title: C-Norm: Cell-Distribution Normalization Enables Precision Recognition of Medical-Cell Image
summary: ThinPrep Cytologic Test (TCT) enables early cervical cancer screening, but manual reading is time-consuming and yields inconsistent diagnostic results among cytopathologists. Existing AI detection models perform poorly under real clinical conditions, primarily restricted by two key constraints: unbalanced spatial distribution of cell populations in TCT slides, and limited high-quality annotated cytology data relying on professional pathologist labeling. To address these limitations, we propose a Cell-Distribution Normalization (C-Norm) method. By decoupling abnormal and normal cells from the original TCT images and re-synthesizing them, this method ensures a uniform distribution of cell populations, thereby mitigating generalization degradation caused by distribution bias. Building upon this, we integrate the YOLOv12 framework with a DINOv3 module. This hybrid architecture leverages the advanced detection capability of YOLO models and the superior feature representations of DINOv3 to capture subtle morphological nuances essential for precise recognition of TCT images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance, significantly outperforming mainstream detection algorithms. The complete implementation is available at: https://github.com/ddw2AIGROUP2CQUPT/Cell-Norm

AI.tldr: Cell-Distribution Normalization (C-Norm) balances cell populations in ThinPrep Cytologic Test (TCT) images by decoupling and re-synthesizing normal and abnormal cells, reducing distribution bias; a YOLOv12-DINOv3 hybrid detector leverages strong detection and rich features to achieve state-of-the-art results in TCT cytology.
AI.motivation: TCT screening faces two major obstacles: (1) highly unbalanced spatial distribution of cell populations on slides, causing biased learning; (2) limited high-quality annotated cytology data due to reliance on professional labeling, hindering generalization.
AI.method: Introduce C-Norm to decouple normal and abnormal cells and re-synthesize samples to produce uniform cell distribution; embed this with a hybrid YOLOv12-DINOv3 architecture that combines YOLO’s detection prowess with DINOv3’s robust feature representations for fine-grained morphological recognition in TCT images.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and significant improvements over mainstream detection algorithms on TCT tasks; code is available at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: C-Norm paired with the YOLOv12-DINOv3 framework enhances generalization under distribution bias and improves recognition of cervical cytology images, representing a strong contribution to AI-enabled cervical cancer screening.

title: Boogu-Image-0.1: Boosting Open-Source Unified Multimodal Understanding and Generation
summary: We introduce Boogu-Image-0.1, an open-source unified multimodal understanding and generation model family, comprising Base, Turbo, Edit, and Edit-Turbo variants. It delivers competitive performance in high-quality text-to-image generation, fast inference, instruction-based editing, and bilingual (Chinese-English) text rendering. Closed-source multimodal systems like Nano-Banana-Pro and GPT-Image-2 achieve strong performance through system-level integration rather than a single model, yet their internal practices remain largely undisclosed. In this work, we demonstrate that targeted improvements in model understanding, data quality, and training pipelines, coupled with agentic inference-time scaling, can substantially enhance generation and editing performance even under highly constrained compute budgets. Comprehensive evaluations show that Boogu-Image-0.1 consistently matches or surpasses other open-source models across standard benchmarks, and achieves results approaching leading closed-source systems. Notably, this is accomplished with only 208.62 million unique images. The base model's theoretical training cost is only approximately \$400K. We share practical discussions that we believe are valuable to the broader research community, and release weights, code, and recipes under Apache 2.0 to advance the open ecosystem for unified multimodal understanding and generation. Our code is available here: https://github.com/Boogu-Project/Boogu-Image.

AI.tldr: Boogu-Image-0.1 is an open-source unified multimodal model family that delivers competitive text-to-image generation, editing, and bilingual rendering with low data usage and compute, released under Apache 2.0.
AI.motivation: To advance accessible, open unified multimodal models and demonstrate that targeted improvements (model understanding, data quality, training pipelines) plus inference-time scaling can compete with closed-source systems under constrained compute.
AI.method: Introduce Base, Turbo, Edit, and Edit-Turbo variants within the Boogu-Image-0.1 family; emphasize improvements in model understanding, data quality, and training pipelines; employ agentic inference-time scaling; train on 208.62 million unique images with an estimated base cost of ~$400k; evaluate on standard benchmarks; release weights/code/recipes under Apache 2.0.
AI.result: Boogu-Image-0.1 consistently matches or surpasses open-source models on standard benchmarks and approaches the performance of leading closed-source systems in text-to-image generation, editing, and bilingual rendering, despite modest data and compute usage.
AI.conclusion: The work supports a robust open ecosystem for unified multimodal understanding and generation, providing practical guidelines, and releasing code and weights to enable broader adoption and further research.

title: A Masked Autoencoder Approach to Unsupervised Steel Surface Defect Recognition
summary: Automated visual inspection of steel surface defects is a recurring quality control task in which labeled defect data is scarce and costly to obtain, while unlabeled surface images are abundant, which motivates self supervised methods that learn useful representations without class labels. A Transformer based Masked Autoencoder is used here to learn representations of steel surface defects for unsupervised grouping. During pretraining, 75% of the input image patches are randomly masked, and a lightweight decoder reconstructs the masked regions from the visible 25%. The encoder is trained jointly with an auxiliary defect localization objective, used only as a training signal and not evaluated as a detector. The decoder reaches a structural similarity score of 0.92 and a mean squared error of 0.47. Features from the pretrained encoder are then clustered using UMAP for dimensionality reduction and Agglomerative clustering, reaching a Hungarian matched accuracy of 91.3% against the six known defect categories.

AI.tldr: Self-supervised Transformer MAE learns representations for steel defect clustering; masking-based pretraining with auxiliary localization; achieves high reconstruction metrics and 91.3% Hungarian accuracy on six defect categories via UMAP + Agglomerative clustering.
AI.motivation: Scarcity of labeled defect data and abundance of unlabeled steel surface images, motivating self-supervised representation learning to enable unsupervised grouping of defects.
AI.method: Train a Transformer-based Masked Autoencoder with 75% patch masking; a lightweight decoder reconstructs masked patches. Encoder jointly trained with an auxiliary defect localization objective (used only during training). After pretraining, extract encoder features, reduce dimensionality with UMAP, then perform Agglomerative clustering; evaluate using Hungarian matching against six defect categories. Reconstruction metrics: SSIM 0.92, MSE 0.47.
AI.result: Clustering of pretrained features achieves 91.3% Hungarian matched accuracy across six known defect categories; the auxiliary localization objective is not evaluated as a detector.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised pretraining via masked autoencoding yields discriminative representations for steel surface defects, enabling accurate unsupervised grouping and effective clustering aligned with ground-truth defect categories.

title: MGFace: Mask-Gated Face Matching via Conditional Similarity Routing
summary: Face identification has achieved remarkable performance under normal conditions. Yet, its accuracy often degrades significantly when query faces are partially occluded, especially by facial masks. Existing re-ranking approaches improve robustness by exploiting patch-level similarities. Still, they often rely on costly, fine-grained matching mechanisms, which limit their efficiency in large-scale retrieval scenarios. In this paper, we propose MGFace, a mask-gated face identification pipeline that predicts the mask status of a query face and conditionally routes the similarity computation accordingly. Specifically, MGFace distinguishes between masked and unmasked queries, applies global embedding matching to unmasked queries, and activates mask-aware patch-level re-ranking only for masked queries. This design focuses on reliable upper-face regions while avoiding unnecessary fine-grained computation. Experiments on the extended LFW-Mask dataset show that MGFace achieves over 80% identification accuracy with the FaceNet backbone and over 90% with the ArcFace backbone. Compared with a previous EMD-based re-ranking method, MGFace achieves better identification performance while reducing query time by approximately 20x. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of MGFace in improving masked-face identification accuracy with low computational overhead. The source code is available at https://github.com/chequanghuy/MGFace.

AI.tldr: MGFace is a mask-gated face identification pipeline that predicts whether a query is masked and routes similarity computation accordingly: global embedding for unmasked queries and patch-level re-ranking for masked queries, achieving strong masked-face accuracy with much lower computation (80%+ with FaceNet, 90%+ with ArcFace; ~20x faster than EMD-based re-ranking).
AI.motivation: Masked-face identification suffers from occlusions, and existing patch-based re-ranking methods are computationally heavy for large-scale retrieval. MGFace aims to maintain accuracy under occlusion while reducing query-time cost by conditionally activating expensive components.
AI.method: Binary mask-status predictor for queries; if unmasked, perform fast global embedding matching; if masked, enable mask-aware patch-level re-ranking (focusing on upper-face regions) instead of full fine-grained matching.
AI.result: On extended LFW-Mask dataset, MGFace yields >80% identification accuracy with FaceNet backbone and >90% with ArcFace backbone; outperforms an EMD-based re-ranking baseline in accuracy while reducing query time by ~20x.
AI.conclusion: MGFace demonstrates effective, computation-efficient masked-face identification by conditionally employing a lightweight global matcher and, only for masked queries, a targeted patch-based re-ranking; code is publicly available.

title: Autonomous UAV Route Planning for Coverage Maximization in Environmental Monitoring: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Environmental monitoring with unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) requires route planning methods that maximize covered area while handling energy limits, operational constraints, and geometric complexity. This paper reports the protocol and preliminary results of an ongoing systematic literature review (SLR) on autonomous UAV route planning for coverage-oriented environmental monitoring. The review follows the PRISMA 2020 framework and searches Scopus and Web of Science for studies published between 2015 and 2026. The protocol focuses on path planning, coverage path planning, and informative path planning, with emphasis on algorithmic families, coverage and energy metrics, obstacle handling, geometric environment representations, and environmental constraints. At the current stage, 562 records have been identified, 161 duplicates have been removed, and 401 unique records have been screened by title, abstract, and keywords. From these, 247 studies were retained for full-text eligibility assessment (235 eligible and 12 borderline records to be resolved during full-text review). A preliminary analysis of the retained studies suggests strong concentration on coverage-oriented formulations, multi-UAV coordination, and energy-aware optimization, while fewer studies explicitly address weather, uncertainty, or obstacle-rich environments. Most retained studies rely on simulation-based validation, highlighting a potential simulation-to-reality gap, and recent publications show increasing interest in reinforcement learning, hybrid optimization, and geometry-aware planning. These early findings indicate an active but fragmented research landscape and support the need for a structured synthesis to identify mature techniques and unresolved gaps for realistic environmental monitoring missions.

AI.tldr: Protocol-based systematic literature review on autonomous UAV route planning for coverage-oriented environmental monitoring; interim findings show focus on coverage, multi-UAV, energy optimization; gaps include weather/uncertainty handling and obstacle-rich scenarios; validation largely simulation-based; rising interest in RL, hybrid optimization, geometry-aware planning; need for structured synthesis to identify mature techniques and gaps.
AI.motivation: To synthesize the current state of research on autonomous UAV route planning for coverage-focused environmental monitoring, identifying mature approaches and research gaps to guide future work.
AI.method: Systematic literature review following PRISMA 2020. Searches in Scopus and Web of Science for studies published 2015–2026. Topics include path planning, coverage path planning, informative path planning. Data extraction covers algorithmic families, coverage/energy metrics, obstacle handling, geometric environment representations, and environmental constraints. Study selection involved de-duplication and screening by title/abstract/keywords, followed by full-text eligibility assessment.
AI.result: Identified 562 records; 161 duplicates removed; 401 unique records screened; 247 full-text assessed (235 eligible, 12 borderline). Preliminary analysis indicates concentration on coverage-oriented formulations, multi-UAV coordination, and energy-aware optimization; fewer studies on weather, uncertainty, or obstacle-rich environments. Most studies rely on simulations; potential simulation-to-reality gap. Emerging interest in reinforcement learning, hybrid optimization, and geometry-aware planning.
AI.conclusion: Research area is active but fragmented. The protocol aims to produce a structured synthesis to identify mature techniques and gaps for realistic missions in environmental monitoring using UAVs.

title: Automatic Differentiation from Scratch: How PyTorch Computes Gradients in Physics-Informed Neural Networks
comment: 25 pages, 9 figures. Educational tutorial on automatic differentiation for Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) using PyTorch. Includes complete numerical derivations and computational graph analysis
summary: This paper traces, with explicit numerical values, how PyTorch's automatic differentiation (AD) engine computes gradients for Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) training -- a setting that requires two levels of differentiation: computing the physics derivative $\hat{y}'(t)=d\hat{y}/dt$ through the network, and computing parameter gradients $\nabla_θL$ of a loss that itself depends on $\hat{y}'(t)$. Using a 1-3-3-1 multilayer perceptron and the initial value problem $y'(t)+y(t)=0$, $y(0)=1$, we trace the complete pipeline at every node: the computational graph built during the forward pass, the reverse-mode backward traversal that computes all 22 parameter gradients in a single pass, and the graph-on-graph mechanism by which \texttt{create\_graph=True} enables correct differentiation through the physics-informed residual. Every adjoint value is verified against the hand derivations of Tahimi (2026), connecting the $P/Q$ sensitivity framework to the vector--Jacobian products used by PyTorch's autograd engine.

AI.tldr: End-to-end gradient tracing for PINNs in PyTorch: a 1-3-3-1 MLP learns y'+y=0; all 22 parameter gradients and the physics residual gradient are computed in a single backprop pass, enabled by create_graph, with adjoint values validated against hand derivations (Tahimi 2026).
AI.motivation: To understand how PyTorch autograd handles higher-order differentiation required by physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and to verify gradient correctness through adjoint and physics residual computations, linking P/Q sensitivity concepts to vector-Jacobian products.
AI.method: Use a 1-3-3-1 MLP to solve y'+y=0, y(0)=1; trace the forward graph, perform reverse-mode backprop to obtain all 22 parameter gradients in one pass, and apply create_graph=True to enable differentiation through the physics-informed residual; verify adjoint values against Tahimi (2026) hand derivations and relate to P/Q sensitivity and vector-Jacobian products.
AI.result: All adjoint values match hand derivations; the full gradient pipeline is demonstrated with 22 parameter gradients computed in a single backward pass; the graph-on-graph approach allows correct differentiation through the physics residual.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a concrete, reproducible account of higher-order gradient computation for PINNs in PyTorch, validating the gradient flow through both the network and the physics residual and demonstrating how create_graph enables differentiation through complex residual terms; it also clarifies the connection between P/Q sensitivity and autograd constructs.

title: OriginBlame: Record- and Token-Level Data Provenance for AI Training Datasets
summary: When a data contributor requests removal, model trainers face a practical gap: unlearning algorithms require a forget set, yet no tool can locate which training records belong to a given author. Existing provenance systems operate at file or dataset level, forcing catastrophic over-deletion. We present ob, a record- and token-level data provenance system that propagates author identity through data processing pipelines and resolves revocation requests into precise forget sets via deterministic queries. Evaluation on 219,555 Wikipedia pages demonstrates that record-level provenance eliminates dataset-level over-deletion (from 101x to 1.3x), while integration adds 1.3-4.0% throughput overhead (HuggingFace) and 2.1-19.0% (Datatrove) on wiki data. On a 1.7B model, provenance-based forget sets improve unlearning by 42% over random baselines.

AI.tldr: Provenance-based forgetting at record/token level enables precise forget sets, reducing over-deletion and improving unlearning with modest overhead.
AI.motivation: Addresses the practical gap where forget-set-based unlearning requires identifying training records associated with an author, which existing systems cannot do at fine granularity, causing over-deletion.
AI.method: Propagates author identity through data processing pipelines to enable deterministic queries that map a forget request to precise training records at record/token granularity; integrates with existing frameworks (e.g., HuggingFace, Datatrove).
AI.result: Eliminates dataset-level over-deletion (from 101x to 1.3x); introduces modest throughput overhead (1.3-4.0% on HuggingFace; 2.1-19.0% on Datatrove); on a 1.7B model, provenance-based forget sets improve unlearning by 42% over random baselines.
AI.conclusion: Record-level provenance substantially mitigates over-deletion while enabling effective unlearning with acceptable overhead, demonstrating practical viability for large-scale models.

title: Self-Supervised Visual Representation Learning: Pretrain-Finetuning or Joint Training?
summary: Self-supervision is a powerful technique for learning visual representations from unlabeled data. Existing techniques primarily adopt a two-stage approach for self-supervised learning (SSL): a pretraining stage on unlabeled data followed by a finetuning stage on labeled data. While this pipeline has demonstrated extreme effectiveness, the interaction between self-supervised and supervised learning objectives remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we systematically investigate whether jointly optimizing the self-supervised and supervised objectives during training provides a better alternative. We compare two training paradigms: (1) the aforementioned pretraining followed by finetuning (PFT) and (2) joint training (JT), where self-supervised and supervised losses are optimized simultaneously in the same network. Across eight representative SSL methods and diverse computer vision tasks on natural, medical, crisis response, and remote sensing data, we evaluate performance under varying percentages of labeled data. Our results reveal that the relative effectiveness of PFT and JT depends strongly on the task at hand, the availability of labeled data, and the complexity of the domain. We find that JT consistently improves data and training efficiency while being robust in low-label settings, while PFT is more reliable in more specialized domains. We further analyze representation quality, robustness, and cross-domain generalization, providing new insights into how self-supervised and supervised objectives interact during optimization. We establish a comprehensive empirical benchmark for hybrid SSL-based semi-supervised learning and offer practical guidance for selecting appropriate training strategies across diverse vision applications.

AI.tldr: Joint training (JT) of self-supervised and supervised objectives often yields data and training efficiency gains and robustness across tasks, though the best strategy depends on domain complexity and label availability.
AI.motivation: To understand how combining SSL and supervised objectives during training compares to the standard pretraining-finetuning (PFT) pipeline across diverse vision tasks and data regimes.
AI.method: Empirical benchmark evaluating PFT vs JT across eight representative SSL methods and tasks in natural, medical, crisis, and remote sensing data, with varying labeled data fractions.
AI.result: JT consistently improves data and training efficiency and is robust in low-label settings; PFT is more reliable in specialized domains. JT also influences representation quality, robustness, and cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: Provides a comprehensive benchmark for hybrid SSL-based semi-supervised learning and practical guidance on choosing between PFT and JT depending on task, label availability, and domain complexity.

title: HRIBench: Benchmarking Interaction-Centric Human-Robot Collaboration
summary: Current vision-language-action (VLA) benchmarks primarily evaluate isolated manipulation skills while leaving human-robot interaction structure largely unmodeled. However, real-world collaboration fundamentally requires coordination under shared agency, including intent understanding, temporal synchronization, protocol adherence, and safe interaction in dynamic environments. To address this gap, we introduce HRIBench, a diagnostic benchmark for intent-aware human-robot collaboration based on executable interaction scenarios. HRIBench represents collaborative tasks as structured scenario scripts that explicitly model agent roles, temporal dependencies, coordination constraints, and human behavior distributions. Building on this abstraction, HRIBench defines three representative interaction roles: Instructor, Collaborator, and Intruder, covering intent communication, joint coordination, and robustness under human intervention. The benchmark contains 13 role-conditioned tasks with over 650 evaluation episodes generated from diverse interaction trajectories and scene variations. Beyond binary task success, HRIBench introduces interpretable interaction-centric metrics spanning synchronization, responsiveness, protocol compliance, and safety. We evaluate adapted policies based on GR00T, pi0.5, and ACT under a unified protocol. Results show that current foundation robot policies struggle substantially in collaborative settings despite strong manipulation ability, revealing major limitations in temporal coordination and intent-aware behavior. Fine-tuning on HRIBench consistently improves collaborative performance. In a real-world adaptation study, simulation data generated by HRIBench improves GR00T N1.5's physical-task success rate from 0.10 to 0.43, demonstrating the benchmark's value for advancing interaction-centric robot learning.

AI.tldr: HRIBench introduces a structured, intent-aware benchmark for human-robot collaboration (HRC) built on executable scenario scripts with three roles (Instructor, Collaborator, Intruder). It contains 13 tasks and 650+ episodes, plus interaction-centric metrics (synchronization, responsiveness, protocol compliance, safety). It reveals current foundation policies struggle with coordination but benefit from HRIBench fine-tuning; real-world adaptation shows simulation data improves GR00T N1.5 performance from 0.10 to 0.43.
AI.motivation: Bridging the gap between existing VLA benchmarks that focus on isolated manipulation and real-world HRC requiring shared agency, intent understanding, temporal coordination, and safety in dynamic environments.
AI.method: Model collaborative tasks as structured scenario scripts with explicit agent roles, temporal dependencies, coordination constraints, and human behavior distributions. Define three roles (Instructor, Collaborator, Intruder). Create 13 tasks and 650+ evaluation episodes across diverse trajectories and scene variations. Propose interaction-centric metrics (synchronization, responsiveness, protocol compliance, safety). Evaluate adapted policies (GR00T, pi0.5, ACT) under a unified protocol. Validate through a real-world adaptation study using HRIBench-generated data to fine-tune policy (GR00T N1.5).
AI.result: Current foundation policies show substantial deficiencies in temporal coordination and intent-aware behavior despite strong manipulation capabilities. Fine-tuning on HRIBench consistently improves collaborative performance. Real-world adaptation study demonstrates HRIBench data can boost GR00T N1.5’s success rate from 0.10 to 0.43, supporting the benchmark’s practical value for interaction-centric robot learning.
AI.conclusion: HRIBench provides interpretable, interaction-centric evaluation for HRC, exposing limitations of existing policies and offering a scalable path to improve intent understanding, coordination, and safety in real-world collaboration through scenario-scripted benchmarking and targeted fine-tuning.

title: Beyond Backbone Backpropagation: A Decoupled Strategy for Efficient Transfer Learning
summary: Deep learning models achieve state-of-the-art image classification but face deployment challenges due to computational costs and energy demands. We propose a lightweight training strategy that adapts normalization layers of the model to the new domain and decouples feature extraction from classifier optimization, reducing overhead by precomputing features only once. A redesigned classifier head with margin-based weighted loss further minimizes ambiguity without end-to-end backpropagation. Evaluated across four CNN architectures (ResNet18, ResNet50, MobileNet, DenseNet121), three Transformer models (ViT, Swin and DeiT) and three medical datasets (Brain Cancer MRI, BreakHis and PatchCamelyon), our approach significantly reduces the required training time with only a marginal accuracy trade-off, often matching or surpassing baseline performance. This efficiency translates to reducing CO2 by orders of magnitude, offering a practical and environmentally sustainable solution for resource-constrained clinical or prototyping environments.

AI.tldr: Lightweight training via domain-adaptive normalization and feature precomputation with a redesigned classifier head, achieving fast training with minimal accuracy loss across CNN/Transformer models on medical datasets, reducing CO2 emissions.
AI.motivation: High training cost and energy demand hindering deployment of DL in resource-constrained clinical/prototyping contexts.
AI.method: Decouple feature extraction and classifier optimization; adapt normalization layers to target domain; precompute features once; margin-based weighted loss; redesigned classifier head; avoid end-to-end backprop; evaluate across multiple architectures and medical datasets.
AI.result: Substantial training-time reduction; marginal accuracy trade-off; sometimes matching or exceeding baselines; CO2 reductions by orders of magnitude in practice.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach offers a practical, environmentally sustainable solution for resource-limited clinical/prototyping environments with little accuracy penalty.

title: SPINE: Bridging the Cyber-Physical Gap with Agentic AI
summary: Foundation models have given robots a sophisticated brain for complex decision-making, yet deploying that intelligence into a physical platform still demands tedious, expert-driven calibration. This deployment gap, the robot's spinal cord, remains a primary bottleneck to scalable Embodied AI. Hence, we propose SPINE (Scalable Physical Integration with ageNtic Expertise): an agentic framework for systematically debugging and deploying bimanual robots with minimal robotics expertise. SPINE's harness comprises two orchestrated multi-agent workflows: a profile builder that creates robot-specific context, and a debugger that cycles through diagnosis, repair, and validation until teleoperation works. Across seven DOBOT X-Trainer debugging scenarios, a robotics novice using SPINE outperformed human operators using Claude Code with the same reference materials, but without SPINE's structured workflow, improving operationalization success from 75% to 100% and reducing mean time-to-teleoperation from 16 min 45 s to 13 min 47 s. On AgileX PiPER, a distinct ROS/CAN bimanual arm, SPINE resolved all 10 implanted bugs, versus 9 out of 10 for the expert baseline, in nearly the same amount of time. Together, these results show that SPINE can transfer across bimanual platforms, reduce dependence on expert calibration, and move embodied AI closer to scalable real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: SPINE enables scalable deployment of bimanual robots by structuring debugging into profile-building and repair-diagnosis workflows, enabling novices to outperform non-structured baselines and transferring across platforms.
AI.motivation: To reduce the deployment gap in embodied AI caused by tedious expert-driven calibration of robot hardware and control stacks.
AI.method: A two-workflow, multi-agent harness: (1) profile builder creates robot-specific context; (2) debugger iterates through diagnosis, repair, and validation until teleoperation works; evaluated on seven DOBOT X-Trainer scenarios with a novice against Claude Code baseline, and on AgileX PiPER (ROS/CAN) against expert baseline.
AI.result: On DOBOT X-Trainer: success rate improved from 75% to 100%; mean time-to-teleoperation decreased from 16m45s to 13m47s. On AgileX PiPER: SPINE resolved all 10 bugs vs 9/10 for expert, with comparable time.
AI.conclusion: SPINE transfers across bimanual platforms, reduces dependence on expert calibration, and advances scalable real-world deployment of embodied AI.

title: Continuously Evolving Deepfake Detection: An Architecture and Public-Benchmark Evaluation of a Dynamic Detection System
summary: Deepfake detectors that achieve near-perfect scores on academic benchmarks collapse on real-world content: recent in-the-wild evaluations report AUC drops of 45-50% for state-of-the-art open-source models. We argue this gap is structural: static detectors are trained once against a moving generative frontier. We present BitMind Forensics (BMF), trained through Bittensor SN34, an open adversarial competition that continually refreshes the training distribution. We evaluate one dated export comprising image, general-video, and human-video checkpoints across nineteen public datasets: the canonical face-swap suites (FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF v1/v2/++, DFDC, DFD, UADFV, DF40) and recent in-the-wild and AI-generated-media benchmarks (Sumsub, Deepfake-Eval-2024, WildRF, Community Forensics, AIGCDetectBench, GenImage, AI-GenBench, AIGIBench, RAID, GenVidBench, GenVideo-100K). BMF reaches 0.936 AUC on Sumsub's original images and 0.872 pooled AUC over its full four-condition manipulation battery (1.4M images), staying robust under perturbation (0.855 JPEG, 0.799 downscaled), while GPEN enhancement improves detection (0.996). On Deepfake-Eval-2024, it matches the best commercial detector on images (0.915 vs 0.90) and exceeds it on video (0.822 vs 0.79), far above the best open-source detectors (0.56 and 0.63). It reaches 0.991 AUC on a 21-generator AI-image panel and 0.918 on GenVidBench, and exceeds the FF++-trained frontier on DFDC (0.947 vs 0.843) and Celeb-DF v2 (0.9985 vs 0.956), both contamination-audited, with statistical parity on Celeb-DF++. In a temporal study, successive dated exports improve on held-out media from generators absent from the static baseline's training (image 0.842 to 0.902; video 0.864 to 0.936). Our evaluation harness is public, and at publication the production API serves the exact evaluated snapshot for independent verification.

AI.tldr: BitMind Forensics (BMF) trains detectors via continual, adversarially refreshed data (Bittensor SN34) to close the real-world performance gap in deepfake detection. It outperforms static FF++ baselines across diverse datasets and maintains robustness under perturbations, with temporal gains as training data evolves.
AI.motivation: Academic benchmarks for deepfake detectors lag behind real-world performance due to a shifting generative frontier; a static detector quickly becomes outdated. A continual learning/distribution-refresh approach can maintain detection effectiveness.
AI.method: Train BMF using Bittensor SN34 adversarial competition to continuously refresh the training distribution; evaluate a dated export across image, general-video, and human-video checkpoints on 19 public datasets (FF++, Celeb-DF variants, DFDC, DFD, UADFV, DF40, plus in-the-wild and AI-generated-media benchmarks); include GPEN enhancement; perform temporal analysis with successive dated exports; use a public evaluation harness.
AI.result: BMF achieves high AUC across datasets: Sumsub original images 0.936; four-condition battery 0.872 (1.4M images) with robustness (JPEG 0.855, downscaled 0.799); GPEN uplift to 0.996. On Deepfake-Eval-2024: images 0.915 vs 0.90 best commercial; video 0.822 vs 0.79; outperforms best open-source. 21-generator AI-image panel 0.991; GenVidBench 0.918; DFDC 0.947 vs 0.843; Celeb-DF v2 0.9985 vs 0.956; Celeb-DF++ parity. Temporal: image 0.842 to 0.902; video 0.864 to 0.936. Public evaluation harness ensures reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: Continual-distribution training via open adversarial competition yields robust, real-world-performing deepfake detectors that outperform static baselines and adapt to generator drift; the framework supports independent verification via a public API.

title: Power from Potential: A Survey of Electrostatic Actuators for Haptics
comment: Copyright 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary:
As haptic interfaces integrate more seamlessly into wearables and everyday environments, they increasingly require actuators that are soft, thin, silent, and energy efficient. However, conventional motors and temperature-responsive polymers often struggle to deliver these properties due to their bulky form factors and high power consumption. High-Voltage Electrostatic Actuators (HVEAs), which generate force by applying an electric field to localized charge concentrations using high voltages and ultra-low currents, have recently emerged as a compelling alternative due to their fast, silent, and low-power operation within highly customizable and compliant form factors.
  This paper presents a focused review of HVEAs for haptics, examining four major classes: electrostatic switchable adhesives, dielectric elastomer actuators, soft electrohydraulic actuators, and electrokinetic pumps. For each class, we describe their mechanisms that enable haptic output; characterize their bandwidths, force densities, and spatial scalability; and evaluate their versatility for rendering cutaneous and kinesthetic feedback across wearable and world-grounded interfaces. Through this cross-technology analysis, we identify common design constraints and emerging strategies for improving ergonomics, streamlining fabrication, and integrating self-sensing. We conclude by outlining where HVEAs are uniquely positioned to advance haptic interaction and highlighting key research directions needed to translate these technologies into practical systems.

AI.tldr: A focused literature review of high-voltage electrostatic actuators (HVEAs) for haptics, organized into four classes, analyzing mechanisms, performance metrics (bandwidth, force density, scalability), and their applicability to wearable/grounded interfaces, with design, fabrication, and sensing considerations and future directions.
AI.motivation: HVEAs offer fast, silent, low-power actuation with highly tunable, soft form factors, addressing limitations of bulky motors and temperature-responsive polymers in wearable haptics.
AI.method: Structured literature review across four HVEA classes—electrostatic switchable adhesives, dielectric elastomer actuators, soft electrohydraulic actuators, and electrokinetic pumps. For each class, describe haptic mechanisms, quantify bandwidths, force densities, and spatial scalability, and assess suitability for cutaneous and kinesthetic feedback in wearable and world-grounded systems. Perform cross-technology analysis to identify design constraints and emergent strategies, with focus on ergonomics, fabrication, and self-sensing, and conclude with future research directions and practical translation considerations.
AI.result: Cross-technology analysis highlights shared constraints (e.g., balancing force output with soft/form-factor constraints, energy efficiency, and safe high-voltage operation) and emerging strategies (e.g., modular fabrication, integrated sensing, configurable stiffness, and scalable actuation architectures). The review delineates how each class supports different haptic modalities and interface contexts, and identifies critical gaps in metrics, reliability, and integration needed to move from lab prototypes to practical wearables and world-grounded devices.
AI.conclusion: HVEAs are uniquely positioned to enable fast, silent, and energy-efficient haptic feedback within soft, slim form factors suitable for wearables. Realizing practical systems requires advances in robust actuation at wearable scales, self-sensing and control integration, safety and reliability for long-term use, standardized performance metrics, and scalable manufacturing. The paper maps promising directions to bridge research and deployment.

title: Federated Explainable Artificial Intelligence: Roles, Architectures, Evaluation, and Open Challenges
summary: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a key paradigm for privacy-preserving collaborative model training across distributed and heterogeneous data sources. By keeping raw data local, FL addresses data confidentiality concerns, yet it does not resolve the opacity of modern machine learning models. In parallel, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has gained attention for improving transparency, trust, and accountability, particularly in high-stakes domains. Their intersection has given rise to Federated Explainable Artificial Intelligence (FedXAI) paradigm, which aims to jointly satisfy privacy and explainability requirements. This survey provides a systematic review of FedXAI, highlighting the transition of explainability from a post-hoc tool to an integral component of the FL lifecycle. We show how explainability supports aggregation, personalization, robustness, coordination, and system-level decision making. To organize the literature, we introduce a taxonomy that classifies FedXAI methods by the role of explainability, model and explainer types, explanation scope, integration level, FL settings, and data heterogeneity. We review approaches ranging from model-agnostic explanations to interpretable federated models and explainability-aware aggregation mechanisms. We also examine evaluation practices and discuss the lack of standardized benchmarks and metrics for measuring explanation quality, stability, privacy leakage, and computational overhead. Finally, we identify key challenges, including explainability under non-IID data, explanation-centric security threats, communication-efficient XAI, continual FedXAI, and the integration of domain knowledge and regulatory constraints. By consolidating existing work and identifying key gaps, this survey serves as a reference framework for designing trustworthy, transparent, and privacy-preserving federated AI systems.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey that systematizes Federated Explainable Artificial Intelligence (FedXAI), offering a taxonomy, synthesis of approaches, evaluation gaps, and directions for trustworthy, privacy-preserving federated AI.
AI.motivation: To reconcile privacy-preserving distributed learning (FL) with explainability (XAI), addressing opacity and governance in decentralized data sources while enabling reliable, accountable AI in high-stakes settings.
AI.method: Systematic literature review of FedXAI works; development of a multi-dimensional taxonomy (explainability role, model/explainer types, explanation scope, integration level, FL settings, data heterogeneity); synthesis of model-agnostic and interpretable federated approaches; review of evaluation practices; gap/challenge analysis.
AI.result: Classifies FedXAI methods into categories such as model-agnostic explanations, interpretable federated models, and explainability-aware aggregation; highlights how explainability supports FL processes (aggregation, personalization, robustness, coordination, system-level decisions); identifies lack of standardized benchmarks/metrics for explanation quality, stability, privacy leakage, computational overhead; outlines evaluation practices and variability; provides a framework for future FedXAI research.
AI.conclusion: The survey offers a reference framework for designing trustworthy, transparent, and privacy-preserving federated AI systems, identifies key challenges (non-IID data, explanation-centric security threats, communication-efficient XAI, continual FedXAI, and regulatory/domain knowledge integration) and calls for standardized benchmarks and practical guidelines to advance FedXAI.

title: Interventional Grounding Audits: Black-Box Premise-Dependency Tests for LLM Chain-of-Thought via Predicate Substitution
comment: Accepted at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Logical Reasoning of Large Language Models (https://iclr.cc/virtual/2026/10017466)
summary: Large language models produce chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that appears logically sound yet may not genuinely depend on its stated premises. We introduce interventional grounding audits, a black-box, step-level test of premise dependency: we intervene on a single premise by substituting its target predicate with a fresh symbol, re-run the model, and check whether each reasoning step's normalized conclusion (canonical predicate form) changes. We evaluate on ProntoQA, a synthetic multi-hop deductive reasoning benchmark with gold proof trees, where step-level premise dependencies are known. Applied to 50 ProntoQA problems with GPT-4o, our method achieves F1 = 0.806 on detecting proof-tree dependencies (F1 = 0.885 on predicate-determining dependencies; Recall = 100%), significantly outperforming a self-consistency baseline (F1 = 0.343; 95% bootstrap CIs non-overlapping). We further identify that 66% of correctly-solved problems contain at least one aligned step insensitive to a direct proof-tree dependency under consistent substitution -- all involving entity-introduction premises, a documented blind spot of the consistent-substitution evaluator -- a "right answer, wrong reasoning" signal invisible to passive methods. All audit certificates, raw outputs, and reproduction scripts are available in a public GitHub repository, and we discuss scope limits beyond formal, parsable benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Introduces interventional grounding audits to test premise dependency in chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning of LLMs as a black-box, step-level intervention method; demonstrates strong detection of premise dependencies and exposes blind spots in prior evaluators using ProntoQA with GPT-4o; provides reproducible artifacts.
AI.motivation: Address the gap where CoT reasoning appears coherent but may not rely on stated premises. Build a black-box, step-level diagnostic to quantify premise-dependency and detect “right answer, wrong reasoning” scenarios that passive evaluators miss.
AI.method: Interventional grounding audits: intervene on a single premise by substituting its target predicate with a fresh symbol, re-run the model, and compare step-level canonical predicates to see if conclusions change. Evaluate on ProntoQA (synthetic multi-hop deductive reasoning with gold proof trees). Use 50 problems with GPT-4o. Measure F1 on proof-tree dependencies and on predicate-determining dependencies; recall 100% for predicate dependencies; compare to a self-consistency baseline.
AI.result: F1 = 0.806 for detecting proof-tree dependencies; F1 = 0.885 for predicate-determining dependencies; recall = 100%. Self-consistency baseline yields F1 = 0.343 (CIs non-overlapping). 66% of correctly-solved items have at least one aligned step insensitive to direct proof-tree dependency under consistent substitution, highlighting a blind spot tied to entity-introduction premises. All audit artifacts (certificates, outputs, scripts) are publicly available on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: The auditing approach robustly exposes premise-dependency signals in LLM-CoT reasoning and reveals blind spots of conventional evaluators. It provides a reproducible, black-box method to diagnose alignment gaps between stated premises and reasoning steps, with implications for evaluation benchmarks and model understanding beyond formal, parsable benchmarks.

title: Active Learning for Efficient Annotation of Surgical Videos with Weak Supervision
summary: Precise spatial-temporal annotation of laparoscopic videos is time-consuming and requires expert knowledge. We propose a human-in-the-loop knowledge acquisition framework that combines active learning with dual-loss optimization to significantly reduce the annotation effort needed for automatic localization and segmentation of objects in the surgical field. Our method employs a foundation model to generate temporally consistent class activation maps (CAMs) from video using two complementary training objectives: a weak supervision loss on video-level tool presence labels for weakly annotated data, and an image-level mask loss on human-corrected annotations obtained through active learning. Rather than requiring dense pixel-level annotation upfront, our pipeline iteratively proposes pseudo-masks that guide the expert annotator to refine the knowledge previously captured by the model. We demonstrate that our framework reduces the effort of surgical video annotation by 50% by the end of training in comparison to fully manual annotation. Through eliminating the need for large, fully annotated datasets from the start, this framework enables scalability to the development of surgical tool segmentation models. This iterative human-in-the-loop refinement supports efficient knowledge acquisition with minimal expert input, providing a practical and deployable strategy for expanding tool segmentation to larger, more diverse datasets and real-world clinical settings.

AI.tldr: A human-in-the-loop framework that uses active learning and dual-loss optimization with a foundation model to generate temporally consistent CAMs for laparoscopic tool segmentation, reducing annotation effort by 50% without dense upfront labels.
AI.motivation: Precise spatial-temporal annotation in surgical videos is labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge; dense pixel-level labels are costly and hinder scalable development of tool segmentation models.
AI.method: A foundation model generates temporally consistent class activation maps (CAMs) from video. Training uses two complementary losses: (1) a weak supervision loss on video-level tool presence labels for weakly annotated data, and (2) an image-level mask loss on human-corrected annotations obtained via active learning. The pipeline iteratively proposes pseudo-masks to guide expert annotation, enabling iterative human-in-the-loop knowledge acquisition without immediate dense labels.
AI.result: Annotation effort is reduced by 50% by the end of training compared to fully manual annotation. The approach eliminates the need for large, fully annotated datasets at start, enabling scalable development of surgical tool segmentation and deployment to larger, more diverse datasets and real-world clinical settings.
AI.conclusion: Iterative human-in-the-loop refinement with active learning and dual-loss optimization provides a practical and deployable strategy for expanding tool segmentation to diverse datasets and real-world clinical settings with minimal expert input.

title: GPUSimBench: Towards Scalable and Reliable GPU-Accelerated Simulators in Embodied AI
summary: Data-driven embodied AI is rapidly transitioning into a paradigm that scales training through massively parallel simulation, where GPU-accelerated simulators serve as the foundational data infrastructure. However, as computational throughput scales, the underlying trade-offs between parallel efficiency, physical fidelity, and execution determinism remain largely unexamined, hindering the development of reliable robot learning. In this paper, we expose the hidden limits of mainstream GPU-based robotic simulators (e.g., Isaac Lab, Genesis) by introducing GPUSimBench, which focuses on scalability, physical consistency, and computational determinism. First, GPUSimBench establishes a physical grounding evaluation with a controlled inclined-plane task, quantifying the distributional alignment between simulated dynamics and their real-world counterparts. Second, we benchmark parallel scalability by measuring throughput and memory footprints across scaling environment counts. Crucially, beyond standard performance metrics, we unveil and quantify the inherent non-determinism introduced by GPU-batched execution, characterized by significant run-to-run and inter-environment variability even under identical initial conditions. Finally, we identify four empirical regimes of stochasticity within current simulator stacks, highlighting that unbounded scaling can compromise reproducibility without explicit constraints.

AI.tldr: GPUSimBench exposes limits in GPU-based robotic simulators: scalability, fidelity, and determinism degrade with parallelism, revealing non-determinism and four stochasticity regimes to guide reproducible robot learning.
AI.motivation: As data-driven embodied AI scales training via massively parallel simulation, it is essential to characterize how GPU-backed simulators balance throughput, physical fidelity, and execution determinism.
AI.method: Introduce GPUSimBench suite with a controlled inclined-plane physical grounding task; benchmark scalability across increasing environment counts; measure throughput and memory footprints; quantify run-to-run and inter-environment non-determinism under GPU-batched execution; identify four empirical stochasticity regimes.
AI.result: 1) Quantified alignment between simulated dynamics and real-world dynamics; 2) Scalability metrics (throughput/memory) across environment counts; 3) Documented substantial non-determinism under batched GPU execution; 4) Identified four stochasticity regimes in current simulator stacks; 5) Demonstrated that unbounded scaling can hurt reproducibility without explicit constraints.
AI.conclusion: Current GPU-based simulators exhibit hidden limits in scalability, fidelity, and determinism; explicit constraints and awareness of stochasticity regimes are needed to maintain reproducible and reliable robot learning at scale.

title: What Your Model Threw Away and Why You'll Want It Back: Masking, Fingerprinting, and Privacy from Discarded Geometry
summary: We develop a framework for the information discarded by machine learning models whose inputs carry a Lie group action. Given a representation $π$ of a Lie group $G$ on a space $V$ and a learned function $f\colon V \to \mathbb{R}$, we define two objects measuring the symmetry invisible to $f$. The null fiber at a point $x \in V$ is the set $N_G(f,x) = \{g \in G : f(π(g^{-1}) \cdot x) = f(x)\}$ of group elements whose inverse action on $x$ is undetectable by $f$. When $N_G(f,x)$ is independent of $x$, it coincides with the stabilizer $\mathrm{Stab}_G(f)$, the largest subgroup of $G$ under which $f$ is invariant. For smooth maps to $\mathbb{R}$, the preimage theorem guarantees that null fibers have dimension at least $\dim G - 1$ at generic inputs, regardless of architecture. For compact groups acting on themselves, the Peter--Weyl theorem yields a spectral characterization of both objects in terms of the Fourier coefficient matrices of $f$. We show that null fiber elements can be computed efficiently via Newton iteration on the orbit map, at a cost comparable to a few gradient evaluations. Applications to data masking, model fingerprinting, and privacy-preserving computation are developed and tested experimentally on molecular property prediction under $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and spherical image classification under the Möbius group $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C})$. The framework applies uniformly to classical neural networks and variational quantum circuits.

AI.tldr: A framework for measuring symmetry information discarded by ML models with Lie group actions. Introduces null fibers N_G(f,x) to quantify detectable invariances, relates to stabilizers, uses preimage theorem and Peter–Weyl for spectral views, and computes null fibers via Newton iterations. Demonstrated on SO(3) and PSL(2,C) with neural nets and quantum circuits, highlighting data masking, fingerprinting, and privacy applications.
AI.motivation: To quantify and exploit the invariances and blind spots induced by symmetry groups in machine learning, enabling principled analysis of what information is hidden from a model due to group actions and enabling privacy-preserving and data-m masking applications.
AI.method: Define N_G(f,x) = {g in G : f(π(g^{-1})·x) = f(x)} as the null fiber of f at x. For constant-x independence, N_G(f,x) matches Stab_G(f). Use the preimage theorem to show null fibers have dimension at least dim G − 1 at generic x for smooth f. For compact G, use Peter–Weyl theorem to spectrally characterize N_G(f,x) via Fourier coefficients of f. Propose Newton iteration on the orbit map to compute null fibers efficiently (cost similar to few gradient evaluations). Apply framework to data masking, model fingerprinting, privacy-preserving computation; experiments on molecular property prediction under SO(3) and spherical image classification under PSL(2, C) (Möbius group). Applicable to classical neural networks and variational quantum circuits.
AI.result: Null fibers have dimension at least dim G − 1 at generic inputs; spectral characterization via Fourier coefficients for compact groups; practical algorithm (Newton iteration) to compute null fibers with cost akin to several gradient evaluations; demonstrated practical relevance in molecular property prediction and spherical image tasks; framework is architecture-agnostic (NNs and VQCs).
AI.conclusion: The work provides a cohesive framework to quantify and compute the symmetry-induced information discarded by ML models, linking geometric, algebraic, and computational perspectives. It offers practical tools for privacy-preserving ML and model analysis, with broad applicability across architectures and domains.

title: Probabilistic Extension of Neuro-Symbolic AGI Robots based on Belnap's Typed Intensional FOL
summary: Neuro-symbolic AI based on $IFOL_B$ is a way to combine neural learning and symbolic reasoning to overcome limitations of purely neural systems (like lack of interpretability and logical structure) with formal logical machinery for self-reference. In this paper we expand the cognitive power of $IFOL_B$ by using the probability computation for the currently unknown sentences, based on Nilsson's probability structure for the $IFOL_B$. We introduce the global symmetry transformation that preserves the current knowledge database and logical deduction, and the local one used for real-time decisions about concrete (sub)problems that involve only a very strict subset of $IFOL_B$ predicates. The computation of probability density function $KI$ in both cases, based on the Shannon's maximum information entropy, is provided by neural networks of this probabilistic neuro-symbolic AGI.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic augmentation of IFOL_B using Nilsson's probability theory and symmetry transforms, implemented with neural nets to reason about unknown sentences under Shannon entropy.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of purely neural systems (interpetability, logical structure) by combining symbolic IFOL_B reasoning with probabilistic semantics; enable self-reference and cognitive enhancement through probabilistic handling of unknown statements.
AI.method: Introduce two symmetry transformations: a global transformation that preserves the entire knowledge base and deductions, and a local transformation for real-time decisions on selected subproblems. Compute the probability density function KI for unknown sentences via Nilsson's probability structure, using Shannon's maximum entropy, implemented by neural networks in a probabilistic neuro-symbolic AGI.
AI.result: Proposes a concrete computational framework for KI in both global and local settings; demonstrates how to realize this probability computation with neural networks within a neuro-symbolic AGI.
AI.conclusion: Extends IFOL_B with a probabilistic, entropy-driven semantics for unknown sentences, enabling more powerful probabilistic reasoning and real-time decision making within a neuro-symbolic AGI.

title: Just-In-Time Scene Graph Growth: Combating Perceptual Saturation in Long-Horizon Robotics
summary: While 3D Scene Graphs (3DSGs) provide crucial structured representations for embodied agents, conventional Ahead-of-Time, build-everything-then-filter pipelines conflict with the real-time, low-latency demands of edge platforms, inducing a perceptual saturation effect via severe observation redundancy. To resolve this, we present JITOMA (Just-In-Time On-demand Memory Activation), a closed-loop framework that unifies task reasoning, perception, and memory into a just-in-time growth process. Instead of exhaustively mapping the entire environment, JITOMA leverages a top-down task heatmap at the frontend to filter continuous observations, routing minimal streams to maintain a global foundation of low-cost, dormant anchors. Upon a cognitive query, the backend Large Language Model (LLM) parses the robotic intent to dynamically awaken task-relevant anchors, triggering resource-intensive operations -- such as dense node captioning and functional inference -- exclusively within the activated local subgraph. To evaluate these dynamic capabilities and study perceptual saturation trade-offs, we introduce JITOMA-Bench, a comprehensive suite for long-horizon multi-tasking and complex multi-step reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that JITOMA substantially reduces active graph size and captioning latency, while maintaining stable processing time under long-horizon task switching.

AI.tldr: Introduces JITOMA, a just-in-time on-demand memory activation framework for 3D scene graphs in edge-enabled embodied systems, reducing observation redundancy and latency by awakening task-relevant anchors via an LLM-driven backend, with JITOMA-Bench benchmarking.
AI.motivation: Edge platforms require real-time, low-latency perception; ahead-of-time 3DSG pipelines generate perceptual saturation due to excessive observation processing and redundancy.
AI.method: A closed-loop system that unifies task reasoning, perception, and memory. A front-end task heatmap filters observations and maintains a minimal set of dormant anchors. On cognitive query, an LLM interprets intent to wake task-relevant anchors and perform selective, resource-intensive operations (e.g., dense node captioning) only within the activated subgraph. Introduces JITOMA-Bench for long-horizon, multi-tasking and complex multi-step reasoning.
AI.result: Significant reductions in active graph size and captioning latency, with stable processing time under long-horizon task switching, validated by extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: JITOMA provides a practical, just-in-time memory activation mechanism for 3D scene graphs on edge devices, enabling efficient real-time perception and establishing a benchmark suite for future evaluation.

title: A Bayesian framework for the uncanny valley in humanoid robot design
summary: The uncanny valley is a long-standing empirical rule in humanoid robot design: making robots more human-like can reduce, rather than increase, affinity. Yet existing guidelines, such as adopting robot-like appearances, avoiding excessive realism, and reducing cross-modal mismatches, remain difficult to use for algorithmic design because they are not expressed as manipulable variables. Here, we propose a hierarchical Bayesian generative model that operationalizes these guidelines as mathematical design variables. The model represents affinity toward humanoid robots as posterior-weighted negative category-conditional surprise and explains category ambiguity and perceptual mismatch as increases in surprise. It maps uncanny-valley mechanisms onto four variables: deviation from the predicted robot-category mean, inconsistency in human likeness across modalities, prediction uncertainty, and observational uncertainty. Simulations showed that category ambiguity and appearance--motion mismatch can produce affinity reductions, and that uncertainty reshapes the valley. In a human-subject experiment with robot--human morphing images, we manipulated prediction uncertainty using blurred prior robot stimuli and observational uncertainty using blurred evaluation stimuli. Increased observational uncertainty attenuated the decrease in familiarity ratings at intermediate human likeness, whereas low prediction uncertainty increased ratings for robot-like appearances. This framework turns empirical uncanny-valley heuristics into a computational basis for algorithmically evaluating and optimizing humanoid robot appearance and behavior.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model converts uncanny valley guidelines into manipulable design variables and demonstrates that category ambiguity, cross-modal mismatch, and varying prediction/observational uncertainty shape affinity, offering a computational basis for optimizing humanoid appearance and behavior.
AI.motivation: To operationalize uncanny valley heuristics as actionable, algorithmic design variables for humanoid robots, enabling principled design optimization.
AI.method: Propose a hierarchical Bayesian generative model with variables: deviation from predicted robot-category mean, cross-modal inconsistency in likeness, prediction uncertainty, observational uncertainty; perform simulations; conduct a human-subject experiment with morphing robot-human images manipulating prior (prediction) and evaluation (observational) uncertainty via blur.
AI.result: Simulations show category ambiguity and appearance–motion mismatch reduce affinity; uncertain predictions/observations reshape the valley; in the human study, increased observational uncertainty attenuated familiarity decline at mid-likeness; low prediction uncertainty raised familiarity for robot-like appearances.
AI.conclusion: Provides a computational, design-meaningful framework to evaluate and optimize humanoid appearance and behavior, turning uncanny-valley heuristics into concrete design variables for algorithmic robotics.

title: Targeted Recovery of Weight-Space Mechanisms From Neural Networks
comment: Accepted at the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop, ICML 2026
summary: Parameter decomposition (PD) decomposes neural networks into interpretable computational components that faithfully reflect the original network's operations. However, scaling PD to large models requires vast compute, making it a costly and risky endeavor. Here we propose targeted PD (tPD), which identifies only the components that process specific inputs of interest -- from isolated prompts to large subtasks -- by introducing a high-rank catch-all component that handles all non-target data. We validate tPD on toy models and on transformer language models trained on The Pile, where it recovers reproducible, mechanistically faithful circuits. We extract a CSS-only submodel of a 4-block transformer using 7% of the FLOPs of its published decomposition, and in a 12-block transformer we surgically ablate and rewire memorized sequences, with negligible side effects on other inputs.

AI.tldr: Targeted PD (tPD) enables input-focused circuit decomposition by introducing a high-rank catch-all for non-target data, allowing scalable, faithful circuit extraction and targeted interventions in large transformers with substantially reduced compute.
AI.motivation: Scaling parameter decomposition (PD) to large neural models is compute-intensive and risky; there is a need for an efficient method that isolates components processing specific inputs of interest.
AI.method: Introduce a high-rank catch-all component to represent all non-target data and define a targeted PD procedure that extracts only the circuitry relevant to chosen inputs. Validate on toy models and transformer language models trained on The Pile; demonstrate CSS-only submodel extraction and surgical manipulation of memorized sequences in deeper transformers.
AI.result: tPD recovers reproducible, mechanistically faithful circuits. It yields a CSS-only submodel of a 4-block transformer using 7% of the FLOPs of the full decomposition. In a 12-block transformer, it allows ablating and rewiring memorized sequences with negligible side effects on other inputs.
AI.conclusion: tPD enables efficient, faithful interpretation and targeted intervention for large models by focusing on input-relevant circuitry, reducing compute and risk compared with full PD.

title: Self-Improvements in Modern Agentic Systems: A Survey
comment: 97 pages, 12 figures. Project page: https://selfimproving-agent.github.io/ Repository: https://github.com/selfimproving-agent/awesome-Self-Improving-Agents
summary: Self-improving autonomous agents are moving from research prototypes to deployed systems. The primary goal is controllable evolution, or adaptation, from experience with minimal or even no human input. This survey frames modern self-improving agents as adaptive systems that convert experience into accumulated capability gains. We offer a system-level framework that represents a modern agent as a configuration coupling a foundation model with an operational scaffold of prompts, memory, tools, and control logic. Within this framework, self-improvement is formalized as a self-induced update operator that obtains and commits updates to model parameters or scaffold components. We organize prior work by update target and by the signals that drive change, then review applications and discuss evaluation, before closing with open problems and future directions. For convenience, we track technical updates on https://github.com/selfimproving-agent/awesome-Self-Improving-Agents.

AI.tldr: A framework for self-improving autonomous agents coupling a foundation model with prompts, memory, tools, and control logic; formalizes self-improvement via a self-induced update operator; surveys prior work by update target and driving signals; discusses evaluation, open problems, and future directions; provides a GitHub tracker.
AI.motivation: As autonomous agents move from prototypes to deployed systems, there is a need for controllable, experience-driven evolution with minimal human input. The paper frames agents as adaptive systems that convert experience into accumulated capability gains and provides a system-level architecture to organize updates to models and scaffolds.
AI.method: Proposes a system-level configuration that couples a foundation model with an operational scaffold (prompts, memory, tools, control logic). Defines self-improvement as a self-induced update operator that obtains and commits updates to model parameters or scaffold components. Organizes prior work by update target and signals driving change, reviews applications and evaluation, and discusses open problems and future directions. Provides a public GitHub resource to track technical updates.
AI.result: The paper offers a unified conceptual framework for self-improving agents, including a taxonomy of update targets and driving signals, and guidance on evaluation and future research directions. It consolidates existing work and points to a community-maintained repository for ongoing updates.
AI.conclusion: Self-improving agents can be systematically developed and evaluated within the proposed framework, but success hinges on well-defined update operators, robust evaluation methods, and addressing open research challenges; a community-driven repository will support coordination and transparency.

title: AffectFlow-DINO: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Task Affect Estimation via Conditional Rectified Flow
summary: We present \textbf{AffectFlow-DINO}, a multi-task learning system for the 11th ABAW challenge that extends a standard deterministic architecture with a conditional rectified-flow head to model the inherent ambiguity of in-the-wild facial behavior. Instead of predicting a single affect estimate, the model learns a conditional generative distribution, enabling uncertainty-aware one-to-many predictions through Monte Carlo sampling. The system jointly estimates continuous valence-arousal, classifies eight facial expressions, and detects twelve Action Units from static face images. Built on a frozen DINOv3 ViT-S/16 backbone, extensive ablation studies show that rectified-flow decoding consistently improves deterministic prediction, particularly for valence-arousal estimation (CCC-V $+0.058$). We further show that post-hoc threshold calibration effectively recovers performance on severely imbalanced rare classes (e.g., Fear: $3.8\% \rightarrow 33.1\%$) without retraining. Combined with backbone fine-tuning and flow retuning, the final model achieves $\mathbf{P_{MTL}=1.177}$, substantially outperforming the official challenge baseline of $P_{MTL}=0.45$.

AI.tldr: AffectFlow-DINO introduces a conditional rectified-flow head to model uncertainty in multi-task affect estimation, achieving state-of-the-art MTL performance on ABAW with improved valence-arousal accuracy and better handling of rare classes via calibration.
AI.motivation: Address the intrinsic ambiguity of in-the-wild facial behavior and severe class imbalance in affective datasets; enable uncertainty-aware, one-to-many predictions while jointly solving valence-arousal, expressions, and action units.
AI.method: Backbone: frozen DINOv3 ViT-S/16. Head: conditional rectified-flow decoding producing a conditional generative distribution; enables Monte Carlo sampling for uncertainty-aware predictions. Tasks: continuous valence-arousal regression, 8 expression classification, 12 Action Unit detection from static faces. Training includes ablations; post-hoc threshold calibration to address rare classes; flow retuning and backbone fine-tuning for final model.
AI.result: Deterministic improvement in valence-arousal (CCC-V +0.058). Post-hoc calibration boosts rare-class performance (e.g., Fear 3.8% → 33.1%). Final multi-task metric P_MTL = 1.177, substantially surpassing the official baseline P_MTL = 0.45.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-aware, multi-task architecture with a rectified-flow head yields robust gains for affect estimation under ambiguity, with effective calibration addressing data imbalance and strong overall MTL performance.

title: A 3DGS-Driven Dynamic Viewpoint and Vibrotactile Framework for Subsea Teleoperation Validated via fNIRS
summary: Teleoperating remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) in flooded, cluttered infrastructure is fundamentally limited by narrow 2D egocentric views and subsea communication latency. We present a multimodal teleoperation architecture built on a ROS-Unity framework that decouples proactive spatial planning from reactive boundary avoidance. The system replaces static camera feeds with a Dynamic Adaptive Viewpoint System (DAVS), which uses continuous optimization and real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to synthesize an occlusion-free exocentric viewpoint from onboard state estimation. To further reduce sensory workload, a torso-mounted vibrotactile suit maps local obstacle clearance to intuitive haptic proximity cues. The architecture was evaluated in a controlled human-subject study (N = 30) using a BlueROV2 navigating a complex simulated underwater facility. A 3 x 4 repeated-measures design compared three interaction modalities (Egocentric, Haptic, Exocentric) under four communication delays (0.0-1.0 s). Performance was quantified using behavioral measures and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to assess task-evoked prefrontal activation. Results show that reactive haptic feedback improves path adherence under minimal delay, whereas the 3DGS-driven exocentric visualization provides superior resilience under severe latency (0.5-1.0 s), significantly outperforming the other modalities. fNIRS further revealed a cognitive disengagement effect: increasing latency during conventional egocentric teleoperation overloaded working memory and reduced prefrontal activation, whereas the proactive spatial context provided by DAVS sustained executive control. These findings demonstrate that spatially grounded, multimodal assistance can substantially improve operator performance and cognitive endurance during latency-degraded underwater teleoperation.

AI.tldr: A ROS-Unity-based multimodal teleoperation framework (DAVS + 3D Gaussian Splatting + haptic feedback) that decouples planning from boundary avoidance; exocentric visualization improves latency resilience, while haptic cues aid under low latency; fNIRS shows cognitive benefits.
AI.motivation: To overcome narrow 2D egocentric views and subsea communication latency in teleoperating ROVs in flooded/cluttered infrastructure by providing a spatially grounded, multisensory, latency-resilient interface.
AI.method: A ROS-Unity architecture implementing Dynamic Adaptive Viewpoint System (DAVS) with real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting to synthesize an occlusion-free exocentric viewpoint from onboard state estimation, plus a torso-mounted vibrotactile suit for haptic proximity cues. Evaluation used N=30 participants in a 3x4 repeated-measures design comparing Egocentric, Haptic, and Exocentric modalities across four delays (0.0–1.0 s) during BlueROV2 navigation in a simulated underwater facility, with behavioral measures and fNIRS for task-evoked prefrontal activation.
AI.result: Reactive haptic feedback improves path adherence under minimal delay; 3DGS-driven exocentric visualization yields superior resilience at higher latency (0.5–1.0 s), outperforming other modalities. fNIRS indicates cognitive disengagement with increasing latency under egocentric teleoperation, while proactive DAVS context sustains executive control.
AI.conclusion: Spatially grounded, multimodal assistance can substantially elevate operator performance and cognitive endurance in latency-degraded underwater teleoperation, especially by combining proactive exocentric visualization with haptic feedback to balance workload across latency regimes.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Sequential Decision Rules for Event-Triggered LLM Invocation in Streaming Systems
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to the ECML PKDD 2026 Research Track
summary: Streaming inference pipelines increasingly pair lightweight fast models with Large Language Models (LLMs) that provide rich semantic understanding at substantial cost. The central question of when to invoke the LLM has received limited formal treatment. We cast this as a risk-based sequential stopping problem, where a trigger policy fires when a risk functional over the observation history exceeds a threshold. Within this framework, we prove six results: a minimum inter-event time bound excluding trigger chattering; optimality of threshold policies via smooth pasting; approximate SPRT guarantees under estimated parameters; O(sqrt(T log T)) regret for stationary streams, extending to O(sqrt((C_T + 1) T log T)) under C_T changepoints; O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence of online gradient descent for adaptive thresholds; and a calibration-to-miss-rate transfer inequality. Several classical trigger families, including event-triggered, optimal stopping, SPRT, CUSUM, and Bayesian triggers, can be expressed as special cases of this framework. On turbofan degradation data (CMAPSS) with real LLM calls, we empirically verify the theoretical assumptions, ablate the risk function design, compare against six baselines including a RouteLLM-style router and contextual bandits, and analyze cost sensitivity and LLM failure modes. The results confirm sublinear regret, with alpha < 1 for all principled triggers; high diagnostic quality, with 92.9 percent of 1600 LLM diagnoses reaching grounding score >= 0.75 under our rubric; and that anomaly-score-driven risk functions dominate alternatives by roughly an order of magnitude on the Pareto AUC.

AI.tldr: A risk-based sequential stopping framework for deciding when to invoke costly LLMs in streaming inference, unifying many trigger schemes.
AI.motivation: Reduce LLM cost while maintaining diagnostic quality by optimally timing LLM calls in a streaming pipeline.
AI.method: Formulates the problem as a risk functional over the observation history that triggers LLM invocation when exceeding a threshold. Proves six results: minimum inter-event time; threshold policy optimality via smooth pasting; approximate SPRT guarantees with estimated parameters; sublinear regret in stationary settings and extended to changepoint streams; online gradient descent convergence for adaptive thresholds; and calibration-to-miss-rate transfer inequality. Shows many classical trigger families are special cases. Empirically evaluates on CMAPSS turbofan data with real LLM calls, ablations, baselines, and cost-sensitivity analyses.
