AI.result: Theoretical guarantees include sublinear regret (alpha<1) for principled triggers, high diagnostic quality with 92.9% of 1600 LLM diagnoses achieving grounding score ≥0.75, and risk-score–driven triggers dominating alternatives by orders of magnitude on Pareto AUC. Empirical results support the proposed framework and the primacy of anomaly-score risk in performance.
AI.conclusion: A unifying, principled trigger framework for LLM invocation in streaming pipelines that yields provable guarantees and strong empirical performance; the anomaly-score-based risk functions are especially effective; multiple classical triggers arise as special cases, enabling broad applicability.

title: Improving Molecular Property Prediction in Small Language Models Using Graph-based Tools
comment: Presented at the 2nd Causal Neuro-symbolic Artificial Intelligence (Causal NeSy): Toward Agentic LLMs with Neuro-Symbolic and Graph Based Reasoning Workshop @ ESWC2026
summary: Small language models (SLMs) have shown promise for zero-shot molecular property prediction from SMILES strings, yet they often suffer from structural blindness because sequence representations under-specify key graph-topological cues. We propose a modular Context-Augmented Prompting framework that enables agentic tool use at inference time: a trained GNN expert model provides a predictive hint with confidence, and a GNN extracts an instance-specific explanatory subgraph (e.g., a subgraph SMILES and an accompanying explanatory paragraph). We evaluate three commonly used SLMs on MUTAG and Tox21 under five prompting configurations ranging from SMILES-only to using all available tools at hand. Across two datasets, enriching prompts with graph-derived context yields substantial accuracy gains, often exceeding 25% relative improvement and up to 74% on Tox21. We further validate the functional relevance of the extracted motifs via a necessity-based edge-drop intervention. Despite the observed gains, a persistent gap remains to specialized GNN models, highlighting both the value and limits of text-conditioned reasoning for molecular structure.

AI.tldr: Enrich SLMs with graph-derived context via a GNN expert and explanations, improving molecular property prediction; gains are substantial but do not fully close the gap to specialized GNNs.
AI.motivation: Address structural blindness in SMILES representations for zero-shot molecular property prediction and enable inference-time tool use to incorporate graph-topology cues.
AI.method: Propose a Context-Augmented Prompting framework: a trained GNN expert provides a predictive hint with confidence, and a GNN extracts an instance-specific explanatory subgraph (subgraph SMILES + explanatory paragraph). Evaluate five prompting configurations from SMILES-only to full tool usage on MUTAG and Tox21.
AI.result: Prompt-enriched prompts yield substantial accuracy gains (often >25% relative; up to 74% on Tox21); edge-drop (necessity-based) validation of motifs; persistent gap to specialized GNN models.
AI.conclusion: Shows the value and limits of text-conditioned reasoning for molecular structure; context augmentation helps SLMs but does not replace specialized graph models; further work needed to bridge the gap.

title: Differentiable Polarized Path Tracing
summary: Physically based differentiable rendering has proven to be a powerful tool for inverse rendering problems (e.g., 3D reconstruction, reflectance estimation, lighting estimation). However, most existing methods operate solely on radiometric intensity, discarding valuable polarization cues that constrain scene geometry and material properties. While forward simulation of polarized light is well-defined via Mueller-Stokes calculus, extending reverse-mode differentiation to this domain presents significant challenges. The rank-deficient nature of common polarimetric operators, such as linear polarizers and diffuse reflections, violates the invertibility assumptions of standard gradient estimators like path replay backpropagation and results in numerical instability. We address this by proposing a robust, polarization-aware differentiable path tracing method. Our approach estimates unbiased gradients through a combination of path replay and local caching. This formulation enables efficient and stable optimization of material and lighting parameters in complex scenes, broadening the applicability of physically based inverse rendering. Project page: https://vcai.mpi-inf.mpg.de/projects/DPPT/

AI.tldr: Polarization-aware differentiable path tracing for inverse rendering that uses Mueller-Stokes calculus and a hybrid path replay + local caching strategy to estimate unbiased gradients, addressing rank-deficiency of polarimetric operators and enabling stable optimization of materials and lighting.
AI.motivation: Polarization cues constrain geometry and material properties beyond radiometric intensity; existing differentiable renderers suffer from gradient instability due to rank-deficient polarimetric operators.
AI.method: Robust differentiable path tracing that incorporates polarization via Mueller-Stokes calculus. Unbiased gradients are estimated by combining path replay with local caching to handle non-invertible polarimetric operators.
AI.result: Enables efficient and stable optimization of material and lighting parameters in complex scenes, extending physically based inverse rendering to polarized light.
AI.conclusion: A polarization-aware DPTR framework mitigating gradient instability from rank-deficient polarimetric operators, broadening the applicability of polarization-informed inverse rendering.

title: HRO: Hierarchical Room-to-Object Framework for Zero-Shot Object Goal Navigation with Large Language Models
comment: Main paper (6 pages). Accepted for publication by IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics 2026 (IEEE SMC 2026)
summary: Zero-shot object-goal navigation aims to enable an intelligent agent to explore and navigate to objects of unknown categories in an unfamiliar environment without specific target training. In zero-shot navigation tasks, pre-trained large models are usually employed to leverage their prior knowledge for guiding the agent's navigation. However, existing zero-shot object-goal navigation methods based on large language models (LLMs) merely utilize LLMs as flat reasoning tools to directly associate objects or regions. They lack the hierarchical spatial cognition modeling of human-like room semantics to object localization, which leads to strong blindness in exploration, insufficient accuracy in semantic association, and failure to fully unleash the common-sense reasoning potential of LLMs. This paper proposes an LLM-driven hierarchical room-to-object (HRO) framework for zero-shot object-goal navigation, which guides the agent to explore and navigate to the target object in a coarse-to-fine manner. Experiments on Gibson and HM3D datasets verify that our HRO framework achieves superior success rate and generalization over existing LLM-based methods, underscoring LLMs' strong potential for zero-shot object-goal navigation.

AI.tldr: LLM-driven hierarchical room-to-object (HRO) enables zero-shot object-goal navigation by using coarse-to-fine room semantics for localization, outperforming flat LLM reasoning.
AI.motivation: LLMs used as flat reasoning tools in zero-shot navigation fail to leverage hierarchical spatial cognition, causing exploration blindness and weak semantic localization; there is a need to integrate room-level semantics with object-level localization to better harness LLM commonsense.
AI.method: Propose an LLM-driven hierarchical room-to-object (HRO) framework that guides exploration from coarse room-level reasoning to fine-grained object localization, combining room semantics with object search in a hierarchical plano-temporal planning loop within unseen environments.
AI.result: Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show that the HRO framework achieves higher success rates and better generalization than existing LLM-based methods for zero-shot object-goal navigation.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating hierarchical room semantics with LLMs unlocks stronger zero-shot navigation capabilities and demonstrates the potential of LLMs for structured spatial reasoning in navigation tasks.

title: TSSM: Triaxial State Space Model for Global Station Weather Forecasting with Temporal-Variable-Historical Modeling
summary: Global Station Weather Forecasting (GSWF) is pivotal for localized and extreme weather prediction over key regions. Despite efforts to exploit look-back windows, existing methods show limited accuracy gains and struggle with extreme events and error accumulation. These limitations stem from overreliance on short-term patterns, which are insufficient to capture chaotic weather dynamics, especially under partial observations. To address this problem, we propose a novel Triaxial State Space Model (TSSM) with a history-enhanced Temporal-VariableHistorical paradigm, which incorporates period-aligned historical weather data to compensate for long-term, large-scale periodic, and full-window weather patterns beyond the temporal lookback window. Specifically, TSSM stacks historical samples into period-aligned batches, where forecasting is causally supported by historical and current observations. Temporal, variable, and historical scanning are designed to capture axial temporal dependencies, variable correlations, and historical evolution. This structure is hierarchically shared to model seasonal to extreme events while alleviating misalignment across historical patterns. TSSM achieves SOTA performance on Weather-5K, the largest station weather dataset to date, with 10% and 61% gains in accuracy and extreme event metrics, and obtains 95% best or second-best results on human-involved datasets. Its advantages are more pronounced in long-horizon and iterative forecasting, reaching a 37.5% gain at 240h and up to 103.5% under a 48h times 5 iterative setting. Moreover, TSSM retains > 90% performance under up to 80% missing observations, compared with < 43% for baselines, demonstrating robustness and practical potential for reliable GSWF in global in-situ observation networks.

AI.tldr: A novel Triaxial State Space Model (TSSM) with a history-enhanced Temporal-VariableHistorical paradigm for global station weather forecasting, leveraging period-aligned historical data to extend beyond short-lookback windows, achieving state-of-the-art results and strong robustness to missing data.
AI.motivation: Current models overrely on short-term patterns and struggle with chaotic dynamics and partial observations. There is a need to incorporate long-term, large-scale periodic patterns through history-aware representations to improve accuracy, extreme-event prediction, and robustness.
AI.method: Proposes Triaxial State Space Model (TSSM) that stacks historical samples into period-aligned batches, enabling causal forecasting with historical and current observations. Introduces temporal, variable, and historical scanning to capture axial temporal dependencies, variable correlations, and historical evolution. The model is hierarchically shared to cover seasonal to extreme events and reduces misalignment across historical patterns.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on Weather-5K with 10% accuracy gains and 61% gains on extreme-event metrics. Attains 95% best or second-best results on human-involved datasets. Long-horizon gains include 37.5% at 240h and up to 103.5% under a 48h×5 iterative setting. Demonstrates robustness with >90% performance under up to 80% missing observations, vs baselines <43%.
AI.conclusion: TSSM effectively mitigates reliance on short-lookback patterns and partial observations, delivering strong performance across horizons and robust operation in incomplete data scenarios, with clear practical potential for reliable global station weather forecasting.

title: Oracle Agent Memory as an Enterprise Memory Substrate for Long-Horizon AI Agents
comment: 23 pages, 7 figures. Technical report on Oracle Agent Memory
summary: Agent memory is a systems problem for long-horizon agents. Practical deployments require retention of task state across extended conversations, recovery of user-specific facts and preferences across sessions, and accumulation of procedural knowledge from prior outcomes. These requirements extend beyond document retrieval: a memory layer must determine which interactions become durable state, how that state is scoped, how it is retrieved under latency constraints, and how it is revised or removed over time. This report studies Oracle Agent Memory as a database-native memory substrate built on Oracle Database. Three themes organize the discussion: memory as a lifecycle spanning ingestion, extraction, consolidation, retrieval, summarization, and revision or removal; a layered architecture that separates an active memory core from a passive memory-store interface with explicit scope control across users, agents, and threads; and evaluation methodology in which downstream task accuracy is complemented by memory-centric measures such as evidence retrieval, recall, latency, and estimated token use. The report summarizes LongMemEval results, reaching 93.8% accuracy, compares Oracle Agent Memory against flat-history baselines, using about 10.7x fewer tokens, and published or reported external baselines where available, and closes with implementation-oriented appendix material covering setup, thread lifecycle, and search semantics.

AI.tldr: Oracle Agent Memory proposes a database-native memory substrate for long-horizon agents, emphasizing lifecycle memory management, a separation between active memory core and passive store, and memory-centric evaluation, achieving 93.8% accuracy on LongMemEval and ~10.7x token efficiency versus flat histories.
AI.motivation: Address long-horizon agent needs: retention across sessions, user-specific facts, and procedural knowledge; overcome limitations of document retrieval by enabling durable state management with explicit scope control and revision.
AI.method: Develop memory substrate on Oracle Database with a layered architecture: an active memory core and a passive memory-store interface with explicit scope control across users, agents, and threads; memory lifecycle operations covering ingestion, extraction, consolidation, retrieval, summarization, and revision/removal; latency-aware retrieval and revision mechanisms; evaluation using LongMemEval and comparisons to flat-history baselines, plus an appendix detailing setup and search semantics.
AI.result: LongMemEval reports 93.8% accuracy; Oracle Agent Memory uses about 10.7x fewer tokens than flat-history baselines; comparisons to published or external baselines when available; robust implementation-oriented appendix.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates feasibility and efficiency of a database-native memory substrate for long-horizon agents, showing scalable memory lifecycle management and concrete gains in accuracy and token efficiency; future directions include optimizing retrieval latency, refining memory pruning, and expanding benchmarks and privacy/ownership considerations.

title: FOLIO: Focused Semantic Memory for Streaming Video Understanding
summary: In online streaming video understanding, a video stream continues to arrive and queries may be issued at any time. Because streaming frames grow without bound, the system must continuously compress and retain information from the observed video prefix while future frames and future queries remain unknown. The core challenge is deciding what information to retain and how to organize the maintained history: as this history grows with the stream, memory cost increases and many redundant visual details are retained, whereas later queries often depend on specific entities, actions, and their temporal changes. To address this challenge, we introduce FOLIO, a training-free focused semantic memory system that records important parts of the stream in higher detail while keeping surrounding context compact. As the stream arrives, FOLIO updates memory at the segment level, guided by a dynamic focus state, combining a short-term visual buffer with a long-term semantic memory organized around observed entities and linked to a visual-evidence cache. At query time, lightweight hybrid retrieval combines direct matching over the structured memory with semantic query expansion. FOLIO achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching 82.0/69.1 Perception/Backward accuracy on OVO-Bench with Qwen3-VL-8B and 74.5 overall accuracy on StreamingBench, while substantially reducing the cost of maintaining streaming memory by reserving detailed records for focused entities and storing surrounding context compactly.

AI.tldr: FOLIO is a training-free focused semantic memory for streaming video that selectively records detailed memory for key entities while keeping context compact, enabling state-of-the-art streaming understanding with reduced memory costs.
AI.motivation: Streaming video understanding requires maintaining useful history under unbounded frames and unknown future queries; naive memory grows with the stream and retains redundant details, hindering efficiency and responsiveness.
AI.method: Segment-level memory updates guided by a dynamic focus state, combining a short-term visual buffer with a long-term semantic memory centered on observed entities and linked to a visual-evidence cache; query-time retrieval uses a hybrid approach of direct memory matching and semantic query expansion.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance: 82.0/69.1 Perception/Backward accuracy on OVO-Bench with Qwen3-VL-8B and 74.5 overall accuracy on StreamingBench; substantial memory-cost reduction by storing detailed records only for focused entities while compactly maintaining surrounding context.
AI.conclusion: FOLIO demonstrates that training-free, selective semantic memory with segment-level updates and hybrid retrieval can achieve high accuracy in streaming video understanding while substantially reducing memory requirements.

title: Worlds in One Demo: A Synthetic Data Engine for Learning Open-World Mobile Manipulation
summary: Learning open-world mobile manipulation policies requires vast data to achieve spatial generalization, long-horizon robustness, and scene generalization. Current prevailing data collection paradigms, teleoperation and UMI, demand prohibitive human effort and cost at scale. To scale beyond the limits of manual data collection, we seek to maximize the value of each human demonstration by scalable data generation. To this end, we introduce WANDA: learning open-World mobile mANipulation from one demonstration via a synthetic DAta engine. WANDA first reconstructs background Gaussian splats and robot-object interaction trajectories from source RGBD observations, as a world substrate for later planning and rendering. It then rearranges contact-rich robot-object interaction segments into extensive spatial configurations, utilizing whole-body motion planning to chain them into new trajectories. To enhance long-horizon robustness, it applies Corrective State Expansion to increase the robot and object state diversity at different stages of mobile manipulation. To unlock cross-environment generalization, trajectories are synthesized on diverse generated 3D worlds from everyday photos. Furthermore, we synthesize photo-realistic observations by compositing rendered robot and object meshes with Gaussian splatting backgrounds. We evaluate our approach on extensive simulation and real-world tasks in various scenes. Experiments show that policies trained with WANDA achieve long-horizon robustness, broad spatial generalization and cross-environment generalization from one real demonstration. Moreover, WANDA naturally supports cross-embodiment data generation, validated by zero-shot deployment on another mobile manipulator with a distinct morphology.

AI.tldr: A one-demonstration-based synthetic data engine (WANDA) enables open-world mobile manipulation with long-horizon robustness, broad spatial generalization, and cross-environment/generalization, including cross-embodiment transfer, through a Gaussian-splat world substrate, rearranged interaction segments, corrective state expansion, multi-world rendering from everyday photos, and photo-realistic compositing.
AI.motivation: To overcome the high data cost of teleoperation/UMI for open-world mobile manipulation, the paper seeks scalable, data-efficient generation that maximizes the value of each human demonstration, enabling spatial generalization, long-horizon robustness, and cross-environment/embodiment transfer.
AI.method: WANDA constructs a reusable world substrate by reconstructing background Gaussian splats and robot-object interaction trajectories from source RGBD. It then rearranges contact-rich segments into diverse spatial configurations using whole-body motion planning, augments diversity via Corrective State Expansion, and synthesizes trajectories on varied 3D worlds created from everyday photos. Observations are rendered photorealistically by compositing robot/object meshes with Gaussian splat backgrounds. The approach supports cross-embodiment data generation and demonstrates zero-shot transfer to a different mobile manipulator.
AI.result: Experiments in simulation and real-world scenes show that policies trained with WANDA achieve long-horizon robustness, broad spatial generalization, and cross-environment generalization using a single real demonstration, with successful zero-shot deployment on another morphology.
AI.conclusion: WANDA provides a scalable, data-efficient framework for open-world mobile manipulation from one demonstration, enabling cross-environment and cross-embodiment generalization through synthetic data generation and photorealistic rendering.

title: Disentangling Knowledge States with Ability and Proficiency Modeling for Knowledge Tracing
summary: Knowledge tracing (KT) aims to predict students' future performance by modeling their evolving knowledge states from historical interactions. Existing KT methods usually treat the raw interaction sequence as a unified behavioral process, overlooking the phase-specific nature of learning behaviors. Our preliminary observations show that students are more likely to correctly answer previously failed knowledge concepts after sufficient practice, suggesting a transition from ability-building to proficiency-oriented learning. Motivated by this, we propose Phase-Aware Knowledge Tracing (PAKT), a KT framework that decomposes student interactions into ability and proficiency phases based on the tailored decomposition mechanism. To effectively exploit the decomposed sequences, we design a multi-branch Transformer with a type-aware readout module to jointly capture phase-specific and holistic knowledge states. We further provide a causal analysis to reveal the confounding bias caused by entangling complex learning behaviors in phase-agnostic KT models. Extensive experiments on six public benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms representative baselines, with a maximum AUC gain of 1.33% and an average gain of 0.82%.

AI.tldr: PAKT introduces phase-aware knowledge tracing by decomposing student sequences into ability and proficiency phases, using a multi-branch Transformer with a type-aware readout; it includes a causal analysis and yields consistent AUC gains (max 1.33%, avg 0.82%) on six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Learners exhibit phase-specific transitions; phase-agnostic KT entangles ability-building with proficiency development, limiting predictive power.
AI.method: Tailored decomposition of interactions into two phases; a multi-branch Transformer that processes phase-specific and holistic signals; a type-aware readout to fuse phase-aware representations; causal analysis to identify confounding biases.
AI.result: Six public benchmarks show consistent improvement over representative baselines; max AUC gain 1.33%; average gain 0.82%.
AI.conclusion: Phase-aware modeling improves KT by separating distinct learning trajectories, with a flexible architecture and analysis supporting robustness across datasets.

title: Learning Safe Agent Behaviour from Human Preferences and Justifications via World Models
comment: 42 pages, 18 figures. Extended version of a paper presented at ICAART 2026; submitted for consideration in the ICAART 2026 post-publication selected-papers volume in Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence
summary: We address the problem of safely training an agent policy and deploying a good and safe policy, in settings where the environment dynamics are unknown and no suitable reward function is available. In the context of safety-critical environments, we consider traditional reinforcement learning impractical and resort to the resource of human input. We introduce DROPJ, a human-centred method for both safe training and deployment. We first learn a world model (a learned simulator) from a dataset of prior real-world trajectories. A human then plays the game in this learned simulator to extract several informative simulated trajectories. From these, we sample pairs of simulated trajectory segments and elicit from a human their preference over these segments, as well as a reason (justification) for their choice. We then train a reward model from these justified preferences and use it, together with the world model, to directly deploy the agent using model predictive control. Running real-user experiments, we find that generating informative simulated trajectories from a user significantly reduces the computational cost during training compared to other strategies, and can also improve the performance during deployment. In the context of training within a learned simulator, we show that the use of preferences rather than other types of feedback substantially improves the performance during deployment. We further demonstrate that safety justifications accompanying preferences can significantly enhance safety or prioritise user-prescribed aspects of safety associated with them during deployment.

AI.tldr: DROPJ uses a learned world model and human-preferring judgments with justifications to safely train and deploy policies in unknown dynamics, achieving lower training cost and improved deployment performance via MPC-driven policy execution.
AI.motivation: In safety-critical settings with unknown dynamics and no suitable reward signals, traditional reinforcement learning is impractical. Human input can guide safe training and deployment by exploring informative trajectories and providing actionable feedback.
AI.method: 1) Learn a world model (simulator) from prior real trajectories. 2) A human plays in the simulator to collect informative simulated trajectories. 3) Sample pairs of trajectory segments; elicit human preference and a justification. 4) Train a reward model from preferences and justifications. 5) Use the world model and reward model to deploy the agent via model predictive control (MPC).
AI.result: Real-user experiments show that informative simulated trajectories from a user reduce training costs versus other strategies and can improve deployment performance. Preferences (vs other feedback) improve deployment performance in training-in-the-loop with a learned simulator, and safety justifications accompanying preferences enhance safety alignment to user-prioritized safety aspects during deployment.
AI.conclusion: DROPJ demonstrates that human-centered preference-based reward modeling within a learned simulator can enable safe training and deployment in unknown dynamics, reducing compute and improving safety-related performance when coupled with MPC.

title: Improving Medical Image Generative Models with Fréchet Distance Loss
summary: Diffusion generative models have demonstrated immense potential for synthetic medical image generation. However, these models often struggle to capture complex morphological characteristics of heterogeneous tumors with irregular boundaries, limiting their utility for downstream clinical tasks such as segmentation. This limitation stems from the standard denoising objective: minimizing a per-pixel error, which smooths high-variance irregular structures characteristic of tumors. To address this, we propose finetuning these generative models with Fréchet Distance loss (FD-loss). FD-loss aligns the first and second order feature statistics of real and generated images in a pretrained encoder space, encouraging the generator to capture complex structural variations characteristic of heterogeneous tumors. We integrate FD-loss across diverse architectural settings, using both natural- and medical-image encoders on multiple liver and brain cancer datasets spanning CT and MRI modalities. Downstream segmentation networks trained on our FD-regularized synthetic data consistently achieve superior performance, improving tumor DSC by $>$$5\%$ over unregularized synthetic augmentation alone. Qualitative analysis suggests these gains are associated with more faithful tumor synthesis and fewer segmentation hallucinations. Our results show FD-loss as an effective regularizer for medical image generative models to improve clinical workflows.

AI.tldr: FD-loss finetunes diffusion models using Fréchet distance in encoder feature space to better reproduce heterogeneous tumor morphology, improving segmentation performance when using synthetic data for augmentation.
AI.motivation: Standard per-pixel denoising objectives blur high-variance, irregular tumor structures, limiting synthetic data utility for downstream tasks like segmentation.
AI.method: Fine-tune diffusion generators with Fréchet Distance loss—matching real and generated feature statistics (first and second order) in a pretrained encoder space. Evaluate across diverse architectures, using both natural and medical encoders, on liver and brain cancer CT/MRI datasets.
AI.result: FD-regularized synthetic data yields improved segmentation performance; tumor DSC improves by >5% over unregularized augmentation; qualitative analysis shows more faithful tumor synthesis and fewer segmentation hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: FD-loss acts as an effective regularizer for medical image generative models, enhancing clinical workflows by producing higher-fidelity tumor structures for downstream tasks.

title: Attitude Estimation Using Inertial and Barometric Measurements
summary: Accurate and robust attitude estimation is a key challenge for autonomous vehicles, particularly in GNSS-denied conditions and during highly accelerated flight. In such conditions, Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) alone are insufficient for reliable tilt estimation due to the ambiguity between gravitational and inertial accelerations. Although auxiliary velocity sensors such as GNSS, Pitot tubes, Doppler radar, or Visual Inertial Odometry are commonly used, they may be unavailable, intermittent, or costly. This paper introduces a barometer-aided attitude estimation architecture that exploits barometric altitude measurements to provide complementary information on the vehicle's vertical motion, thereby enhancing attitude estimation within nonlinear observers on SO(3). The contributions are twofold. First, we design a deterministic Riccati observer cascaded with a complementary filter, ensuring almost-global asymptotic stability (AGAS) under a uniform observability (UO) condition while preserving the geometric structure of the attitude dynamics. Second, we propose a nonlinear observer evolving on SO(3)xR2, which integrates IMU measurements as inputs and barometer and magnetometer measurements as outputs within a unified framework, guaranteeing local exponential stability (LES) under relaxed uniform observability conditions. The proposed approaches are validated using both simulated and real flight data. The results demonstrate that barometer-aided estimation provides a lightweight, reliable, and effective complementary sensing modality for attitude estimation in minimal-sensing configurations, offering a practical alternative when conventional velocity measurements are unavailable or degraded.

AI.tldr: Barometer-aided attitude estimation using barometer data to complement IMU for attitude estimation on SO(3), with two observers (Riccati + complementary filter; nonlinear observer on SO(3)xR^2), stability guarantees (AGAS and LES under UO conditions), validated with simulations and flight data; enables reliable attitude estimation in GNSS-denied/minimal-sensing configurations.
AI.motivation: Attitude estimation in GNSS-denied or highly accelerated flight where IMU data alone cannot resolve gravity-acceleration ambiguity; velocity sensors (GNSS, Pitot, Doppler, VIO) may be unavailable or unreliable, prompting the need for a lightweight complementary sensor.
AI.method: Two observer designs: 1) a deterministic Riccati observer cascaded with a complementary filter, achieving almost-global asymptotic stability under a uniform observability condition while preserving attitude dynamics; 2) a nonlinear observer on the manifold SO(3)×R^2 that ingests IMU measurements and outputs from barometer and magnetometer, yielding local exponential stability under relaxed uniform observability. Barometer measurements provide information about vertical motion to assist tilt estimation.
AI.result: Validation on both simulated and real flight data shows that barometer-aided estimation provides a lightweight, reliable complementary sensing modality for attitude estimation in minimal-sensing configurations, particularly when conventional velocity measurements are unavailable or degraded.
AI.conclusion: Barometer-assisted attitude estimation is a practical, robust approach for attitude estimation with minimal sensing, offering a viable alternative to traditional velocity-based aiding in GNSS-denied or degraded environments while preserving geometric structure.

title: STKAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
summary: Real-world traffic data exhibit heterogeneous spatial correlations and nonlinear temporal dynamics, posing substantial challenges for accurate spatio-temporal forecasting. Existing approaches have developed increasingly sophisticated graph, attention, and decomposition architectures, while the influence of the underlying nonlinear function approximator has received comparatively less attention. In this work, we propose STKAN, a spatio-temporal forecasting architecture that introduces Taylor-polynomial Kolmogorov--Arnold Network modules into spatial and temporal token mixing. STKAN first constructs high-level spatial representations through a learnable soft node-group assignment mechanism, applies group-wise spatial mixing, and subsequently models temporal dependencies over the compressed sequence. Spatial and temporal self-attention layers are further employed to capture long-range interactions. Experiments on five traffic forecasting benchmarks show that STKAN achieves competitive performance and performs better than the evaluated MLP-based variant in the tested settings. These results suggest that the design of nonlinear function approximators can serve as a useful complement to architectural design in spatio-temporal forecasting.

AI.tldr: STKAN introduces Taylor-polynomial Kolmogorov--Arnol'd Network modules for spatio-temporal forecasting, integrating nonlinear function approximators into spatial and temporal token mixing via learnable soft node-grouping and group-wise mixing, achieving competitive results on five traffic benchmarks and outperforming an MLP-based variant.
AI.motivation: Real-world traffic data show nonlinear temporal dynamics and heterogeneous spatial correlations; existing architectures emphasize architectural components (graph, attention, decomposition) but underexplore the role of nonlinear function approximators.
AI.method: STKAN constructs high-level spatial representations with a learnable soft node-group assignment, applies group-wise spatial mixing, models temporal dependencies on the compressed sequence, and then applies spatial and temporal self-attention layers. The nonlinear function approximator is implemented via Taylor-polynomial Kolmogorov–Arnol'd Network modules within the mixing steps.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on five traffic forecasting benchmarks shows STKAN achieves competitive performance and outperforms the evaluated MLP-based variant in the tested settings.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear function approximators can complement architectural design in spatio-temporal forecasting, with STKAN illustrating the utility of Taylor-polynomial based modules in improving forecasting performance.

title: CayleyR: Solving the TopSpin puzzle via cycle intersection
summary: We present cayleyR, an R package for solving permutation puzzles by detecting cycle intersections in Cayley graphs. The core algorithm performs an iterative bidirectional search: from both the initial and target permutation states, random operation sequences generate cycles in the Cayley graph of the symmetric group Sn; their intersection yields a connecting path. When no direct intersection is found, a distance-guided bridge selection narrows the gap, and the process repeats. The package targets the TopSpin(n,k) puzzle, whose state space is a Cayley graph of Sn generated by a cyclic shift and a prefix reversal. We describe the mathematical framework, the algorithm, and its implementation, which combines a C++ hash-indexed state store with optional Vulkan GPU acceleration. The software is publicly available on CRAN.

AI.tldr: Introduces cayleyR, an R package for solving permutation puzzles via cycle-intersection searches in Cayley graphs; targets TopSpin(n,k); uses iterative bidirectional randomized search with distance-guided bridging and a hash-indexed state store, with optional GPU acceleration; available on CRAN.
AI.motivation: Provide a practical, scalable toolkit to solve permutation puzzles by exploiting the algebraic structure of their state spaces (Cayley graphs of Sn), enabling efficient search via cycle intersections and bidirectional exploration.
AI.method: Constructs queries by performing random operation sequences from both initial and target states to generate cycles in the Cayley graph of Sn. Intersections of these cycles yield connecting paths. When no direct intersection is found, distance-guided bridge selection narrows the gap and the process repeats. Implementation uses a C++ hash-indexed state store with optional Vulkan GPU acceleration.
AI.result: A complete software package with an underlying mathematical framework and algorithm; implemented in C++/R with Vulkan support, and released publicly on CRAN.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a practical approach to solving TopSpin puzzles by leveraging Cayley graph structure and bidirectional search, with a scalable implementation that can leverage GPU acceleration for performance gains.

title: Accuracy Without Grounding: Diagnosing Visual Dependency Dissociation in Video LLM Benchmarks
comment: Accepted, ACM International Conference on Multimedia 2026 (ACM MM)
summary: Benchmark accuracy in video large language models (LLMs) is often treated as evidence of visual understanding. We audit this assumption across twenty models spanning 2-78B parameters and ten architecture families. We introduce the Visual Dependency Gap (VDG), the difference in per-question correctness between original-video and black-screen conditions. Paired McNemar tests on MVBench show that accuracy and visual dependency are separable: models differ on original video (p = 0.0003) but not on black screens (p = 0.53). Across models, task-type rankings are stable: Attribute Perception is strongly visual, whereas Temporal Reasoning approaches the language-only baseline. A diagnostic ladder from black screen to single frame, shuffled frames, and original video reveals that frame diversity supplies most of the visual benefit, while temporal order contributes near-zero accuracy across sixteen open-weight models. An ablation from 0.5 to 24 FPS rules out sparse sampling as the cause. H.264 experiments further show that stable aggregate accuracy conceals bidirectional question-level answer flips. The diagnostic also generalizes to four API-accessed models, whose VDG values range from 0.025 to 0.315. These results motivate VDG as a standard audit for whether video benchmarks measure visually grounded capability. Code is available at https://github.com/JaeLee18/accuracy-without-grounding.

AI.tldr: Introduces Visual Dependency Gap (VDG) to audit whether video benchmarks truly measure visually grounded understanding in video-language models. Finds that per-question accuracy on original video vs. black-screen conditions diverge, indicating that frame content—not temporal order—drives most visual benefit; VDG is stable across architectures and APIs; code is released.
AI.motivation: Question the assumption that benchmark accuracy equates to visual grounding in video LLMs and develop a robust diagnostic (VDG) to separate visual understanding from language-only processing.
AI.method: Evaluate twenty models (2–78B parameters) across ten architecture families on MVBench. Compare per-question accuracy between original video and black-screen conditions using paired McNemar tests. Use a diagnostic ladder (black screen → single frame → shuffled frames → original video) to identify sources of visual benefit. Perform ablation from 0.5 to 24 FPS, conduct H.264 experiments, and test both open-weight and API models. Report VDG values and analyze effect across task types.
AI.result: Accuracy and visual dependency are separable: models differ on original video (p=0.0003) but not on black screens (p=0.53). Across models, Attribute Perception is highly visual, while Temporal Reasoning aligns with language-only baselines. Frame diversity supplies most of the visual benefit; temporal order contributes near-zero accuracy for sixteen open-weight models. Sparse sampling is ruled out as the cause (0.5–24 FPS). H.264 experiments reveal bidirectional, per-question flips masked by stable aggregate accuracy. API models show VDG values from 0.025 to 0.315. Code available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: VDG should be adopted as a standard audit for video benchmarks to ensure they measure visually grounded capability, rather than relying solely on aggregate accuracy that can mask underlying grounding deficiencies.

title: Parsimonious disturbance-aware minimum-time planning with parametric uncertainty
summary: This study presents and validates a minimum-lap-time planning (MLTP) framework for motorsport applications that embeds robustness against both state disturbances and parameter uncertainty. The methodology builds upon a prior disturbance-aware framework that, at each track point, propagates stochastic vehicle dynamics over a short horizon and tightens tyre-friction constraints based on the worst-case scenario at horizon end. We extend the formulation to account for uncertainty in key vehicle parameters: moment of inertia, centre-of-mass position, and aerodynamic drag coefficient. To keep the extended formulation computationally tractable, a spatially selective, parsimonious activation strategy confines the robust constraints to the circuit segments where they are most critical. We demonstrate the improved driveability of the robust references by employing a model predictive controller (MPC) as a virtual test driver. For each reference, the same MPC drives a simulated FSAE (Formula SAE) car over 1000 runs on a representative Barcelona-Catalunya sector, with randomly realised impulsive disturbances and parameter scatter. We compare a nominal reference, planned without robustness, against its robust counterparts. The latter yield consistently fewer failed runs and, at a moderate sector-time cost, show tighter dispersion of key signals (vehicle inputs, axle saturations) around the reference values, evidence of better trackability.

AI.tldr: Robust MLTP for motorsport with disturbances and parameter uncertainty; spatially selective activation; MPC-based validation; improved driveability with modest time cost.
AI.motivation: Improve reliability and trackability of lap-time planning under disturbances and parameter uncertainty for high-performance driving.
AI.method: Extend existing disturbance-aware MLTP to include uncertain inertia, COM position, drag; propagate stochastic dynamics over short horizon; tighten tyre friction at horizon end; spatially selective activation to keep tractable; validate with MPC driving an FSAE car over 1000 runs on Barca track sector with impulsive disturbances and parameter scatter.
AI.result: Robust references reduce failed runs and tighten signal dispersion, at moderate sector-time cost.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating parameter uncertainty into MLTP with selective robust constraints enhances driveability and trackability under disturbances; practical for real-time MPC contexts; further work needed on real-world validation and computational scaling.

title: A Hybrid Mamba for Audio-Visual Navigation
comment: Main paper (6 pages). Accepted for publication by IEEE International Conference on Systems and Man and Cybernetics 2026 (IEEE SMC 2026)
summary: Since the paradigm centered on convolutional neural networks and recurrent architectures was established in 2020, the fundamental backbone networks for audio-visual navigation have undergone no essential changes for more than five years, making them inadequate to support efficient representation of dynamic multimodal sequences. This paper proposes Samba(A Hybrid Mamba for Audio-Visual Navigation). It uses the adaptive selection-enabled Mamba State Encoder (M-SE) to replace conventional GRUs for temporal aggregation, and constructs an Audio Mamba Encoder (AME) to remedy the limitations of convolutional operators in capturing global time-frequency dependencies in spectrograms. Experiments demonstrate that Samba exhibits exceptional generalization performance when facing unheard sound sources and unseen scenes. On the Matterport3D dataset, it improves the navigation success rate (SR) by 11.3\% compared with existing state-of-the-art models, and the performance gain is even more pronounced on the Replica dataset, which features finer scene structures. Such modernized architectural reconstruction unlocks stronger embodied representation capabilities at a lower computational cost, thereby providing a highly robust technical pathway for paradigm evolution in the field of audio-visual navigation.

AI.tldr: Hybrid audio-visual navigation model Samba replaces GRUs with a Mamba State Encoder (M-SE) for temporal aggregation and introduces an Audio Mamba Encoder (AME) to capture global time-frequency dependencies in spectrograms. It achieves strong generalization to unseen sounds and scenes, with notable SR gains (+11.3% on Matterport3D; larger gains on Replica) at lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Address the stagnation of backbone architectures in audio-visual navigation since 2020 and the insufficiency of conventional convolutions/GRUs for dynamic multimodal sequence modeling. Propose an architectural reconstruction to improve representation and efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce Samba architecture that substitutes GRUs with an adaptive, selection-enabled Mamba State Encoder (M-SE) for temporal aggregation and adds an Audio Mamba Encoder (AME) to model global time-frequency dependencies in spectrograms.
AI.result: Empirical results show enhanced generalization to unseen sound sources and scenes. On Matterport3D, SR improves by 11.3% over state-of-the-art. On Replica, gains are larger due to finer scene structures.
AI.conclusion: A modernized architectural approach can deliver stronger embodied representations at lower computational cost, providing a robust pathway for paradigm evolution in audio-visual navigation.

title: Networked Intelligence: Active Shared Context Graphs for Human-AI Team Science
summary: Most AI-for-science systems focus on scaling a single reasoning process through better models, larger context windows, long-horizon agentic execution, or digital co-scientists working with one principal user. However, challenging scientific problems are rarely solved by one reasoner alone. They are solved by teams whose members bring different priors, experimental backgrounds, tacit knowledge, and domain-trained intuitions. The open problem is therefore not only how to scale models, but how to cultivate networked intelligence: scaling the connections between humans and AI systems so that a result or hypothesis produced in one context reaches another person, agent, instrument, or robot that can act on it. We introduce Mycelium, an active shared workspace that automatically connects researchers and AI agents as a multi-user co-scientist. As human users and agents work, the system captures important observations and hypotheses, tracks how they relate to the team's evolving model, and routes them to the person or agent whose next decision they can inform. We evaluate Mycelium in its first empirical test, a biological multi-omics campaign in which routed shared context turned a local analytical finding into a cross-expert mechanistic constraint and ultimately into an experimental design. We also give networked intelligence a computational account as sparse conditional computation over distributed scientific contexts. This account distinguishes when a scaled standalone agent can match the network from when independent expertise and non-mergeable contexts make the network irreducible.

AI.tldr: Mycelium is a multi-user co-scientist platform that connects researchers and AI agents in a shared workspace, enabling networked intelligence. In a biological multi-omics study, routing shared context across experts transformed a local finding into cross-expert constraints and an experimental design. The authors propose sparse conditional computation over distributed contexts to explain when networked collaboration helps versus scaled standalone agents.
AI.motivation: Current AI-for-science work often scales a single reasoning process; however, complex scientific problems require distributed expertise and propagation of results across different humans and agents. There is a need to cultivate networked intelligence that connects contexts, agents, and instruments.
AI.method: Develop Mycelium as an active shared workspace that automatically captures observations and hypotheses, tracks their relation to the evolving model, and routes them to the most relevant human or agent. Evaluate in a biological multi-omics campaign. Provide a computational account via sparse conditional computation across distributed scientific contexts.
AI.result: In the empirical test, routed shared context turned a local analytical finding into a cross-expert mechanistic constraint and ultimately into an experimental design, demonstrating the practical potential of networked intelligence.
AI.conclusion: Networked intelligence can outperform isolated agents in cross-context scientific problems. The paper offers a computational framework (sparse conditional computation) to determine when networked collaboration is necessary or irreducible due to non-mergeable contexts.

title: Reflecting Process Expertise in Procedural Material Generation
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://materialapprentice.github.io
summary: Procedural material creation underpins applications in digital content creation, visual effects, and 3D asset design. Achieving high-quality results requires more than reproducing node graphs -- it demands understanding the process by which experts construct materials. We formulate procedural material generation as retrieval-time process reasoning over expert demonstrations, elevating process to a first-class representation beyond graph-only synthesis. Concretely, we represent expert workflows as process traces: textual records of construction steps, parameters, and design intent. To instantiate this idea, we use a pretrained LLM-based ProcessSynthesizer to synthesize a process trace aligned with a user's intent and a pretrained LLM-based Compiler to ground the process trace into an executable Blender material graph. Because procedural expertise is most naturally conveyed through demonstrations, we leverage tutorial videos as a source of process knowledge and extract textual, LLM-compatible traces using automated video analysis tools. In an expert study with five Blender artists (avg. 7.5 years of experience), materials generated by reflecting expert demonstrations were found to produce workflows requiring fewer edits, and more closely match professional design strategies than methods operating solely on static artifacts. A user study with 150 participants further shows that our approach achieves superior generation and editing performance compared to prior procedural systems. All code, models, and data will be available at https://materialapprentice.github.io

AI.tldr: Procedural material creation is reframed as retrieval-time process reasoning over expert demonstrations, using LLMs to synthesize and ground process traces into executable Blender graphs, improving fidelity and edit efficiency over graph-only approaches.
AI.motivation: Move beyond static graph-based synthesis by capturing construction process, parameters, and design intent from expert demonstrations (e.g., tutorial videos) to enable more faithful, editable procedural materials.
AI.method: Represent expert workflows as textual process traces; use a pretrained ProcessSynthesizer (LLM) to generate traces aligned with user intent; employ a pretrained Compiler (LLM) to convert traces into executable Blender material graphs; extract traces from tutorial videos via automated video analysis; validate via expert study (n=5, avg 7.5 years) and a user study (n=150).
AI.result: Expert-generated materials using reflected demonstrations required fewer edits and better matched professional design strategies than graph-only methods. In a larger user study, the approach achieved superior generation and editing performance compared with prior procedural systems.
AI.conclusion: Process traces provide a first-class, interpretable representation of procedural knowledge that improves alignment with expert workflows and enables more efficient material generation and editing; code, models, and data will be released.

title: Adapting Generalist Vehicle Models for High-Speed MPC Across Terrains
summary: High-speed off-road autonomy requires precise closed-loop control for a target vehicle while remaining robust across changing terrains. Recent forward kinodynamic (FKD) prediction foundation models suggest a promising path, starting from a generalist model and specializing it to the target platform. However, effective specialization remains challenging, as it often requires substantial real-world data, and models adapted to one setting can still overfit to specific terrains or driving regimes. We present OptCar (Optimized Car), a recipe for bridging the gap from generalist to specialist FKD models that preserves cross-terrain generalization while optimizing performance for a specific vehicle. $\texttt{OptCar}$ introduces a history-conditioned dynamics adaptation module that encodes recent state-action observations into a dynamics context token, and then fine-tunes the generalist model using limited real-world data together with targeted synthetic rollouts from environment-specific system identification. In closed-loop model predictive control (MPC) experiments across three terrains and an out-of-distribution cart-pulling task, the largest gains appear at 6~m/s, the highest speed evaluated and the regime in which slip dominates tracking error. On vegetation and dirt, the most slip-diverse terrain, OptCar reduces 6~m/s trajectory tracking error by roughly 55% relative to a fine-tuned AnyCar baseline, and remains the most accurate even when an unseen cart payload changes the dynamics. With only 5 minutes of real data per terrain, OptCar is competitive on road with a specialist trained on 30 minutes of road data, and substantially outperforms it once the terrain changes.

AI.tldr: OptCar provides a recipe to specialize generalist forward kinodynamic (FKD) models to a target vehicle across terrains by introducing a history-conditioned dynamics adaptation module and leveraging limited real-world data plus synthetic rollouts, achieving major performance gains in high-speed off-road MPC.
AI.motivation: Robust high-speed off-road autonomy requires cross-terrain generalization. Generalist FKD models must be specialized for a target vehicle without overfitting to specific terrains or requiring large real-world datasets.
AI.method: Introduce a history-conditioned dynamics adaptation module that encodes recent state-action observations into a dynamics context token. Fine-tune the generalist FKD model using limited real-world data together with targeted synthetic rollouts from environment-specific system identification.
AI.result: Closed-loop MPC experiments across three terrains and an out-of-distribution cart-pulling task show the largest gains at 6 m/s. On vegetation and dirt (most slip-diverse terrains), OptCar reduces 6 m/s trajectory tracking error by ~55% relative to a fine-tuned AnyCar baseline and remains the most accurate even when an unseen cart payload changes dynamics. With only 5 minutes of real data per terrain, OptCar is competitive on road with a specialist trained on 30 minutes of road data, and substantially outperforms it when terrain changes.
AI.conclusion: OptCar effectively bridges the generalist-to-specialist gap for FKD models, preserving cross-terrain generalization while optimizing performance for a specific vehicle. It achieves strong gains with limited real data and synthetic rollouts, including robustness to unseen payload changes.

title: CoDiffGRN: Rethinking Gene Regulatory Network Inference via the BEELINE-KGC Benchmark and Co-evolutionary Discrete Diffusion
summary: Inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from single-cell transcriptomic data is crucial for biological discovery, yet existing approaches suffer from a fundamental misalignment with real-world needs. Researchers typically seek a small set of high-confidence regulatory interactions for experimental validation, often involving previously unseen genes. However, current benchmarks rely on transductive splits with global classification metrics, while prevailing models struggle to generalize under inductive settings. To bridge this gap, we reformulate GRN inference as an inductive, ranking-centric graph completion problem and introduce \textbf{\benchmark}, a new benchmark that incorporates an inductive gene-holdout split together with knowledge graph completion metrics to better evaluate top-ranked predictions. Building on this, we propose \textbf{\method}, the first co-evolutionary discrete diffusion framework that jointly models biologically coherent discretized gene expression states and regulatory interactions for robust inductive generalization and improved top-ranked regulatory discovery. We further introduce TF-ALL Subgraph Sampling (TASS) for scalable training. Extensive experiments on {\benchmark} show that {\method} establishes new state-of-the-art performance, significantly outperforming existing methods in novel regulatory discovery, and ablation studies further verify the effectiveness of our design.

AI.tldr: Inductive, ranking-based graph completion for gene regulatory network inference using a new inductive benchmark and a co-evolutionary discrete diffusion model, achieving state-of-the-art performance on novel regulatory discovery with scalable training via targeted subgraph sampling.
AI.motivation: There is a practical need for high-confidence regulatory interactions involving unseen genes, but prevailing benchmarks are transductive and rely on global classification metrics, hindering generalization to inductive settings.
AI.method: Introduce an inductive gene-holdout benchmark with knowledge-graph completion-style metrics. Propose a co-evolutionary discrete diffusion framework that jointly models discretized gene expression states and regulatory interactions, and a TF-ALL Subgraph Sampling (TASS) strategy for scalable training.
AI.result: Experiments show state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark, especially in novel regulatory discovery; ablations validate the design choices.
AI.conclusion: Recasting GRN inference as inductive ranking on graph completion improves generalization to unseen genes and enhances top-ranked regulatory discovery; the benchmark and method together offer a more realistic evaluation framework for practical GRN inference.

title: AI-Native Insurance for Agentic AI: Pricing, Underwriting, and End-to-End Automation
summary: Agentic AI introduces new insurance challenges because autonomous AI systems can make decisions, invoke tools, modify external environments, and interact with third-party services. This paper develops an AI-native mathematical framework for underwriting, pricing, and contract design for agentic AI deployments. A deployment is represented by a risk state that captures autonomy level, operational authority, permission exposure, governance maturity, and dependency concentration. The framework maps the risk state to event probabilities, loss severities, governance costs, premiums, deductibles, coverage allocation, and policy covenants, and formulates an optimization problem for insurance contract design under participation, profitability, and incentive compatibility constraints. The paper establishes structural properties of insurability, including characterization of an insurability region, monotone deterioration of feasibility with increasing exposure, and governance certification thresholds. Insurance is further interpreted as both an operational cost and a regulatory mechanism for AI deployment. A healthcare case study illustrates contract optimization, sensitivity analysis, and automated claims processing for agentic AI systems.

AI.tldr: An AI-insurance framework for agentic AI deployments that links a risk state (autonomy, authority, exposure, governance, dependency) to probabilistic risks and contract terms, then optimizes insurance design under participation and incentive constraints; establishes insurability regions and governance thresholds, and demonstrates via a healthcare case study.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI enables autonomous decision-making, tool use, and environment interaction, creating novel risk profiles not captured by traditional insurance models. A formal, AI-native underwriting framework is needed to price, contract, and regulate deployments while providing incentives for safer behavior.
AI.method: Define an AI-native risk state capturing autonomy, authority, permission exposure, governance maturity, and dependency concentration. Map this state to event probabilities, loss severities, governance costs, premiums, deductibles, coverage, and covenants. Formulate an optimization problem for contract design under participation, profitability, and incentive compatibility constraints. Establish structural properties of insurability (insurability region, monotone deterioration with exposure, governance certification thresholds). Interpret insurance as cost and regulatory mechanism. Validate via a healthcare case study with contract optimization, sensitivity analysis, and automated claims processing for agentic AI.
AI.result: Derived an insurability region and thresholds; showed how increasing exposure deteriorates feasible contracts; provided a framework to compute optimal premiums, deductibles, and covenants; demonstrated potential for automated claims handling in a healthcare AI deployment.
AI.conclusion: An AI-native insurance design can both economically manage agentic AI deployment risk and function as a regulatory lever, with practical viability demonstrated through a healthcare case study and clear directions for contract optimization and governance requirements.

title: SARFA: Segment Anything with Radiomic Feature Alignment
summary: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) has demonstrated strong generalizability across a variety of segmentation tasks. However, SAM often struggles in situations where the target to be segmented is ambiguous. This poses a problem in medical imaging, where accurate delineation of targets such as tumors is vital, but even expert radiologists can disagree on the appropriate boundary for a target. Addressing this, we propose SARFA (Segment Anything with Radiomic Feature Alignment), a novel framework for improved medical image segmentation. Via probabilistic prompting, SARFA generates a diverse set of plausible masks for each input image and optimizes them with a radiomics-driven training objective based on Fréchet Radiomic Distance (FRD) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). By minimizing the FRD between masked predicted and ground truth regions within each image, SARFA encourages segmentation outputs whose anatomical and textural characteristics align with clinically meaningful ground truth representations, without relying solely on pixel-level overlap. Evaluated on computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) benchmarks, SARFA outperforms existing ambiguous segmentation methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of radiomic feature alignment and DPO-style candidate mask ranking as a training objective. Our code is available at https://github.com/tbwa233/SARFA.

AI.tldr: SARFA enhances ambiguous medical image segmentation by aligning radiomic features between predicted masks and ground truth using a Fréchet Radiomic Distance objective, aided by probabilistic prompting and DPO-style mask ranking.
AI.motivation: Ambiguity in medical image boundaries leads to disagreement among experts and unreliable pixel-wise overlap metrics; incorporating radiomic texture and anatomical information can produce clinically meaningful segmentations.
AI.method: Builds on SAM with probabilistic prompting to generate diverse candidate masks per image. Introduces a radiomics-driven training objective combining Fréchet Radiomic Distance (FRD) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style ranking to select masks. The loss minimizes FRD between masked predictions and ground truth within each image and ranks candidate masks without relying solely on pixel-wise overlap.
AI.result: On CT and MRI benchmarks, SARFA outperforms existing ambiguous segmentation methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of radiomic feature alignment and DPO-style candidate mask ranking.
AI.conclusion: Radiomic feature alignment improves segmentation under boundary ambiguity in medical imaging; SARFA is effective and code is available for replication.

title: Design and Characterization of a Limb Encircling Actuator
summary: Lower-limb powered exoskeletons have demonstrated substantial improvements in mobility and function, but most designs place actuation components lateral to the legs or remotely at the waist or back. These configurations often extend beyond the body's natural envelope, making devices intrusive in everyday use and potentially limiting societal adoption. We posit that rethinking actuation geometry could enable exoskeletons that conform more closely to the body. Here, we explored an actuation layout in which the actuator encircles the limb in a plane orthogonal to the limb axis, potentially reducing its spatial footprint around the body. We developed the Limb-Encircling Actuator (LEA) and characterized its electromechanical properties using a custom-built testbed. The LEA also features a novel radial bearing layout with potential as a lightweight or lower-cost alternative to traditional large-diameter bearings. The actuator achieved a continuous torque density of 7.5 Nm/kg with a mass of 894 g. Despite this high torque density and innovative layout, the system remained difficult to contain close to the body. These results highlight opportunities and challenges in limb-encircling actuation and provide insights into torque-dense exoskeleton designs that could integrate more readily into everyday apparel if challenges in actuator sizing and geometry are overcome.

AI.tldr: A limb-encircling actuator (LEA) is proposed to reduce actuation footprint by surrounding the limb in a plane perpendicular to the limb axis. The device achieves a high torque density (7.5 Nm/kg) with a compact 894 g package, and introduces a novel radial bearing layout, but remains challenging to contain close to the body for everyday use.
AI.motivation: Conventional exoskeleton actuation is bulky and mounted laterally or remotely, causing intrusion and limiting wearable adoption. A limb-encircling actuation geometry could improve body conformity and social acceptability.
AI.method: Design and build the Limb-Encircling Actuator (LEA) that encircles the limb in a plane orthogonal to the limb axis. Develop a custom testbed to characterize electromechanical properties and evaluate a radial bearing layout as a lightweight, low-cost alternative to traditional bearings. Measure torque density and mass to assess compactness.
AI.result: The LEA achieved a continuous torque density of 7.5 Nm/kg with a total mass of 894 g. Despite high torque density and novel geometry, the device remains difficult to contain in close proximity to the body, highlighting both the potential and the practical constraints of limb-encircling actuation.
AI.conclusion: Limb-encircling actuation offers a promising path toward more body-conforming exoskeletons and potentially wearables, but significant challenges in sizing, geometry, and integration must be overcome before everyday apparel-like use is feasible.

title: ShortOPD: Recovering Pruned LLMs with Short-to-Long On-Policy Distillation
summary: Structured pruning is a hardware-friendly way to compress LLMs, but it is mostly validated on multiple-choice recognition tasks, while the same compressed checkpoints can collapse on the free-form generation that deployment actually requires. Two observations trace this gap. First, greedy \textsc{pass}@$1$ nearly vanishes after compression, yet \textsc{pass}@$k$ recovers substantially under repeated sampling: useful generations are demoted, not erased. Second, the recoverable regime fails mainly through suffix repetition. Recovery should therefore train on the compressed model's own on-policy states with dense token-level supervision, which On-Policy Distillation (OPD) provides by reusing the pre-compression model as a frozen teacher. However, long on-policy rollouts spend early recovery budget on low-information repetitive suffixes, delaying loss descent. To mitigate this waste, we propose \textbf{\shortopd}, a short-to-long OPD schedule that detects teacher-confirmed repetitive suffixes, treats the surviving prefix as each rollout's effective length, and allocates future rollout budgets to the effective lengths the policy can currently use. Across math, code, and open-ended generation, \shortopd\ raises the compressed model's score to about $9\times$ its unrecovered value and $1.6$--$4.4\times$ standard recovery recipes (SFT w/o KD, KD, and SeqKD), and it matches a fixed $8192$-token rollout horizon within two points using a quarter of the training time ($8.5$ vs.\ $35.9$ hours) and $71\%$ fewer rollout tokens. We hope this recipe helps move structured pruning beyond marginal gains on perplexity and multiple-choice benchmarks, a step closer to deployment-ready generation quality.

AI.tldr: ShortOPD is a short-to-long on-policy distillation schedule that mitigates repetitive suffix waste in compressed LLMs, enabling structured pruning to recover near full generation quality with far less compute and rollout length than standard methods.
AI.motivation: To close the gap between structured pruning performance on multiple-choice tasks and free-form generation, where suffix repetition and long on-policy rollouts hinder recovery.
AI.method: Introduce ShortOPD: detect teacher-confirmed repetitive suffixes, treat the surviving prefix as the rollout's effective length, and allocate future rollout budgets to these effective lengths. Uses on-policy distillation with a frozen teacher (pre-compression model) and compares against standard recovery methods across math, code, and open-ended generation.
AI.result: OPD with ShortOPD raises the compressed model’s score to ~9× its unrecovered value and 1.6–4.4× higher than SFT w/o KD, KD, or SeqKD. It matches an 8192-token rollout horizon within two points, using only 8.5 hours of training versus 35.9 hours, and 71% fewer rollout tokens.
AI.conclusion: The recipe advances structured pruning toward deployment-ready generation quality, moving beyond marginal perplexity gains and multiple-choice metrics.

title: Cost-Optimal Foundation Model Deployment Portfolio for Transportation Management
summary: Foundation models, including large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), are increasingly used for transportation management center (TMC) tasks such as anomaly detection, incident reporting, and traveler information. Deploying multiple such models across TMC functions raises a portfolio question: which model should serve each function, in which deployment mode, and under what shared hardware budget? We formulate this as the Foundation Model Deployment Portfolio (FMDP) problem, a mixed-integer program minimizing total cost of ownership (TCO) subject to per-function quality, latency, and safety constraints over shared GPU capacity. We prove the problem NP-hard by reduction from the 0-1 knapsack problem and propose a polynomial-time greedy heuristic. In an illustrative case study with five TMC functions and 19 candidate (model, mode) pairs, FMDP identifies a mixed portfolio costing $34/mo (97% below the cheapest feasible all-closed-API baseline) by routing four functions to open-source APIs and the one function whose quality floor no open-source model meets to a closed API. Break-even analysis shows that on-premise GPU investment becomes reasonable only above approximately 309 vision queries/hour or if API prices double.

AI.tldr: Foundation Model Deployment Portfolio (FMDP) optimizes allocating multiple foundation models to transportation management center (TMC) tasks under a shared GPU budget. It formulates a mixed-integer program minimizing total cost of ownership with per-function quality, latency, and safety constraints; proven NP-hard via 0-1 knapsack; a polynomial-time greedy heuristic is proposed. A case study with 5 functions and 19 model/mode candidates achieves $34/month (97% cheaper than a feasible all-closed-API baseline) by mixing open-source APIs and one function requiring a closed API; break-even for on-prem GPUs occurs only above ~309 vision queries/hour or if API prices double.
AI.motivation: To optimize the portfolio of foundation models deployed across diverse TMC tasks by jointly selecting models, deployment modes, and hardware under budgetary and QoS constraints, thereby reducing total cost of ownership while ensuring performance and safety.
AI.method: Formulate as a mixed-integer program (MIP) that minimizes total cost of ownership (TCO) subject to per-function quality, latency, and safety constraints, over a shared GPU capacity. Prove NP-hardness via reduction from the 0-1 knapsack problem. Propose a polynomial-time greedy heuristic for practical deployment. Validate with a case study of five TMC functions and 19 candidate (model, mode) pairs.
AI.result: The FMDP yields a mixed portfolio with total cost of $34/month, achieving about 97% savings relative to the cheapest feasible all-closed-API baseline. Four functions are routed to open-source APIs; the fifth requires a closed API to meet its quality floor. Break-even analysis indicates on-premise GPU investment becomes cost-effective only when workload exceeds ~309 vision queries/hour or if API prices double.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that mixed deployment—leveraging open-source models where feasible and reserving closed APIs for unmet floors—substantially reduces TCO under shared hardware budgets. GPU investments are only justified under higher-than-threshold workloads or API pricing shifts, highlighting the value of portfolio-level optimization for TMCs.

title: Delving into the Temporal Challenges of Unified Video Protection Against Image-to-Video and Fine-Tuning-based Customization
comment: This work provides a basis for the ECCV 2026 LifeGenIP Challenge on Unlearnable Videos against Diffusion-based Customization. Challenge page: https://lifegenip.cc/competition. Evaluation code: https://github.com/tmllab/ECCV26_LifeGenIP_starting_kit. Project page: https://saythe17.github.io/TC-UAP/
summary: Recent diffusion-based video generation models have enabled high-quality personalized video customization through both tuning-based pipelines, which fine-tune a video diffusion model, and reference-based pipelines such as image-to-video generation. However, these capabilities raise serious concerns about personal privacy, identity ownership and intellectual property protection. Existing anti-customization works focus on protecting images, while protection for videos against both reference- and tuning-based customization remains largely underexplored. Protecting videos in this setting raises three challenges: (i) Image-level perturbations, optimized frame by frame, cannot survive temporal compression by 3D video VAE. (ii) A video-level perturbation optimized on a single video is vulnerable to temporal editing and fails to protect unseen videos. (iii) Temporally inconsistent perturbations are not robust to temporal attacks. To address these challenges, we propose Temporally Consistent Universal Adversarial Perturbations (TC-UAP), the first protection method against both reference- and tuning-based video customization. TC-UAP optimizes an identity-level multi-frame UAP over sliding windows from multiple videos, accounting for local temporal dependencies induced by temporal compression in video VAE and enabling a single perturbation to protect unseen videos of varying lengths. Moreover, we introduce intrinsic temporal modeling and an extrinsic surrogate temporal-attack loss, which make the perturbation temporally consistent and robust to unseen temporal attacks. Empirically, quantitative and qualitative results show that TC-UAP achieves the strongest identity protection compared with existing methods under both reference- and tuning-based video customization, and remains robust under multiple unseen temporal attacks.

AI.tldr: Proposes Temporally Consistent Universal Adversarial Perturbations (TC-UAP) to protect videos from both reference- and tuning-based diffusion-based customization by learning a multi-frame universal perturbation over sliding windows from multiple videos, accounting for temporal compression and ensuring temporal consistency; achieves strong identity protection and robustness against unseen temporal attacks.
AI.motivation: Protect video content against illicit personalization via diffusion models, addressing privacy, identity ownership, and IP concerns. Existing anti-customization methods focus on images and fail to generalize to videos, especially under temporal compression and editing.
AI.method: Introduce a multi-frame universal adversarial perturbation (UAP) learned over sliding windows from several videos, forming an identity-level perturbation. Incorporate intrinsic temporal modeling and an extrinsic surrogate temporal-attack loss to enforce temporal consistency and robustness to unseen temporal attacks.
