The perturbation is designed to survive temporal compression and generalize to unseen videos of varying lengths.
AI.result: Empirical results demonstrate TC-UAP provides the strongest identity protection compared with existing methods under both reference- and tuning-based video customization, and remains robust under multiple unseen temporal attacks, across diverse videos and lengths.
AI.conclusion: TC-UAP is the first protection method against both reference- and tuning-based video customization, achieving temporally consistent, robust protection for unseen videos of varying lengths despite temporal compression and attacks.

title: Safe Overtaking for Autonomous Racing Using Hierarchical Optimization and Learning-Based Control
summary: Autonomous racing overtaking requires balancing competitive performance with safety under nonlinear vehicle dynamics and real-time constraints. Model Predictive Control (MPC) combined with Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provides a principled mechanism for certifying forward invariance of a safe set. However, commonly used fixed-decay discrete-time CBF formulations can become overly conservative in interactive racing scenarios, limiting overtaking performance and requiring manual tuning across track conditions. This paper proposes a hierarchical overtaking framework that explicitly separates maneuver-level decision making from safety-certified trajectory control, reducing conservatism while preserving safety. A high-level Mixed-Integer Quadratic Program (MIQP) resolves the combinatorial passing-side selection problem by selecting a feasible overtaking topology, while a nonlinear Frenet-frame MPC enforces vehicle dynamics and safety through embedded discrete-time CBF constraints. This decomposition isolates the combinatorial complexity of maneuver selection from the continuous trajectory optimization. To further mitigate the sensitivity of fixed-decay barrier constraints, a reinforcement learning policy adapts the discrete-time CBF decay parameter online, enabling context-dependent modulation of safety margins without directly controlling vehicle inputs. Simulation and scaled-hardware experiments show that no single fixed decay parameter achieves uniformly strong performance across tracks, whereas the adaptive strategy attains the highest aggregate success rate and consistently strong safety--performance trade-offs without per-track tuning, improving robustness to environment variation while maintaining safety constraint satisfaction in nominal operation.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical control framework for autonomous racing overtaking that combines a high-level MIQP-based maneuver planner with a nonlinear Frenet-frame MPC and embedded discrete-time CBF safety constraints, augmented by a reinforcement learning policy to adapt the CBF decay online. This structure reduces conservatism from fixed-decay CBFs, while preserving safety and improving robustness and performance across varying tracks.
AI.motivation: To address the conservatism of fixed-decay discrete-time CBFs in interactive racing, which limits overtaking performance and requires manual tuning for different track conditions; and to achieve safe, high-performance, real-time operation through a decomposition of maneuver decision and trajectory optimization.
AI.method: 1) High-level MIQP selects the overtaking topology (which car passes where). 2) Nonlinear Frenet-frame MPC enforces dynamics and safety with embedded discrete-time CBF constraints, representing a continuous trajectory optimization with safety guarantees. 3) A reinforcement learning policy adjusts the discrete-time CBF decay parameter online to adapt safety margins to context without controlling inputs. 4) The overall hierarchy decouples combinatorial maneuver planning from continuous trajectory optimization.
AI.result: Simulations and scaled hardware experiments show that no single fixed CBF decay parameter achieves uniformly strong performance across tracks; the adaptive strategy yields the highest aggregate success rate and robust safety–performance trade-offs without per-track tuning, improving robustness to environment variation while ensuring nominal safety constraint satisfaction.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical separation of maneuver decision from safety-certified trajectory control, together with online adaptation of CBF decay via reinforcement learning, reduces conservatism and enhances performance and robustness in autonomous racing overtaking while maintaining safety constraints.

title: HEDGEHOG: Hierarchical Evaluation of Drug Generators Through Rigorous Filtration
comment: 29 pages (including References and Appendix sections), 8 tables, 7 figures, 2 supplementary files
summary: Generative molecular models can support early drug discovery by proposing new candidate compounds de novo. In practice, useful candidates must balance target-relevant activity, synthetic accessibility, physicochemical properties, and other multiparameter design constraints. However, metrics commonly used to evaluate molecular generators only weakly reflect whether the generated compounds are medicinally plausible and suitable for downstream computation. This can produce false positives in model evaluation, incorrect assumptions, and inefficient use of computational resources. We introduce HEDGEHOG, a unified six-stage filtration benchmark that is inspired by industrial hit identification workflows: (i) preprocessing; (ii) physicochemical descriptor screening; (iii) structural alerts and graph-sanity checks; (iv) synthesis feasibility; (v) docking and binding affinity estimation; and (vi) three-dimensional pose and interaction checks. We evaluate 23 molecular generators across three model classes under a standardized protocol. Across 230,000 generated molecules, only 0.65% of initial molecules survive all stages. Our results expose a central limitation of current molecular generators: molecules that appear acceptable under isolated criteria rarely satisfy medicinal chemistry, synthesis, docking, and 3D pose filters simultaneously.

AI.tldr: HEDGEHOG: a six-stage filtration benchmark for generative molecular models; across 230k generated molecules, only 0.65% survive all stages, revealing that current generators produce many misleading candidates when evaluated under realistic medicinal chemistry constraints.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between common generator evaluation metrics and real-world medicinal chemistry requirements (plausibility, synthetic feasibility, docking, and 3D interactions); reduce false positives and wasted computational effort in drug discovery pipelines.
AI.method: Six-stage pipeline: (i) preprocessing; (ii) physicochemical descriptor screening; (iii) structural alerts and graph-sanity checks; (iv) synthesis feasibility; (v) docking and binding affinity estimation; (vi) 3D pose and interaction checks. Evaluates 23 molecular generators across three model classes under a standardized protocol, across ~230k molecules.
AI.result: Only 0.65% of initial molecules survive all stages, indicating that molecules deemed acceptable by isolated criteria rarely meet multi-criteria medicinal chemistry, synthesis, docking, and 3D pose requirements.
AI.conclusion: Holistic, multi-stage benchmarking is essential for realistic evaluation of molecular generators. HEDGEHOG reveals a substantial gap between traditional metrics and practical viability, guiding future development to reduce false positives and computational waste.

title: Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable,Navigable, and Editable
summary: The capability of a modern AI agent depends not only on its foundation model but also on its harness, which constructs prompts, manages state, invokes tools, and coordinates execution. As models, APIs, environments, and requirements evolve, the harness must be continually modified. Before such a change can be made, a developer or coding agent must identify all code locations that implement the target behavior. This is difficult because production harnesses are large, tightly coupled, and behaviorally distributed, while modification requests describe what the system should do and repositories are organized by files and modules. Code search, repository indexing, and long-context processing ease inspection, but still leave this behavior-to-code mapping to be recovered by hand. Behavior localization is therefore a central bottleneck in harness evolution. We introduce the Harness Handbook, a behavior-centric representation synthesized automatically from a harness codebase via static analysis and LLM-assisted structuring, linking each behavior to its corresponding source. We also introduce Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD), which guides agents from high-level behaviors to relevant implementation details and verifies candidate locations against the current source. On diverse modification requests from two open-source harnesses, Handbook-Assisted planning improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality while using fewer planner tokens, with the largest gains on scattered sites, rarely executed paths, and cross-module interactions. Evolving complex agentic systems thus depends not only on generating edits, but also on determining where those edits should be made.

AI.tldr: Behavior-centric harness evolution through Harness Handbook and Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD) improves localization of edits and planning quality, reducing reliance on planner tokens.
AI.motivation: To overcome the bottleneck of mapping high-level modification requests to specific code locations in large, distributed, and tightly coupled harnesses where code is organized by files/modules rather than behavior.
AI.method: Introduce Harness Handbook, a behavior-centric representation automatically synthesized from a harness codebase using static analysis and LLM-assisted structuring; link each behavior to its source. Introduce BGPD to guide agents from high-level behaviors to relevant implementation details and verify candidate edits against the current source. Evaluate on modification requests from two open-source harnesses, comparing Handbook-Assisted planning to baselines.
AI.result: Handbook-Assisted planning improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality while using fewer planner tokens, with the largest gains on scattered sites, rarely executed paths, and cross-module interactions.
AI.conclusion: Evolving complex agentic systems requires not only generating edits but also determining where those edits should be made; behavior-centric representations and guided disclosure help locate and verify edits effectively.

title: Marker-free deformable registration and fusion for augmented reality-guided positive margin localization during tumor resection surgery
summary: Positive margins in head and neck oncologic surgery require mapping specimen-side pathology findings to the patient resection bed. This is challenging because pathologists identify the positive margin on slices of the resected, deformed specimen, while surgeons must relocate the corresponding site on the resection bed using only verbal descriptions and no visual guidance. We present a marker-free augmented reality (AR) workflow for mapping a margin label from a three-dimensional specimen scan to the resection bed. The method combines contour-constrained deformation, residual alignment to a depth scan, surface-based fusion to a head-mounted display, and target projection onto the reconstructed bed. Bead-suture correspondences estimate specimen deformation, whereas patient-to-display fusion does not require external fiducial markers. Following formative experiments, five residents and surgeons performed cadaveric cheek and scalp re-resection tasks under verbal guidance, verbal guidance with specimen examination, and AR guidance. Deformation target errors were $7.63 \pm 3.74$ mm for the cheek and $3.72 \pm 1.02$ mm for the scalp; residual specimen-to-bed distances were $2.43 \pm 2.15$ mm and $2.19 \pm 1.06$ mm, respectively. Fusion error did not differ significantly between marker-free and marker-based methods on either cadaver; overall marker-free fusion error was $2.15 \pm 0.87$ mm. End-to-end margin localization error decreased from $21.40 \pm 3.84$ mm with verbal guidance and $16.09 \pm 4.30$ mm with specimen examination to $6.19 \pm 1.79$ mm with AR guidance ($p < 0.001$). Online fusion required $5.23 \pm 0.34$ s. These results demonstrate effective marker-free AR guidance for positive-margin localization and support more precise tumor resection.

AI.tldr: Marker-free AR maps margins from a 3D specimen to the resection bed for head and neck cancer surgery, using bead-suture deformation estimation, depth-scAN residual alignment, and surface fusion to a headset. End-to-end margin localization improved to ~6.2 mm with AR vs ~21/16 mm with verbal guidance; online fusion ~5.2 s; validated in cadaveric cheek/scalp tasks with marker-free fusion matching marker-based methods.
AI.motivation: Accurate positive-margin localization is difficult because pathologists identify margins on a deformed specimen while surgeons must re-localize on the bed using verbal guidance. Marker-free AR aims to provide an intuitive, fiducial-free guidance workflow to improve precision and reduce reoperation risk.
AI.method: Contour-constrained deformation with bead-suture correspondences to estimate specimen deformation; residual alignment to a depth scan; surface-based fusion to a head-mounted display; target projection onto the reconstructed bed; marker-free patient-to-display fusion.
AI.result: Deformation target errors: cheek 7.63±3.74 mm; scalp 3.72±1.02 mm. Residual specimen-to-bed distances: cheek 2.43±2.15 mm; scalp 2.19±1.06 mm. Marker-free fusion error: 2.15±0.87 mm. End-to-end margin localization error: 21.40±3.84 mm (verbal) and 16.09±4.30 mm (specimen exam) reduced to 6.19±1.79 mm with AR (p<0.001). Online fusion time: 5.23±0.34 s.
AI.conclusion: Marker-free AR guidance enables effective positive-margin localization and supports more precise tumor resection, without external fiducials; feasible in a cadaveric validation and promising for clinical translation.

title: A Hybrid Sampling-Based Trajectory Planner with Game-Theoretic Guidance for Autonomous Racing
summary: Autonomous racing demands planning algorithms that balance vehicle dynamics at the limits of handling with strategic decision-making in competitive multi-agent scenarios. Game theory provides a mathematical framework for modeling these interactions, enabling interactive trajectory planning and strategic behaviors, such as blocking. However, directly solving full dynamic games online is computationally prohibitive and challenging to integrate into robust, high-frequency autonomous software stacks. This paper proposes a hybrid architecture that integrates game-theoretic reasoning into a sampling-based motion planner, combining strategic interactions with robust trajectory generation. Building upon an $α$-potential game formulation, we utilize an offline-learned potential function to capture multi-agent interactions. During online operation, a gradient-based optimization dynamically refines interaction parameters to generate an \textit{Interaction Reference Path}. This path serves as a dynamic cost bias within a high-frequency sampling planner. We evaluate our approach in a high-fidelity simulation environment on the Yas Marina Circuit. Qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our approach successfully induces defensive behaviors like blocking without carrying the computational burden of full dynamic game solvers.

AI.tldr: Hybrid game-theoretic sampling planner for autonomous racing using offline-learned α-potential interactions and online gradient refinement to generate an Interaction Reference Path, enabling defensive behaviors like blocking with real-time computation.
AI.motivation: Need to balance aggressive/defensive multi-agent strategies with real-time feasibility; full dynamic-game solvers are intractable for high-frequency autonomous racing stacks.
AI.method: Hybrid architecture: α-potential game formulation with offline-learned potential function to capture multi-agent interactions; online gradient-based optimization refines interaction parameters to produce an Interaction Reference Path; the path biases a high-frequency sampling-based planner as a dynamic cost.
AI.result: Qualitative and quantitative results in a high-fidelity Yas Marina Circuit simulation show the method induces defensive behaviors such as blocking and achieves these strategies without the computational burden of full dynamic game solvers.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective integration of game-theoretic reasoning into real-time motion planning, enabling strategic behavior while maintaining computational practicality.

title: SteinGate: Tail-Sensitive Safe Reinforcement Learning via Stein Discrepancy
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Safe reinforcement learning typically enforces safety by bounding expected cumulative costs, a criterion that often fails to detect rare but catastrophic tail events. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces SteinGate, a boundary-aware distributional safety certificate that replaces fragile tail fitting with a robust consistency check using Kernelized Stein Discrepancy while accounting for boundary atoms induced by clipped costs. SteinGate evaluates whether observed policy rollout costs remain consistent with a safe reference distribution, providing a non-parametric safety certificate. This certificate is used to dynamically adapt the learning regime: favoring reward-improving policy updates when rollouts remain consistent with the safe reference and switching to recovery behavior when the cost tail deviates. Experiments on continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate that SteinGate significantly reduces both the frequency and severity of constraint violations during training while maintaining competitive returns relative to state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: SteinGate provides a boundary-aware, non-parametric safety certificate for reinforcement learning that uses Kernelized Stein Discrepancy to detect tail-risk in rollout costs and adapt learning between safety-focused recovery and reward-improving updates, reducing constraint violations while preserving performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional safety via bounding expected cumulative costs often misses rare but catastrophic tail events. There is a need for a robust tail-risk detector that accounts for boundary effects due to clipped costs and avoids fragile tail fitting.
AI.method: SteinGate computes Kernelized Stein Discrepancy on observed rollout costs against a safe reference distribution, explicitly handling boundary atoms introduced by cost clipping. It serves as a non-parametric safety certificate that governs the learning regime: if rollouts are consistent with the safe reference, favor reward-improving updates; if not, switch to recovery behavior.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on continuous-control benchmarks shows SteinGate substantially reduces the frequency and severity of constraint violations during training while maintaining competitive returns relative to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: SteinGate delivers a robust, boundary-aware, non-parametric safety certificate for RL that improves tail safety during training and enables adaptive learning without sacrificing performance.

title: Theory-Level Autoformalization: From Isolated Statements to Unified Formal Knowledge Bases
summary: Autoformalization translates informal natural language into formal, machine-verifiable languages. While most work focuses on individual statements, real formalization efforts are inherently theory-level: they require an entire web of axioms, definitions, and lemmas before target theorems can even be stated. In this position paper, we argue for theory-level autoformalization: formalizing complete theories, including all their inter-dependencies, as structured libraries. We examine the significance of this shift, address alternative views, identify open challenges, and propose three promising paths forward. Our survey of autoformalization is available at https://github.com/marcusm117/Awesome-Autoformalization.

AI.tldr: Autoformalization should extend from individual statements to theory-level formalization by building complete, interdependent libraries of axioms, definitions, and lemmas; this position paper advocates for this shift and outlines significance, challenges, and three forward paths, with a survey link.
AI.motivation: Current autoformalization focuses on single statements, neglecting the theory-level dependencies needed for verifiable formalization; without library-level structure, target theorems cannot be properly stated.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis: argue for theory-level approach, discuss significance, compare with alternatives, identify open challenges, propose three paths forward; provide a community survey resource.
AI.result: A position paper proposing a shift to theory-level autoformalization and outlining challenges and three directions, to guide future work.
AI.conclusion: Theory-level autoformalization is necessary and promising for scalable, machine-verifiable formal knowledge; progress hinges on developing structured theory libraries and following the three proposed paths; survey link provided.

title: Audio-Text Cross-Attention with Psycholinguistic Support Features for Ambivalence/Hesitancy Recognition
summary: We present an audio-text system for the Ambivalence/Hesitancy Video Recognition Challenge of the 11th ABAW Competition. The method excludes visual frames and represents each video as overlapping 5-second windows aligned with transcript timestamps. Each window combines a 320-dimensional prosodic audio descriptor, a 768-dimensional emotion-oriented RoBERTa embedding, and 74 handcrafted features capturing uncertainty, hedging, and attitudinal conflict. Audio and text are fused via temporal cross-attention, while support features are injected prior to gated multiple-instance learning (MIL) pooling to modulate the window's importance. Predictions from five independently initialized models are averaged. On the labeled public development set, the ensemble achieved an average precision of 0.875 and a macro-F1 of 0.72. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Liga-de-IA-PUCPR/abaw-11-ah-challenge/.

AI.tldr: Audio-text only model for Ambivalence/Hesitancy recognition using overlapping 5s windows; combines prosodic features, RoBERTa embeddings, and 74 handcrafted hedging/uncertainty features; uses temporal cross-attention and gated MIL pooling with support features; ensemble of five models; AP 0.875 and macro-F1 0.72 on the development set; code released.
AI.motivation: Tackle ambivalence and hesitancy in speech by leveraging audio-text cues and transcript-aligned windows, avoiding reliance on visual data.
AI.method: Video is represented as overlapping 5-second windows aligned to transcript timestamps. Each window concatenates a 320-dimensional prosodic audio descriptor, a 768-dimensional emotion-oriented RoBERTa embedding, and 74 handcrafted features capturing uncertainty/hedging/attitudinal conflict. Audio and text are fused via temporal cross-attention; support features are injected before gated multiple-instance learning (MIL) pooling to modulate window importance. Predictions from five independently initialized models are averaged.
AI.result: On the labeled public development set, the ensemble achieves average precision 0.875 and macro-F1 0.72.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective audio-text fusion with cross-attention and MIL for ambivalence recognition; ensemble boosts robustness; code is publicly available for reproducibility.

title: Min-Max Regret Task Allocation and Planning of Heterogeneous Multi-Robot System in Partially Known Environments
summary: Efficient task allocation for large-scale Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems (HMRS) is critical, yet dealing with complex temporal logic tasks in partially known environment (PKE) remains a computational bottleneck. Existing approaches often struggle to balance exploring uncertain regions and exploiting known resources, while also suffering from exponential computational complexity. To address these issues, this paper presents a robust planning framework that simultaneously handles high-level logical constraints and environmental uncertainty without sacrificing scalability. We formulate the problem as a min-max regret optimization, proposing a Region-Binding Atomic Proposition (RbAP) to capture resource uncertainty within the automaton structure. To solve this, we propose the Extended Planning Decision Tree (E-PDT) equipped with a novel Regret-based Branch-and-Bound (BnB) strategy. Unlike traditional methods that rely on prior probabilities or worst-case analysis, our approach dynamically prunes suboptimal policies, effectively balancing the need for information gathering (exploration) and task completion (exploitation). Theoretical analysis confirms the feasibility and completeness of our approach. Extensive numerical and physical experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves near-linear scalability with respect to the number of robots and types, significantly outperforming MILP-based baselines in both solution quality and computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: A scalable robust planning framework for large-scale heterogeneous multi-robot systems under partial knowledge, using min-max regret optimization with Region-Binding Atomic Propositions and an Extended Planning Decision Tree, achieving near-linear scalability and outperforming MILP baselines in both quality and speed, with theoretical guarantees of feasibility and completeness.
AI.motivation: Address the computational bottleneck of handling high-level temporal logic tasks in partially known environments for large HMRS, by balancing exploration and exploitation while maintaining scalability.
AI.method: Formulate the problem as a min-max regret optimization. Introduce Region-Binding Atomic Proposition (RbAP) to encode resource uncertainty within the automaton. Develop Extended Planning Decision Tree (E-PDT) with a Regret-based Branch-and-Bound (BnB) strategy that prunes suboptimal policies dynamically, avoiding reliance on prior probabilities or worst-case analyses.
AI.result: The approach achieves near-linear scalability with respect to the number of robots and types and significantly outperforms MILP-based baselines in solution quality and computational efficiency. Theoretical analysis confirms feasibility and completeness, with extensive numerical and physical experiments supporting the claims.
AI.conclusion: A robust, scalable planning framework for HMRS under uncertain environments that effectively integrates high-level logical constraints with environmental uncertainty, offering strong theoretical guarantees and practical performance advantages over traditional MILP approaches.

title: Concurrent Image Understanding and Generation: Self-Correcting Coupled Markov Jump Processes
summary: Human cognition does not separate understanding and generation. A teacher at a whiteboard speaks and draws $\textit{together}$, each modality reshapes the other. In this paper, we bring this coupled loop to artificial systems. Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) are ideally suited to this task, yet existing samplers either decode text and image interleavedly or independently update them in parallel branches that share only previous-step history, but not the other modality's latest decisions $\textit{within}$ the same step; combined with MDMs' inability to remask, cross-modal contradictions are neither detected nor repaired. We introduce $\textbf{Self-Correcting Coupled Markov Jump Processes (SC-CMJP)}$, a framework in which one modality's transition rates are functionals of the other modality's confidence score, as weighted by cross-modal attention. Furthermore, a remasking jump retracts commitments the moment cross-modal evidence turns against them. In conjunction with SC-CMJP, we introduce $\texttt{CO}_\texttt{2}\texttt{Jump}$ (Self-$\underline{\text{CO}}$rrecting $\underline{\text{CO}}$upled $\underline{\text{Jump}}$), a novel training-free single-pass sampler for joint multimodal geneneration. For training and evaluation purposes, we have created and will release three large-scale joint multimodal generation corpora: $\text{JEdit-1M}$, $\text{JMaze-200K}$, $\text{JNono-200K}$, with matching in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks. $\texttt{CO}_\texttt{2}\texttt{Jump}$ achieves best joint performance for image understanding and editing as well as visual reasoning (maze and nonogram solving). The performance of the sampler scales monotonically with the number of denoising steps, evidence that the benefits of cross-modal coupling $\textit{compound}$ across the trajectory. Project page: https://coupled-jump.github.io

AI.tldr: Introduces a self-correcting, coupled diffusion framework for joint multimodal generation and a training-free single-pass sampler (CO2Jump) that uses cross-modal attention and remasking to repair contradictions.
AI.motivation: Current diffusion samplers either process text and image separately or in parallel without incorporating the latest decisions from the other modality, leading to cross-modal inconsistencies that are not detected or repaired.
AI.method: Propose Self-Correcting Coupled Markov Jump Processes (SC-CMJP) where one modality’s transition rates are functionals of the other’s confidence via cross-modal attention, plus a remasking jump that retracts commitments when cross-modal evidence flips. Introduce CO2Jump, a training-free single-pass joint multimodal sampler. Build three large corpora (JEdit-1M, JMaze-200K, JNono-200K) for evaluation.
AI.result: CO2Jump achieves state-of-the-art joint performance for image understanding/editing and visual reasoning. Performance improves with more denoising steps, indicating benefits compound across the coupled trajectory. The method is training-free and scalable.
AI.conclusion: Coupled, self-correcting diffusion dynamics with remasking enable more coherent and repairable joint multimodal generation. CO2Jump offers an efficient, training-free solution for joint generation, with strong empirical gains on new multimodal datasets.

title: EZSMT Version 3, Matured
comment: Under consideration in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP)
summary: Constraint Answer Set Programming (CASP) is a hybrid reasoning paradigm that combines Answer Set Programming (ASP) with Constraint Processing and Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT), enabling powerful declarative encodings of complex combinatorial search problems. This paper presents the design and implementation of EZSMTV3, an extensible SMT-based CASP framework that advances the translational approach to CASP solving. Building upon the foundation of the EZSMT+ system, EZSMTV3 introduces a more expressive input language, supports optimization via weak constraints, and offers foundations for streamlined integration of new constraint types. Rather than implementing custom search procedures, EZSMTV3 leverages state-of-the-art SMT solvers, such as CVC5, YICES, and Z3 to perform reasoning. The paper provides benchmarking results comparing EZSMTV3 with its CASP peers such as CLINGCON, CLINGO[DL], and CLINGO[LP], while showcasing its ability to handle mixed-domain constraints involving both integers and reals. The system provides a robust platform for future extensions and theoretical exploration within the CASP domain.

AI.tldr: EZSMTV3 is an extensible SMT-based CASP framework that extends EZSMT+ with a richer input language, weak-constraint optimization, and SMT-solver reasoning, enabling mixed-integer/real constraints without custom search procedures.
AI.motivation: To advance scalable, declarative CASP solving by leveraging mature SMT solvers and creating a flexible foundation for integrating new constraint types, thereby bridging ASP with constraint processing in a practical, extensible system.
AI.method: Design and implement EZSMTV3 on the translational CASP approach, expanding the input language, incorporating weak constraints for optimization, and enabling seamless use of SMT backends (CVC5, YICES, Z3) instead of bespoke search procedures, with EZSMT+ as its precursor.
AI.result: Benchmarking against CASP peers (CLINGCON, CLINGO[DL], CLINGO[LP]) shows competitive performance and demonstrates the system’s ability to handle mixed-domain (integers and reals) constraints, underscoring its practicality and extensibility.
AI.conclusion: EZSMTV3 provides a robust, extensible platform for future CASP research and development, validating the translational approach and offering a flexible path for incorporating additional constraint types and SMT backends.

title: Detector Confidence Signals Presence Rather Than Occlusion in Cluttered Manipulation
summary: Occlude a named object until about an eighth of it remains visible, and an open-vocabulary detector's confidence that the object is present barely changes; as the clutter around it grows the confidence can even rise. On real video the detector still reports the object present in 99% of occluded frames, on another instance of the same category. This matters because that confidence is widely read as a visibility signal, used to threshold detections, evaluate open-vocabulary detectors, ground language, retrieve instances, and gate active perception. We audit whether it reflects occlusion by pairing every view with a geometry-segmentation oracle that gives detector-free ground-truth visibility. As true visibility falls from every scene to one in eight, the confidence stays nearly constant and uncorrelated with visibility, and the detector reports the target present in about nine of ten scenes, firing on same-category distractors: it signals that the category is present somewhere, not that the specific target is visible. The failure holds across three detectors (Grounding DINO, OWLv2, and Segment Anything Model 3), nine object categories, two simulators with different renderers and object sets, built and natural occlusion, and real video. Two consequences follow: a confidence-based metric understates the value of resolving occlusion by about ten times (8 against 88 points in our active-perception setting), and a confidence-based gate fires exactly when the object is hidden. No single-view signal we tried, including a realizable localization check, flags the occlusion, because the occluders sit where the target is. We connect the effect to detector miscalibration and object hallucination, release the controlled benchmark, and recommend target-grounded signals for gating and evaluation.

AI.tldr: Open-vocabulary detectors overreact to occlusion: confidence stays high while true visibility collapses, miscalibrating signals and gating; a grounded, target-specific signal is needed for evaluation and active perception.
AI.motivation: To determine whether detector confidence serves as a reliable visibility proxy under occlusion and to quantify its impact on gating, evaluation, and downstream tasks.
AI.method: Audit detector confidence by pairing each view with a geometry-segmentation oracle providing ground-truth visibility; evaluate three detectors (Grounding DINO, OWLv2, SAM3) across nine categories, two simulators with varied renderers/occluders, built and natural occlusion, and real video; analyze correlation between confidence and true visibility, test single-view signals, and assess consequences for active perception and evaluation.
AI.result: Detector confidence remains nearly constant as true visibility declines to one-eighth; on real video detectors report the target present in ~99% of occluded frames and in a different instance of the same category; detectors often fire on same-category distractors, signaling presence of the category rather than the specific target visibility; this pattern holds across all three detectors, nine categories, two simulators, and both synthetic and real occlusions; consequence: confidence-based metrics undervalue the benefit of resolving occlusion by ~10x and gate on occlusion; no single-view signal flags occlusion; miscalibration and object hallucination are implicated; a controlled benchmark is released and target-grounded signals are recommended for gating and evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights that confidence-based signals are unreliable proxies for visibility under occlusion; it advocates for target-grounded signals for gating and evaluation and provides a controlled benchmark to facilitate this shift.

title: WNOJ-LIO: A White-Noise-on-Jerk Motion-Prior EKF for High-Dynamic LiDAR-IMU Fusion
summary:
LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) is a key component of autonomous navigation, but high-dynamic driving exposes two coupled challenges: intra-scan motion distortion and vibration-contaminated inertial measurements. Most real-time LiDAR-inertial pipelines propagate the system state by integrating raw IMU measurements and then use the propagated trajectory for point cloud de-distortion, thereby propagating inertial noise into both the corrected scan and the subsequent scan-to-map registration. This paper presents WNOJ-LIO, a LiDAR-IMU fusion framework based on a White-Noise-on-Jerk (WNOJ) Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). WNOJ-LIO employs a decoupled WNOJ prior on $\R^3 \times \SO(3)$ for state prediction and treats the IMU as a high-frequency measurement source rather than the driver of state propagation. The resulting posterior state history is then used for LiDAR scan de-distortion and subsequent point-to-plane LiDAR updates. The decoupled process model enables closed-form covariance propagation, thereby bridging the gap between batch WNOJ Gaussian process (GP) trajectory priors and recursive filtering.
  Simulation results demonstrate improvements in acceleration and angular-velocity denoising, scan de-distortion, and localization accuracy over a FAST-LIO-style baseline.
  Real-world experiments were conducted using an autonomous racing car on four driving segments with maximum speeds ranging from 53 to 208~km/h, covering a wide range of vehicle vibration levels. The experiments further validate the proposed method and provide a comprehensive evaluation of its performance in estimating acceleration, angular velocity, body-frame linear velocity, attitude, and position under highly dynamic driving. The source code of WNOJ-LIO is publicly available at https://github.com/LvJohny/wnoj-ekf-lio.git.

AI.tldr: Proposes WNOJ-LIO: a LiDAR-IMU fusion framework using a decoupled White-Noise-on-Jerk prior EKF for state prediction, with IMU as a measurement source. It yields posteriors used for scan de-distortion and LiDAR updates, and closes the gap between batch GP priors and recursive filtering. Validated in simulations and real-world high-speed driving with open-source code.
AI.motivation: High-dynamic driving causes intra-scan motion distortion and vibration-contaminated inertial measurements. Traditional real-time LIO pipelines propagate inertial noise into scans and map updates, degrading accuracy.
AI.method: Use a decoupled WNOJ prior on R^3 × SO(3) for state prediction within an EKF; treat the IMU as a high-frequency measurement source rather than the state driver; propagate closed-form covariance; recover a posterior trajectory for LiDAR de-distortion and subsequent point-to-plane updates; bridge batch WNOJ GP priors with recursive filtering.
AI.result: Simulation shows improved acceleration and angular-velocity denoising, scan de-distortion, and localization accuracy over a FAST-LIO-style baseline. Real-world tests on an autonomous racing car (53–208 km/h) confirm robustness across high dynamics, evaluating acceleration, angular velocity, body-frame velocity, attitude, and position. Source code released at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: The decoupled WNOJ EKF-based LIO improves robustness to high-dynamics, enhances de-distortion and localization, and effectively bridges GP trajectory priors with real-time filtering; the approach is validated both in simulation and real driving, with open-source implementation.

title: EMAGN: Efficient Multi-Attention Graph Network via Learned Clustering for Scalable Traffic Forecasting
summary: Traffic forecasting is highly challenging due to complex and nonlinear spatial and temporal dependencies. Self-attention mechanisms have been widely adopted to model dynamic and long-range dependencies, achieving state-of-the-art performance, but suffer from limited scalability due to quadratic computational and memory complexity. To address this, we propose an Efficient Multi-Attention Graph Network (EMAGN) that linearises the spatial attention mechanism itself, inspired by the theory of fast high-dimensional Gaussian filtering. Two learned clustering matrices C_k and C_v adaptively group key and value vectors into M super-clusters, reducing complexity from O(N^2 d) to O(NMd) without sacrificing the flexibility of attention for dynamic dependency modelling. Experimental results on PEMS-BAY and METR-LA show that EMAGN achieves accuracy within 2.7-3.2% MAE of full-attention GMAN while reducing training time by 32%, inference time by 38%, and GPU memory by 58%. Critically, at K=16 attention heads, full-attention GMAN runs out of memory on a standard 11 GB GPU entirely while EMAGN continues to operate, demonstrating a categorical expansion of feasible model configurations. EMAGN also surpasses Linformer and Performer in both accuracy and efficiency within the same backbone, owing to its traffic-network-aware adaptive clustering.

AI.tldr: Efficient, scalable multi-attention graph network (EMAGN) for traffic forecasting that linearizes spatial attention via adaptive clustering, achieving near full-attention accuracy with substantial efficiency gains.
AI.motivation: Reduce the quadratic complexity of spatial attention in traffic forecasting models to enable scalable modeling of dynamic long-range dependencies while preserving expressive power.
AI.method: Introduce EMAGN with two learned clustering matrices C_k and C_v to group key and value vectors into M super-clusters, yielding complexity O(NMd) from O(N^2d); evaluate on PEMS-BAY and METR-LA within the GMAN backbone; compare against full-attention GMAN, Linformer, and Performer.
AI.result: EMAGN achieves MAE within 2.7–3.2 percentage points of full-attention GMAN; reduces training time by 32%, inference time by 38%, and GPU memory by 58%; at K=16 heads, full-attention GMAN runs out of memory on 11 GB GPU while EMAGN remains feasible; also surpasses Linformer and Performer in both accuracy and efficiency within the same backbone.
AI.conclusion: A traffic-network-aware, adaptive clustering–based linearized attention approach enables scalable, memory-efficient traffic forecasting with minimal loss in accuracy compared with full-attention models, expanding feasible model configurations and outperforming generic linear-attention baselines.

title: Set-shifting Behavioral Test for Harnessed Agents
summary: What happens to an LLM agent's tool choice when the reliable tool silently changes within an ongoing session? We borrow set-shifting from cognitive psychology to study how well agents adapt to hidden reliability shifts. Our benchmark mounts tool-skill libraries with redundancies, where many tools solve the same task but differ in hidden reliability. In our evaluation framework, a branched schedule shifts the reliable tool group at hidden boundaries and pairs every shift with a no-shift control. We find that agents, by default, settle on a small recurring routine within a few turns of each boundary, with call shares concentrating on a few discrete values after each reliability shift. We score the set-shifting accuracy for each agent trajectory: the joint probability of routing to the target tool group in every post-shift window. We test open-weight LLMs in an open-source agentic harness and find qualitatively distinct failure modes across the same set of routines. We also find that set framing, how the toolset presents the alternatives as competing or complementary, shifts the routing dynamics.

AI.tldr: LLM agents adapt their tool choices when hidden tool reliability changes; agents converge to recurring routines after shifts, with tool-use concentration; framing affects routing dynamics; open-weight models show varied failure modes.
AI.motivation: Assess robustness of tool use under covert reliability shifts, and understand adaptation and failure modes in agentic tool routing.
AI.method: Create a benchmark with redundant tool libraries and a branched schedule that changes the reliable tool group at hidden boundaries; compare post-shift windows with no-shift controls; measure joint probability of selecting the target tool group; evaluate open-weight LLMs in an open-source agent harness; vary set framing (competing vs complementary) to study routing dynamics.
AI.result: Agents rapidly settle into a small recurring routine after each boundary; call shares concentrate on a few discrete tools post-shift; the set-shifting accuracy is defined as the probability of choosing the target tool group in post-shift windows; open-weight LLMs exhibit qualitatively distinct failure modes across routines; set framing shifts routing dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Reliability shifts induce rapid, low-diversity adaptation in tool-use; presentation of the toolset (framing) can modulate routing decisions; findings inform robust tool-usage design and benchmarking for dynamic reliability.

title: DiffGI: Differentiable Geometry Images for High-Fidelity Thin-Shell 3D Generation
summary: Existing 3D generative models predominantly rely on implicit volumetric representations, which enforce watertight topology and struggle to represent thin-shell and non-manifold geometries such as garments. Geometry image-based approaches offer a surface-centric alternative, but existing methods rely on discrete binary occupancy maps whose resolution-dependent boundary encoding causes staircase artifacts and information loss upon downsampling, while surface reconstruction remains a non-differentiable post-processing step disconnected from the learning pipeline. To address this, we propose Differentiable Geometry Image (DiffGI), an end-to-end 3D-to-2D mapping framework that seamlessly integrates surface representation and geometric optimization. DiffGI replaces binary maps with a continuous 2D Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF), which encodes boundary position at subpixel precision within a fixed grid resolution, eliminating resolution-dependent staircase artifacts even under aggressive downsampling. Building on this continuous field, we introduce a differentiable Marching Squares algorithm based on analytical linear interpolation, allowing gradients from 3D surface losses to propagate back to the 2D latent space. Leveraging this differentiable pipeline, we train a DiffGI-VAE augmented with a geometry-aware normal rendering loss to compress complex 3D surfaces into an ultra-compact 32X32 latent space, and instantiate a transformer-based latent diffusion model with a flow-matching objective on top of this space for conditional 3D generation. Extensive experiments on garment and object datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior reconstruction fidelity and boundary precision compared to prior geometry-image and voxel-based approaches, while requiring significantly fewer computational resources.

AI.tldr: Introduces Differentiable Geometry Image (DiffGI): a differentiable 3D-to-2D geometry framework using a continuous 2D TSDF and differentiable Marching Squares to enable end-to-end geometry learning; achieves compact 32x32 latent representations via DiffGI-VAE and transformer-based latent diffusion for conditional 3D generation, with superior boundary precision and efficiency on garments and objects.
AI.motivation: Current 3D generative models rely on implicit watertight representations and discrete geometry-image occupancy maps, which fail for thin-shell, non-manifold geometries and produce boundary artifacts; existing surface extraction is non-differentiable and decoupled from learning.
AI.method: Replace binary occupancy with a fixed-grid 2D Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) to encode boundary with subpixel precision; implement differentiable Marching Squares via analytical linear interpolation to backpropagate surface losses into the 2D latent space; train a DiffGI-VAE with a geometry-aware normal rendering loss to obtain a compact 32x32 latent; stack a transformer-based latent diffusion model with a flow-matching objective for conditional 3D generation.
AI.result: Experiments on garment and object datasets show higher reconstruction fidelity and sharper boundary precision than prior geometry-image and voxel methods, while consuming significantly less computational resources.
AI.conclusion: DiffGI provides a unified, end-to-end differentiable geometry-image pipeline that overcomes boundary artifacts and rigidity of occupancy-based methods, enabling compact latent representations and effective conditional 3D generation for complex, non-watertight surfaces.

title: Ego-Dynamics-Augmented World Model for Autonomous Driving with Zero-Shot Cross-Chassis Adaptation
summary: World model (WM)-based reinforcement learning enables sample-efficient end-to-end autonomous driving learning by imagining long-horizon trajectories in latent space. However, most driving WMs operate on bird's-eye-view (BEV) representations that are inherently egocentric: the transition between consecutive frames entangles the ego vehicle's own motion with scene dynamics. As a result, the WM devotes significant capacity to recovering ego-motion from warped observations, at the cost of scene modeling fidelity and imagination accuracy. This work proposes DynaDreamer, a dynamics-augmented Dreamer-style reinforcement learning method to address this problem by augmenting the WM with an explicit ego-dynamics prior. A physics-informed ego-dynamics encoder-decoder extracts the ego-state history into a compact and identifiable context, which modulates a causal Transformer WM to condition both its prior and posterior latents. During imagination, the ego-dynamics predictor propagates this context forward to keep the ego-dynamics prior synchronized with the rollout. An information-theoretic analysis shows that conditioning on this context reduces both the predictive entropy of the observation transition and the prior--posterior Kullback--Leibler divergence, confining the WM's modeling burden to the scene dynamics beyond ego-motion. An additional benefit is zero-shot cross-chassis adaptation: the ego-dynamics context depends on identifiable chassis parameters, so that a vehicle with previously unseen dynamic characteristics can adapt the WM to the new chassis without retraining. Experiments demonstrate that DynaDreamer improves task success rates over the strongest baseline by 28% and 61% in urban and highway driving scenarios, respectively, with the advantage rising to 73% when extrapolating to unseen chassis.

AI.tldr: DynaDreamer augments Dreamer-style WMs with an explicit ego-dynamics prior to separate ego-motion from scene dynamics, improving imagination fidelity and enabling zero-shot cross-chassis adaptation; yields substantial gains (urban +28%, highway +61%; unseen chassis up to +73%).
AI.motivation: Egocentric BEV-based world models entangle ego-motion with scene dynamics, wasting capacity on ego-motion recovery and limiting scene modeling fidelity; disentangling ego-dynamics should improve planning and allow cross-chassis adaptation.
AI.method: Introduce a physics-informed ego-dynamics encoder–decoder to extract the ego-state history; condition a causal Transformer-based WM's priors and posteriors on this context; during imagination, propagate the ego-dynamics context with an ego-dynamics predictor; provide information-theoretic justification that conditioning reduces predictive entropy and prior–posterior KL divergence; enables zero-shot cross-chassis adaptation via chassis-parameter–dependent context.
AI.result: Empirical gains: +28% task success in urban driving, +61% in highway driving; up to +73% on unseen chassis; demonstrates improved modeling efficiency and adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling ego-motion via an ego-dynamics prior confines the WM’s burden to scene dynamics, improving imagination fidelity and enabling cross-chassis adaptation without retraining.

title: Reassessing Muon for Matrix Factorization
summary: Muon has recently emerged as a strong optimizer for large-scale deep learning, where it reshapes gradient updates through approximate orthogonalization and has been reported to outperform Adam and AdamW in large language model training. Its empirical success has motivated a growing body of theoretical work that interprets Muon as steepest descent under the spectral norm. Yet it remains unclear which of Muon's advantages stem from its update rule itself and which are artifacts of the scale, architecture, and data of modern deep networks. In this work, we isolate the optimizer from these confounding factors by studying Muon on a simple, well-understood, and spectrally structured problem: low-rank matrix factorization. Through a controlled comparison against carefully tuned adaptive baselines, we find that Muon does not consistently outperform AdamW in this setting and that several previously reported advantages are sensitive to hyperparameter choices. Our results provide a more nuanced picture of when spectrum-aware orthogonalization is beneficial and argue for evaluating modern optimizers on controlled problems in addition to end-to-end benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Muon's advantages over AdamW do not robustly transfer to a controlled, spectrally structured task; hyperparameter sensitivity suggests limited generality of spectrum-aware orthogonalization.
AI.motivation: To dissociate optimizer-specific effects from scale, architecture, and data by testing Muon on a simple, well-understood problem with spectral structure—low-rank factorization.
AI.method: Controlled experiments comparing Muon to carefully tuned adaptive baselines (e.g., AdamW) on low-rank matrix factorization with a spectrally structured setting.
AI.result: Muon does not consistently outperform AdamW on this setting; several claimed benefits are sensitive to hyperparameters.
AI.conclusion: Spectrum-aware orthogonalization offers nuanced, task-dependent gains; evaluators should use controlled problems in addition to end-to-end benchmarks to assess modern optimizers.

title: LAPO: Leave-One-Turn Attribution for Self-Generated Process Rewards in Multi-Turn Search Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning for multi-turn search reasoning typically relies on terminal outcome rewards, which cannot distinguish useful, redundant, and harmful intermediate interactions. We propose LAPO, a self-generated process-supervision method based on backward leave-one-turn attribution. For each search turn, LAPO replaces the turn and its retrieval observation with a fixed [DELETE] placeholder and measures the resulting change in the current policy's mean log-likelihood of the gold answer. This Answer-Likelihood Gain estimates the turn's contribution while preserving all downstream interactions, allowing early evidence to be evaluated in the complete reasoning context. LAPO further applies sign-consistency gating, retaining only normalized process advantages whose directions agree with their raw attribution scores. The method requires no additional reward model, teacher, verifier, or LLM-as-a-Judge. Across seven knowledge-intensive question-answering datasets with local retrieval, LAPO achieves an average exact-match score of 0.326, outperforming the strongest step-reward baseline, IGPO, by 0.053. Ablations show complementary benefits from backward attribution and sign-consistency gating, demonstrating that policy-derived retrospective attribution can provide effective process supervision for multi-turn search agents.

AI.tldr: LAPO introduces backward leave-one-turn attribution to provide process supervision for multi-turn search reasoning. It measures the impact of deleting a turn on the policy's likelihood of the gold answer, plus sign-consistency gating, without extra reward models. It outperforms step-reward baselines (IGPO) on seven QA datasets with local retrieval (EM 0.326, +0.053).
AI.motivation: Terminal rewards in multi-turn reasoning cannot distinguish useful, redundant, or harmful intermediate steps; there is a need for retrospective, policy-derived supervision to credit or blame intermediate turns within the full reasoning context.
AI.method: For each turn, replace the turn and its retrieval observation with a [DELETE] placeholder and compute the resulting change in the policy's mean log-likelihood of the gold answer (Answer-Likelihood Gain). This retroactively attributes turn-level contribution while preserving downstream interactions. Apply sign-consistency gating to retain only normalized process advantages aligned with raw attribution. No extra reward model, teacher, verifier, or LLM judge is required.
AI.result: LAPO achieves an average exact-match score of 0.326 across seven knowledge-intensive QA datasets with local retrieval, outperforming IGPO (the strongest step-reward baseline) by 0.053. Ablations show that backward attribution and sign-consistency gating contribute complementary benefits.
AI.conclusion: Policy-derived retrospective attribution can provide effective process supervision for multi-turn search agents, enabling improved decision-making without external evaluators or reward models.

title: RoughNet: Mapping Arctic Sea Ice Roughness Using Diffusion-Based Super-Resolution of Satellite Imagery
summary: Accurate estimation of landfast sea ice roughness is critical for climate modeling and safe Arctic over-ice travel, yet existing approaches rely on costly airborne surveys or sparse in-situ measurements, limiting spatial coverage and operational scalability. Here we show that high-resolution sea ice topography can be reconstructed directly from optical satellite imagery using a conditional diffusion framework. Our approach, RoughNet, learns to map 10 m Sentinel-2 multispectral images to locally normalized 1 m surface elevation residual fields, enabling fine-scale roughness characterization from widely available satellite data. Trained on airborne LiDAR data from two Arctic regions and evaluated on an unseen third Arctic region, the model generalizes across diverse ice conditions and partially reproduces small-scale topographic structure. The best-performing model achieves an out-of-domain root mean squared error of 9 cm while preserving the statistical and spectral properties of the underlying roughness field. These results demonstrate that generative diffusion models can recover physically meaningful surface structure from optical imagery alone, providing a scalable pathway for high-resolution sea ice mapping and roughness estimation in data-sparse environments.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based model RoughNet maps Sentinel-2 imagery to high-resolution sea-ice roughness, achieving 9 cm RMSE on an unseen Arctic region, enabling scalable mapping.
AI.motivation: Need for large-area, high-resolution roughness maps without costly airborne surveys in data-sparse Arctic regions.
AI.method: Conditional diffusion framework that outputs locally normalized 1 m elevation residuals from 10 m multispectral inputs; trained on airborne LiDAR data from two Arctic regions and evaluated on an unseen third region to test cross-region generalization; emphasizes preserving roughness statistics and spectral properties.
AI.result: Best-performing model achieves out-of-domain RMSE of 9 cm and maintains statistical/spectral characteristics of the roughness field; partially recovers small-scale topography.
AI.conclusion: Generative diffusion approaches can recover physically meaningful surface structure from optical data, enabling scalable, high-resolution sea-ice roughness mapping in data-sparse environments.

title: Generalizable VLA Finetuning via Representation Anchoring and Language-Action Alignment
summary: Finetuning a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) on robot demonstrations via behavior cloning (BC) has become the standard recipe for vision-language-action (VLA) policies. However, BC finetuning progressively overwrites the pretrained representations that support visual and semantic generalization. Co-training on web image-text data, a common remedy, does not prevent this; it applies language and action losses to separate observations, leaving VLAs with language-action misalignment that standard manipulation benchmarks do not expose. We propose Anchor-Align, which augments BC with two objectives: Vision-Language Anchoring distills layer-wise representations from a frozen VLM copy to prevent this drift, while Language-Action Alignment converts each action target into a discrete motion-direction label and jointly trains language and action prediction on the same robot observation. On a physical xArm7 robot, across two widely used VLA architectures, Anchor-Align improves real-robot success on both (28% to 54% and 37% to 60%). At scale in simulation, we demonstrate consistent improvements on OOD perturbations, perceptual robustness, and long-horizon control across LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN, respectively, suggesting that preserving pretrained representations and effective action learning are not fundamentally at odds. Project page: anchoralignvla.github.io

AI.tldr: Anchor-Align improves vision-language-action policies by preserving pretrained VLM representations and aligning language with discrete action labels, yielding substantial real-robot and simulation gains across multiple architectures and platforms.
AI.motivation: Standard BC fine-tuning on VLA policies overwrites pretrained visual/semantic representations, harming generalization. Co-training with web data alone does not fix language-action misalignment, which is not exposed by standard benchmarks.
AI.method: Two objectives: (1) Vision-Language Anchoring — distill layer-wise representations from a frozen VLM copy to prevent representation drift; (2) Language-Action Alignment — convert action targets into discrete motion-direction labels and jointly train language and action predictions on the same robot observation.
AI.result: Real-robot: improved success on two VLA architectures (e.g., from 28% to 54% and 37% to 60%). Simulation at scale shows robust improvements on OOD perturbations, perceptual robustness, and long-horizon control across LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN.
AI.conclusion: Preserving pretrained representations and learning effective actions are compatible, enabling significant gains in both real and simulated environments; Anchor-Align offers a practical approach to mitigate BC drift and misalignment in VLA policies. Project page: anchoralignvla.github.io

title: Deconstructing Actor-Critic: A Large-scale Empirical Study of Design Components for Practitioners
summary: Reinforcement learning is increasingly being considered for controlling real-world systems, from fusion plasma and autonomous vehicles to drug discovery and drinking water treatment, where reliability is essential and tuning budgets are limited. Actor-critic algorithms share a set of design decisions, such as how the policy is updated, how it represents the distribution over actions, how its gradient is estimated, and how often it is updated relative to the value estimator. Using a control task derived from a real water treatment plant, we analyze over 33,000 experiments to determine how these components affect variability across runs and sensitivity to hyperparameters. Common defaults, such as Gaussian action distributions with pathwise gradient estimators, are among the least reliable configurations, whereas bounded distributions with adaptive update schedules remain robust across a wide range of settings. These findings offer empirical guidance to practitioners across scientific and engineering domains for understanding and making component-level decisions when adapting actor-critic methods to new real-world control settings.

AI.tldr: Bounded action distributions with adaptive update schedules yield robust performance in actor-critic control across real-world tasks; common defaults like Gaussian actions with pathwise gradients are fragile and sensitive to hyperparameters.
AI.motivation: Assess how architectural and training choices in actor-critic algorithms affect reproducibility and hyperparameter sensitivity in real-world control tasks.
AI.method: Empirical study on a control task derived from a real water treatment plant, evaluating over 33,000 experiments by varying components: policy update method, action distribution, gradient estimator, and update frequency relative to the value estimator.
AI.result: Bounded action distributions with adaptive update schedules improve robustness across diverse settings; Gaussian action distributions with pathwise gradient estimators are among the least reliable defaults; many standard choices cause high variability and sensitivity to hyperparameters.
AI.conclusion: Provide practical guidance for practitioners to select component designs when adapting actor-critic methods to real-world control problems, highlighting robustness of bounded distributions and adaptive update schedules and cautioning against common defaults.

title: How Far Can Root Cause Analysis Go on Real-World Telemetry Data?
summary: Identifying root causes in production microservice failures requires reasoning over large-scale, multimodal telemetry spanning metrics, logs, and traces, a problem that has proved resistant to both classical and LLM-based approaches. The OpenRCA dataset exemplifies these challenges: it is large-scale, multimodal, and lacks detailed domain knowledge, and yields consistently low accuracy across all existing methods. We show that classical causal discovery methods and existing LLM-based multi-agent systems fail to reliably identify root causes on this benchmark, and present a Structured Multi-Agent RCA pipeline that substantially outperforms existing LLM-based and classical baselines, supporting both domain-knowledge and knowledge-free operating modes. To diagnose where failures originate, we introduce a reverse reasoning agent that, given the correct answer, identifies which signals in the extracted anomalies support it and determines whether Stage~1 had access to those signals, classifying each failure as Reasoning Gap (evidence present but unused) or Data Ambiguity (evidence genuinely absent). This analysis reveals that the required evidence is present in the vast majority of failures: the bottleneck is not data access but the agent's ability to reason over it correctly. We further introduce an automated rule mining pipeline that systematically extracts discrimination rules from reverse reasoning reports, reducing reliance on manual knowledge curation. Across all configurations, model reasoning capability and domain knowledge are the primary constraints: stronger models embed more domain expertise, and explicit knowledge injection partially compensates for this gap. Reasoning performance remains practically bounded even when evidence extraction is perfect: scaffold engineering and better data pipelines alone cannot close this gap; progress requires improvements at the model level.

AI.tldr: A Structured Multi-Agent RCA framework outperforms baselines on OpenRCA, revealing bottlenecks in reasoning and domain knowledge. It introduces a reverse reasoning agent and automated rule mining; data access is not the main bottleneck, and progress hinges on model reasoning and explicit knowledge integration.
AI.motivation: Root-cause analysis (RCA) for production microservices requires reasoning over large-scale, multimodal telemetry (metrics, logs, traces). The OpenRCA benchmark exposes limitations of classical and LLM-based methods, including lack of domain knowledge and poor accuracy across methods.
AI.method: Propose a Structured Multi-Agent RCA pipeline with domain-knowledge and knowledge-free modes. Incorporates a reverse reasoning agent that analyzes which signals support the correct answer and whether Stage 1 had access to them, classifying failures as Reasoning Gap or Data Ambiguity. Introduces automated rule mining to extract discrimination rules from reverse reasoning reports. Evaluates across configurations against baselines.
AI.result: The pipeline substantially outperforms existing LLM-based and classical baselines across configurations. Model reasoning capability and domain knowledge emerge as primary constraints: stronger models encode more domain expertise; explicit knowledge injection partially compensates. Even with perfect evidence extraction, reasoning remains a bottleneck; scaffolding and data pipelines alone cannot close the gap.
AI.conclusion: Advancing RCA in large-scale multimodal settings requires improvements at the model level for reasoning and domain knowledge integration. The reverse reasoning analysis and automated rule mining reduce manual curation and offer diagnostic insights, but progress hinges on better reasoning capabilities and knowledge incorporation in models.

title: FM$^2$: Unified Federated Foundation Models for Heterogeneous Multimodal Medical Imaging
comment: Accepted by ACM MM 2026 (Main Track): the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia
summary: Building foundation models for medical imaging requires pooling data across institutions, yet privacy regulations prohibit centralized aggregation. Existing Federated Foundation Models either fine-tune natural-image models with poor medical-domain transfer, or train from scratch within a single modality, lacking the flexibility to unify tasks. We identify an under-explored challenge, Imaging Modality Heterogeneity, where clients operate under two structural regimes: Overlapped (shared modalities with heterogeneous label distributions) and Non-overlapped (fully disjoint modalities per client). We propose FM$^2$, a unified framework that trains the core backbone from scratch to preserve medical domain fidelity while optionally incorporating biomedical pretrained encoders for vision-language alignment. FM$^2$ equips each client with dual Mixture-of-Experts modules (a Class-wise MoE for personalized category knowledge and a Domain-wise MoE for shared cross-modality representations), coupled with a Heterogeneous Modality Alignment (HMA) regularizer that explicitly aligns modality-specific expert parameters, admitting provable $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence and generalization guarantees. FM$^2$ further incorporates Caption-Enhanced Learning (CEL), where locally retained GPT-4o-generated captions serve as a textual semantic bridge enabling representation transfer across clients with disjoint modalities, and demonstrates extensibility to Federated Medical VQA. Experiments on our MIMH benchmark (classification and CEL) and real-world medical VQA datasets confirm consistent superiority over state-of-the-art federated baselines and strong out-of-modality generalization across all three tasks.

AI.tldr: FM^2 is a unified Federated Foundation Model framework for modality-heterogeneous medical imaging, using dual Mixture-of-Experts and a Heterogeneous Modality Alignment regularizer, plus Caption-Enhanced Learning with GPT-4o captions; it provides convergence guarantees and generalizes across tasks including VQA.
AI.motivation: Enable privacy-preserving learning across medical institutions when imaging modalities are heterogeneous, addressing overlapped and non-overlapped modalities while preserving medical-domain fidelity and enabling cross-task transfer.
AI.method: Train the backbone from scratch to preserve domain fidelity; optionally incorporate biomedical pretrained encoders for vision-language alignment; per-client dual MoEs (Class-wise MoE for category knowledge, Domain-wise MoE for cross-modality representations); Heterogeneous Modality Alignment (HMA) regularizer to align modality-specific expert parameters with provable O(1/√T) convergence and generalization; Caption-Enhanced Learning (CEL) using locally retained GPT-4o-generated captions as a textual bridge for cross-client transfer; extensible to Federated Medical VQA.
AI.result: Empirical results on the MIMH benchmark (classification and CEL) and real-world medical VQA datasets show consistent superiority over state-of-the-art federated baselines and strong out-of-modality generalization across all three tasks.
AI.conclusion: FM^2 offers a principled, scalable solution for modality-heterogeneous federated medical learning, preserving domain fidelity while enabling cross-modality transfer, supported by theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance; the framework is extensible to related tasks like VQA.

title: Stress-Sharing: A Bio-Inspired Approach to Decentralized Fault Repair in Modular Spacecraft
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems
summary: Structural damage in modular spacecraft can disrupt mechanical and communication connectivity, reducing system capability. Existing approaches rely on redundancy or preplanned reconfiguration and do not enable autonomous repair under local information and physical constraints. We model the spacecraft as a lattice-constrained graph and introduce a fully decentralized, asynchronous stress-sharing repair policy inspired by biological wound healing: local distress signals guide surviving modules toward damaged regions to close fragmented gaps, after which each displaced module locally retraces its own motions to recover the pre-damage shape, using only local information and no absolute position sensing. We evaluate the policy in PyBullet rigid-body simulation across structures of up to 160 modules, three fault densities (10, 20, 30%), and random and localized damage. The policy consolidates the surviving modules into a single connected body: even in the most severe case tested, where 30% of modules fail at random, it gathers roughly 80% or more of the surviving modules into one connected component, and this fraction improves with assembly size, making the approach well suited as a swarm-scale repair policy for large modular spacecraft.

AI.tldr: A decentralized, asynchronous wound-healing–inspired repair policy for modular spacecraft that uses local distress signals to guide surviving modules to damaged regions, closes gaps, and locally retraces motions to recover pre-damage shape without absolute positioning.
AI.motivation: Enable autonomous repair under local information and physical constraints, avoiding reliance on redundancy or preplanned reconfiguration.
AI.method: Model the spacecraft as a lattice-constrained graph and implement a fully decentralized, asynchronous stress-sharing policy. Distress signals guide nearby modules toward damaged areas to close gaps; displaced modules then retrace their own local motions to restore the original shape, using only local information and no absolute position sensing.
AI.result: The policy yields a consolidated, connected surviving structure. In tests with up to 160 modules and fault densities of 10–30%, it gathers 80%+ of surviving modules into a single connected component in the worst random-failure case, with higher consolidation as assembly size increases, across random and localized damage.
AI.conclusion: The approach is well suited as a swarm-scale repair policy for large modular spacecraft, offering robust, decentralized repair under local information constraints and without absolute positioning.

title: Tabular Foundation Models for Discrete Choice Estimation
summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) generate predictions on structured data via in-context learning, without task-specific estimation. We ask whether TFMs can be effectively applied to discrete choice, a central demand estimation framework in marketing and operations, and find that directly applying TFMs yields limited performance. The gap is structural: TFMs assume row-independent observations, whereas discrete choice is inherently set-valued and subject to persistent consumer preference heterogeneity. We propose a reformulation that encodes both choice-set dependence and individual heterogeneity within a row-based learning framework. Evaluated on a yogurt scanner panel, individual-level heterogeneity encoding is the dominant driver of predictive accuracy. The best reformulation outperforms hierarchical Bayesian estimation by 8\% in holdout log-likelihood and 3.6\% in hit rate, running 16 times faster, a practical advantage for large-scale demand estimation. The advantage is largest in the medium-data regime (10--40 purchase occasions per consumer), where parametric Bayesian shrinkage most distorts estimates for atypical consumers. Fine-tuning on population choice data provides additional gains for consumers with shallow purchase histories, where in-context learning has limited individual-specific signal to condition on. These results establish a principled approach for applying foundation models to consumer choice problems more broadly.

AI.tldr: Tabular foundation models underperform on discrete choice due to row-independence assumptions; a row-based reformulation that encodes both choice-set dependence and individual heterogeneity yields substantial gains, surpassing hierarchical Bayesian estimation in accuracy and speed, especially in medium-data regimes; fine-tuning on population data provides additional gains for sparse histories.
AI.motivation: Assess whether Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) can be effectively applied to discrete choice in marketing and operations, and address structural mismatches by integrating choice-set dependence and individual heterogeneity within a row-based learning framework.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation on a yogurt scanner panel comparing direct TFM application to a reformulated row-based approach that encodes both choice-set dependence and individual heterogeneity. Key metrics include holdout log-likelihood and hit rate. Benchmarks against hierarchical Bayesian estimation. Analysis of data regimes (low/medium/high purchase occasions) and speed, plus investigation of fine-tuning on population choice data for consumers with shallow histories.
AI.result: Best reformulation outperforms hierarchical Bayesian estimation by 8% in holdout log-likelihood and 3.6% in hit rate, while running 16× faster. Individual-level heterogeneity encoding is the dominant driver of predictive accuracy. The advantage is largest in the medium-data regime (10–40 purchase occasions per consumer), where parametric Bayesian shrinkage distorts estimates for atypical consumers. Fine-tuning on population data yields additional gains for consumers with shallow purchase histories.
AI.conclusion: A principled, scalable framework for applying foundation models to consumer choice problems is established, emphasizing heterogeneity encoding and choice-set structure; the approach offers practical speed advantages and improves predictive performance, suggesting broader applicability to demand estimation tasks.

title: Multi-Agent Collaborative Reasoning with Tool-Augmented Evidence for Urban Region Profiling
