summary: Urban region profiling constitutes a core problem in urban computing, supporting applications such as population estimation, economic assessment, and environmental monitoring. Existing methods typically formulate this task as multimodal representation learning, fusing heterogeneous urban data, e.g., satellite imagery, points of interest, textual descriptions, and 3D building information, into latent embeddings for prediction. However, these approaches are largely correlation-driven, assume cross-modal consistency, and rely on static pipelines, which limit their robustness in heterogeneous or unseen urban regions. We propose UrbanAgent, an agentic framework that reframes urban region profiling as a reasoning-driven inference problem. UrbanAgent instantiates an independent agent for each data modality and performs structured multi-agent collaborative reasoning to explicitly address cross-modal inconsistencies rather than absorbing them into a single representation. In addition, UrbanAgent extends indicator prediction as a closed-loop process of active evidence acquisition and iterative reasoning, enabling agents to verify uncertain inferences through tool-augmented retrieval of external knowledge optimized via reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments on global urban datasets for Carbon emissions, GDP, and Population estimation show that UrbanAgent consistently outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average improvement of 8.1% in R2, and exhibiting strong generalization performance in unseen-city settings.

AI.tldr: UrbanAgent uses per-modality agents with collaborative, reasoning-driven inference and active evidence gathering to tackle cross-modal inconsistencies in urban region profiling, yielding robust, generalizable predictions; it achieves about 8.1% improved R2 and good unseen-city performance.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal urban profiling methods are largely correlation-driven, assume cross-modal consistency, and rely on static pipelines. They struggle with heterogeneity and unseen regions, motivating a shift to agent-based, reasoning-driven inference with active evidence acquisition.
AI.method: Introduce independent agents for each data modality that engage in structured multi-agent collaborative reasoning to address cross-modal inconsistencies. Extend indicator prediction as a closed-loop process of active evidence acquisition and iterative reasoning, using tool-augmented retrieval of external knowledge optimized via reinforcement learning to verify uncertain inferences.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on global urban datasets for Carbon emissions, GDP, and Population estimation shows consistent performance gains over baselines, with an average improvement of 8.1% in R2 and strong generalization to unseen-city settings.
AI.conclusion: UrbanAgent demonstrates that an agentic, reasoning-driven framework with active evidence gathering can outperform traditional multimodal fusion in urban region profiling, offering enhanced robustness and generalization across multiple targets and cities.

title: AnomExpert: Identifying and Selecting Anatomical Planes for Prenatal Ultrasound Anomaly Diagnosis
comment: It has been accepted early by MICCAI2026
summary: Life-limiting congenital anomalies require accurate prenatal diagnosis for appropriate clinical decision-making. Prenatal ultrasound (US) examinations involve multiple anatomical planes, and diagnosis depends on identifying anatomical planes and selecting diagnostically relevant planes for each anomaly. Existing automated methods either rely on plane-level annotations or aggregate heterogeneous images without explicitly modeling these diagnostic capabilities. We propose AnomExpert, a prototype-driven framework for prenatal US anomaly diagnosis using only case-level supervision. AnomExpert introduces learnable plane prototypes to organize unordered images into latent representations corresponding to anatomical planes without requiring plane annotations. A disease-aware sparse selection mechanism further selects diagnostically relevant planes for each anomaly. Experiments on a multi-center dataset of 3,654 cases show that AnomExpert consistently outperforms nine representative multi-instance learning methods. Using a ViT-small backbone, it achieves 86.9% accuracy and 84.2% F1-score while maintaining parameter efficiency. These findings indicate that modeling anatomical plane identification and disease-specific plane selection improves weakly supervised multi-plane prenatal US anomaly classification. The code is available at https://github.com/TIanCat/AnomExpert.

AI.tldr: Proposes AnomExpert, a prototype-driven weakly supervised framework for prenatal ultrasound anomaly diagnosis that uses learnable plane prototypes to organize unordered images into anatomical planes and a disease-aware sparse selector to pick diagnostically relevant planes; achieves high accuracy on 3,654 cases with ViT-small backbone, outperforming MIL baselines.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of plane-level annotations in prenatal US and the need to model diagnostic plane identification to improve weakly supervised multi-plane anomaly classification.
AI.method: Introduce learnable plane prototypes that cluster images into latent anatomical planes without explicit plane annotations; apply disease-aware sparsity to select relevant planes per anomaly; use ViT-small backbone; evaluate on multi-center dataset; compare to nine MIL methods.
AI.result: Consistent outperformance of nine representative MIL methods; accuracy 86.9%, F1 84.2% on 3,654 cases; parameter-efficient; code released.
AI.conclusion: Modeling anatomical plane identification and disease-specific plane selection improves weakly supervised multi-plane prenatal US anomaly classification.

title: Learning Physics-Guided Residual Dynamics for Deformable Object Simulation
summary: Simulating deformable objects is essential for a wide range of robotic manipulation applications, yet accurately predicting their dynamics remains challenging. We propose Physics-Guided Residual Dynamics (PGRD), a hybrid simulation framework that combines the advantages of physics-based and learning-based approaches. Specifically, PGRD combines an optimizable spring-mass simulator as a backbone with a learned neural network that predicts residual corrections to the physics-based predictions. We adopt a velocity-based formulation to ensure stable simulation and a sliding-window transformer architecture to capture temporal dependencies. We show that PGRD produces more accurate results than both purely physics-based and learning-based methods on a set of diverse real-world deformable objects. We further demonstrate the utility of PGRD in two applications: manipulation planning via Model Predictive Control, including a language-conditioned setting with a generated goal image; and interactive simulation via action-conditioned video prediction by 3D Gaussian Splatting.

AI.tldr: A hybrid physics-guided residual dynamics (PGRD) framework for deformable object simulation that blends an optimizable spring-mass physics backbone with a neural residual predictor, using velocity-based integration and a sliding-window transformer, achieving superior accuracy and enabling planning and interactive simulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Deformable object dynamics are hard to predict accurately, which hinders manipulation planning and interactive simulation; a hybrid approach can leverage physical priors while learning complex residuals.
AI.method: Backbone: optimizable spring-mass simulator. Residual: neural network predicting corrections to physics-based predictions. Temporal modeling via a sliding-window transformer. Velocity-based formulation for stability. Applications include MPC-based manipulation planning (language-conditioned with goal image) and action-conditioned video prediction using 3D Gaussian Splatting.
AI.result: PGRD outperforms purely physics-based and purely learning-based methods on diverse real-world deformable objects.
AI.conclusion: A physics-guided residual framework can improve deformable object simulation accuracy and enable practical planning and interactive tasks, by integrating physics priors with learned residual dynamics and temporal modeling.

title: Accuracy-Preserving Stability Regularization for Large-Scale Retail Demand Forecasting
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, accepted for presentation at ICEME 2026
summary: Retail demand forecasts are reused across replenishment, capacity, labor, and transportation planning cycles. Point-error objectives do not constrain abrupt movement between adjacent forecasts, while post-hoc smoothing acts only after model fitting. We ask whether a training-time penalty on consecutive within-series movement can improve horizontal forecast-path stability without materially changing point accuracy. The penalty is evaluated in a temporal-structured pipeline combining recent-demand embeddings with calendar, price, hierarchy, item, and store features. On selected M5 demand series at 1000, 3000, and 4000-series scales, the stability-aware hybrid model improves Forecast Stability Score over XGBoost by 6.91%, 6.66%, and 7.68%, respectively, while RMSE changes remain within 0.72% across three random seeds. Post-hoc exponential smoothing attains lower raw movement but incurs a larger RMSE cost; training-time regularization preserves more point accuracy and performs favorably under normalized stability. These findings extend forecast evaluation from point-error minimization toward an accuracy-stability trade-off perspective for operational retail forecasting.

AI.tldr: A training-time penalty for within-series movement improves forecast path stability with minimal RMSE change, evaluated on large-scale M5 demand series; post-hoc smoothing reduces movement but hurts RMSE; suggests an accuracy-stability trade-off in retail forecasting.
AI.motivation: Retail forecasts feed multiple planning cycles; point-error optimization can produce abrupt forecast moves that hinder operational stability. A training-time stability regularizer aims to constrain consecutive forecast changes, improving path stability without sacrificing point accuracy.
AI.method: A temporal-structured pipeline combines recent-demand embeddings with calendar, price, hierarchy, item, and store features. A regularization penalty during training penalizes consecutive movement within an item/store time series. Compared against post-hoc exponential smoothing and baseline models (on M5 series at 1k/3k/4k scales).
AI.result: Forecast Stability Score improves by 6.91%, 6.66%, and 7.68% over XGBoost at the three scales, while RMSE changes are within 0.72% across three seeds. Post-hoc smoothing reduces raw movement but increases RMSE; training-time regularization maintains point accuracy and performs well under normalized stability.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating a training-time stability penalty yields more stable forecast paths with minimal loss (or even preservation) of point accuracy, reframing forecast evaluation toward an accuracy-stability trade-off in operational retail forecasting.

title: AI advice suppresses people's willingness to say "I don't know", even when the advice is wrong and accuracy is incentivized
summary: Knowing when to say "I don't know" is fundamental to human judgment, yet AI assistants offer a fluent answer to almost any question. In five experiments (N = 3,132; four preregistered, one direct replication), participants answered difficult questions and could always decline to respond. We engineered the questions so that AI advice was wrong, separating AI use from its accuracy. Merely having access to AI nearly eliminated participants' willingness to suspend judgment, and this held whether the advice was actively requested or simply displayed. Consequently, participants answered more questions but were correct about a third as often as when AI was unavailable-yet their confidence nearly doubled. Incentivizing accuracy and penalizing inaccuracy led participants to seek and follow AI advice less, answer more accurately, and suspend judgment more often, though still far less than when AI was unavailable. As AI suggestions grow ubiquitous and unsolicited, they may not simply affect answer accuracy; they may even alter the metacognitive threshold at which people decide whether they know enough to answer.

AI.tldr: AI advice presence dramatically reduces willingness to suspend judgment, causing more answers but lower accuracy when AI is wrong; incentives for accuracy can mitigate this but do not restore performance to the no-AI baseline; AI may shift metacognitive thresholds.
AI.motivation: To understand how ubiquitous AI advice affects human judgment and metacognition, and to distinguish the effects of AI access from its accuracy.
AI.method: Five experiments (N = 3,132; four preregistered, one direct replication). Questions engineered so AI advice was wrong. Manipulated AI access (requested vs displayed) and incentives (accuracy vs penalties).
AI.result: Access to AI almost eliminates suspension of judgment; more questions attempted but with only about one third the accuracy of when AI is unavailable; confidence nearly doubles. Incentivizing accuracy or penalizing errors reduces AI reliance, improves accuracy, and increases suspending judgment, but not to no-AI levels.
AI.conclusion: Ubiquitous, unsolicited AI advice can alter metacognitive thresholds, affecting not only accuracy but also when people feel they know enough to answer. Design and policy implications for AI systems to preserve human metacognition and appropriate reliance.

title: MultiAnimate: A Unified Framework for Controllable Multi-Character Animation
summary: Recent advances in generative models and technological innovations have significantly addressed the fundamental challenges of character image animation. However, existing approaches predominantly focus on character animation from a single reference image, substantially limiting their applicability in scenarios such as multiple character interaction animation. To fill this gap, this paper introduces MultiAnimate, a comprehensive framework that enables concurrent animation of multiple characters within a shared environment while preserving both identity consistency and spatial relationships. The framework achieves these objectives through multiple well-designed mechanisms. First, we incorporate an identity-specific reference net that enables appearance extraction from multiple reference images, distinguishing MultiAnimate from existing approaches constrained to single reference inputs. Second, we implement an identity-aware pose encoder to address the character-pose binding challenge, wherein an attention mechanism enables the network to accurately differentiate and process multiple pose sequences during generation. Third, we introduce an interaction guider module that enhances the framework's capability to handle complex inter-character interactions by leveraging character-specific mask information, serving as an optional component that refines the pose sequences. Extensive experiments and ablation analyses demonstrate our framework's superiority in multiple character animation, particularly in scenarios involving complex motion sequences.

AI.tldr: MultiAnimate enables concurrent multi-character animation from multiple references while preserving identity and spatial relations, using dedicated modules for appearance extraction, pose discrimination, and optional interaction guidance.
AI.motivation: Existing methods rely on a single reference image, which hinders multi-character interactions and reduces identity and spatial consistency in shared scenes. A framework is needed to (1) extract appearances from multiple references, (2) bind poses to multiple characters without confusion, and (3) handle complex inter-character interactions.
AI.method: Proposes a three-component framework: (i) an identity-specific reference net that extracts appearance from multiple reference images; (ii) an identity-aware pose encoder with an attention mechanism to differentiate and process multiple pose sequences; (iii) an interaction guider that leverages character-specific mask information to refine pose sequences, optional but beneficial in complex interactions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and ablation analyses show that MultiAnimate achieves superior performance in multi-character animation, especially for complex motion sequences, by improving identity consistency, pose fidelity, and interaction plausibility compared to single-reference or single-character baselines.
AI.conclusion: MultiAnimate fills the gap in multi-character animation by enabling concurrent, identity-preserving, and spatially coherent animation in shared environments, with demonstrated benefits from the proposed modules and ablation studies; the interaction guider further enhances handling of inter-character dynamics.

title: Reverse to Advance: Teleoperation-Cost Effective Hard Policy Learning from Reversed Easy Tasks
summary: High-quality teleoperation datasets are costly to collect, particularly for hard tasks. We observe that many tasks exhibit directional asymmetry: completing the forward hard task is difficult, whereas reversing it by relaxing or disrupting the environment is comparatively easy. This suggests that reversed easy-task trajectories can serve as a scalable supervision signal for the hard task, reducing the cost of manual demonstration collection. However, reversed data can be noisy, and directly training on it may yield suboptimal policies. To enable largely automated acquisition and effective use of reversed data, we propose a teleoperation-cost effective framework for hard policy learning via temporal reversal of easy tasks, consisting of three key components: a closed-loop data collection pipeline that alternates between hard-task and easy-task policies to autonomously reset the environment and generate diverse trajectories; a hierarchical data refinement pipeline that temporally inverts easy-task rollouts and filters low-quality motion using kinematic priors and a critic-guided advantage filter; and an iterative policy learning method that trains the hard-task policy using both initial reversed easy-task demonstrations and the filtered reversed data in a continuous online learning loop. By combining automated collection, hierarchical refinement, and iterative learning, our method enables scalable, reliable training of complex, high-precision manipulation tasks. Across two simulated benchmarks and real-robot experiments, we demonstrate that our method improves hard-task success rates with higher data efficiency and more stable training compared to reversal-based and reinforcement-learning baselines, without requiring extensive hard-task teleoperation.

AI.tldr: A framework to learn hard-teleoperation policies by leveraging temporally reversed easy-task trajectories, with automated closed-loop data collection, hierarchical data refinement, and iterative learning, achieving improved data efficiency and stability over reversal-based baselines on simulated and real robots.
AI.motivation: High-quality teleoperation data for hard manipulation is costly. The authors exploit directional asymmetry where easy-to-return-from (reversed) easy tasks can supervise hard tasks, reducing manual data collection though reversed data is noisy; thus a scalable, robust pipeline is needed.
AI.method: 1) Closed-loop data collection alternating hard-task and easy-task policies to autonomously reset and diversify trajectories. 2) Hierarchical data refinement: temporally invert easy-task rollouts and filter low-quality motion using kinematic priors and a critic-guided advantage filter. 3) Iterative policy learning: train hard-task policy using initial reversed easy-task demonstrations plus filtered reversed data in a continuous online loop.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on two simulated benchmarks and real-robot experiments shows improved hard-task success rates, better data efficiency, and more stable training compared with reversal-based and RL baselines, without requiring extensive hard-task teleoperation.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables scalable, reliable training of complex, high-precision manipulation tasks by combining automated collection, hierarchical refinement, and iterative learning, addressing the data bottleneck in teleoperation for hard tasks.

title: Agora: Collective and Permissionless Internet-Scale Pretraining of Large Language Models
summary: Training large language models at the multi-billion to trillion parameter scale is confined to datacenters, where data-parallel (DP) and model-parallel (MP) techniques presume homogeneous accelerators, high-speed interconnects, and a single orchestrating entity. Frontier model development is thereby concentrated among the few groups able to assemble such clusters. Meanwhile, an enormous pool of compute remains unusable for training: consumer and professional GPUs that are heterogeneous, preemptible, individually owned, and connected only by the internet. We present Agora, a system that makes efficient use of this compute. Agora combines bandwidth-efficient pipeline-parallel model sharding over internet-grade links with multi-party, fault-tolerant collective operations. Each participant holds only one stage of the model, and no single party ever possesses the full weights. We term this setup Protocol Learning: it enables collectively trained, collectively owned models, opening a path to open-source frontier training with economic sustainability. This report presents the outcome of a research effort spanning communication-efficient parallelism, asynchronous optimization, and fault-tolerant systems design. It culminates in the first demonstration of its kind: Pluralis-8B, an open, permissionless pretraining run of an 8.6B-parameter model on 500B tokens of FineWeb-Edu. The model was trained over 40 days by 330 contributor nodes, predominantly consumer GPUs on internet connections, joining and leaving throughout. The run sustained ~170k tokens/s and 4.2 tokens per TFLOP of pooled compute, 63% of the efficiency of a centralized H100 baseline, and converged to within a small margin of a centralized reference run.

AI.tldr: Agora enables open, distributed frontier-model training by pipeline-parallel sharding over internet-grade links with fault-tolerant multi-party coordination; demonstrates Pluralis-8B using 330 contributor nodes over 40 days, achieving ~170k tokens/s and 63% efficiency vs a centralized baseline.
AI.motivation: Lower the barrier to frontier model training by leveraging heterogeneous, preemptible, globally distributed compute and ownership, enabling economically sustainable open-source development of large models.
AI.method: Protocol Learning: each participant holds a single model stage; no party has full weights. Bandwidth-efficient pipeline-parallel model sharding over internet-grade links combined with fault-tolerant collective operations and asynchronous optimization. Open, permissionless setting enables collectively trained models with distributed governance. Demonstrated with Pluralis-8B (8.6B params) trained on 500B tokens (FineWeb-Edu) by 330 contributor nodes (consumer GPUs) over 40 days, with dynamic join/leave.
AI.result: Achieved ~170k tokens/s and 4.2 tokens per TFLOP of pooled compute, at 63% efficiency relative to a centralized H100 baseline, converging to within a small margin of the centralized reference run.
AI.conclusion: First demonstration of collectively trained, collectively owned frontier models via Protocol Learning. Validates feasibility of open, permissionless pretraining on heterogeneous internet-scale compute, and outlines directions for scalability, reliability, governance, and economic sustainability.

title: SAFETY SENTRY: Context-Aware Human Intervention via EXECUTE-ASK-REFUSE Routing
summary: LLM agents act on real-world environments through tool calls, and a single misjudged action can cause irreversible harm. The standard safeguard is a guard model that labels each proposed action as safe or unsafe, but this binary view conflates two distinct decisions: whether the action is harmful in itself, and whether it is appropriate given the user's context. It also operates at the granularity of action categories rather than individual instances, producing routine interruptions that erode autonomy and train users to wave through the most consequential alerts. We reframe the problem as a per-instance three-way routing decision over {EXECUTE, ASK, REFUSE} and instantiate it with Safety Sentry, a lightweight guard model whose inference reduces to a single decoding call. A single decoding-time threshold lets one fixed checkpoint be re-positioned across deployments of differing risk tolerance without retraining. Safety Sentry outperforms a broad set of open-weight and frontier closed-source baselines on overall accuracy and safety-related recall, while controlling both directional error rates simultaneously.

AI.tldr: Reframe LLM safety as per-instance routing with {EXECUTE, ASK, REFUSE} using a lightweight guard (Safety Sentry) that uses a single decoding call and a fixed threshold, enabling risk-tolerance deployment without retraining; outperforms baselines on accuracy and safety recall while balancing directional errors.
AI.motivation: Traditional guard systems treat safety as a binary, action-category-level classification, which conflates harm with context and causes unnecessary interruptions, reducing autonomy. A per-instance, tripartite routing approach aims to separate harm assessment from contextual appropriateness and minimize user disruption.
AI.method: Propose per-instance three-way routing ({EXECUTE, ASK, REFUSE}) and instantiate with Safety Sentry—a lightweight guard whose inference is a single decoding pass. Implement a single decoding-time threshold so one fixed checkpoint can be repositioned across deployments with different risk tolerances without retraining.
AI.result: Safety Sentry surpasses a broad set of open-weight and frontier closed-source baselines in overall accuracy and safety-related recall, while simultaneously controlling directional error rates.
AI.conclusion: Per-instance, three-way routing with a lightweight guard enables adaptable, accurate safety decisions for LLM agents, achieving better performance and stability across varying risk tolerances without retraining.

title: ScanFocus: A Coarse-to-Fine Framework for Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding
comment: this paper has already been accepted by ECCV 2026
summary: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to retrieve the visual trajectory of a specific object from a video stream as described by a natural language expression. However, most advanced methods struggle to balance global context modeling with precise boundary localization. Due to the prohibitive computational costs of processing long videos, these approaches typically resort to low-rate temporal downsampling and implicit motion modeling. This inevitably suppresses high-frequency boundary cues and neglects the explicit inter-frame dependencies required for precise boundary delineation. To address these limitations, we present \textbf{ScanFocus}, a novel coarse-to-fine framework that decouples the STVG task into a global spatio-temporal scan and a local boundary focus. Specifically, we utilize a unified vision-language fusion encoder combined with a lightweight Deformable Semantic-Motion Fusion module to efficiently align multimodal features and generate coarse proposals. To recover the suppressed fine-grained details, we introduce the Semantic-Guided Temporal Aggregator (SGTA) in the refinement stage. By densely sampling around coarse boundaries, SGTA explicitly models short-term temporal interactions under semantic guidance, capturing rapid motion changes for precise timestamp regression. Extensive experiments on three widely used benchmarks demonstrate the performance superiority of our proposed method over previous approaches. Code will be released at https://github.com/TenMinutes209/ScanFocus.

AI.tldr: ScanFocus introduces a coarse-to-fine STVG framework that decouples global spatio-temporal scanning from local boundary refinement, leveraging a vision–language fusion encoder, a lightweight Deformable Semantic-Motion Fusion module for coarse proposals, and a Semantic-Guided Temporal Aggregator (SGTA) for dense, semantically-guided boundary refinement.
AI.motivation: Current STVG approaches struggle to balance global context modeling with precise boundary localization due to long videos requiring downsampling, which suppresses high-frequency boundary cues and neglects explicit inter-frame dependencies essential for exact timestamp delineation.
AI.method: A two-stage coarse-to-fine framework: (i) global stage with a unified vision–language fusion encoder and a lightweight Deformable Semantic-Motion Fusion module to produce coarse proposals; (ii) refinement stage with Semantic-Guided Temporal Aggregator (SGTA) that densely samples around coarse boundaries to model short-term temporal interactions under semantic guidance for precise timestamp regression.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three standard STVG benchmarks show that ScanFocus outperforms prior methods.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively balances global context and boundary precision; SGTA enables fine-grained temporal localization, and the framework is efficient for long videos; code is to be released.

title: Joint On-and-Off Policy Learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) necessitates an embodied agent to navigate in the physical world by adhering to natural language instructions. Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLM) have propelled the development of VLM-based VLN methods with two predominant paradigms: (1) imitation learning (IL) on expert demonstrations, followed by the Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) algorithm to bolster error recovery capabilities; (2) reinforcement learning (RL) driven by verifiable rewards to enhance reasoning and exploration. A notable gap is the absence of integration between these two distinct paradigms. This paper introduces JOP-VLN, a novel VLN framework that synergistically combines off-policy imitation learning and on-policy exploration within a three-stage training pipeline. Initially, IL is employed on expert demonstrations to acquire basic navigation skills. Subsequently, the DAgger algorithm is utilized to generate heuristic exploration trajectories, which are then used for imitation learning to improve error recovery capabilities. Finally, a joint on-and-off policy learning framework is implemented, featuring high-entropy trajectory sampling to enhance RL training efficiency and an error-correction-prioritized trajectory sorting strategy for effective error correction. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of JOP-VLN, achieving success rates of 69.9% and 68.0% on the VLN-CE R2R and RxR benchmarks, respectively, setting a new state-of-the-art on R2R. Project page: https://qingrongh.github.io/JOP-VLN.

AI.tldr: A three-stage VLN framework (JOP-VLN) unifies off-policy imitation learning with on-policy RL: (1) IL on expert demos, (2) DAgger-guided heuristic exploration with imitation learning for error recovery, (3) a joint on/off policy training with high-entropy sampling and error-priority trajectory sorting, achieving SOTA on R2R and RxR benchmarks.
AI.motivation: VLN methods either focus on imitation-learning with error recovery via DAgger or on reinforcement learning; there is a gap in integrating these paradigms to leverage complementary strengths for better exploration, error handling, and navigation performance.
AI.method: A three-stage training pipeline: (1) off-policy IL on expert demonstrations, (2) DAgger to collect heuristic exploration trajectories and IL updates to enhance error recovery, (3) joint on-off policy learning with high-entropy trajectory sampling and an error-correction-prioritized trajectory sorting strategy, evaluated on VLN-CE R2R and RxR benchmarks.
AI.result: Empirically strong performance, achieving 69.9% on VLN-CE R2R and 68.0% on RxR, setting a new state-of-the-art on R2R.
AI.conclusion: Integrating off-policy imitation learning with on-policy RL in a structured three-stage framework yields robust VLN agents with improved error recovery and exploration efficiency, and establishes new state-of-the-art results on major VLN benchmarks.

title: Weight Feedback Computes the Jacobian Transpose Locally in Modern Deep Networks
summary: Predictive Coding (PC) offers a biologically motivated alternative to backpropagation via local weight updates, yet routing error between layers still relies on an autograd Jacobian-transpose ($J^\top$) product - the last non-local operation in PC. We show that this dependency is largely avoidable. For any layer $f(x)=\mathrm{Act}(\mathrm{Norm}(L(x)))$ with frozen normalization statistics, the exact $J^\top$ factors into three locally available terms, $J^\top v = L^\top(s \odot σ'(z) \odot v)$, where $σ'$ is the activation derivative, $z$ is the pre-activation, and $s=γ/σ_{\mathrm{run}}$ is the normalization gain. Prior weight-feedback methods omitted both corrections; restoring them closes the transport gap for this layer class. Locality here holds up to three assumptions, which we state upfront: weight symmetry ($L^\top$ mirrors the forward operator, as assumed by all PC), a soft spectral-norm control that is not synapse-local, and a nearest-neighbour approximation for MaxPool. Substituting the identity into PC yields WF-Act-PC, which removes the autograd backward pass from error transport. On CIFAR-10/100 (50 epochs, 5 seeds), WF-Act-PC is the only PC method whose accuracy improves with depth, surpassing iPC - the strongest classical PC baseline - by 2.7-22.3 pp on CIFAR-10. With both methods tuned per architecture, it matches or exceeds a comparably-tuned backpropagation baseline on the deeper CIFAR-10 architectures (VGG-9: 93.57% vs. 92.43%; ResNet-18: 92.76% vs. 91.54%) and on the harder Tiny-ImageNet benchmark, while trailing tuned BP on the deeper CIFAR-100 VGG cells. Our WF-Act-PC implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/jlshen025/pcax

AI.tldr: Derives a local factorization of the autograd Jacobian-transpose in Predictive Coding (PC), enabling WF-Act-PC which removes the non-local backward pass; achieves competitive or superior accuracy to backpropagation on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny-ImageNet for deeper architectures, with notable depth sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Address the non-local error transport bottleneck in PC by expressing J^T as a product of locally available terms under frozen normalization statistics, improving both plausibility and performance of PC.
AI.method: Analytical derivation for a layer f(x)=Act(Norm(L(x))) with frozen statistics showing J^T v = L^T(s ⊙ σ'(z) ⊙ v); identify three locality-supporting assumptions (weight symmetry, soft spectral-norm control non-local, nearest-neighbor MaxPool); propose WF-Act-PC by substituting the identity for error transport, and evaluate on CIFAR-10/100 (50 epochs, 5 seeds) and Tiny-ImageNet, comparing to iPC and tuned BP; provide open-source implementation.
AI.result: WF-Act-PC yields depth-aware gains on CIFAR-10, surpassing iPC by 2.7–22.3 percentage points; when architectures are tuned, it matches or exceeds tuned BP on deeper CIFAR-10 models (VGG-9: 93.57% vs. 92.43%; ResNet-18: 92.76% vs. 91.54%); performs well on Tiny-ImageNet; on CIFAR-100 VGG cells, BP slightly outperforms WF-Act-PC; code released at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: By removing the autograd backward pass from error transport for the specified layer class, the transport gap is closed under three stated locality assumptions, enabling PC methods to scale with depth and approach BP performance in several settings; the approach hinges on frozen normalization statistics and specific architectural approximations, with publicly available implementation.

title: Automatic Ordinary Differential Equations Discovery For Biological Systems Using Large Language Model Powered Agentic System
summary: Automatic scientific discovery has long been a goal of computational scholars - a machine that can discover nature's secrets on its own, moving computational systems beyond data-fitting tools toward the generation and refinement of mechanistic models of the universe. Recent advances in symbolic regression (SR) and large-language-model (LLM)-based agents suggest that such systems can recover equations from data, incorporate domain priors, and automate parts of the research workflow. However, most existing approaches either focus on narrow equation-discovery benchmarks or broad end-to-end automation pipelines, while biological systems remain comparatively underexplored. Here, we introduce the MEDA system, an LLM- and SR-powered agentic framework for discovering ordinary-differential-equation (ODE) models of biological and biologically inspired dynamical systems. MEDA retrieves background knowledge, defines admissible variables, generates mechanistic constraints, proposes candidate ODEs, and fits and evaluates them. We evaluate it across canonical model retrieval, reasoning-based extrapolation to unseen variants, and open-ended discovery, with and without experimental data. Across these settings, MEDA recovered the correct state variables, achieved strong structural recovery in retrieval and extrapolation tasks, and produced biologically plausible discovery-oriented models. Ablation and robustness analyses show that knowledge-guided formalization and mechanistic constraints are load-bearing components, whereas numerical fitting alone can preserve trajectory-compatible but biologically incorrect equations.

AI.tldr: MEDA combines LLM-based knowledge integration with symbolic regression to autonomously discover mechanistic ODE models for biology, achieving correct variables, strong structural recovery, and biologically plausible models; ablations show the necessity of constraints and knowledge formalization.
AI.motivation: Automated discovery of mechanistic biological models has long been desired, but existing SR and LLM approaches either target narrow benchmarks or broad automation without adequate domain constraints, limiting biological applicability.
AI.method: MEDA is an agentic framework that uses an LLM to retrieve background knowledge and define admissible variables, generates mechanistic constraints, proposes candidate ODEs via symbolic regression, and fits and evaluates models. It operates across retrieval, extrapolation to unseen variants, and open-ended discovery, with or without experimental data.
AI.result: MEDA correctly identifies state variables, shows strong structural recovery in retrieval and extrapolation tasks, and yields biologically plausible discovery-oriented models. Ablation studies show that knowledge-guided formalization and mechanistic constraints are essential; numerical fitting alone can yield trajectory-consistent yet biologically incorrect equations.
AI.conclusion: Integrating LLM-driven knowledge with symbolic regression and explicit mechanistic constraints enables robust discovery of biologically plausible ODE models, highlighting the critical role of domain knowledge in mechanistic discovery.

title: CLIP-Guided Label-Free Discriminative Region Scoring for Fine-Grained Classification
summary: Recent vision models such as CLIP and SAM enable training-free segmentation and semantic encoding for fine-grained classification. A common approach is to compare the representations of segmented image regions with the text prompt embeddings of the corresponding labels. However, it remains unclear how different local regions and CLIP-based scoring strategies affect the selection of discriminative evidence, especially when ground-truth labels are unavailable. In this paper, we propose a unified CLIP-guided label-free region scoring framework for fine-grained classification. The framework evaluates cosine similarity-based, margin-based, and entropy-based scoring strategies using both SAM-generated masks and random crops, and introduces two label-free pseudo-label variants based on global image embeddings and local region embeddings. We conduct experiments on five fine-grained classification datasets to systematically compare different region generation methods and scoring strategies. The results show that Soft Negative Margin scoring achieves the strongest performance, and pseudo-label scoring closely approximates true-label performance. Although SAM produces semantically meaningful masks, random-crop-based pseudo-label scoring consistently outperforms SAM-based scoring across all datasets, suggesting that random crops preserve surrounding information and provide more stable semantic context when pseudo-labels are noisy. In addition, SAM masks benefit from aggregating embeddings from all regions, whereas random crops tend to perform better with a smaller top-k subset. These findings provide new insights for fine-grained classification.

AI.tldr: A unified CLIP-guided, label-free region scoring framework for fine-grained classification; it compares cosine similarity, margin-based, and entropy-based scoring using SAM masks and random crops, with two pseudo-label variants. Soft Negative Margin scoring performs best; pseudo-label scoring closely matches true-label performance; random crops outperform SAM-based scoring; SAM benefits from embedding aggregation, while random crops favor small top-k. Provides new insights for FG classification.
AI.motivation: To understand how local region selection and CLIP-based scoring influence discriminative evidence in fine-grained classification when ground-truth labels are unavailable, and to evaluate label-free strategies that align with CLIP/segmentation models.
AI.method: Propose a unified CLIP-guided, label-free region scoring framework that evaluates cosine similarity-based, margin-based, and entropy-based scoring strategies using both SAM-generated masks and random crops; introduce two label-free pseudo-label variants based on global image embeddings and local region embeddings; conduct experiments on five fine-grained datasets to compare region generation methods and scoring strategies.
AI.result: Soft Negative Margin scoring achieves the strongest performance; pseudo-label scoring closely approximates true-label performance; random-crop-based pseudo-label scoring consistently outperforms SAM-based scoring across all datasets; SAM masks benefit from aggregating embeddings from all regions, while random crops perform better with a smaller top-k subset.
AI.conclusion: The study provides new insights: random crops maintain surrounding context and provide stable semantic cues under label noise, while SAM masks gain from embedding aggregation; pseudo-label scoring is a viable proxy for true labels; guidance is offered for choosing region generation and scoring strategies in CLIP-based FG classification.

title: EgoHTR: Egocentric 4D Demonstrations of Human Terrain Traversal
summary: Deploying humanoid robots in unstructured terrain remains an open problem. While classic reinforcement learning struggles with the sheer complexity of real-world interactions, more promising methods leveraging human priors remain limited to models lacking contextual awareness. The restricted motion synthesis is a direct consequence of existing dataset pipelines failing to capture human-scene sequences in challenging environments. To bridge this gap between humanoid learning and scene reconstruction, we introduce the Egocentric Human-Terrain Reconstruction (EgoHTR) dataset. We develop and open-source a reconstruction pipeline capturing 55 scene-aligned 4D human motion sequences in diverse, complex environments using a multi-sensor setup of egocentric wearables and a portable 3D scanner. The resulting dataset comprises over 150k frames, which we evaluate against motion-capture ground truth, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy and establishing a rigorous benchmark for human motion analysis and synthesis. Further, we leverage this data to train perceptive locomotion policies, demonstrating hardware deployment on a Unitree G1 for reconstructed reference motions. Our pipeline enables community-driven dataset extensions and factors the problem to help researchers build foundational, context-aware robots that reliably traverse uneven terrain.

AI.tldr: A large egocentric 4D human motion dataset (EgoHTR) with 55 scene-aligned sequences totaling >150k frames, captured via multi-sensor wearables and 3D scanning; used to train perceptive locomotion policies and deployed on a Unitree G1. Provides an open-source pipeline and a benchmark for context-aware humanoid locomotion in unstructured terrain.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between human-prior-based motion synthesis and scene understanding; address the lack of context-rich, scene-aligned human motion data in challenging environments; enable robust learning and real-world deployment of locomotion policies.
AI.method: Collect 4D human motion data with egocentric wearables and portable 3D scanner across diverse, unstructured environments; assemble 150k frames in 55 scene-aligned sequences; evaluate against motion-capture ground truth; develop and open-source a reconstruction pipeline; train perceptive locomotion policies from EgoHTR data; validate via hardware deployment on a Unitree G1 using reconstructed reference motions; design the pipeline for community-driven extensions.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy against mocap ground truth; provides a rigorous benchmark for human motion analysis and synthesis; demonstrates practical usefulness by hardware deployment; offers an extensible, open-source pipeline for future dataset growth.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a foundational resource for context-aware humanoid locomotion in uneven terrain, enabling researchers to train and deploy perceptive locomotion policies and to extend the dataset via a community-driven pipeline.

title: Where Should RL Post-Training Compute Go? Model Size, Search, Learning, and Feedback
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training is increasingly used to adapt foundation models for reasoning, planning, and feedback-driven robot-learning pipelines, but constrained post-training resources are often summarized by a single total FLOP budget. We study the fixed-budget decision problem behind this practice: under the same post-training budget, should one use a larger policy, train a smaller policy longer, generate more rollout search, or spend compute on stronger reward feedback? We introduce a FLOP-accounting framework for GRPO post-training that decomposes compute into rollout/search, policy-update/learning, and reward- or feedback-model evaluation. Across LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5 policies, we find conditional allocation frontiers: the best observed allocation changes with model size, compute budget, reward system, and evaluation target. Same-FLOP model-size comparisons show that model choice and training allocation are coupled because larger policies consume more per-token compute and therefore buy fewer updates or rollouts under the same budget. Reward systems also change the accounting: rule-based rewards spend nearly all non-update compute on policy rollouts, while PRM-style feedback allocates a visible part of the budget to reward-model inference. We present RACE as a diagnostic pilot-grid protocol, not a guarantee of held-out improvement, for identifying allocation regimes before expensive validation runs; our results suggest that RL post-training papers should report total FLOPs together with how compute is divided among model size, search, learning, and feedback.

AI.tldr: Under a fixed FLOP budget, optimal RL post-training strategy depends on model size, reward system, and evaluation target; use FLOP accounting to balance rollout/search, learning, and reward-model work; RACE helps map allocation regimes.
AI.motivation: Constrained post-training compute creates tradeoffs among policy size, training duration, rollout/search, and feedback quality; understanding these tradeoffs is essential for efficient RL post-training.
AI.method: Propose a FLOP-accounting framework that decomposes compute into rollout/search, policy-update/learning, and reward-model evaluation; apply it to LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5 policies; compare allocations at the same FLOP budget across different sizes and reward systems; introduce RACE as a diagnostic pilot-grid protocol.
AI.result: Found conditional allocation frontiers: optimal compute allocation changes with model size, budget, reward system, and evaluation target; larger models consume more per-token compute, reducing updates/rollouts possible under the same FLOP; rule-based rewards channel most non-update compute into rollouts, while PRM-style feedback allocates a visible portion to reward-model inference; same-FLOP comparisons show coupling between model choice and training allocation; RACE identifies allocation regimes before costly validation; recommends reporting total FLOPs and how compute is divided.
AI.conclusion: RL post-training studies should report total FLOPs and the split of compute among model size, search, learning, and feedback to enable fair comparisons and regime identification; RACE provides a diagnostic step prior to expensive validation.

title: STOCKTAKE: Measuring the Gap Between Perception and Action in LLM Agents with a Fair Oracle
summary: LLM agents are increasingly evaluated on multi-week decision tasks in which the state that drives cost is never directly observed. On such tasks the final cost cannot say why an agent failed: it may have misread the world, or read it correctly and still failed to act (the knowing-doing gap). Existing evaluations cannot separate these two failures; their reference policies either read privileged information the agent never sees, or are missing altogether. We introduce STOCKTAKE, a 26-week supply-chain replenishment benchmark built as a factored partially observable Markov decision process with six hidden factor processes, designed so that a fair reference policy is computable: an exact Bayes filter per factor drives a rollout policy on the identical observation stream the agent receives. Scoring each run between a symptom-blind base-stock floor (0) and this oracle (1) yields a skill score, and grading each week's written rationale yields a stated-belief detection lag and a knowing-doing rate, so state estimation and control are measured separately. On fifty seeds with curated stress profiles, Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.4, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Grok 4.5 detect 84-88% of hidden failures, typically within a week of onset, yet span skill scores from 0.62 to -0.23: two of the four end below the symptom-blind floor while naming factors slightly faster than the two that beat it. The failure has two faces. Where stress persists, 34-43% of correctly diagnosed stress weeks still end in stockout for every model, a rate that partly reflects the severity of the weeks models notice. That rate also runs opposite to skill: the two models under the floor stock out least on diagnosed weeks, so under-response is only one face of the gap, and their traces point to the other, responses whose cost exceeds what they protect. STOCKTAKE measures both directions of that failure.

AI.tldr: A new benchmark, STOCKTAKE, evaluates LLM agents on a 26-week supply-chain replenishment task framed as a factored partially observable Markov decision process. It uses an exact Bayes filter per hidden factor as an oracle to separate state estimation from control, and introduces skill, detection lag, and knowing-doing metrics to reveal both estimation and action failures.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations fail to distinguish whether failures come from misreading the world or from not acting appropriately after reading it. A fair reference policy is needed to measure true skill in long-horizon, uncertainty-rich tasks.
AI.method: A 26-week replenishment benchmark (stocking under uncertainty) with six hidden factor processes. It is a factored POMDP where an exact Bayes filter per factor drives a rollout policy on the agent’s observation stream. A symptom-blind base-stock floor (0) vs an oracle policy (1) yields a skill score; weekly rationales measure stated-belief detection lag and knowing-doing rate.
AI.result: Across 50 seeds with curated stress profiles, leading LLMs detect 84–88% of hidden failures within about a week. Reported skill scores range from 0.62 to −0.23; some models underperform the floor on stockouts. 34–43% of diagnosed-stress weeks still end in stockouts, indicating that stress severity and misalignment between detection and response contribute to failures.
AI.conclusion: STOCKTAKE enables separate assessment of state estimation and control, reveals two faces of failure (missed/stressed state estimation and costly responses), and provides a realistic, fair evaluation framework for long-horizon, partially observable tasks.

title: DreamSat-Pose: Spacecraft Pose Estimation from Single-View 3D Reconstructions and Learned 2D-3D Feature Matching
summary: 6-DoF pose estimation is a critical task in autonomous rendezvous and proximity operations. In the case of an unknown target, this task becomes challenging as it shall be paired with the reconstruction of the target shape model. In this article, we propose a novel framework for single-shot shape and pose estimation of unknown spacecraft objects. Given a single image, we first reconstruct a 3D shape model of the target, then estimate the relative six-degrees-of-freedom pose by learning dense 2D-3D correspondences. The image features are extracted using a frozen DINOv3 vision transformer, while the geometric features are computed from the reconstructed point cloud using a trainable dynamic graph convolutional neural network encoder. A dual-stream transformer matcher refines descriptors through alternating self- and cross-attention, producing soft correspondences that are passed to a Perspective-$n$-Point solver for pose recovery. We evaluate the method on the SPE3R dataset and consider FoundationPose as a representative baseline for current state-of-the-art capabilities. Results show reliable pose estimates achieving 0.157 degrees mean pointing error using only a single image and reconstructed geometry, demonstrating strong generalization to unseen spacecraft.

AI.tldr: A single-shot framework for unknown spacecraft pose estimation by reconstructing a 3D shape from one image and computing dense 2D-3D correspondences to recover 6-DoF pose; achieves 0.157° mean pointing error on SPE3R, outperforming FoundationPose, with strong generalization to unseen spacecraft.
AI.motivation: Address the combined problem of unknown target geometry and 6-DoF pose estimation from a single view, essential for autonomous rendezvous where prior CAD models are unavailable.
AI.method: Pipeline: 1) reconstruct 3D target shape from a single image; 2) extract image features with frozen DINOv3; 3) derive geometric features from the point cloud via a trainable dynamic graph CNN encoder; 4) refine dense descriptors with a dual-stream transformer matcher to yield soft 2D-3D correspondences; 5) recover pose with a Perspective-n-Point solver.
AI.result: On SPE3R, with FoundationPose as baseline, the method achieves 0.157 degrees mean pointing error using only a single image and reconstructed geometry, showing strong generalization to unseen spacecraft.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates effective joint 3D reconstruction and pose estimation from a single image, leveraging transformer-based matching and graph-based geometry to deliver accurate 6-DoF pose estimates for unknown targets.

title: Deformable State Estimation for Autonomous Surgical Tissue Retraction Under Partial Observability
comment: Accepted to the ICRA 2026 RASEI Workshop
summary: Surgical tissue retraction requires effective manipulation planning under partial and noisy perception. We study state estimation for deformable tissue retraction, where only sparse observations of the tissue surface are available at decision time. We propose a learned state estimator that reconstructs the full deformable mesh state from 40 noisy vertex observations. The estimator combines a multilayer perceptron with a low-dimensional PCA latent representation and is trained using geometry-aware regularization that encourages smooth and physically plausible deformations. We evaluate the approach in a 2D deformable sheet simulation using single-step and multi-step retraction planning. Results show that the learned estimator achieves 98.1% of oracle performance in multi-step retraction while supporting efficient inference. These results demonstrate that learned, geometry-regularized state estimation can support effective deformable manipulation under realistic perception constraints.

AI.tldr: A geometry-regularized learned state estimator reconstructs the full deformable tissue mesh from 40 noisy vertex observations, enabling near-oracle multi-step retraction in a 2D simulation with efficient inference.
AI.motivation: Deformable tissue retraction under partial/noisy perception presents a state-estimation challenge for planning. Accurate full-state knowledge is needed for effective manipulation, but sensors provide sparse, noisy data.
AI.method: Combine a multilayer perceptron with a low-dimensional PCA latent representation to predict the latent state from 40 observations; train with geometry-aware regularization promoting smooth, physically plausible deformations; evaluation in 2D sheet simulation with single- and multi-step retraction planning.
AI.result: Achieves 98.1% of oracle performance in multi-step retraction and supports efficient inference.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that learned, geometry-regularized state estimation can enable effective deformable manipulation under realistic perception constraints.

title: Self-Improving is Often Sudden: Enlightenment-style Finetuning for Large-Scale Models
summary: The pursuit of autonomously self-improving models has attracted growing interest in the era of large-scale foundation models. Drawing inspiration from the concept of "enlightenment" or "aha moment" in human brain, we hypothesize that large models exhibit an analogous enlightenment phenomenon-a latent capacity for sudden capability boost. Then, we propose Enlightenment, a novel training-free post-tuning paradigm for large-scale models. Our approach modifies shortcuts for key modules/layers without weight updates, while existing training-free ones predominantly manipulate attention weights. We introduce two architecture-specific instantiations: i) For large language models, we propose attention head-mixing shortcuts that recalibrate attention weights by linking the initial attention head's output to all other target heads, modulated by an adaptive scaling factor initialization strategy. ii) For vision-language models, we apply a lightweight scalar-modulated factor to residual connections in the decoder layers, regulating information flow. Extensive experiments show that Enlightenment efficiently unlocks the latent potential of pre-trained networks, yielding remarkable performance improvements across diverse benchmarks and models.

AI.tldr: A training-free post-tuning approach, Enlightenment, unlocks latent capabilities of large models by architecture-level shortcuts without weight updates, with two instantiations for LLMs (attention head-mixing) and vision-language models (residual modulation).
AI.motivation: Large foundation models may harbor latent capabilities that can be elicited without traditional fine-tuning. A training-free method that reconfigures information flow could trigger sudden performance boosts (an 'enlightenment' moment) with minimal cost.
AI.method: Introduce architecture-specific shortcuts that modify signal flow without gradient updates. For LLMs, apply attention head-mixing by linking the original head output to other heads with an adaptive scaling factor. For vision-language models, add a scalar-modulated factor to residual connections in decoder layers to regulate information flow.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows meaningful performance gains across diverse benchmarks and models, indicating the latent potential of pre-trained networks can be unlocked efficiently via architectural shortcuts without weight updates.
AI.conclusion: Enlightenment demonstrates a practical, training-free route to enhance large models by leveraging architecture-aware shortcut strategies, enabling rapid gains with low computational overhead.

title: UESF-Bench: Benchmarking and Probing for Unified Embodied Seeking and Following
summary: Language-guided human following is an important capability for embodied agents, but existing benchmarks typically assume that the target person is visible at the start of an episode. This setting simplifies the problem and overlooks a more realistic requirement: an agent often needs to first find a language-described target and then persistently follow that target in a dynamic environment. While recent work has started to study human search, existing settings are typically evaluated in task-specific scenarios and often rely on stronger prior knowledge of the environment. Moreover, they usually treat searching and following as separate tasks and still lack a unified benchmark for systematic evaluation. To address these limitations, we introduce the Unified Embodied Seeking and Following Benchmark (UESF-Bench), a large-scale and diverse benchmark for embodied human seeking and following. The benchmark requires agents to handle semantic-guided exploration, reliable behavior switching and recovery, and delayed identity grounding. To this end, we propose SeekFollow-VLA, a vision-language-action framework with a task-driven routing mechanism for latent phase inference and transition modeling between seeking and following. Experimental results show that SeekFollow-VLA achieves clear improvements over both single-head and dual-head baselines across single-person and multi-person environments, establishing a baseline for unified embodied seek-and-follow.

AI.tldr: Proposes Unified Embodied Seeking and Following Benchmark (UESF-Bench) and SeekFollow-VLA, a vision-language-action framework with latent phase routing to unify semantic-guided searching and following in embodied agents; shows improved performance over baselines in single- and multi-person environments.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks treat seeking and following separately, assume initial visibility of the target, rely on environment priors, and lack a unified framework for evaluating integrated search-and-follow behavior. A unified benchmark is needed to study semantic-guided exploration, reliable behavior switching, and delayed identity grounding in dynamic environments.
AI.method: UDI: Introduces SeekFollow-VLA, a vision-language-action framework with a task-driven routing mechanism for latent phase inference and transition modeling between seeking and following. The router decides when to search, follow, or recover, enabling seamless switching and robust behavior in the presence of dynamic targets and distractions.
AI.result: Empirical results show that SeekFollow-VLA outperforms single-head and dual-head baselines in both single-person and multi-person environments, establishing a baseline for unified embodied seek-and-follow.
AI.conclusion: UESF-Bench provides a large-scale, diverse benchmark for integrated seeking and following in embodied agents and, together with SeekFollow-VLA, offers a baseline framework for future research on unified seek-and-follow tasks.

title: Symbiosis-Inspired Knowledge Distillation for Incremental Object Detection
summary: Incremental object detection (IOD) aims to extend detectors to new categories while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Existing methods often adopt a class incremental learning perspective, separating feature spaces to sharpen decision boundaries. However, this separation-oriented paradigm may overlook object symbiosis in detection, where co-occurrence and occlusion introduce spatial and semantic dependencies that benefit from shared representations. Ignoring these dependencies distorts the shared representations, exacerbates confusion between old and new classes, and accelerates catastrophic forgetting. To address this, we propose Symbiosis-Inspired Knowledge Distillation (SIKD), which explicitly leverages object symbiosis at two complementary levels. Spatial Symbiosis Distillation (SpSD) focuses on symbiotic regions where the old model responds with high overlap to objects in the new task. It preserves generalizable old class cues, suppresses class-specific bias and redundancy, and distills the refined evidence to the new model at matched spatial locations with slot-aligned supervision. Semantic Symbiosis Distillation (SeSD) maintains class level structure by forming confidence weighted prototypes for old classes and aligning their inter class soft ranks over the old class logits, which stabilizes the semantic topology during adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: A two-level distillation framework, Symbiosis-Inspired Knowledge Distillation (SIKD), for incremental object detection that leverages spatial and semantic symbiosis via SpSD and SeSD to preserve old knowledge while learning new categories.
AI.motivation: Object symbiosis—co-occurrence and occlusion—creates spatial and semantic dependencies that are not exploited by traditional separation-based class incremental learning, leading to distorted representations and catastrophic forgetting in incremental object detection.
AI.method: SIKD comprises two complementary distillation modules. Spatial Symbiosis Distillation (SpSD) preserves generalizable cues in spatial regions where the old model strongly responds to new-task objects, reduces class-specific bias and redundancy, and distills evidence at matched spatial locations with slot-aligned supervision. Semantic Symbiosis Distillation (SeSD) builds confidence-weighted prototypes for old classes and aligns their inter-class soft ranks over the old logits to stabilize semantic topology during adaptation.
AI.result: Empirical results on standard incremental object detection benchmarks demonstrate that SI KD achieves superior performance against strong baselines, validating the effectiveness of leveraging object symbiosis.
AI.conclusion: Modeling both spatial and semantic symbiosis in IKD effectively mitigates forgetting and improves integration of new classes while preserving old ones in incremental object detection.

title: VAMP-MR: Vector-Accelerated Motion Planning and Execution for Multi-Robot-Arms
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. To appear in the Proceedings of IROS 2026
summary: Multi-robot-arm motion planning is a key challenge in deploying multiple manipulators for industrial tasks such as manufacturing. Existing search-based and sampling-based solvers often require significant computation time to produce collision-free, high-quality motions suitable for safe real-world execution. In this work, we introduce a new suite of multi-robot-arm motion planners capable of near real-time motion generation, combining classical planning algorithms with state-of-the-art vectorized collision-checking techniques. Based on CPU SIMD instructions, our new planners accelerate their primary bottleneck, collision checking, and achieve up to two orders of magnitude speedup in both motion planning and execution postprocessing for multi-arm manipulation tasks. We also release our implementation to lower the barrier for research and development of multi-robot-arm planning and manipulation problems. Code is available at https://vamp-mr.github.io/vamp-mr

AI.tldr: A suite of multi-robot-arm motion planners using CPU SIMD-based vectorized collision checking to enable near real-time planning, achieving up to 100x speedups; code released.
AI.motivation: Reduce computation time for generating collision-free, high-quality motions in multi-arm manipulation, addressing the inefficiency of existing search- and sampling-based planners for industrial tasks.
AI.method: Combine classical planning algorithms with state-of-the-art vectorized collision checking on CPU SIMD to accelerate collision checks, speeding up both planning and execution postprocessing for multi-robot-arm tasks; release an open-source implementation.
AI.result: Up to two orders of magnitude speedup in planning and postprocessing; near real-time motion generation for multi-arm manipulation; code available at the provided URL.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates practical real-time capable multi-robot-arm planning, with a ready-to-use implementation to foster research and industrial adoption.

title: Is the Statistical Advantage Worth the Cost? An Empirical Comparison of KANs and MLPs for Structured Data Classification
comment: To be presented at the 9th International Conference on Machine Learning and Machine Intelligence (MLMI 2026), Tokyo, Japan
summary: This study presents an empirical benchmarking comparison between Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) and Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) on structured tabular classification tasks. Motivated by the growing interest in KANs as an alternative function-approximating architecture, we evaluate their out-of-the-box performance on twelve publicly available datasets spanning binary, multiclass, multilabel, and ordinal problems. Both models were trained under standardized preprocessing, architecture, and fixed hyperparameter settings, with performance assessed using test accuracy and F1-Score, paired hypothesis testing, and effect size analysis. Results show that KANs statistically outperform MLPs in binary and multiclass domains and achieve a significant aggregate advantage across all datasets. However, the observed medium effect size (d = -0.46) raises an important cost-benefit consideration: while KANs offer superior generalization through adaptive spline-based mappings, this advantage comes with substantially higher parameter and computational complexity relative to the MLP baseline. These findings suggest KANs are the preferred choice for high-precision applications, while MLPs remain a robust and efficient option for resource-constrained environments. Future work should extend this analysis to additional data modalities to further refine these architectural selection criteria.

AI.tldr: KANs outperform MLPs on structured tabular classification with higher complexity; medium effect size; best for high-precision, not resource-limited settings.
AI.motivation: Assess the potential of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) as an alternative function-approximating architecture for structured tabular data and benchmark against standard MLP baselines.
AI.method: Empirical benchmarking across twelve public datasets spanning binary, multiclass, multilabel, and ordinal tasks. Standardized preprocessing, architecture, and fixed hyperparameters. Performance assessed via test accuracy and F1-score, with paired hypothesis testing and effect size analysis.
AI.result: KANs statistically outperform MLPs in binary and multiclass domains and show a significant aggregate advantage across all datasets. The observed medium effect size (d = -0.46) indicates a meaningful but costlier improvement, with higher parameter and computational complexity relative to MLPs due to adaptive spline-based mappings.
AI.conclusion: KANs are preferred for high-precision applications on tabular data, while MLPs remain robust and efficient for resource-constrained environments. Future work should test additional data modalities to refine architectural selection criteria.

title: Explaining Reinforcement Learning Agents via Inductive Logic Programming
summary: Explainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL) seeks to make Reinforcement Learning (RL) policies more transparent and interpretable, a key requirement in safety-critical and human-centric scenarios. However, it is mostly based on user studies, thus targeting the needs of a specific audience and lacking shared evaluation metrics. On the other hand, logic-based approaches within eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) provide compact, human-readable abstractions of decision-making. However, the systematic quantification of the explainability degree of logical representations remains an open problem. This work aims to advance the state of the art in XRL by introducing objective and planning-oriented metrics for policy explainability in RL settings. At the same time, it contributes to the field of logic for XAI by providing a principled way to quantify the explainability of logical rules, moving beyond common-sense assessments and simple propositional fragments. We employ Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) to extract symbolic representations of RL policies and define a novel set of explainability metrics, including activation rate, feature coverage, syntactic distance and semantic distance. These metrics quantify alignment between symbolic rules and agent behavior, the role of features in decision-making, and the evolution of policies during training and across agents in single and multi-agent RL. Experiments across different RL domains show that the proposed metrics highlight action-specific learning dynamics beyond global return, provide fine-grained insights into domain features beyond classical approaches for global feature importance estimation, and uncover coordination, specialization, and adaptation patterns in MARL. Moreover, they provide crucial insights for the transfer and generalization of action-specific policies.

AI.tldr: Introduces objective metrics for explainability in RL and logic-based XAI by extracting symbolic rules via ILP and defining action- and policy-focused metrics.
AI.motivation: XRL and logic-based XAI currently lack shared, objective explainability metrics; need quantifiable measures to assess how well explanations align with agent behavior and learning dynamics, including multi-agent coordination.
AI.method: Apply Inductive Logic Programming to extract symbolic representations of RL policies. Define metrics: activation rate (rule-action activation frequency), feature coverage (features used by rules), syntactic distance (differences in rule syntax), semantic distance (differences in meaning/behavior). Evaluate in single- and multi-agent RL to track policy evolution during training and across agents.
AI.result: Metrics reveal action-specific learning dynamics beyond global return; offer fine-grained feature importance over traditional global measures; uncover coordination, specialization, and adaptation in MARL; support transfer and generalization of action-specific policies.
AI.conclusion: Proposes objective, planning-oriented explainability metrics for RL and a principled quantification of logical rule explainability, advancing both XRL and logic-focused XAI; metrics enable deeper insights into policy behavior, feature roles, and cross-agent dynamics.

title: GeoAnchor: Collaborative Reasoning via Latent Decomposition for 3D Spatial Understanding
summary: Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, understanding 3D spatial relationships from 2D images remains a critical challenge. Existing methods primarily rely on symbolic text tokens, which inherently lack the fidelity to represent continuous geometric information. While recent methods use latent representations to enhance reasoning, relying on a single latent type cannot adapt to the diversity of spatial tasks, leading to misalignment in complex geometric scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose GeoAnchor, an interleaved text-latent reasoning framework. GeoAnchor decomposes 3D spatial information into three complementary components: position latents for object grounding, direction latents for relational orientation, and geometry latents for scene structure. These components are recombined in a structured space to construct local evidence while capturing global context, enabling dynamic and interpretable reasoning. Furthermore, we introduce a collaborative training strategy that guides the model from local spatial perception to comprehensive 3D understanding. Extensive experiments on diverse and complex 3D reasoning tasks demonstrate that GeoAnchor outperforms the state of the art, validating its effectiveness and generalization capabilities.

AI.tldr: GeoAnchor introduces an interleaved text-latent reasoning framework that decomposes 3D spatial understanding into three latent types—position, direction, and geometry—to ground, relate, and structure scene information, with collaborative training to connect local perception to full 3D understanding, achieving state-of-the-art results on diverse 3D reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Understanding 3D spatial relationships from 2D imagery remains challenging for multimodal LLMs due to reliance on symbolic tokens or a single latent representation, which fail to faithfully capture continuous geometry and diverse spatial tasks.
AI.method: Decompose 3D information into three complementary latents (position for grounding, direction for relational orientation, geometry for scene structure) and interleave their use with text in a structured space. Recombine latents to form local evidence while maintaining global context, enabling dynamic and interpretable reasoning. Introduce a collaborative training strategy that guides the model from local spatial perception to holistic 3D understanding.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on varied and complex 3D reasoning tasks show GeoAnchor outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating strong effectiveness and generalization.
AI.conclusion: A multi-latent, text-latent interleaved framework with structured combination and collaborative training provides improved 3D reasoning from 2D inputs, offering interpretable, dynamic reasoning and strong generalization across tasks.

title: Topology-Agnostic Mesh Reconstruction of Deformable Objects from Sparse Touch
comment: Accepted to the RSS 2026 DAROMA Workshop
summary: Estimating the full shape of a deformable object is especially challenging when vision is unavailable: in the dark, inside an opaque bag, behind the manipulating hand, or under heavy self-occlusion. Touch is the natural sensor in these settings, but touches are sparse and local. We present a single topology-agnostic estimator that reconstructs the full mesh of a deformable object from only a few touches and no vision, using one permutation-invariant cross-attention architecture that handles a 1D rope, a 2D cloth, and a 3D volumetric soft body. The learned estimator reduces reconstruction error by roughly two-thirds relative to non-learned geometric mesh completion and a Gaussian-process surface baseline, and it outperforms a simpler global-pool set encoder, with the gap growing as more touches are observed. We then show that the estimator's deep-ensemble uncertainty can be used to learn where to touch next, which lowers error further and beats both random touching and a Gaussian-process active baseline at sparse budgets. This gain is modest on average but grows with self-occlusion and on the error tail. When vision is also available, where to touch barely matters, motivating the vision-free setting we study.
