In this paper, we propose CASA-SDF (Curriculum-Aware Spatial Adaptation for SDF), a unified framework that addresses this challenge via complementary adaptations of supervision and representation capacity. Specifically, Hybrid Spatially-Adaptive Uncertainty Annealing (SAUA) fuses semantic and photometric uncertainties to construct a pixel-wise curriculum for monocular prior supervision. This strategy maintains regularization in reliable regions while attenuating unreliable supervision early in training to enable data-driven photometric refinement. Meanwhile, Curvature-Aware Locally Adaptive Density Transformation (CALADT) progressively modulates the sharpness of the SDF-to-density mapping via a curvature proxy to enhance the representation of thin structures. Extensive experiments on benchmark indoor datasets demonstrate that CASA-SDF improves surface completeness and detail recovery on high-frequency structures, without compromising the stability of planar surfaces.

AI.tldr: CASA-SDF combines a curriculum-driven monocular supervision strategy with a curvature-aware SDF-to-density mapping to handle indoor geometric heterogeneity, achieving better high-frequency detail without breaking planar regions.
AI.motivation: Indoor scenes exhibit strong geometric heterogeneity: large texture-less planes require strong smoothing, while thin structures demand sharp, adaptive representations. Global SDF-to-density priors and indiscriminate supervision hinder balance between regularization and detail.
AI.method: Hybrid Spatially-Adaptive Uncertainty Annealing (SAUA) fuses semantic and photometric uncertainties to create a pixel-wise curriculum for monocular prior supervision, reducing unreliable supervision early in training to allow data-driven refinement. Curvature-Aware Locally Adaptive Density Transformation (CALADT) adjusts the sharpness of the SDF-to-density mapping via a curvature proxy to better represent thin structures.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on standard indoor benchmarks shows improved surface completeness and recovery of high-frequency details, while maintaining stability of planar surfaces.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CASA-SDF framework effectively balances planar regularization and fine geometric detail in indoor neural implicit representations, yielding more complete and detailed reconstructions without sacrificing planar stability.

title: Agile perceptive multi-skill locomotion for quadrupedal robots in the wild
comment: Project page: https://skillquadsr.github.io/ ,This is the author's version of the work. It is posted here by permission of the AAAS for personal use, not for redistribution. The definitive version was published in Science Robotics on 7.15.2026; doi: 10.1126/scirobotics.adz7397. Jun-Gill Kang and Jaehyun Park are co-first authors. Seungwoo Hong and Hae-Won Park are co-corresponding authors
summary: Enabling quadrupedal robots to traverse complex terrains-from rugged outdoor environments to urban landscapes-requires seamless integration of multiple motor skills, smooth transitions between gaits, and high-speed perceptive locomotion using only onboard sensors. We present APT-RL (Action Pretrained Transformer-based Reinforcement Learning), a unified framework that enables multi-skill locomotion to achieve high-speed traversal in complex environments through autonomous skill transitions utilizing only onboard perception and computation. Our approach generates large-scale, feature-rich 2D motion datasets through trajectory optimization with simplified dynamics. These datasets enable training of diverse, reusable locomotion skills that transfer effectively to a real quadruped robot operating on complex uneven terrains. The resulting high-quality skills serve as strong priors for efficient learning of complex downstream tasks and extend naturally to 3D environments, enabling smooth, high-speed multi-skill locomotion in deployed policy. Real-world experiments demonstrate the framework's capabilities: the robot performs agile maneuvers through complex indoor obstacles and outdoor wild environments, including dynamic drop-down maneuvers that reach instantaneous peak speeds of up to 6 meters per second. A single onboard policy enables robust traversal of diverse obstacles, including stairs, hurdles, stepping stones, gaps, and fallen branches, demonstrating the versatility and effectiveness of our approach.

AI.tldr: A transformer-based reinforcement learning framework (APT-RL) that pretrains a library of locomotion skills from large synthetic datasets and uses a single onboard policy to achieve high-speed, robust, multi-skill traversal of a quadruped across diverse terrains using only onboard perception.
AI.motivation: To enable seamless, high-speed, perception-based locomotion on quadrupeds across complex environments by learning transferable, reusable skills and smooth gait transitions entirely onboard.
AI.method: Generate large-scale 2D motion datasets via trajectory optimization with simplified dynamics. Train diverse, reusable locomotion skills as priors. Use a transformer-based policy (Action Pretrained Transformer) to condition and transition between skills, transferring skills to a real quadruped. Extend to 3D environments and deploy a single onboard policy capable of robust traversal of stairs, hurdles, stepping stones, gaps, and branches. Demonstrate on real robot with onboard perception and computation.
AI.result: Real-world experiments show agile indoor and outdoor obstacle traversal, including dynamic drop-down maneuvers reaching instantaneous peak speeds up to 6 m/s. A single onboard policy enables robust traversal of diverse obstacles (stairs, hurdles, stepping stones, gaps, fallen branches).
AI.conclusion: APT-RL provides a unified, perception-driven framework for high-speed, multi-skill quadruped locomotion by leveraging dataset-derived skill priors and a single onboard policy, enabling smooth transitions and effective transfer from synthetic data to real-world deployment.

title: Distributionally Robust and Safe Imitation Learning
summary: Imitation learning (IL) has achieved remarkable success in complex decision-making tasks. However, its performance is highly sensitive to distribution shifts, which can pose significant safety risks. We propose a distributionally robust and safe IL framework that explicitly addresses both policy-induced and uncertainty-induced distribution shifts. Our approach develops a unified framework leveraging Taylor Series Imitation Learning (TaSIL) to mitigate policy-induced shifts and distributionally robust adaptive control to handle uncertainty-induced shifts. This architecture enables the formulation of an IL problem that optimizes performance under distributional uncertainty while systematically accounting for safety constraints. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) case study where the UAV performs a task in an uncertain environment while avoiding unsafe regions.

AI.tldr: A distributionally robust and safe IL framework that addresses both policy-induced and uncertainty-induced distribution shifts, using TaSIL for policy shifts and robust adaptive control for uncertainty, validated on a UAV task with safety constraints.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning often suffers under distribution shifts, which can threaten safety. The work aims to address both kinds of shifts—policy-induced and uncertainty-induced—to enable safer, more reliable IL in safety-critical tasks.
AI.method: Unify Taylor Series Imitation Learning (TaSIL) to mitigate policy-induced shifts with distributionally robust adaptive control to handle uncertainty-induced shifts. Formulates an IL problem that optimizes performance under distributional uncertainty while enforcing safety constraints.
AI.result: Demonstrates effectiveness in a UAV case study where the vehicle operates in an uncertain environment while avoiding unsafe regions, indicating improved robustness to distribution shifts and adherence to safety.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses both distribution-shift types in imitation learning and is applicable to safety-critical tasks; future work could explore broader domains, scalability, and tighter safety guarantees.

title: AI-accelerated End-to-End Framework for Rapid Professional Upskilling
summary: By 2030, 59 of every 100 workers will need reskilling or upskilling, yet the average time to close an enterprise skills gap grew from roughly 3 days in 2014 to 36 days in 2018. Most current frameworks accelerate single stages of upskilling programs and generally lack industry validation. We present an end-to-end framework that applies AI acceleration across five stages of knowledge acquisition, content development, content review and verification, teaching, and assessment development; with a strong focus on both production and learning efficiency. Three strong external signals validates the framework: the US National Association of State Boards of Accountancy reviewed and approved an upskilling program built on the framework for continuing-professional-education credits; 3 learners followed the program and passed the NVIDIA Certified Professional in Agentic AI exam in a significantly short amount of time, with 14 more in progress; the program's knowledge base supports complex downstream analysis such as the production of a robust 1,267 risk item dataset for managing multi-agent AI system risks.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end AI-accelerated five-stage framework for enterprise upskilling with external validation signals.
AI.motivation: To address widening enterprise skills gaps and longer closure times; current approaches accelerate only single stages and lack industry-wide validation.
AI.method: Proposes AI acceleration across five stages: knowledge acquisition, content development, content review and verification, teaching, and assessment development; emphasizes production and learning efficiency; validated by external signals: NASBA approval for a CPE-based program, three learners passing the NVIDIA Certified Professional in Agentic AI exam (with 14 more in progress), and a knowledge base enabling a 1,267-item risk dataset for multi-agent AI risk management.
AI.result: Three validation signals: NASBA approval for continuing-professional-education credits; three learners passed the NVIDIA Agentic AI exam in a significantly shortened timeframe (14 more in progress); robust knowledge base supporting complex downstream analyses such as a 1,267-item risk dataset for multi-agent AI risk management.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end AI-accelerated upskilling framework shows promise for scalable, validated training; external validations bolster credibility and wider adoption potential, though additional quantitative outcomes would strengthen evidence.

title: M2P-AD: Memory-to-Prototype Learning with Boundary-aware Score Refinement for 3D Anomaly Detection
summary: 3D anomaly detection has recently emerged as an important research topic in computer vision. Although existing methods have achieved high performance, excessive anomaly responses in normal regions and false positives near object boundaries remain unresolved challenges. To address these challenges, we propose a novel 3D anomaly detection model, Memory-to-Prototype Anomaly Detection (M2P-AD), which effectively models the distribution of normal features while suppressing excessive anomaly scores in normal regions and false positives near object boundaries. Specifically, we introduce a Memory-to-Prototype (M2P) module that learns representative prototypes from normal feature embeddings to preserve important structural information of objects. In addition, a Boundary extraction (BE) module is integrated to identify object boundaries, and a Boundary-aware score refinement (BSR) strategy is applied to recalibrate anomaly scores by incorporating boundary characteristics. The proposed method is evaluated on Real3D-AD, Anomaly-ShapeNet, and MulSen-AD, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Qualitative results demonstrate that excessive anomaly scores in normal regions are reduced and false positives near object boundaries are suppressed, resulting in more accurate and stable anomaly localization. The results indicate that the proposed approach enables more reliable 3D anomaly detection and provides a robust solution applicable to real-world industrial environments.

AI.tldr: Proposes M2P-AD for 3D anomaly detection, combining a Memory-to-Prototype module to model normal feature distributions, a Boundary extraction module to locate object boundaries, and a Boundary-aware score refinement strategy to adjust anomaly scores. Achieves state-of-the-art results on Real3D-AD, Anomaly-ShapeNet, and MulSen-AD, while reducing false positives in normal regions and near boundaries.
AI.motivation: 3D anomaly detection suffers from excessive anomaly responses in normal regions and false positives near object boundaries. There is a need to preserve structural information of objects while accurately differentiating anomalies.
AI.method: Introduce Memory-to-Prototype (M2P) module that learns representative prototypes from normal feature embeddings to model normal distribution and preserve structure; integrate a Boundary extraction (BE) module to identify object boundaries; apply a Boundary-aware score refinement (BSR) strategy to recalibrate anomaly scores by leveraging boundary characteristics.
AI.result: Empirically achieves state-of-the-art performance on Real3D-AD, Anomaly-ShapeNet, and MulSen-AD. Qualitative results show reduced excessive anomaly scores in normal regions and suppressed false positives near boundaries, leading to more accurate and stable anomaly localization.
AI.conclusion: The M2P-AD framework provides a robust and reliable solution for 3D anomaly detection, well-suited for real-world industrial settings, by effectively modeling normal feature distributions and incorporating boundary-aware refinements to suppress spurious detections.

title: Active Trust Management for Successful Human-Robot Teaming: Moving from a Trust Repair to a Trust Satisficing Perspective
summary: Integrating mobile robots into human teams promises significant capability improvements for tasks such as searching hazardous environments. Unlike existing teleoperated robots, future robot systems will increasingly be endowed with some level of artificial intelligence (AI), giving them a degree of autonomy in how they pursue mission goals. This autonomy could make a human-agent (robot) team more effective but also put inter-agent trust under strain if robots make a mistake, or (appear to) pursue task priorities that conflict with the team's best interest. During a mission, agents' trust states are anticipated to vary according to the situation as understood by each teammate (trustor). If component-level (agent) or system-level trust falls below sufficient levels for cooperative tasks to be completed, it could critically affect mission success . We argue that active trust management will be an important precondition for the success of human-robot teams (HRTs, a subcategory of human-agent teams with embodied agents), especially in dynamic, high-risk environments. We present a trust satisficing perspective which acknowledges and attempts to account for the fluctuating, multi-faceted, and context-dependent nature of trust and trust requirements even under normal operating conditions. Our outline of a trust management framework for human-robot teaming includes online measurement of proxy metrics for trust, closed-loop adaptation of robot behavior, and variable autonomy to give space for human responsibility in situations requiring value judgements. We refer to a recent experimental exploration of 'swift trust' and a novel behavioral trust metric for HRT, and we highlight issues for further investigation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a trust management framework for human-robot teams in dynamic, high-risk environments, using a trust-satisficing perspective with online trust metrics, adaptive behavior, and variable autonomy to sustain effective collaboration.
AI.motivation: Human-robot teams in hazardous settings require reliable trust between teammates; fluctuations in trust can jeopardize mission success, thus active trust management is needed.
AI.method: Conceptual framework: trust satisficing approach; online measurement of proxy trust metrics; closed-loop adaptation of robot behavior; variable autonomy to preserve human responsibility; references to Swift Trust experiments and a behavioral trust metric as supporting work.
AI.result: No empirical results reported in the abstract; presents a theoretical framework and identifies direction for future work, with mention of related experimental exploration of trust concepts.
AI.conclusion: Active trust management is essential for effective human-robot teams; the proposed framework aims to handle fluctuating, context-dependent trust and outlines areas for further investigation.

title: PQFA: Parallel Quantum Feature Augmentation of Fused Representations for Multimodal Classification
summary: Most multimodal learning methods improve how heterogeneous representations are aligned and fused, while post-fusion enhancement remains less explored. We propose Parallel Quantum Feature Augmentation (PQFA), a hybrid quantum-classical framework that applies multiple shallow variational quantum circuits to fused multimodal features. Text and image representations extracted by frozen RoBERTa and ViT encoders are processed through bidirectional cross-attention, attentive pooling, and adaptive gated fusion. The fused feature is then amplitude-encoded into parallel quantum circuits, whose measurement readouts are concatenated with the classical representation for prediction. We evaluate PQFA on MM-IMDb and N24News through controlled comparisons using the same encoders, fusion backbone, data splits, projection dimension, and augmentation output width. PQFA consistently outperforms both the fusion backbone without quantum augmentation and a width-matched MLP augmentation baseline, while using approximately 2.2K augmentation parameters compared with 24.0K for the MLP branch. Missing-modality experiments further show improved robustness when textual or visual inputs are incomplete, with particularly clear gains when the more informative textual modality is severely degraded. Controlled ablations and feature-space analyses indicate that the improvement cannot be reproduced by random feature mappings, increased classical width, or untrained quantum transformations. Quantum-state diagnostics additionally show stable predictive performance across the tested simulated noise levels and distinct branch-specific transformations of the encoded states. These results establish PQFA as an effective and parameter-efficient strategy for post-fusion augmentation in hybrid quantum-classical multimodal learning.

AI.tldr: PQFA introduces parallel quantum feature augmentation to post-fusion multimodal learning, achieving parameter-efficient improvements on text+image tasks with better robustness to missing modalities.
AI.motivation: Post-fusion augmentation is underexplored; aim to leverage quantum circuits to augment fused multimodal representations while keeping parameter count low and robustness high.
AI.method: Extract text via frozen RoBERTa and image via frozen ViT; compute fused features via bidirectional cross-attention, attentive pooling, adaptive gated fusion; amplitude-encode into parallel variational quantum circuits; concatenated quantum readouts with classical features for prediction; benchmark on MM-IMDb and N24News; compare to fusion backbone without quantum augmentation and width-matched MLP augmentation; ablations and noise analyses.
AI.result: PQFA outperforms baselines consistently; gains in missing-modality scenarios; augmentation uses ~2.2k parameters vs 24k for MLP branch; robustness improvements; ablations indicate effect not due to random mappings, wider classical width, or untrained quantum transforms; quantum-state diagnostics show stability under simulated noise and branch-specific transformations.
AI.conclusion: PQFA is an effective and parameter-efficient post-fusion augmentation strategy for hybrid quantum-classical multimodal learning.

title: Earthquaker-AI: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework with Rubric-Based Assessment for Primary School Earthquake Education
summary: This paper presents Earthquaker-AI, a hybrid educational framework building upon a previously implemented educational robotics project by integrating a conversational AI assistant based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation. It aims to enhance earthquake preparedness and conscious action among primary-school students. The system extends the award-winning STEM project Earthquaker moving from mechanical simulation with Lego WeDo2 to cognitive and metacognitive processing. The robotics component uses Lego WeDo2 automation to simulate seismic response, letting students interact with sensors and actuators as tangible representations of protective actions. The assistant operates as a guided learning mechanism aligning student responses with safety guidelines, while providing rubric-based verbal feedback that supports self-regulated learning and calmness under emergency conditions. Earthquaker-AI follows a progressive learning trajectory aligned with cognitive development. In early grades, the focus is on basic recognition of safety actions through multiple-choice questions, assessed via a two-dimensional rubric. In middle grades, students identify correct action sequences through multiple-choice questions, evaluated via a three-axis rubric. In upper grades, the approach shifts to verbal production, requiring short written responses assessed via a four-dimensional rubric that includes clarity of expression. The dialogic module uses RAG to match student queries semantically with official guidelines, generating safe, accurate responses. Experimental evaluation shows high groundedness and accuracy, with a low hallucination rate. Overall, Earthquaker-AI combines hands-on engagement, information processing, and reflective practice. Combining robotics, rubrics, and AI promotes technological literacy, self-regulation, and responsible use of digital systems, contributing to early crisis-management skills.

AI.tldr: Earthquaker-AI integrates Lego WeDo2 robotics with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation assistant to teach earthquake preparedness to primary students via a progressive, rubric-based curriculum that evolves from recognition to action sequences to verbal responses, combining hands-on STEM with AI-guided metacognition.
AI.motivation: Address the need for early crisis-management education, leveraging tangible robotics and AI to foster safety knowledge, self-regulation, and calm decision-making under emergencies; extend a successful STEM project to cognitive and metacognitive processing.
AI.method: Hybrid educational framework: Lego WeDo2-based robotic simulations of seismic responses plus a RAG-based conversational assistant aligned with safety guidelines; progressive assessment rubrics (2D, 3-axis, 4D) across grade bands; dialogic module retrieves official guidelines and provides safe, accurate responses; experimental evaluation on groundedness, accuracy, hallucination rate.
AI.result: High groundedness and accuracy; low hallucination rate; effective integration of robotics, rubrics, and AI to promote technological literacy, self-regulation, and early crisis-management skills.
AI.conclusion: Earthquaker-AI demonstrates a scalable approach to integrate robotics, AI, and assessment for early safety education, fostering cognitive development and responsible digital-system use in crisis contexts.

title: Attention-Free and Lightweight Token Reduction for Efficient Vision-Language Models
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in multimodal understanding, yet remain challenging to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices due to the substantial computational overhead of processing numerous visual tokens. Token reduction is a promising direction for accelerating VLMs inference, but existing approaches either rely on attention maps that are incompatible with modern acceleration frameworks or depend on computationally intensive pairwise similarity comparisons, which undermine scalability and negate their practical benefits in deployment. In this paper, we propose an attention-free and lightweight token reduction framework as a plug-and-play module for VLMs, which preserves both important and diverse tokens to produce a compact visual representation. First, to enable attention-free importance estimation, we adopt an information-theoretic perspective and quantify token information using a novel entropy-based criterion, retaining those with more expressive and less degenerate feature representations. Second, to ensure diverse visual coverage in a lightweight manner, we introduce a transformation-induced consistency signal where similar tokens yield similar signals, such that sorting by this signal places similar tokens close to each other and enables stride-based selection to produce a diverse token set. Extensive experiments across multiple VLMs benchmarks demonstrate that our framework achieves a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, maintaining competitive performance under aggressive compression.

AI.tldr: An attention-free, lightweight token reduction module for vision-language models that preserves informative and diverse tokens for efficient edge deployment, using entropy-based importance and a transformation-induced consistency signal with stride-based selection.
AI.motivation: VLMs suffer from heavy computational overhead due to processing many visual tokens; existing token-reduction methods rely on attention maps (incompatible with accelerators) or expensive pairwise similarity. A fast, plug-and-play solution is needed for edge devices.
AI.method: 1) Entropy-based information criterion to identify expressive, non-degenerate tokens without attention. 2) Transformation-induced consistency signal ensures similar tokens yield similar outputs, enabling sorting and stride-based selection to maintain token diversity with minimal compute.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple VLM benchmarks show the approach achieves a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, maintaining competitive performance under aggressive token compression.
AI.conclusion: An attention-free, plug-and-play token-reduction framework that preserves both important and diverse visual tokens, enabling efficient inference on resource-constrained devices without sacrificing much accuracy.

title: Semantic Anchoring for Robotic Action Representations
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models inherit rich semantic representations from pretrained Vision-Language Models, yet fine-tuning on limited robot demonstrations degrades this structure and undermines generalization. A fundamental question therefore arises: what constitutes a good action representation? Inspired by the mirror neuron theory's insight that observation and execution share an intention-level encoding, we examine whether a robot's action representations preserve the semantic structure captured by pretrained encoders. Systematic probing confirms that this structure erodes during finetuning, and that its quality synchronizes with both task success and out-of-distribution generalization. We further introduce a plug-and-play method that anchors action representations to a semantic manifold while decomposing representations into a shared semantic channel and a private channel, all discarded at inference, leaving the deployed model unchanged. Validated on different VLA backbones across simulation and real-world benchmarks, our method yields up to +18.7% on real-world in-distribution tasks and +21.5% on out-of-distribution generalization.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning degrades pretrained semantic structure in Vision-Language-Action models; a plug-and-play semantic-manifold anchor with a shared/private channel improves both in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance without changing the deployed model.
AI.motivation: To understand what makes a good action representation by testing whether robot action encodings preserve the semantic structure captured by pretrained encoders, inspired by mirror neuron theory that observation and execution share intention-level encoding.
AI.method: Introduce a plug-and-play semantic anchoring method that restricts action representations to a semantic manifold and decomposes them into a shared semantic channel and a private channel, with the private channel discarded at inference. Training-time changes only; deployed model remains unchanged. Evaluated across multiple VLA backbones in both simulation and real-world benchmarks.
AI.result: Systematic probes show the semantic structure erodes during finetuning and its quality tracks task success and OOD generalization. The proposed method yields up to 18.7% gains in real-world in-distribution tasks and 21.5% gains in OOD generalization.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring action representations to a semantic manifold preserves the pretrained semantic structure, improving task performance and generalization without altering the deployed model, demonstrated across backbones and settings.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Anomaly Detection in Banking Transactions: An Internal Audit Perspective
comment: 9 pages, 2 tables. Author's preprint. A revised version of this work has been published in the International Journal of Engineering Development and Research (IJEDR)
summary: The banking sector increasingly relies on automated systems to monitor electronic transactions for signs of fraud, yet conventional rule-based approaches struggle with high false-positive rates and offer no justification for their outputs, limiting their utility for compliance teams. This paper introduces an Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) framework tailored for banking transaction anomaly detection within internal audit workflows. An Isolation Forest (iForest) model performs unsupervised anomaly scoring, while a SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) layer provides transaction-level, feature-attributed explanations grounded in cooperative game theory [8]. A lightweight Streamlit dashboard renders these outputs in a form accessible to audit professionals without machine learning expertise. Evaluation on a synthetic banking dataset yields 0.91 precision and 0.88 recall, outperforming three unsupervised baselines. Expert feedback confirms that feature-level explanations measurably improve auditor confidence and decision quality. The framework advances the practical deployment of accountable, transparent AI in regulated financial environments.

AI.tldr: Explainable AI for banking transaction anomaly detection using iForest with SHAP explanations, evaluated on synthetic data; improved precision/recall vs baselines; auditor-friendly dashboard.
AI.motivation: Reduce false positives and provide rationale for detections to comply with regulatory auditing requirements and to integrate ML outputs into internal audit workflows.
AI.method: Unsupervised Isolation Forest for anomaly scoring; SHAP layer attributes feature-level explanations grounded in cooperative game theory; Streamlit dashboard for accessible visualization to auditors; evaluated on a synthetic banking dataset against three unsupervised baselines.
AI.result: Achieves 0.91 precision and 0.88 recall, outperforming baselines; feature-level explanations improve auditor confidence and decision quality according to expert feedback.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates practical deployment of accountable, transparent AI in regulated financial environments by coupling high-performing anomaly detection with interpretable explanations and audit-facing tooling.

title: Deep Interaction: An Efficient Human-AI Interaction Method for Large Reasoning Models
summary: The emergence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has significantly enhanced the ability of large language models (LLMs) to tackle complex, multi-step tasks. However, when errors occur, current interaction approaches typically involve re-generating another response that may make mistakes again, or users laboriously flag the faulty step in follow-up turns that may get responses <You are right, I made a mistake here> followed by similar errors recurring. To address this issue, we propose an efficient human intervention mechanism for precisely correcting reasoning errors in LLMs, termed Deep Interaction. Our approach enables direct editing of the original response, allowing erroneous parts to be corrected while preserving accurate reasoning steps. We refine the edited CoT into a distilled prompt, which then steers the LLM along the corrected reasoning path. Experimental results show that our method achieves over a 25% improvement in correction success rate and reduces token usage by approximately 40% on STEM tasks reasoning compared to baseline approaches.

AI.tldr: Edit-based correction of chain-of-thought (CoT) outputs, then distill into a prompt to steer the model along corrected reasoning; shows 25% higher correction success and ~40% token savings on STEM tasks.
AI.motivation: CoT improves multi-step reasoning but error propagation remains a bottleneck. Re-generating or flagging errors is inefficient. An editable CoT with prompt distillation offers precise, economical correction.
AI.method: Directly edit the original CoT response to fix erroneous segments while preserving valid reasoning steps; convert the edited reasoning into a distilled prompt that guides the LLM along the corrected path to generate final results.
AI.result: Experimental results indicate >25% improvement in correction success rate and ~40% reduction in token usage on STEM-task reasoning relative to baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: Deep Interaction provides an efficient, precise mechanism for correcting reasoning errors in CoT, reducing user effort and token cost while maintaining or improving reasoning quality.

title: DP-BOA: Dirichlet-Process Birth-or-Assign for On-the-Fly Category Discovery
summary: On-the-fly category discovery requires deciding for each incoming test sample whether to assign it to an existing category or spawn a new one. Existing methods typically implement this decision through matching-based heuristics, such as radius- or hash-based rules. While effective in practice, these methods usually treat category birth implicitly as a fallback when no existing category matches confidently, rather than as an explicit alternative supported by its own statistical evidence. To address this, we propose DP-BOA, a posterior-predictive decision framework based on an online Dirichlet-process Gaussian mixture model with a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior. During training, we use labeled data to calibrate a shared NIW prior over category Gaussians and warm-start the known-category posteriors. At test time, for each incoming sample, DP-BOA compares the posterior predictive evidence for assignment to existing categories against the evidence for spawning a new category induced by the DP prior, and then updates category statistics online after the decision. The method captures anisotropic category geometry and naturally adapts decision confidence as evidence accumulates. Across standard OCD benchmarks, DP-BOA consistently outperforms strong baselines and delivers particularly strong novel-class discovery performance while maintaining competitive known-class accuracy.

AI.tldr: DP-BOA is an online Bayesian framework for open-world category discovery that uses a Dirichlet-process Gaussian mixture with a NIW prior to decide whether to assign an incoming sample to an existing category or create a new one, updating online; it achieves strong novel-class discovery on OCD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing open-set/category discovery methods rely on heuristic matching and treat category birth as a fallback. There is a need for explicit statistical evidence for new-category creation, with the ability to capture anisotropic geometries and to accumulate evidence over time.
AI.method: Train with labeled data to calibrate a shared NIW prior over category Gaussians and warm-start known-category posteriors. At test time, compute posterior predictive evidence for assigning to existing categories versus spawning a new category via the DP prior; decide and update category statistics online. The approach is an online DP-Gaussian mixture model with NIW prior, accommodating anisotropic covariance.
AI.result: DP-BOA consistently outperforms strong baselines on standard OCD benchmarks, with particularly strong performance in novel-class discovery while maintaining competitive accuracy on known classes.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled Bayesian decision framework for open-world (novel-class) discovery, with an explicit birth mechanism, adaptive confidence as evidence accumulates, and effective online updates that capture category geometry; shows practical gains in OCD tasks.

title: An Empirical Study on Stage-Information Interfaces for VLA Fine-Tuning
summary: One high-level instruction in long-horizon manipulation can cover several action stages. We use segmented action annotations as an intermediate representation between the full-task instruction and VLA action chunks. A progress module tracks the active stage, while the action policy receives stage information either as current-stage text or as a normalized ordinal stage index in robot state. We compare these interfaces with GR00T N1.6 on LIBERO-10 under direct fine-tuning and continuation fine-tuning from a full-task instruction baseline. Under direct fine-tuning, full-task instruction, current-stage text, and Ordinal Stage-State achieve mean success rates of 57.45%, 50.24%, and 54.36%, respectively, showing that explicit stage information does not automatically improve the policy. Under continuation, the corresponding means are 49.07%, 50.00%, and 53.75%, with Ordinal Stage-State exceeding both alternatives in all three paired runs. The observed benefit differs across interface representations and training arrangements.

AI.tldr: Segmented, intermediate stage annotations are evaluated as interfaces between full-task instructions and action policies for long-horizon manipulation. Ordinal Stage-State representations outperform current-stage text under continuation fine-tuning from a full-task baseline, while direct fine-tuning shows no universal benefit from explicit stage information.
AI.motivation: To determine whether intermediate stage representations can bridge high-level Instructions and low-level action policies, potentially improving policy performance in long-horizon robotic manipulation.
AI.method: The study uses segmented action annotations as an intermediate representation. A progress module tracks the active stage, and the policy consumes stage information either as current-stage text or as a normalized ordinal stage index embedded in robot state. Comparisons are made against GR00T N1.6 on LIBERO-10 under two regimes: direct fine-tuning from a full-task instruction baseline, and continuation fine-tuning from that baseline.
AI.result: Direct fine-tuning: full-task instruction 57.45%, current-stage text 50.24%, Ordinal Stage-State 54.36%. Continuation fine-tuning: full-task instruction 49.07%, current-stage text 50.00%, Ordinal Stage-State 53.75%. Ordinal Stage-State surpasses both alternatives in all three paired runs under continuation, while under direct fine-tuning the full-task instruction performs best."
AI.conclusion: The benefit of explicit stage information is context-dependent, varying with interface representation and training regime. Ordinal Stage-State offers a clear advantage under continuation fine-tuning, suggesting structured, state-embedded stage representations can be beneficial when leveraging full-task baselines, though benefits are not universal across all training setups.

title: DeepLoop: Depth Scaling for Looped Transformers
summary: Looped Transformers scale sequential computation by applying a compact stack of physical blocks for multiple rounds, increasing unrolled depth without increasing stored parameters. This reuse changes the residual-scaling problem: in an untied Transformer, each residual branch receives and applies its own parameter update, whereas in a looped Transformer one shared update aggregates gradients from repeated visits and is read back by those same visits in the next linearized forward pass. We formalize this tied-depth effect through a first-order perturbation bound controlled by a visit-alignment coefficient $κ_R$. The bound recovers the DeepNorm exponent when visits decorrelate, but in the conservative aligned regime it requires the exponent to increase from $1/4$ to $1/2$ as loop count grows at fixed physical depth. The resulting method, \textbf{DeepLoop}, keeps the Post-LN DeepNorm architecture and sets $α=(2N)^{1/2}$ and $β=(8N)^{-1/2}$ for unrolled depth $N$. On GPT-style looped language models at GPT-2 small and GPT-2 medium scale, DeepLoop is neutral when no physical block is revisited and improves validation loss and downstream accuracy once recurrent depth is activated. These results show that stable recurrent depth requires residual scaling rules that account for parameter visits, not only nominal layer count.

AI.tldr: DeepLoop extends DeepNorm to looped Transformers by introducing visit-aware residual scaling. It uses a first-order perturbation bound with a visit-alignment coefficient κ_R, and prescribes α=(2N)^{1/2}, β=(8N)^{-1/2} for unrolled depth N. Empirically, it is neutral without revisits and improves performance when recurrent depth is activated, highlighting the need to account for parameter visits in residual scaling.
AI.motivation: To address how looped Transformers with shared parameter updates across repeated visits alter residual scaling dynamics, necessitating a formal bound and stable scaling rules that go beyond nominal layer count.
AI.method: Formalize the tied-depth effect via a first-order perturbation bound controlled by a visit-alignment coefficient κ_R. Show that the bound recovers the DeepNorm exponent under decorrelation of visits; in the aligned regime, the exponent must grow from 1/4 to 1/2 with increasing loop count at fixed physical depth. Propose DeepLoop by keeping Post-LN DeepNorm and setting α=(2N)^{1/2}, β=(8N)^{-1/2} for unrolled depth N.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on GPT-2 small and GPT-2 medium looped language models shows DeepLoop is neutral when no physical block is revisited, and yields improvements in validation loss and downstream accuracy once recurrent depth is activated.
AI.conclusion: Residual scaling for stable recurrent depth must account for parameter visits, not just nominal layer count; visit-aware scaling is essential for looped Transformers to maintain training stability and performance.

title: TRACE-PCa: Predicting Prostate Cancer Progression from Longitudinal MRI During Active Surveillance
summary: Active surveillance (AS) is the preferred strategy for favorable-risk prostate cancer, yet current protocols rely on scheduled repeat biopsies, most of which reveal no progression and are unnecessary. Existing risk-stratification tools operate on single time-point imaging or depend on explicit lesion segmentation, limiting their ability to capture longitudinal change and excluding patients without an MRI-visible lesion. In this study, we propose an end-to-end temporal and multimodal model for predicting pathological progression during AS without lesion segmentation. We encode each serial scan with a pretrained 3D MRI foundation model and introduce a temporal attention gate that recalibrates the multi-visit features to amplify focal imaging changes associated with progression. The gated imaging representation is then fused with clinical variables in a multimodal framework to estimate the probability of progression. Validated on a longitudinal AS cohort, our approach consistently outperforms competing baselines and performs comparably to the radiologist assessment representing current clinical practice. It maintains high negative predictive value while achieving higher positive predictive value, demonstrating its potential to safely reduce unnecessary biopsies during surveillance.

AI.tldr: End-to-end temporal multimodal model for predicting pathological progression during active surveillance of prostate cancer, using a pretrained 3D MRI foundation model with a temporal attention gate, without lesion segmentation, fused with clinical data; outperforms baselines and matches radiologist assessment, with improved PPV/NPV, suggesting potential reduction of unnecessary biopsies.
AI.motivation: Current active surveillance protocols rely on scheduled repeat biopsies, many of which are unnecessary. Existing risk tools use single time-point imaging or require lesion segmentation, missing longitudinal changes and excluding MRI-invisible lesions. A method that captures longitudinal imaging changes without segmentation could reduce biopsies while maintaining safety.
AI.method: Encode each serial MRI visit with a pretrained 3D MRI foundation model. Introduce a temporal attention gate to recalibrate multi-visit features, emphasizing imaging changes linked to progression. Fuse the gated imaging representation with clinical variables in a multimodal framework to estimate progression probability. Validate on a longitudinal AS cohort and compare to baselines and radiologist assessment.
AI.result: The proposed approach consistently outperforms competing baselines and achieves performance comparable to radiologist assessment. It maintains high negative predictive value and achieves higher positive predictive value, indicating potential to safely reduce unnecessary biopsies during surveillance.
AI.conclusion: A temporal, multimodal model without lesion segmentation can effectively predict pathological progression in AS for prostate cancer, matching radiologist performance and enabling safer, fewer biopsies during surveillance.

title: Design, Modeling and Experimental Validation of a Miniature Hybrid Underwater Glider With Large-Range Foldable Deflectable Wings
summary: Miniature hybrid underwater gliders have attracted increasing attention for long-endurance ocean observation and confined-space inspection. Large-range wing reconfiguration offers a promising yet largely unexplored approach for simultaneously enhancing maneuverability and shape adaptability in constrained underwater environments. However, such morphing introduces substantial challenges in mechanical integration, dynamic modeling, and hydrodynamic characterization. This paper presents FoDeGlider, a miniature hybrid underwater glider equipped with two independently actuated wings capable of large-range folding and deflection. To capture configuration-dependent variations in mass distribution, center-of-geometry location, and hydrodynamic loading, a multibody dynamics model is developed by treating wing configuration as a structural variable. A composite rigid body algorithm (CRBA)-based projection formulates the composite inertia, wrench transformations, and component-level hydrodynamics into a unified Fossen-form dynamic model applicable to arbitrary wing configurations. A sequential parameter-identification framework is further proposed to estimate fuselage and wing hydrodynamic coefficients, resulting in an open benchmark dataset for model identification and validation. Extensive experiments are conducted, the results of which demonstrate accurate dynamic modeling and parameter identification across diverse morphing configurations. Gate traversal experiments further validate FoDeGlider's ability to actively reconfigure its morphology during locomotion, enabling enhanced navigation in confined underwater environments.

AI.tldr: FoDeGlider introduces a miniature hybrid underwater glider with two independently actuated wings that fold/deflect over a large range; it combines a multibody dynamics model with CRBA-based inertia/hydrodynamics formulation into a Fossen-form dynamic model across morphologies, plus a sequential parameter identification framework and an open dataset; experimental validation confirms modeling accuracy and morphing-enabled navigation in confined spaces.
AI.motivation: Need for long-endurance, highly maneuverable underwater platforms capable of operating in constrained environments; morphing wings promise enhanced maneuverability and adaptability, but pose significant modeling and integration challenges.
AI.method: Represent wing configuration as a structural variable in a multibody dynamics model; use CRBA-based projection to compute composite inertia and hydrodynamic effects; convert to a unified Fossen-form dynamic model for arbitrary morphologies; implement a sequential parameter-identification workflow to estimate hull and wing hydrodynamic coefficients; provide an open benchmark dataset for model identification and validation; perform extensive experiments including morphing during locomotion.
AI.result: Accurate dynamic modeling and parameter identification across diverse morphing configurations; validated by experiments and gate traversal demonstrations showing active morphing improves navigation in confined environments; presence of an open dataset.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables reliable, morphology-dependent dynamics for miniature underwater gliders, enabling efficient, adaptive operation in constrained spaces; suggests practical viability of large-range wing morphing for enhanced control and endurance.

title: A VAE-Driven Multi-Task Satellite-Aided Semantic Communication Framework for 6G-Enabled Connected Autonomous Vehicles
summary: The development of smart transportation systems and the introduction of 6G wireless communication technologies have significantly changed vehicle network topologies. Future connected autonomous vehicle (CAV) networks require bandwidth-efficient, reliable, and low-latency communication for safety-critical applications such as traffic sign recognition and decision-making. Conventional communication systems transmit raw data regardless of task relevance, which is inefficient in resource-constrained satellite channels where uplink bandwidth is scarce and propagation losses are large. Semantic communication addresses this limitation by transmitting task-relevant information instead of full signal representations. It extracts and conveys essential semantic features and leverages deep learning to optimize task performance at the receiver. Therefore, we present a Variational Autoencoder (VAE)-based multi-task semantic communication framework for satellite-assisted autonomous driving. Unlike deterministic autoencoder-based methods, the proposed model uses probabilistic latent representations for more robust and efficient encoding. The learned features are transmitted over noisy wireless channels to perform traffic sign reconstruction and classification. The framework is trained end-to-end to jointly optimize both tasks. Results show that the proposed approach achieves significant bandwidth reduction of up to 87.23\% to 98.17\% while maintaining stable performance across varying signal-to-noise ratio conditions.

AI.tldr: Variational autoencoder-based multi-task semantic communication for satellite-assisted autonomous driving; achieves substantial bandwidth savings by transmitting task-relevant semantic features with probabilistic latent representations, end-to-end trained for traffic sign reconstruction and classification; bandwidth reductions up to ~87–98% with robust performance across SNR.
AI.motivation: In satellite channels with limited uplink bandwidth and high loss, conventional raw-data transmission is inefficient for safety-critical CAV applications; semantic communication can improve efficiency by transmitting task-relevant information.
AI.method: Propose a VAE-based multi-task semantic communication framework; uses probabilistic latent representations; transmits learned features over noisy channels; end-to-end training to jointly optimize traffic sign reconstruction and classification tasks.
AI.result: Bandwidth reduction of 87.23% to 98.17% achieved while maintaining stable performance across varying SNR; demonstrates robustness.
AI.conclusion: Probabilistic latent VAE semantic communication is effective for satellite-assisted CAVs, enabling significant bandwidth savings without sacrificing safety-critical task performance; multi-task end-to-end training yields robust, efficient communication.

title: DriveFace: A Cross-Spectral Through-Glass Face Dataset for On-the-Move Vehicular Border Control
summary: The continuous growth in cross-border mobility places increasing pressure on existing border control infrastructures, motivating on-the-move biometric authentication, in which travellers are identified directly inside their vehicles at checkpoints. Face recognition is well-suited to this setting, as it can be acquired passively and at a distance. Its development, however, is hindered by the lack of representative datasets: existing benchmarks are collected in controlled environments and do not capture the challenges inherent to vehicular acquisition, including motion blur, variable illumination, occlusions, and cross-spectral enrollment. To address this gap, we introduce a dataset for on-the-move face recognition in border-control scenarios, comprising NIR vehicle-crossing videos paired with smartphone-based pre-enrollment data. Baseline evaluations with state-of-the-art models show clear performance limitations under these realistic conditions, highlighting the need for dedicated methods to advance the field.

AI.tldr: Introduces an on-the-move face recognition dataset for border-control scenarios using NIR vehicle-crossing videos and smartphone pre-enrollment data; reveals performance gaps of state-of-the-art models in realistic conditions, underscoring need for specialized methods.
AI.motivation: Growing cross-border mobility pressures demand passively acquired biometric identification inside moving vehicles at checkpoints. Existing benchmarks rely on controlled settings and fail to capture vehicular challenges (motion blur, variable illumination, occlusions, cross-spectral enrollment). A representative dataset is needed to drive method development.
AI.method: Dataset creation: NIR vehicle-crossing videos paired with smartphone-based pre-enrollment data. Baseline evaluations performed with state-of-the-art face recognition models to establish performance under realistic border-control conditions.
AI.result: Baseline evaluations show clear performance limitations of current models under motion, lighting, occlusions, and cross-spectral enrollment scenarios, highlighting the need for dedicated methods.
AI.conclusion: The dataset fills a gap for evaluating on-the-move border-control recognition and provides a benchmark to motivate the development of methods tailored to vehicular acquisition and cross-spectral enrollment.

title: From Language to Navigation Goals: A Vision-Language Approach for Semantic Navigation of Mobile Robots Using RGB-D Perception
summary:
Natural language interaction provides an intuitive way for non-expert users to communicate with robotic platforms. However, transforming user requests into executable navigation actions remains a challenging task, requiring the integration of language understanding, environment perception, and autonomous navigation. This work presents a language-driven navigation framework that enables mobile robots to interpret user requests in natural language to move the robot to a destination and autonomously navigate towards it.
  The framework is composed of modular ROS 2 components that cooperate to transform natural language instructions into navigation actions. Given a natural language request referring to a target in the environment (e.g., "go to the mail box"), the system identifies the referenced object, estimates its position using RGB-D data, and generates a navigation goal, which is then executed through the ROS 2 Nav2 navigation stack. The ROS 2-based implementation facilitates portability across different robotic platforms, requiring only the configuration of the corresponding topics and services.
  The system is evaluated in both simulation and real-world scenarios using a TurtleBot3 Waffle and a Unitree Go2 robot with a RealSense camera. Experimental results show that the framework successfully interprets both direct commands and contextual requests, generates meaningful natural-language feedback, and navigates towards the desired target. These results demonstrate the feasibility of combining semantic perception and autonomous navigation to provide an intuitive human-robot interaction paradigm. Code will be released as open source upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: A modular ROS 2 framework translating natural language requests into navigation actions by detecting referents, localizing them with RGB-D, and issuing Nav2 goals; demonstrated on TurtleBot3 and Unitree Go2; open-source planned.
AI.motivation: To lower the barrier for non-experts to command mobile robots via natural language by integrating language understanding, perception, and autonomous navigation.
AI.method: Modular ROS 2 components: natural-language parsing to identify the target; referent grounding and pose estimation using RGB-D data; generation of a navigation goal; execution through the ROS 2 Nav2 stack; ability to provide natural-language feedback; portable across platforms via configurable topics/services.
AI.result: Evaluated in simulation and real-world with TurtleBot3 Waffle and Unitree Go2 (RealSense). The framework successfully interprets direct and contextual commands, generates meaningful natural-language feedback, and navigates to the target. Demonstrates feasibility of combining semantic perception and autonomous navigation for intuitive HRI; code to be released as open source upon acceptance.
AI.conclusion: Shows that integrating semantic perception with autonomous navigation enables intuitive language-driven HRI for mobile robots; modular, ROS 2-based architecture supports cross-platform deployment and open-source dissemination.

title: Factorized Spectral Representations for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Learning a compact model of the world from interaction data is central to sample-efficient deep reinforcement learning. Spectral representation methods have become the leading paradigm for representation learning in continuous control by taking a matrix view of the transition kernel, with state-action pairs on one side and next states on the other, and learning a low-rank factorization through self-supervised contrastive objectives. We take this view one step further. The transition kernel is naturally a three-mode tensor over states, actions, and next states, and a CP decomposition gives one feature map per mode. We propose FaStR, which fits this decomposition with a noise contrastive objective, producing separate state, action, and next-state encoders that together form a single spectral representation. The factored form yields a smaller hypothesis class, and the sample size needed for representation learning shrinks by a factor that scales with the smaller of the state and action dimensions. Empirically, FaStR delivers its largest gains on high-dimensional locomotion tasks whose dynamics align with the factored structure, and the learned state encoder transfers intact across actuator shift while only the action encoder is retrained.

AI.tldr: FaStR extends spectral RL representations to a three-way (state, action, next-state) transition view, fitting a CP decomposition with a noise-contrastive objective to produce separate state, action, and next-state encoders that combine into a single spectral representation. This yields a smaller hypothesis class and improved sample efficiency, especially when the dynamics are factored, and enables transfer of the state encoder across actuator shifts with retraining limited to the action encoder.
AI.motivation: Spectral methods in continuous control typically treat the transition kernel as a 2D matrix (state-action vs next state). However, the true transition tensor is three-mode (state, action, next state). Exploiting this structure with a CP decomposition can reduce the hypothesis class, potentially lowering sample complexity and enabling modular transfer of representations.
AI.method: Propose FaStR, which fits a CP decomposition of the three-mode transition kernel using a noise-contrastive objective. This yields separate encoders for states, actions, and next states that together constitute a unified spectral representation. The method leverages the factored form to shrink the required sample size, scaling with the smaller of state/action dimensions.
AI.result: Empirically, FaStR delivers the largest gains on high-dimensional locomotion tasks where the dynamics align with factored structure. The learned state encoder transfers intact across actuator shift, while only the action encoder requires retraining.
AI.conclusion: Factored CP-based spectral representations reduce the effective hypothesis class and improve sample efficiency in RL when the transition dynamics are amenable to a state-action-next-state factorization. The approach also supports modular transfer, notably preserving the state encoder across actuator changes with selective retraining of the action encoder.

title: VGIF-Score: Interpretable and Diagnostic Evaluation of Spatio-Temporal Instruction Following in Video Generation
summary: Recent video generation models (VGMs) have made substantial progress in visual fidelity, yet their ability to follow long, compositional instructions remains insufficiently evaluated. Existing evaluation protocols often rely on prompts that are short and semantically shallow, with limited atomic constraints and weak spatio-temporal dependencies. They also frequently depend on costly human evaluation or handcrafted vision pipelines, while providing little diagnostic insight into which instruction constraints succeed or fail. To address this gap, we propose VGIF-Score, a highly automated and interpretable framework for evaluating instruction following in video generation. VGIF-Score consists of two complementary components: an objective completion branch that parses prompts into a Spatio-Temporal Directed Acyclic Graph (ST-DAG) and performs dependency-aware QA with short-circuit diagnostics, and a subjective satisfaction branch that uses instruction-conditioned AutoRubric to assess cinematography, visual purity, motion smoothness, and physics adherence. Together, these components produce a unified score that captures both objective completion and perceptual satisfaction. We instantiate this framework on VGIF-Bench, a benchmark of 223 long, structurally entangled prompts paired with approximately 4.3K fine-grained evaluation items. Experiments on 14 proprietary and open-source VGMs across more than 3K generated videos show that VGIF-Score provides reliable, interpretable, and diagnostically useful evaluation of video generation instruction following. The code will be available at https://github.com/PRIS-CV/VGIF-SCORE.

AI.tldr: VGIF-Score: an automated, interpretable framework to evaluate instruction-following in long-form video generation via objective ST-DAG parsing plus subjective AutoRubric, validated on VGIF-Bench with 3k+ videos across 14 VGMs; provides diagnostic insights.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation protocols rely on short prompts, limited atomic constraints, and expensive human evaluation, offering little diagnostic insight into constraint success/failure. A scalable, interpretable framework is needed to assess instruction following in video generation.
AI.method: Two-branch approach: (1) objective completion branch parses prompts into a Spatio-Temporal Directed Acyclic Graph (ST-DAG) and performs dependency-aware QA with short-circuit diagnostics; (2) subjective satisfaction branch uses instruction-conditioned AutoRubric to assess cinematography, visual purity, motion smoothness, and physics adherence. Produces a unified score.
AI.result: VGIF-Score yields reliable, interpretable, and diagnostically useful evaluation of instruction following in VGMs. Tested on 14 VGMs over 3K+ generated videos, on VGIF-Bench (223 long, structurally entangled prompts and ~4.3K evaluation items). Code will be released at the provided URL.
AI.conclusion: VGIF-Score provides a robust, interpretable diagnostic tool for instruction-following in video generation, enabling both objective completion assessment and perceptual satisfaction, with broad applicability to long-horizon prompts and structured evaluation.

title: Design and Control of the "QuadBoat": A Quadruped Surface Vehicle for Drowning Rescue
summary: Prompt extraction of victims from water is crucial in water surface rescue missions. However, previous research on rescue robots has seldom addressed this issue. This paper presents QuadBoat, a bio-inspired unmanned surface vehicle (USV) designed to track and retrieve victims from water. QuadBoat features a quadrupedal robot configuration, enabling it with highly adaptable and agile maneuverability through its actively adjustable posture. Employing an inverse kinematics-based controller and cascaded model predictive control (MPC)-PID controller for overall movement, QuadBoat can accurately track and retrieve objects on the water surface. Maneuverability demonstrations validate QuadBoat's high agility, while a series of tracking experiments, including leg action tracking and trajectory tracking, confirm its high motion accuracy and system mobility. Finally, visual-based tracking and object pickup experiments further verify QuadBoat's target tracking capabilities and its effectiveness in executing rescues, both indoors and outdoors.

AI.tldr: QuadBoat is a bio-inspired quadrupedal unmanned surface vehicle designed to rapidly locate and retrieve victims on water surfaces using IK-based control and a cascaded MPC-PID controller, demonstrating high agility and accurate tracking both indoors and outdoors.
AI.motivation: Prompt victim extraction from water is critical in water surface rescue; existing rescue robots provide limited agility and adaptability on water; a biologically inspired, adjustable-leg USV could enhance maneuverability and pickup accuracy.
AI.method: QuadBoat employs a quadrupedal configuration with actively adjustable posture; an inverse-kinematics-based controller guides leg-like actuators; a cascaded MPC-PID framework controls overall motion; experiments include leg action tracking, trajectory tracking, and visual-based tracking with object pickup; tests conducted indoors and outdoors.
AI.result: Showed high agility in maneuverability demonstrations; accurate leg action and trajectory tracking; effective visual tracking and object pickup confirming rescue capability in varied environments.
AI.conclusion: QuadBoat demonstrates effective victim-tracking and water-surface rescue capabilities; the combination of IK-based control and cascaded MPC-PID supports precise, agile operation; further work could address robustness, stability under waves, and real-world deployment.

title: CDS: Counterfactual Directionality Score for Structured Interventions in Spatial Graphs
summary: Quantifying directional influence between node populations is a fundamental problem in graph-based modeling, particularly in spatial biological systems where cell-cell interactions shape functional outcomes. Existing approaches based on attention, attribution, or correlation capture associations but do not provide a principled framework for evaluating directional effects under controlled perturbations. We introduce a framework for structured counterfactual interventions in graph-based models to estimate directional influence between node types. Our approach trains a Neighbor Influence Model (NIM) to predict node states from local neighborhoods and applies constrained interventions that modify neighborhood composition while preserving key spatial and structural properties. We define the Counterfactual Directionality Score (CDS), which measures the change in predicted node state induced by targeted perturbations, and provide a theoretical interpretation of CDS as a finite-difference measure of local intervention sensitivity. To obtain valid uncertainty estimates, we introduce a core-level bootstrap procedure that accounts for dependencies within spatial samples. Experiments on synthetic spatial graphs with known directional structure show that CDS recovers directional influence, remains well calibrated under null conditions, and is robust to confounding signals, while preliminary results on spatial transcriptomics data reveal biologically plausible and consistent interactions across tissue cores.

AI.tldr: A principled framework for estimating directional influence in graph-based spatial models via counterfactual interventions; introduces a Neighbor Influence Model (NIM), Counterfactual Directionality Score (CDS), and a core-level bootstrap; validated on synthetic graphs and spatial transcriptomics.
AI.motivation: Existing methods (attention, attribution, or correlation) capture associations but do not provide a principled, perturbation-based measure of directional effects in spatial graphs under controlled perturbations.
AI.method: Train a Neighbor Influence Model (NIM) to predict node states from local neighborhoods; apply constrained, structure-preserving interventions that modify neighborhood composition; define Counterfactual Directionality Score (CDS) as a finite-difference measure of how targeted perturbations alter predicted states; introduce a core-level bootstrap to obtain valid uncertainty estimates accounting for dependencies in spatial samples.
AI.result: CDS recovers directional influence, is well-calibrated under null conditions, and robust to confounding signals in synthetic tests; preliminary results on spatial transcriptomics show biologically plausible and consistent interactions across tissue cores.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled, perturbation-based framework to quantify directional influence in graph-based spatial systems; CDS offers an interpretable directional metric; validated on synthetic data with promising preliminary results on real biological data, warranting further validation across datasets.

title: ThinkBLOX: 3D Indoor Scene Generation with Progressive Reasoning
summary: While traditional graphics methods often synthesize 3D indoor scenes autoregressively or hierarchically, recent vision-language model (VLM)-based generators predominantly adopt a one-shot paradigm where the full layout is planned at once. This one-shot approach often requires global re-optimization or complete reconstruction during interactive editing (e.g., inserting or moving objects) and can lead to physically or semantically poorly organized arrangements. To address these challenges, we propose ThinkBLOX, a VLM-based progressive reasoning framework that iteratively designs and refines 3D scenes. ThinkBLOX treats layout generation as a state-conditioned, step-by-step reasoningand-action process. To power this, we construct the ThinkBLOX-Data-200K dataset, containing 224,757 procedural placement pairs annotated with multi-view scene context, explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rationales, and structured JSON layouts. Through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on this dataset, the VLM learns to bridge the reasoning-action gap under incremental updates. Furthermore, recognizing that scene synthesis is inherently a multisolution task where SFT suffers from reward conflict, we introduce Tier-Decoupled GDPO. This reinforcement learning scheme organizes heterogeneous rewards into distinct tiers, stabilizing policy optimization across physical validity, semantic plausibility, and reasoning-action consistency. Extensive experiments show that ThinkBLOX significantly outperforms recent one-shot and iterative baselines in physical plausibility, semantic alignment, and interactive editability. Additionally, we show that it supports diverse applications, including both global and local generation and rearrangement of 3D scenes.

AI.tldr: A progressive, state-conditioned VLM-based 3D scene generator (ThinkBLOX) that uses iterative reasoning-and-action loops, a CoT-annotated dataset, and tiered GDPO RL to improve physical plausibility, semantic alignment, and interactive editability over one-shot methods.
AI.motivation: One-shot (global) VLM-based generation often requires full re-optimization or reconstruction during interactive edits, leading to physically/semantically incoherent arrangements. Progressive, reasoning-guided design aims to improve scene organization and editability.
AI.method: ThinkBLOX enables step-by-step reasoning-action cycles with a ThinkBLOX-Data-200K dataset (224,757 procedural placement pairs; multi-view context; explicit Chain-of-Thought rationales; structured JSON layouts). It uses supervised fine-tuning to bridge reasoning-action gaps and Tier-Decoupled GDPO reinforcement learning to stabilize optimization with tiered rewards for physical validity, semantic plausibility, and reasoning-action consistency.
AI.result: Experiments show ThinkBLOX outperforms recent one-shot and iterative baselines in physical plausibility, semantic alignment, and interactive editability; supports global and local generation and rearrangement of 3D scenes across diverse applications.
AI.conclusion: Progressive, reasoned scene synthesis with structured data and tiered RL yields robust, editable 3D scene generation, addressing limitations of one-shot approaches and enabling multiple generation/editing modes.

title: Anatomy of Uncertainty: Expressive Descriptors of Robotic Manipulator Motion for Non-verbal Communication in Human-Robot Collaboration
summary: Robots operating in human-robot collaboration must communicate not only their intended actions but also uncertainty arising from incomplete or ambiguous perception. This work introduces a mathematical framework for expressing perceptual uncertainty through robotic manipulator motion. Drawing on Laban Movement Analysis, robot behavior is organized in a Commitment-Vigilance state space that maps uncertainty-related states - confidence, curiosity, hesitance, fear, and inactivity - to distinct Laban Effort signatures. Five motion primitives - approach, pause, retreat, exploration, and oscillation - are then parameterized using eleven kinematic and geometric descriptors, including acceleration, pause and retreat characteristics, gaze angles, tilt, and shiver amplitude. A video-based human-subject study evaluated recognition of four expressive trajectories and the influence of individual descriptors on perceived intensity. Participants reliably identified the intended behavioral states, while several descriptors significantly modulated expressiveness. The results establish a perceptually grounded basis for encoding robot uncertainty in motion and support future autonomous trajectory generation using parametric movement representations for collaborative tasks in shared environments. Code, videos, questionnaire and appendices are available at "https://bit.ly/github-aou".

AI.tldr: A perceptual framework for encoding robotic uncertainty in human-robot collaboration by mapping perceptual states to Laban movement patterns; introduces five motion primitives parameterized by 11 descriptors and validated via a video-based study on trajectory expressiveness.
AI.motivation: To enable robots to communicate uncertainty to human collaborators through motion, addressing ambiguity in perception and intent during shared tasks.
AI.method: Define a Commitment–Vigilance state space with states: confidence, curiosity, hesitance, fear, inactivity; map these to distinct Laban Effort signatures. Specify five motion primitives (approach, pause, retreat, exploration, oscillation) parameterized by 11 kinematic/geometric descriptors (e.g., acceleration, pause/retreat dynamics, gaze angles, tilt, shiver amplitude). Conduct a video-based human-subject study evaluating recognition of four expressive trajectories and assess how descriptors influence perceived intensity.
AI.result: Participants reliably recognized the intended behavioral states; several descriptors significantly modulated expressiveness; the work provides a perceptually grounded basis for encoding perceptual uncertainty in motion and supports future trajectory-generation for collaborative tasks.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a principled, perceptually grounded approach to express robotic uncertainty via motion, enabling parametric, human-friendly trajectory generation for shared autonomy in collaborative settings; code and materials are provided for replication.

title: ExTernD: Expanded-Rank Ternary Decomposition Ternary LLM PTQ with Accuracy Approaching Any Quantization Level
summary: We introduce ExTernD (Expanded-rank Ternary Decomposition), a post-training factorization of each LLM weight matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ into $A \approx B \mathrm{diag}(D) C$ with ternary factors $B \in \{-1,0,+1\}^{m \times k}$, $C \in \{-1,0,+1\}^{k \times n}$ and a real scale vector $D \in \mathbb{R}^k$. The inner rank $k = μ\min(m,n)$ is deliberately expanded beyond full rank ($μ> 1$), so that components past full rank correct the quantization error of earlier ones. We prove the residual decreases monotonically in $k$ and can be driven below any $\varepsilon > 0$: ExTernD approaches bf16 accuracy arbitrarily closely, which no ternary scheme with a fixed plane count can do. Memory and compute scale continuously with $μ$, and factor sparsity continuously with a threshold $τ$, so an accuracy target is hit exactly rather than rounded to the next bit-width. ExTernD matches Q4_K's per-matrix accuracy at 5.2-5.5 effective bpw (5.1-5.5 with importance weighting) on Gemma-4-E2B and Qwen3.5-4B, and a full Qwen3.5-4B conversion at $μ= 3$ reaches 10.10 wikitext-2 perplexity against 9.78 for bf16 (+3.2%), placing it near the Q4_K/Q5_K accuracy band at ~5.7 effective bpw.

AI.tldr: Post-training, expanded-rank ternary factorization of LLM weight matrices: A ≈ B diag(D) C with B,C ternary, D real; expands rank beyond full to iteratively reduce quantization error, approaching bf16 accuracy; scalable memory/computation via μ and sparsity via τ; achieves competitive accuracy on large models (Q4_K/Q5_K band).
AI.motivation: To achieve high-accuracy weight quantization for LLMs using ternary factors while overcoming fixed-plane limitations, enabling closer bf16 performance with controllable memory and sparsity.
AI.method: Factor each weight matrix A into B diag(D) C where B,C ∈ {−1,0,+1} and D∈R^k; increase inner rank k = μ min(m,n) with μ>1; prove monotonic decrease of residual with k and existence of ε-near bf16 accuracy; introduce sparsity via threshold τ and adjust μ for memory/computation; evaluate on Gemma-4-E2B and Qwen3.5-4B.
AI.result: The residual can be driven below any ε>0; achieves bf16-like accuracy; matches Q4_K per-matrix accuracy at ~5.2–5.5 effective bpw (5.1–5.5 with weighting); full Qwen3.5-4B conversion at μ=3 achieves perplexity 10.10 vs 9.78 bf16 on wikitext-2; places near Q4_K/Q5_K accuracy band at ~5.7 bpw.
