AI.motivation: To address limitations of purely reactive or purely cognitive strategies for localising intermittent chemical plumes by combining fast, reactive behaviours with robust belief-driven planning; reduce exploration and manual tuning.
AI.method: Introduce a detection-triggered switching mechanism that transitions between crossflow exploration (reactive) and source-directed motion (exploitation). Parameterise behavioural switches from belief metrics, eliminating manual tuning, and integrate bio-inspired reactivity into belief-based planning.
AI.result: Simulations across three turbulence regimes and field tests with an autonomous surface vehicle in the Mondego River show up to 50% reduction in travelled distance, 86% localisation success, and 3.2 m average localisation error.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid approach yields adaptive reactivity grounded in belief metrics, improving efficiency and robustness for chemical source localisation without manual parameter tuning.

title: Maximally Robust Satisficing Bayesian Optimization
comment: Accepted to the Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI) 2026
summary: Many design tasks can be cast as black-box function optimization, enabling use of Bayesian optimization to find an ideal design with minimal number of trials. However, often we do not actually need the optimum but instead a sufficiently good solution is enough, for instance a material that is durable enough for its intended use. In most cases there are multiple satisfactory solutions, forming a superlevel set of the function, raising a key question of which one to prefer. We answer this by explaining why robustness to input perturbations that may occur when the solution is deployed is a good criterion and by introduce a Bayesian optimization method that efficiently finds satisficing solutions that are robust to maximally large perturbations. In contrast to previous works, we assume the inputs can be accurately controlled during optimization, but will be perturbed after the deployment.

AI.tldr: Bayesian optimization for robust satisficing under perturbations; finds designs in the performance superlevel set that remain acceptable under maximal input perturbations, assuming controllable design variables during optimization.
AI.motivation: In many design tasks, a sufficiently good solution is preferable to the exact optimum; selecting among multiple satisfactory designs requires considering robustness to deployment perturbations.
AI.method: A Bayesian optimization framework that targets robust-satisficing over a defined perturbation set. It models performance under perturbations, and uses an acquisition strategy that seeks high performance within the superlevel set while maximizing robustness to the worst-case perturbation.
AI.result: The proposed approach efficiently locates robust satisficing solutions with fewer evaluations and demonstrates improved robustness to deployment perturbations compared to non-robust baselines.
AI.conclusion: Robust satisficing via Bayesian optimization provides a practical design criterion under deployment disturbances, leveraging controllable optimization inputs to focus search on stable, satisfactory designs.

title: FreeLit: Paired-Free Indoor Relighting via Physics-Guided Diffusion
comment: Accepted to ACM Multimedia (ACM MM) 2026. This is the accepted manuscript prior to publication
summary:
Image-based indoor scene relighting remains challenging due to the complex interplay between cluttered geometry and local illumination, requiring precise modeling of light position, color, and intensity. Existing data-driven methods implicitly learn this relationship via paired multi-illumination datasets. Nevertheless, this data is costly and fails to scale, which is essential for accurate light-source-level control. Conversely, inverse-rendering methods reduce the data dependency by incorporating physical priors; however, they lack the robustness of intrinsic estimation in challenging conditions.
  In this paper, we present FreeLit, a paired-free framework for controllable indoor relighting that explicitly manipulates light-source location, color, and intensity. Instead of relying on paired supervision, we construct a physics-guided illumination prior from intrinsic scene properties, generating a structured lightmap along with a pseudo-relit image to guide diffusion-based synthesis. To address instability in intrinsic estimation, especially in low-light scenes, we introduce a relighting-guided intrinsic stabilization strategy that enforces illumination-invariant reflectance through structure-aware distillation and consistency constraints. Furthermore, we propose controllability-oriented evaluation metrics to quantify alignment with user-specified illumination color and intensity. Experimental results demonstrate that FreeLit achieves stable, physically consistent, and controllable relighting, with improved robustness in low-light indoor scenes, without requiring paired supervision.

AI.tldr: FreeLit offers a paired-free, physics-guided indoor relighting method that jointly constructs a lightmap/pseudo-relit and uses diffusion with intrinsic stabilization to achieve controllable, robust relighting without paired data.
AI.motivation: Paired multi-illumination data for indoor relighting is costly and does not scale. Inverse-rendering approaches reduce data needs but struggle with robustness in challenging or low-light conditions. A data-efficient, controllable framework is needed.
AI.method: Build a physics-guided illumination prior to generate a structured lightmap and a pseudo-relit image to guide diffusion-based synthesis. Address instability in intrinsic estimation with a relighting-guided intrinsic stabilization strategy that enforces illumination-invariant reflectance via structure-aware distillation and consistency constraints. Propose controllability-oriented evaluation metrics to quantify alignment with user-specified illumination color and intensity.
AI.result: Experiments show stable, physically plausible, and controllable relighting, with improved robustness in low-light indoor scenes, without requiring paired supervision.
AI.conclusion: FreeLit provides a robust, controllable relighting framework that reduces data dependency and improves performance under challenging conditions, presenting a practical alternative to paired-supervision methods.

title: Learning Forward & Reverse Skills from a Single Unfinished Demonstration for Constrained Manipulation Tasks
summary: Learning from demonstration (LfD) enables robots to learn manipulation skills directly from expert demonstrations but remains challenging for contact-rich tasks involving geometric constraints and force interaction. Existing approaches typically require multiple complete demonstrations and do not support reverse skill execution. In this paper, we present a unified one-shot framework for constrained manipulation that learns both forward and reverse execution from a single, possibly unfinished demonstration. Our method decomposes demonstrations into non-contact and contact phases, with non-contact motion encoded with dynamic movement primitives (DMP), and contact motion represented as a sequence of screw motion primitives segmented by our proposed geometry-driven twist-direction segmentation algorithm. During execution, screw primitives are executed sequentially under admittance-guided pose correction and speed regulation, enabling task completion beyond the demonstrated trajectory length as well as reverse skill execution without additional learning data. Experiments on peg insertion, battery insertion, lock opening, and screw driving tasks demonstrate improved success rates and robustness over segmentation and one-shot trajectory learning baselines. Details are available on the project website: https://tuwien-asl.github.io/LfD-Screw/.

AI.tldr: One-shot framework for constrained manipulation enabling forward and reverse execution from a single, possibly unfinished demonstration, using non-contact DMPs and contact screw primitives with geometry-driven twist-direction segmentation and admittance-guided execution.
AI.motivation: LfD on contact-rich tasks is data-hungry, struggles with incomplete demonstrations, and lacks reverse skill execution; a unified one-shot approach is needed for robust, extendable manipulation under geometric constraints.
AI.method: Split demonstrations into non-contact and contact phases. Non-contact motion is encoded with Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMP); contact motion uses a sequence of screw motion primitives segmented by a geometry-driven twist-direction algorithm. Execution applies sequential screw primitives under admittance-guided pose correction and speed regulation, enabling completion beyond the demonstrated trajectory and enabling reverse skill execution without extra data.
AI.result: Experiments on peg insertion, battery insertion, lock opening, and screw driving show improved success rates and robustness compared with segmentation and one-shot trajectory learning baselines.
AI.conclusion: Introduces a unified one-shot approach for constrained manipulation that supports forward and reverse execution from a single demonstration, with demonstrated robustness and applicability to several contact-rich manipulation tasks.

title: The Hyperspherical Geometry of CLIP Latent Space: A Semantic Mixture Model
summary: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) representations form a semantic embedding space governed by cosine similarity, reflecting an intrinsic hyperspherical geometry. However, existing probabilistic interpretations typically rely on Gaussian assumptions, which fail to capture this directional and multimodal structure. We propose a principled density model for the CLIP latent space based on Mixtures of von Mises-Fisher (MovMF) distributions defined on the unit hypersphere. Using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, we efficiently learn a probabilistic model in which each mixture component corresponds to a coherent semantic concept. This formulation yields a closed-form likelihood naturally aligned with hyperspherical geometry, enabling accurate and interpretable density estimation. Empirically, our model significantly improves long-tailed and out-of-distribution detection and provides a natural semantic decomposition, representing each embedding as a sparse probabilistic combination of interpretable concepts. These results suggest that CLIP latent space is more faithfully characterized as a hyperspherical semantic mixture rather than an isotropic Gaussian, establishing a simple and geometrically consistent probabilistic framework for modeling and understanding multimodal representations. Project page is available at https://xiaoyuzhizi.github.io/movmf-clip/.

AI.tldr: A hyperspherical probabilistic model for CLIP: MovMF mixtures on the unit sphere learned via EM, offering interpretable semantic components and improved OOD/long-tail detection over Gaussian baselines.
AI.motivation: CLIP embeddings lie on the unit hypersphere with directional and multimodal structure; Gaussian assumptions fail to capture geometry and multimodality, motivating a spherical mixture model for principled density estimation.
AI.method: Mixtures of von Mises-Fisher distributions on the unit hypersphere (MovMF) with EM learning. Each mixture component corresponds to a coherent semantic concept; closed-form hyperspherical likelihood enables dense probabilistic density estimation; results include sparse, interpretable combination of concepts.
AI.result: Improved long-tail and out-of-distribution detection; natural semantic decomposition with embeddings represented as sparse probabilistic mixtures of interpretable concepts; better alignment with hyperspherical geometry than isotropic Gaussians.
AI.conclusion: CLIP latent space is better modeled as a hyperspherical semantic mixture rather than a Gaussian; MovMF provides a simple, geometrically consistent probabilistic framework for multimodal representations and density estimation.

title: Fine-grained CLIP fine-tuning with self-annotated region alignment
summary: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) has been shown to have limitations in its fine-grained dense feature representation, due to its pre-training focusing on matching the whole image to a text description. Considering the large data and computational burden in pre-training a vision-language model from scratch, a series of works aim to enhance the fine-grained ability of CLIP through a fine-tuning scheme. However, existing works suffer from a variety of limitations: additional region annotations are usually required, which limits the semantic diversity due to the predefined categories and leads to a large effort to process the training data; and they usually sacrifice CLIP's original ability for global visual representation. To bypass these limitations, we propose SFF-CLIP (Self-annotated Fine-grained Fine-tuning for CLIP), which only uses image-text pairs as input to boost the fine-grained representation ability in the CLIP fine-tuning, while maintaining the global visual-semantic consistency. Concretely, a run-time region-phrase alignment scheme is designed, which obtains concept phrases from the input sentence, and aligns them with corresponding extracted region-based features using text-specific heat maps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SFF-CLIP leads to significant performance improvements on fine-grained dense feature representation, as well as maintaining the performance of the original CLIP on image-level tasks. Code will be released later.

AI.tldr: SFF-CLIP introduces a self-annotated, fine-grained fine-tuning approach that uses runtime region-phrase alignment from the input text to align with region-based features, improving dense representations while preserving CLIP’s image-level performance, using only image-text pairs.
AI.motivation: CLIP’s dense, fine-grained representation is weak because pre-training targets whole-image–text matching. Obtaining region annotations is costly and restricts semantic diversity, and fine-tuning often harms global CLIP quality. A lightweight, annotation-free method is needed to boost local alignments without sacrificing global vision-language consistency.
AI.method: During fine-tuning, extract concept phrases from the input sentence, compute region-based features from the image, and align phrases with regions using text-specific heat maps. This run-time region-phrase alignment leverages only image-text pairs (no extra region annotations) to improve dense feature representations while preserving global image-level CLIP performance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show significant gains in fine-grained dense feature representation and no degradation of the original CLIP’s image-level tasks.
AI.conclusion: SFF-CLIP provides a scalable, annotation-free path to enhance CLIP’s fine-grained representation without sacrificing global vision-language alignment, with code to be released later.

title: S-squared-VLA: Decoupling Semantic and Spatial Streams in Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential for high-level reasoning in autonomous driving, yet they fundamentally struggle to generate precise, low-level control actions. This limitation is rooted in a semantic-physical gap caused by the inherent mismatch between discrete language tokens and continuous trajectory planning. While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures attempt to bridge this gap by unifying perception and control into a single policy, this entanglement creates a new bottleneck. Standard VLAs experience a severe spatial representation collapse, which irreversibly degrades the fine-grained spatial and geometric priors essential for safe, boundary-aware navigation. To address this limitation, we propose the S-squared-VLA, which explicitly decouples the semantic and spatial streams in Vision-Language-Action models. The semantic stream leverages hierarchical bridging to extract multi-scale VLM features for robust intent reasoning. In parallel, an independent spatial stream bypasses the autoregressive language bottleneck, directly preserving uncompressed spatial features from the visual encoder. By integrating auxiliary perception supervision, this stream explicitly equips the model with rich spatial and geometric priors. Finally, a dual-stream planning adapter fuses high-level semantic intent with precise spatial constraints via cascaded attention mechanisms. Evaluations on the NAVSIM closed-loop benchmark show that S-squared-VLA achieves a Predictive Driver Model Score (PDMS) of 87.1, establishing a new state-of-the-art for VLA models under a purely supervised fine-tuning (SFT) setting. By mitigating the spatial representation collapse of traditional VLMs, our framework significantly outperforms baselines, achieving the highest No Collision (NC) rate of 98.4 among all evaluated methods.

AI.tldr: A decoupled dual-stream Vision-Language-Action (S-squared-VLA) approach improves low-level control in autonomous driving by separating semantic reasoning from spatial perception, addressing spatial representation collapse. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM in SFT settings (PDMS 87.1; No Collision 98.4).
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action models entangle semantic and spatial information, causing a semantic-physical gap and a collapse of fine-grained spatial priors essential for boundary-aware navigation. Decoupling streams is proposed to preserve spatial priors while enabling robust intent reasoning.
AI.method: Introduce S-squared-VLA with two streams: (1) semantic stream using hierarchical bridging to extract multi-scale VLM features for intent reasoning; (2) independent spatial stream that preserves uncompressed spatial features from the visual encoder and uses auxiliary perception supervision to inject spatial/geometric priors. A dual-stream planning adapter fuses high-level semantic intent with precise spatial constraints via cascaded attention.
AI.result: On NAVSIM closed-loop benchmark, PDMS = 87.1, achieving a new state-of-the-art for VLA models under supervised fine-tuning. No Collision rate reaches 98.4, outperforming baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicit decoupling of semantic and spatial streams mitigates spatial representation collapse, yielding improved perception-control alignment and safety in VLA-based autonomous navigation; the dual-stream design with hierarchical bridging and auxiliary supervision demonstrates strong empirical gains.

title: Optimal and Efficient Contextual Combinatorial Semi-bandits with General Function Approximation
comment: 59 pages (11 pages main body, 17 pages supplementary materials)
summary: We study the contextual combinatorial semi-bandit (CCSB) problem with general reward function approximation. At each round, the learner observes a context, selects a combinatorial action consisting of a subset of basic arms, and receives the reward of each selected arm; the goal is to maximize the cumulative reward over time. We propose SquareCB.Comb, a computationally efficient algorithm that, at each round, solves a convex optimization problem to sample a combinatorial action that balances exploration and exploitation. SquareCB.Comb scales to large arm sets and imposes no structural assumptions on the action set beyond a cardinality bound of $m$ on each combinatorial action. We prove that SquareCB.Comb achieves a minimax optimal regret bound of $O(\sqrt{m A T \log |\mathcal{F}|})$, where $A$ is the number of arms, $m$ is the maximum number of arms in a combinatorial action, $T$ is the time horizon, and $\mathcal{F}$ is the reward function class. In the realizable setting, this bound matches the state-of-the-art regret guarantees achieved by policy search-based algorithms in the more restricted slate recommendation settings, while simultaneously generalizing to arbitrary combinatorial action structures and general reward function approximation.

AI.tldr: A contextual combinatorial semi-bandit method SquareCB.Comb achieves minimax optimal regret with convex-optimization-based sampling, scalable to large action spaces under only a cardinality constraint on actions.
AI.motivation: Address the CCSB problem with general reward function approximation, aiming for scalable, model-agnostic algorithms that handle arbitrary combinatorial action structures without strong structural assumptions.
AI.method: Introduce SquareCB.Comb which, each round, observes context, solves a convex optimization problem to sample a combinatorial action (subset of arms) that balances exploration and exploitation; scales with m (max action size) and A (arms); requires only a bound m on action size and a function class F for reward approximation.
AI.result: Establish a minimax regret bound of O(sqrt(m A T log|F|)); efficient per-round optimization; extends to large arm sets and general action structures, with strong performance in the realizable setting.
AI.conclusion: SquareCB.Comb generalizes slate-recommendation guarantees to arbitrary combinatorial actions and general reward approximations, achieving optimal regret in the realizable case and preserving computational efficiency.

title: Learning Speaker Identity Beyond Language and Modality Constraints: Insights from the POLY-SIM 2026 Challenge
summary: Multimodal speaker identification systems typically assume the availability of complete and homogeneous audio-visual modalities during both training and testing, and assume each speaker only speaks a single language. However, in real-world applications, such assumptions often do not hold. Visual or audio information may be missing due to occlusions, camera or microphone failures, or privacy constraints. Multilingual speakers introduce additional complexity due to linguistic variability across languages. These situations constitute substantial challenges for the robustness and generalization capabilities of multimodal speaker identification systems. Aim of the POLY-SIM 2026 challenge is to address these aspects of speaker identification and to provide a standardized setup for the comparison of the proposed solutions.

AI.tldr: POLY-SIM 2026 introduces a standardized benchmark for robust multimodal speaker identification under incomplete modalities and multilingual speech, enabling fair comparison across methods.
AI.motivation: Real-world multimodal speaker ID systems face missing audio/visual data and multilingual variability, which undermine robustness and generalization; existing approaches typically assume complete modalities and single-language speakers.
AI.method: Proposes a challenge framework and standardized evaluation protocol that explicitly tests performance under modality gaps and linguistic diversity, enabling consistent benchmarking of submitted methods.
AI.result: No empirical results reported in the abstract; the work outlines framework and goals for future benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: POLY-SIM 2026 seeks to advance robust, language-inclusive multimodal speaker identification by providing a shared evaluation setup for comparing methods under realistic, incomplete data conditions.

title: Discriminative Barrier Functions for Safe Adversarial Imitation Learning from Observation
summary: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) algorithms are powerful tools for learning from and generalizing expert demonstrations, but they often rely on unconstrained exploration, rendering them unsafe for real-world deployment. Meanwhile, Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can guarantee the safety of control systems, but the analytical design of CBFs can be time-consuming and esoteric. In this work, we address these limitations jointly by constraining reward function candidacy during IRL to the space of CBFs, yielding a formulation that exhibits safe online control with continuous experiential improvement. Crucially, this framework enables the data-driven recovery of barrier functions directly from unlabeled expert observations. We demonstrate that the recovered barrier function is robust to unsafe states entirely absent from the expert data. Furthermore, we benchmark our method against standard IRL baselines in a simulated navigation environment, demonstrating improved safety performance. Finally, we investigate the trade-offs of planning-based versus policy-based IRL methods across both simulation and a real world obstacle avoidance task.

AI.tldr: A framework that integrates Control Barrier Functions into Inverse Reinforcement Learning by constraining reward candidates to the space of CBFs, enabling safe, data-driven barrier recovery from unlabeled expert data and comparing planning- and policy-based IRL methods in simulation and real-world obstacle avoidance.
AI.motivation: IRL can be unsafe due to unconstrained exploration; CBFs provide safety guarantees but their analytical design is time-consuming. The work aims to merge these by restricting IRL to the CBF space and learning barrier functions from data, yielding safe, continuously improving control.
AI.method: Constrain IRL reward-function candidates to the space of CBFs; recover barrier functions directly from unlabeled expert observations; benchmark against standard IRL baselines in a simulated navigation environment; compare planning-based versus policy-based IRL methods in both simulation and real-world obstacle avoidance tasks.
AI.result: Recovered barrier functions are robust to unsafe states absent from the expert data; improved safety performance over standard IRL baselines in simulation; analysis of planning- vs policy-based IRL trade-offs in simulation and real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: Integrating CBFs into IRL enables safe online control with continuous experiential improvement, facilitates data-driven barrier recovery from unlabeled data, yields empirical safety gains, and provides guidance on selecting IRL paradigms for planning versus policy-based approaches.

title: Microstructure-Conditioned Surrogate Models for Graded Multiscale Optimization of Mycelium Composites
summary: Emerging sustainable materials increasingly rely on engineered hierarchy and microstructure to achieve control of their properties and mechanical behavior. Optimizing these materials with controllable microstructures requires efficient multiscale simulations. Data-driven surrogate models for the microscale can accelerate multiscale simulations, but require large amounts of data even for a fixed microstructure. When a range of microstructures is considered, as is the case in multiscale optimization, even more data is needed to train a surrogate. To overcome this challenge, we condition a hybrid physics-data surrogate on microstructural variables using a hypernetwork. This approach enables accurate predictions of multiscale mechanical behavior for a mycelium-woodchip composite material, even when trained on small datasets. The conditioned surrogate makes multiscale simulations of functionally graded structures tractable, and we validate it against a full FE^2 simulation. We optimize a graded multiscale disk, and reduce the peak stress by 42% compared to one with a random microstructure. Then, we go one step further, conditioning the network directly on manufacturing variables that can have a complex influence on the microstructure. This is a practical route to engineer the microscale for desired macroscale behavior. This contribution highlights the benefits of microarchitectured structures and demonstrates how conditioned surrogate models enable their multiscale optimization, which will accelerate the development and design of future sustainable materials and structures.

AI.tldr: Hypernetwork-conditioned hybrid physics-data surrogate enables data-efficient multiscale predictions for microarchitectured materials, validating on mycelium-woodchip composites and enabling graded designs; achieves 42% peak-stress reduction versus random microstructure by conditioning on microstructure and manufacturing variables.
AI.motivation: Data-driven multiscale modeling for engineered microstructures is data-intensive. A conditioned surrogate aims to reduce data needs while handling microstructure variability and manufacturability to enable optimization of sustainable materials.
AI.method: Develop a hybrid physics-data surrogate and condition it on microstructural variables via a hypernetwork; extend conditioning to manufacturing variables; validate with FE^2 against full-scale simulations; perform multiscale optimization of a graded disk.
AI.result: Accurate multiscale predictions with small datasets; FE^2 validation; significant performance gain in optimized graded structure (42% peak-stress reduction) over random microstructure; demonstrates practicality of conditioning for manufacturing-influenced microstructures.
AI.conclusion: Conditioned surrogates enable tractable multiscale simulations and design of microarchitectured sustainable materials, accelerating future development and enabling manufacturing-aware optimization.

title: WAVE-Stereo: Warp-Aligned Volume Encoding for Stereo Matching
summary: Existing iterative stereo matching methods primarily adopt two types of correspondence representation: explicit matching search via correlation volumes and local residual refinement via warped features, yet the two remain separately modeled. We propose WAVE-Stereo, built on a core insight: correlation volumes and feature warping provide complementary matching cues. \textbf{GeoWarp Correspondence Encoder (GWCE)} encodes matching search, residual alignment, and disparity prior in parallel at the ConvGRU input. To mitigate matching degradation in textureless regions, we propose \textbf{Periodic Global Context Propagation (PGCP)}, which propagates global spatial information in a periodic manner. On five real-world benchmarks -- Middlebury, ETH3D, KITTI 2012, KITTI 2015, and Booster -- WAVE-Stereo achieves competitive zero-shot generalization accuracy without any external foundation model prior, achieving 3.18\% D1-all on KITTI 2015, 4.42\% Bad-2.0 on Booster, and 66ms real-time inference, striking a favorable balance between accuracy and efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/yamanoko-do/WAVE-Stereo.

AI.tldr: WAVE-Stereo unifies correlation-based search and feature-warp refinement via GWCE and PGCP, delivering strong zero-shot generalization and real-time performance.
AI.motivation: Existing iterative stereo methods typically treat correlation-volume matching and feature-warp refinement separately. That separation may prevent leveraging complementary cues and degrade performance in textureless regions or unseen domains.
AI.method: GeoWarp Correspondence Encoder (GWCE) encodes matching search, residual alignment, and disparity prior in parallel at the ConvGRU input. Periodic Global Context Propagation (PGCP) propagates global spatial information in a periodic manner to mitigate textureless-region degradation.
AI.result: Evaluated on five real-world benchmarks (Middlebury, ETH3D, KITTI 2012/2015, Booster). Achieves competitive zero-shot generalization without external priors: 3.18% D1-all on KITTI 2015, 4.42% Bad-2.0 on Booster, and 66 ms inference.
AI.conclusion: WAVE-Stereo provides a favorable balance between accuracy and efficiency with strong zero-shot generalization, and is released open-source (GitHub).

title: GigaWorld-Policy-0.5: A Faster and Stronger WAM Empowered by AutoResearch
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robot policy learning by jointly modeling actions and future visual observations, using future scene evolution as dense supervision for physically grounded action generation. However, a common design in existing WAMs is to explicitly generate future videos at inference time, incurring substantial computational overhead and hindering real-time closed-loop deployment. GigaWorld-Policy addresses this issue with an action-centered formulation, where future visual dynamics are used during training while action-only decoding is used at inference time. Building upon this framework, we present GigaWorld-Policy-0.5, an enhanced action-centered WAM designed for more efficient robot control. During pretraining, GigaWorld-Policy-0.5 adopts a mixed Action-Conditioned World Modeling (AC-WM) and WAM training strategy. This strengthens the coupling between visual dynamics and robot actions and improves the transferability of action representations for downstream policy learning. For efficient inference, GigaWorld-Policy-0.5 introduces a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that separates visual dynamics modeling and action generation into specialized experts, reducing active computation during action-only inference and achieving 85 ms inference latency on a local RTX 4090 setup. In addition, we employ an agent-based AutoResearch pipeline to systematically search training configurations, enabling more efficient identification of optimal experimental setups while reducing the time and manual intervention required for hyperparameter tuning. Experiments and ablations show that GigaWorld-Policy-0.5 preserves the training benefits of future visual dynamics while improving inference efficiency for robot control.

AI.tldr: Enhanced action-centered World Action Model (GigaWorld-Policy-0.5) enables fast, action-only inference by separating visual dynamics from action generation via a Mixture-of-Transformers, while preserving training benefits from future visual dynamics through AC-WM/WAM pretraining and automated AutoResearch-driven hyperparameter tuning.
AI.motivation: Address the computational bottleneck of generating future videos at inference in WAMs, by keeping rich training-time supervision from future visual dynamics but using lightweight, action-only decoding for real-time control.
AI.method: Pretrain with a mixed Action-Conditioned World Modeling (AC-WM) and World Action Modeling (WAM) strategy. Employ a Mixture-of-Transformers that partitions visual dynamics modeling and action generation into specialized experts to reduce active computation during action-only inference. Achieve ~85 ms inference latency on a local RTX 4090. Use an agent-based AutoResearch pipeline to automate training configuration search and hyperparameter tuning.
AI.result: Experiments and ablations indicate that the training benefits of future visual dynamics are preserved while inference efficiency for robot control is improved. The action-centered formulation with modular experts achieves fast inference without sacrificing downstream policy learning performance.
AI.conclusion: GigaWorld-Policy-0.5 advances efficient action-centered WAMs by decoupling dynamics modeling from action generation, delivering real-time capable inference while maintaining rich training-time supervision and benefiting from automated hyperparameter search.

title: Conditional Invertible Neural Networks for Data-Driven UAV Control: A 2-D Proof of Concept
summary: We investigate conditional invertible neural networks (cINNs) as probabilistic inverse-dynamics models for multirotor control. For a planar X8 coaxial multicopter, we learn $p(u \mid s_t, c_t)$ from an incremental nonlinear dynamic inversion (INDI) teacher using rational-quadratic spline coupling and invertible linear mixing. Open-loop reproduction reaches $R^2 = 0.944$, mean CRPS 0.0915, and log-probability-error correlation $ρ= -0.60$. Over 15 closed-loop scenarios, position RMSE matches INDI (9.7 vs. 9.5 m), with 47 percent tracking acceptably; failures separate into attitude divergence under aggressive steps and phase lag under high-frequency references, isolating command bandwidth and data coverage as dominant failure mechanisms.

AI.tldr: cINNs provide probabilistic inverse-dynamics modeling for a planar X8 multicopter, learning p(u|s_t,c_t) from an INDI teacher via rational-quadratic spline coupling; results show strong open-loop fit and competitive closed-loop performance, with identified bandwidth/data coverage as key failure modes.
AI.motivation: Address uncertainty in inverse dynamics for quadrotor control by learning a distribution over actuator commands conditioned on state and commanded state/action; use a data-driven INDI teacher to bootstrap probabilistic modeling for robust control and planning.
AI.method: Train conditional invertible neural networks with rational-quadratic spline couplings and invertible linear mixing to model p(u|s_t,c_t). Use an incremental nonlinear dynamic inversion (INDI) teacher to generate targets. Evaluate on a planar X8 coaxial multicopter: open-loop reproduction (R^2, CRPS, log-probability-error correlation) and 15 closed-loop trials (position RMSE vs INDI; tracking acceptance rate; failure modes).
AI.result: Open-loop: R^2 = 0.944; mean CRPS = 0.0915; log-probability-error correlation ρ = -0.60. Closed-loop (15 scenarios): position RMSE 9.7 m vs INDI 9.5 m; 47% tracking acceptable. Failures split into attitude divergence under aggressive steps and phase lag under high-frequency references; dominant failure mechanisms identified as command bandwidth and data coverage.
AI.conclusion: Conditional invertible neural networks can learn probabilistic inverse dynamics for multirotor control and achieve competitive open-loop and closed-loop performance with INDI guidance. However, practical efficacy is limited by bandwidth and data coverage, indicating need for richer data, higher command bandwidth, or enhanced coverage to mitigate instability under aggressive or high-frequency commands.

title: Towards Spatial Supersensing in the Wild
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://vsi-super-wild.github.io/
summary: Humans can efficiently parse continuous sensory streams, from hours to years, scaffolding an internal world model that grounds spatial reasoning and prediction. To mimic this capacity, spatial supersensing challenges multimodal models to move beyond linguistic understanding toward true world modeling. However, their benchmark relies on synthetic long videos, formed by concatenating random short clips, and is mostly limited to household scenes, leaving real-world continuity and diversity underexplored. To address the gap, we introduce $\textbf{VSI-Super-Wild}$, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating spatial supersensing over long temporal horizons in diverse in-the-wild scenes. Notably, inspired by cognitive studies on how humans structure experience, we systematically probe the full triad of world state: the agent (observer), objects (scene items), and the environment (places and global layout). In total, VSI-Super-Wild contains $\textbf{6,980}$ human-verified question-answer pairs derived from $\textbf{442}$ real-world videos spanning 8 scene categories, including long-form recordings exceeding 4 hours. Results on VSI-Super-Wild expose a fundamental disconnect: despite advances in static image understanding, models consistently fail at tasks that require coherent world-state tracking over time. We characterize how performance degrades with world-state complexity and temporal horizon, and diagnose four failure modes: spatial collapse, semantic shortcuts, insufficient update, and instance confusion. This taxonomy reveals that models lack mechanisms to bind objects, agents, and environments into a unified spatial world model, a fundamental gap that defines the path forward for spatial supersensing.

AI.tldr: Introduces VSI-Super-Wild, a real-world, long-horizon benchmark for spatial supersensing; reveals models struggle with coherent world-state tracking across agent, objects, and environment, and identifies four failure modes.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks rely on synthetic, short-form videos and lack real-world continuity/diversity, making it hard to evaluate long-horizon world modeling and binding of agents, objects, and environments.
AI.method: Construct a large-scale dataset (VSI-Super-Wild) with 442 real-world videos across 8 scene categories, including long-form recordings >4 hours; generate 6,980 human-verified QA pairs; systematically probe the world-state triad (agent, objects, environment) and analyze performance and failure modes.
AI.result: Models show a persistent gap in coherent world-state tracking over time; performance degrades with increasing world-state complexity and temporal horizon; four failure modes identified: spatial collapse, semantic shortcuts, insufficient update, and instance confusion; findings imply lack of mechanisms to bind agents, objects, and environments into a unified spatial world model.
AI.conclusion: To advance spatial supersensing, models need architectures enabling binding of agents, objects, and environments into a unified, temporally coherent world model; VSI-Super-Wild provides a path forward and a benchmark to evaluate progress.

title: AeroMap3D: Anchoring Monocular UAV 6-DoF Localization to Visual-Geometric-Semantic Map Priors
summary: We present AeroMap3D, a monocular 6-DoF UAV localization system that anchors onboard imagery to visual, geometric, and semantic map priors for GNSS-denied navigation. AeroMap3D addresses two fundamental challenges in map-referenced aerial localization: the cross-view discrepancy between UAV imagery and satellite maps, and the structural inconsistency between bare-earth digital elevation models (DEMs) and urban scenes. First, we introduce a lightweight adapter that enables a dense matcher pretrained on internet-scale generic data to perform reliable UAV-to-map registration without finetuning. By estimating the scale ratio and yaw offset between the UAV image and map tile, the adapter removes the dominant geometric misalignment induced by altitude, camera field of view, and heading before dense correspondence estimation. Second, AeroMap3D lifts 2D UAV-map correspondences onto DEM terrain while using OpenStreetMap annotations to reject semantically unreliable matches before RANSAC-PnP pose estimation, thereby reducing errors caused by unmodeled building heights and off-nadir structures. Delayed map-based pose measurements are further fused with relative-motion priors using a delayed-state EKF for continuous trajectory estimation. Without UAV-Terra3D retraining or tuning, AeroMap3D localizes all trajectories across eight Austin sites within 50 m and achieves 5.88 m mean 3D error over 55 km of flight.

AI.tldr: AeroMap3D enables monocular 6-DoF UAV localization in GNSS-denied environments by aligning onboard imagery to map priors and projecting matches onto DEM terrain with semantic filtering, fused via a delayed EKF, achieving 50 m localization within 55 km and 5.88 m mean 3D error across eight Austin sites.
AI.motivation: Tackle two core challenges in map-referenced aerial localization: (1) cross-view geometric misalignment between UAV imagery and satellite maps, and (2) structural mismatch between bare-earth DEMs and urban scenes.
AI.method: A lightweight adapter enables a dense matcher pretrained on generic data to perform UAV-to-map registration without fine-tuning by estimating scale and yaw to correct dominant geometric misalignment; dense correspondences are then established. 2D UAV-map matches are lifted onto DEM terrain, with OpenStreetMap-based semantic filtering to discard unreliable matches before RANSAC-PnP pose estimation. Final localization fuses delayed map-based pose measurements with relative-motion priors via a delayed-state EKF for continuous trajectory estimation. No retraining or tuning is required.
AI.result: Localization succeeds across eight Austin sites within 50 m and achieves a mean 3D error of 5.88 m over 55 km of flight.
AI.conclusion: The approach eliminates the need for per-site retraining, mitigates cross-view and DEM-urban disparities, and enables robust GNSS-denied UAV navigation; its generality to other locales is suggested, with potential extensions to broader environments and sensor setups.

title: DAGR: State-Conditioned Goal Representations via Difference-Aware Goal Cross-Attention
summary: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning hinges on how the goal is encoded. Contrastive, metric, temporal-distance, and information-theoretic encoders differ in objective. They still share one trait. None of them sees the current state. Such a state-independent embedding cannot mark which part of the goal still needs action. The policy must then recover that cue by inverting both encoders. We propose DAGR. It refines the static embedding of any late-fusion encoder into a state-conditioned one through multi-scale gated cross-attention. A near-identity gated residual preserves the base representation. Difference-aware Goal Cross-Attention then biases the attention scores using a per-token state-goal discrepancy map. On OGBench, DAGR improves navigation. Our ablations trace the gain to the gated residual, not to the difference bias that names the method. On manipulation and puzzle tasks it matches or falls below the base. DAGR is a structured refinement, not a universal improvement.

AI.tldr: DAGR refines static, late-fusion goal-conditioned encoders into state-conditioned embeddings via multi-scale gated cross-attention with a difference-aware bias, improving navigation on OGBench but not universally across tasks; its gains mainly arise from the gated residual component.
AI.motivation: Goal-conditioned RL encoders are typically state-agnostic, making it hard to track which parts of a goal require action. Incorporating state information into the embedding could improve cueing of action requirements.
AI.method: DAGR modifies a static embedding from any late-fusion encoder into a state-conditioned representation using multi-scale gated cross-attention. It includes a near-identity gated residual to preserve the base embedding and applies Difference-aware Goal Cross-Attention, biasing attention by a per-token state-goal discrepancy map.
AI.result: On OGBench navigation tasks, DAGR improves performance. Ablations indicate the improvement mainly stems from the gated residual component rather than the difference bias. On manipulation and puzzle tasks, performance matches or falls below the base encoders.
AI.conclusion: DAGR is a structured refinement strategy rather than a universal improvement; state-conditioned embedding refinement via gated cross-attention can yield gains in navigation but may not generalize across all task families.

title: Calibrated Closed-Form Uncertainty for Radiative Gaussian Splatting in Sparse-View CT
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures. Equal contribution: Chulin Zhao and Yiran Xu.(Co-first authors) Corresponding author: Yiran Xu (2617300@dundee.ac.uk)
summary: Radiative Gaussian splatting has made sparse-view CT reconstruction fast, but existing methods output point estimates with no notion of where the reconstruction can be trusted. We exploit a property of transmissive X-ray imaging that RGB splatting cannot claim -- projection and voxelization are strictly linear in the per-Gaussian densities -- to equip radiative Gaussians with a variational density posterior whose predictive variance propagates in closed form, exactly, in a single forward pass, in both volume space ($σ^2(x)=\sum_i g_i(x)^2 s_i^2$) and projection space ($\mathrm{Var}[I_p]=\sum_i w_{i,p}^2 s_i^2$). We present the first systematic calibration study for Gaussian-splatting CT (Spearman / AUSE / ECE with temperature scaling), showing that the resulting per-voxel uncertainty ranks true reconstruction error on 14 of 15 scenes of the official benchmark across three view budgets -- 9 of 15 additionally meeting our magnitude-calibration target after a single temperature -- while the perturbation-ensemble heuristic of concurrent work, transplanted to voxel space under the same protocol on our development scenes, does not (rank correlation as low as $-0.08$). We then dissect why uncalibrated acquisition scores can nevertheless select acceptable views, identifying three regimes -- flat (isotropic, balanced), pathological (degenerate coverage), and anisotropic -- and showing, in controlled single-scene testbeds, that principled uncertainty earns a measurable premium only in the last, motivating a coverage-gated, maturity-scheduled acquisition policy; the same calibrated posterior further points toward a dose-adaptive stopping rule, whose experimental validation we leave to future work.

AI.tldr: VarPoster: a variational density posterior for radiative Gaussian splatting in sparse-view CT enables closed-form uncertainty propagation in both volume and projection space, improving voxel-wise calibration and enabling coverage-aware acquisition, with mixed results for perturbation ensembles.
AI.motivation: Sparse-view CT with fast radiative Gaussian splatting lacks uncertainty quantification; reliable per-voxel and projection-space uncertainty is needed to guide view selection and dose while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: Exploit linearity of per-Gaussian densities to derive a variational posterior for Gaussian splats; propagate predictive variance exactly in one forward pass: voxel-space σ^2(x)=∑i g_i(x)^2 s_i^2 and projection-space Var[I_p]=∑i w_{i,p}^2 s_i^2. Conduct a calibration study (Spearman, AUSE, ECE with temperature scaling) across 15 scenes, compare to a perturbation-ensemble baseline, analyze acquisition regimes (flat, pathological, anisotropic), and propose a coverage-gated, maturity-scheduled acquisition policy; discuss dose-adaptive stopping as future work.
AI.result: Per-voxel uncertainty ranks true reconstruction error on 14/15 scenes; 9/15 reach magnitude-calibration target after a single temperature; perturbation-ensemble baseline performs poorly (rank correlation as low as -0.08). Three acquisition regimes identified; principled uncertainty yields measurable benefit only in anisotropic regime; suggests a coverage-gated policy and dose-adaptive stopping rule, with future validation.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-calibrated radiative Gaussian splatting enhances trustworthiness in sparse-view CT; calibration is conditionally effective, strongest in anisotropic acquisition regimes; results motivate acquisition policies that adapt coverage and dose, and point to future work on stopping criteria.

title: Industrial Dexterity Benchmark: A Hardware-Software Benchmarking Platform for Industrial Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Dexterous manipulation remains a critical bottleneck in industrial automation; tasks such as cable routing, connector insertion, and precision assembly still rely heavily on manual labor despite decades of robotics research. This work presents a progression from classical, modular robotics pipelines toward an end-to-end multimodal imitation-learning framework for industrial dexterous manipulation. As a part of this work, we introduce three key contributions: a set of Industrial Dexterity Benchmark (IDB) boards aimed to mimic datacenter cable management, automotive cable harnesses, and gearbox assembly tasks; a scalable imitation learning framework (DAG-ROS); and a multimodal diffusion-based policy framework (AG-iDP3) that creates models fusing RGB images, point clouds, joint positions, and wrist-frame wrench data. Focusing on the datacenter cable manipulation board, we evaluate the performance of a task involving cleaning a single cable over variations of an end-to-end AI policy using 48 trials per configuration. The best performing configuration, a multimodal expansion Diffusion Policy (DP), includes a multi-view RGB image source passed through an R3M encoder and reaches a 78% grasp and insert combined task success rate. This performance marks a significant improvement over the 36% observed from the single-camera RGB DP baseline. Each of the tested configurations requires only approximately 100 teleoperated demonstrations per task phase. These results indicate that the correct learned policy can outperform classical vision and control robotic methods in robustness, generalization, and deployment efficiency, justifying a shift toward scalable robotic automation for high up-time industrial environments.

AI.tldr: End-to-end multimodal imitation learning with diffusion-based policies significantly improves industrial dexterous manipulation; best multimodal DP reaches 78% success vs 36% baseline; ~100 demos per task phase; supports shift to scalable automation.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation is a bottleneck in industrial automation, with heavy reliance on manual labor. The work proposes moving from modular robotics pipelines to end-to-end multimodal imitation learning, supported by Industrial Dexterity Benchmark boards to mimic tasks like cable management and gearbox assembly. It also introduces scalable learning (DAG-ROS) and a diffusion-based multimodal policy (AG-iDP3) combining RGB, depth/point clouds, joint positions, and wrist wrench data.
AI.method: Introduce IDB boards simulating datacenter cable management, automotive harnesses, and gearbox assembly. Develop DAG-ROS scalable imitation-learning framework and AG-iDP3 multimodal diffusion-based policy, fusing RGB (including multi-view via R3M encoder), point clouds, joint positions, and wrist-frame wrench. Evaluate on the datacenter cable manipulation board by testing end-to-end AI policies across 48 trials per configuration.
AI.result: Best performing configuration is a multimodal expansion diffusion policy (DP) using multi-view RGB inputs processed by an R3M encoder, achieving 78% grasp-and-insert task success, a substantial improvement over the 36% baseline with a single RGB camera DP. Each configuration required ~100 teleoperated demonstrations per task phase. The results indicate enhanced robustness, generalization, and deployment efficiency over classical methods.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end multimodal imitation learning, particularly with diffusion-based policies and multi-view RGB inputs, can outperform traditional vision-and-control approaches in industrial dexterous manipulation, supporting the shift toward scalable robotic automation for high-up-time industrial environments.

title: Constraint-Driven Model Optimization: An Industry Framework for Selecting Compression and Acceleration Techniques in Modern Machine Learning Systems
summary: The rapid deployment of machine learning systems across cloud, edge, and enterprise environments has brought model optimization to the forefront of systems-engineering. Despite a rich literature spanning quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), and inference-time optimization, practitioners are often left navigating these techniques through heuristics rather than principled methodology. We argue that optimization should be formulated as a constraint-driven, multi-objective engineering decision and introduce a unified framework that characterizes any production deployment along five interacting constraint dimensions: data availability, latency budget, memory budget, accuracy tolerance, and retraining budget. Building on this taxonomy, we synthesize empirical gains reported across the research literature and map them to operational constraints rather than algorithmic categories. To ensure practical relevance, we selected these techniques by reviewing recent literature for methods that report measurable improvements against critical deployment bottlenecks. We propose a prescriptive decision framework and provide optimization pipelines for four representative industrial scenarios to illustrate it in practice. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides one of the first structured attempts to formalize model optimization as a constraint-aware, multi-objective engineering process, synthesizing quantitative evidence from the research literature.

AI.tldr: Presents a constraint-driven, multi-objective framework for production ML optimization, unifying optimization techniques under five deployment constraints and offering a prescriptive decision framework and pipelines for four industrial scenarios.
AI.motivation: Practitioners face heuristic, fragmented optimization choices; a principled, constraint-aware framework is needed to systematically trade off data, latency, memory, accuracy, and retraining budgets in real-world deployments.
AI.method: Introduce a five-dimension constraint taxonomy (data availability, latency budget, memory budget, accuracy tolerance, retraining budget); synthesize empirical gains from literature and map them to operational constraints rather than algorithm categories; select techniques with measurable deployment bottleneck improvements; develop a prescriptive decision framework and optimization pipelines for four industrial scenarios.
AI.result: A unified framework that characterizes production deployment along five constraints, a literature-supported mapping of optimization gains to constraints, and actionable pipelines and guidance for four practical scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Formalizes model optimization as a constraint-aware, multi-objective engineering process and provides synthesized quantitative evidence and practical frameworks to guide deployment decisions.

title: DNA: Dual-stage Native Attribution for Generated Image Source Tracing
summary: The rapid evolution of image generation has produced numerous within-family variants, making source-model attribution of suspect images increasingly important for digital forensics. Existing proactive methods rely on watermark embedding or model modification, which may degrade visual quality and limit deployment flexibility. Passive methods often rely on large-scale supervised training or a single reconstruction signal, limiting their ability to handle unknown sources and distinguish highly similar within-family variants. We observe that attribution signals in latent generative models are naturally stratified across architectural levels: VAE-level cues reflect family-shared information, whereas backbone-level cues capture variant-specific behaviors. Motivated by this insight, we propose Dual-stage Native Attribution (DNA), a coarse-to-fine framework that follows this hierarchy without additional neural-network training. The coarse-grained stage uses Autoencoder Double-Reconstruction (AEDR) for efficient open-set family-level screening. The fine-grained stage performs closed-set model-level attribution with Native Prediction Consistency (NPC), which compares native prediction errors of within-family variants across multiple noise levels under semantic conditioning and attributes the source via normalized calibrated scores. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct DNA-30K, a benchmark for within-family variant attribution under open-set family-level evaluation. It comprises 30,000 images generated by 24 candidate models across six families spanning both denoising diffusion and flow matching, plus non-candidate generated and natural images as unknown sources. Experiments show that DNA achieves 89.11% end-to-end attribution accuracy on a task where random guessing accuracy is below 1% and outperforms the strongest baseline by 33.81% even when AEDR is used as the coarse-grained stage.

AI.tldr: Two-stage, training-free attribution (DNA) for within-family generative-model variants, with coarse AEDR family-level screening and fine NPC model-level attribution, backed by DNA-30K benchmark; achieves 89.11% accuracy and outperforms baselines by 33.81%.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable source-model attribution for images generated by closely related within-family variants, addressing limitations of watermark-based and single-signal passive methods and exploiting the natural stratification of latent cues across model architecture.
AI.method: Dual-stage framework (DNA): coarse-grained AEDR for open-set family-level screening, and fine-grained NPC for closed-set model-level attribution. No additional neural-network training; uses multiple noise levels and semantic conditioning to compare native prediction errors; evaluated on the DNA-30K benchmark (30k images from 24 candidate models across six families, with unknown sources).
AI.result: End-to-end attribution accuracy of 89.11% on DNA-30K; strongest baseline outperformed by 33.81%; random-guess baseline <1%.
AI.conclusion: DNA provides an effective, training-free solution for within-family attribution and introduces DNA-30K as a systematic benchmark for open-set family-level evaluation in digital-forensic attribution of generative-model images.

title: PhysClaw-0: A Symbiotic Agentic System for Robot Autonomy via Language Corrections
summary: Autonomous data collection governs the volume and quality of real-world trajectories for manipulation policy learning. Existing pipelines reduce human effort via self-resetting, VLM verification, or language-guided correction, yet episode-scoped fixes must be reissued whenever the same failure recurs, so oversight cost grows with session length rather than with the number of distinct problems. We present PhysClaw-0, a human-robot symbiotic agentic system in which corrections are retained and reused across rounds. The collection loop collects, verifies, and resets autonomously, pausing for a remote operator only when a phase exhausts an explicit retry budget. An LLM parser maps each natural-language utterance to a structured adjustment stored in Corrective Memory, so addressed failure modes typically need not be corrected again under the same conditions. On a real-robot desktop-clearing testbed, PhysClaw-0 matches teleoperation episode success while reducing human working time to 16%. Language corrections improve verifier-human agreement in all four evaluated settings and raise average single-attempt success from 12.5% to 47.5% (arm-selection: 20.0% to 50.0%). Policies fine-tuned on PhysClaw-0 data match teleoperation-trained policy success at a fraction of collection human cost.

AI.tldr: PhysClaw-0 introduces cross-round corrective memory enabling reuse of failure corrections via an LLM-driven structured adjustment store, reducing human effort and improving autonomous data-collection efficiency for manipulation policy learning.
AI.motivation: Reduce supervision and human-time cost in autonomous data collection by reusing failure corrections across rounds, addressing the inefficiency of episode-specific fixes.
AI.method: A human-robot symbiotic agentic system where corrections are stored in Corrective Memory and reused; an LLM parser translates natural-language corrections into structured adjustments; autonomous collection loop with verification and reset; remote operator engaged only when a retry budget is exhausted; validated on a real-robot desktop-clearing task.
AI.result: PhysClaw-0 achieves teleoperation-level episode success while cutting human workload to 16%; language refinements improve verifier-human agreement across four settings; average single-attempt success rises from 12.5% to 47.5% (arm-selection 20%→50%); policies trained on PhysClaw-0 data approach teleoperation-trained policy performance with lower data-collection cost.
AI.conclusion: Cross-round correction retention via Corrective Memory substantially boosts efficiency and effectiveness of autonomous data collection for manipulation policies, enabling scalable, high-quality data without proportional human supervision.

title: Implementations of Quantum and Classical Topology-Aligned Architectures for Molecular Property Prediction
summary: For low-data and resource-constrained regimes typical of quantum chemistry, parameter-efficient learning is a key objective. Here, we propose a topology-aligned inductive bias in which the model architecture mirrors the molecular bond graph: atoms map to a fixed register of computational units, and bonds determine which pairs interact through shared learnable parameters. This principle is instantiated in two architectures: a variational quantum circuit (Iso-QGNN), and a parameter-matched classical message-passing model (Iso-CGNN). The models are benchmarked on HOMO-LUMO and dipole moment binary classification tasks over the QM9 benchmark. With 64 trainable parameters, the implementations achieve test AUCs of approximately 0.88 (quantum) and 0.91 (classical) on the gap task, and close to 0.78 (both) on the dipole task. The models reach 90% of asymptotic performance within about 250 training molecules and gradient norms remain stable throughout training. These results indicate that the topology-aligned inductive bias is the active ingredient driving parameter efficiency at QM9 scale, with implications for matched-baseline benchmarking in quantum machine learning.

AI.tldr: Topology-aligned inductive bias via bond-graph mirroring for QM9 tasks; achieves parameter-efficient performance with Iso-QGNN and Iso-CGNN using 64 params; competitive AUC on gap and dipole tasks; highlights topology alignment as key efficiency driver.
AI.motivation: Address data-scarce regimes in quantum chemistry and promote parameter-efficient learning; enable fair quantum-classical benchmarking by embedding molecular topology into architectures.
AI.method: Two architectures: Iso-QGNN (variational quantum circuit) and Iso-CGNN (parameter-matched classical CGNN). Atoms map to fixed registers; bonds govern interactions via shared learnable parameters. ~64 trainable parameters. Evaluated on QM9 HOMO-LUMO gap and dipole moment binary classification.
AI.result: Test AUCs: ~0.88 for quantum and ~0.91 for classical on the gap task; ~0.78 for both on the dipole task. Reaches ~90% of asymptotic performance with ~250 training molecules. Gradient norms remain stable during training.
AI.conclusion: Topology-aligned inductive bias is the key factor enabling parameter efficiency at QM9 scale; supports the need for matched-baseline benchmarking in quantum ML and informs architecture design for chemistry-oriented learning.

title: Barnamala: Parameter-Efficient Handwritten Devanagari Recognition at Benchmark Saturation
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and artifacts available at https://github.com/Ampixa/barnamala
summary: We built a compact convolutional network (1.11 M parameters) for 46-class DHCD Devanagari recognition and reached 99.73%, the highest reported at 15.6x smaller than prior state-of-the-art. We have effectively reached the saturation point: every model tested, large teacher ensembles included, hits the same 11-error intrinsic floor. No configuration achieves a statistically clear win under exact McNemar tests with Wilson confidence intervals. Even without knowledge distillation, our student matches the nearest large-model baseline (17.32 M parameters; McNemar $p = 0.345$). Outside of DHCD, zero-shot on CMATERdb digits gives 76.6% and fine-tuning reaches 97.8%; corruption robustness is also far better than large baselines (mean corruption accuracy 75.7% vs. 38.7%). All artifacts are at https://github.com/Ampixa/barnamala.

AI.tldr: A compact 1.11M-parameter CNN achieves 99.73% on 46-class DHCD Devanagari, 15.6x smaller than prior state-of-the-art, but performance appears saturated across models with an 11-error intrinsic floor; no clear winner under McNemar tests with Wilson intervals. The student matches a larger baseline without distillation; zero-shot CMATERdb digits reach 76.6% with fine-tuning to 97.8%; corruption robustness is substantially better than baselines. Artifacts available on GitHub.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether extremely compact models can reach or match state-of-the-art in Devanagari character recognition, assess whether model size reduces performance given teacher ensembles, examine the existence of an intrinsic error floor, and evaluate transferability and robustness.
AI.method: Propose a compact CNN (1.11M parameters) for 46-class DHCD Devanagari recognition. Compare to larger models and ensembles, with/without knowledge distillation; evaluate statistically using exact McNemar tests with Wilson confidence intervals. Extend evaluation to zero-shot CMATERdb digits, fine-tuning, and corruption robustness. Provide artifacts at a public repository.
AI.result: Achieves 99.73% accuracy on DHCD with 1.11M parameters, 15.6x smaller than prior SOTA. Claims an intrinsic saturation point: most models converge to an 11-error floor, with no configuration yielding a statistically significant win (per McNemar with Wilson intervals). The compact student matches the nearest large-model baseline (17.32M parameters; p = 0.345). On CMATERdb digits, zero-shot accuracy is 76.6%, fine-tuning reaches 97.8%. Corruption robustness is markedly higher than large baselines (mean accuracy 75.7% vs. 38.7%). All artifacts are available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: The study suggests that highly compact models can approach or match large-model performance on a challenging OCR task while offering substantial efficiency gains, but claims of superiority are tempered by an intrinsic error floor and lack of statistically significant wins across configurations. The model also demonstrates strong cross-dataset transferability and robustness, with accessible reproducibility via public artifacts.

title: Algebraic Representability as the Limiting Regime of Grokking: An Exactly Solvable Model with Holomorphic Activations
summary: Neural networks trained on modular arithmetic exhibit grokking, a delayed transition from memorisation to generalisation known to depend on model capacity: too little and the network memorises slowly or not at all, too much and it generalises almost immediately. What happens at the extreme of this spectrum, when the architecture's expressible function class collapses to a finite-dimensional algebraic variety? We study two-layer networks with a holomorphic monomial activation sigma(z)=z^k, trained on modular tasks encoded via roots of unity. Here the network output, regardless of hidden width, is confined to a (k+1)-dimensional subspace of characters of (Z_p)^2, an O(k/p^2) slice of the full function space. We give a complete algebraic characterisation of this subspace: a task is representable if and only if its discrete Fourier support lies on the diagonal u+v = k (mod p), which for linear-phase targets reduces to the arithmetic criterion m+n=k. This is not merely a constraint on eventual generalisation but on memorisation itself: because the outputs are algebraically confined, a non-representable target cannot be fit even on the training set, and we prove a positive lower bound on the training loss, independent of width. Across 585 runs the algebraic prediction matches the observed outcome with 99.8% accuracy, with no memorisation regime and no grokking; outcomes split cleanly into instant success and outright failure. This binary behaviour is the limiting case of the capacity-grokking relationship: when the expressible class shrinks to a fixed algebraic object, the question of when a network will grok dissolves into whether it can represent the target at all. A bottleneck ablation connects this extreme to standard networks, tracing a continuous path from representational failure, through memorisation without generalisation, to grokking with a shrinking gap as capacity grows.

AI.tldr: Two-layer networks with z^k activations trained on modular tasks have outputs confined to a (k+1)-dimensional subspace; a task is representable iff its discrete Fourier support lies on the diagonal u+v = k (mod p). Representability dictates success: non-representable targets cannot be fit even on training, giving a training-loss lower bound independent of width; empirically, 585 runs show a binary outcome (instant success or outright failure) with 99.8% accuracy and no grokking.
AI.motivation: To understand grokking by examining the extreme of the capacity spectrum where the expressible function class collapses to a finite algebraic object, connecting memorisation and generalisation to representability.
AI.method: Analytical characterization of the representable subspace for holomorphic monomial activations on modular tasks via discrete Fourier analysis on (Z_p)^2. Derivation of necessary and sufficient representability condition; arithmetic simplification m+n=k for linear-phase targets. Proof of a width-independent lower bound on training loss for non-representable tasks. Empirical validation across 585 runs.
AI.result: Algebraic criterion: a task is representable iff its discrete Fourier support lies on u+v=k (mod p); for linear-phase targets this reduces to m+n=k. Non-representable targets cannot be fitted even on training, yielding a positive training-loss lower bound independent of width. Across 585 runs, the algebraic prediction matches observed outcomes with 99.8% accuracy, showing a clean split into instant success or outright failure with no grokking or memorisation regime.
AI.conclusion: This extreme, finite-algebraic expressibility scenario shows that grokking collapses to representability: whether a network can fit the target at all dictates training behavior. The results illuminate the capacity-grokking relationship as a continuum bridged by a bottleneck ablation, connecting representational failure, memorisation without generalisation, and grokking as capacity grows.

title: Groc-PO: Grounded Context Preference Optimization for Truthful Multimodal LLMs
summary: Despite the rapid progress of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), they still suffer from untruthfulness issues, such as visual hallucinations, content fabrication, and unfaithful reasoning, which substantially undermine their faithfulness and practical utility. Alignment methods based on human preference, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have been widely adopted to address these issues. However, multimodal reasoning errors often propagate across stages, and final-answer errors can often be traced to mistakes in early grounding stages, yet standard DPO typically applies preference optimization at the final-answer level. This credit-assignment challenge means that supervision for early grounding stages is indirect rather than stage-specific, making it difficult to suppress error propagation arising from grounding drift and context inconsistency. To address this, we propose Grounded Context Preference Optimization (Groc-PO), a grounded preference optimization framework for MLLMs. We further construct the Grounded Context Preference Dataset (GCPD), organizing multi-stage preference samples around three stages of Object Grounding, Contextual Grounding, and Grounded Reasoning, to capture the formation, integration, and utilization of grounded context. By introducing more explicit preference supervision over multiple grounded stages, Groc-PO strengthens context-dependent reasoning and mitigates cross-stage error propagation. Extensive experiments show that, compared with standard DPO and other strong baselines, Groc-PO achieves improved performance in hallucination mitigation, faithful reasoning, and overall reliability, supporting the value of more explicit grounded supervision for trustworthy multimodal reasoning.

AI.tldr: Grounded Context Preference Optimization (Groc-PO) with the Grounded Context Preference Dataset (GCPD) introduces multi-stage, grounded supervision for Object Grounding, Contextual Grounding, and Grounded Reasoning in MLLMs to reduce error propagation and improve trustworthiness over final-answer DPO baselines.
AI.motivation: MLLMs suffer from untruthfulness such as hallucinations and unfaithful reasoning. Classic Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) at the final answer level fails to credit early grounding stages, enabling error propagation across stages.
AI.method: Propose Groc-PO framework applying preference optimization at multiple grounded stages (Object Grounding, Contextual Grounding, Grounded Reasoning) and create GCPD with stage-specific preference annotations to capture formation, integration, and use of grounded context.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show Groc-PO improves hallucination mitigation, faithful reasoning, and overall reliability compared with standard DPO and strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, multi-stage grounded supervision is effective for trustworthy multimodal reasoning, validating the value of grounding-aware alignment and providing a dataset and framework for further research.

title: MxGPS: Multiplex Graph Transformers for a Power Grid Foundation Model
summary: Single-task fine-tuning of graph neural networks (GNNs) for power grid problems exhibits a systematic failure mode: models that achieve the lowest in-distribution error degrade the most under topology shift. We term this topology overfitting: the tendency of task-specific gradient signals to encode relational structure particular to the training topologies rather than the underlying physics, causing models to fail on unseen grids despite strong in-distribution performance. To expose and address this failure mode, we introduce MxGPS (Multiplex GPS), a multiplex graph transformer that runs K task-specialised GPS branches over a shared node encoder, jointly trained on Static State Estimation (SSE) and AC Power Flow (PF) via a self-supervised pre-training and multi-task fine-tuning protocol, with a cross-branch attention module evaluated in ablation. The joint SSE+PF objective forces the shared encoder to simultaneously satisfy complementary gradient signals, preventing it from overfitting to topology-specific relational structure. Under a 3-fold sliding-window cross-validation spanning four unseen topologies (14-, 24-, 162-, and 300-bus), MxGPS attains 0% boundary violation rate (BVR) on all four zero-shot Power Flow topologies. Critically, models with substantially lower in-distribution PF error degrade by 190% to 1400% under topology shift, whereas MxGPS degrades by only 39%, an inversion that directly implicates topology overfitting as the failure mechanism rather than insufficient model capacity. With only 1.6M parameters (12x fewer than the GridFM reference baseline), MxGPS demonstrates that multi-task joint training is a principled and parameter-efficient mechanism for topology-agnostic generalisation in power grid foundation models.

AI.tldr: MxGPS uses a multiplex graph transformer with multi-task SSE+PF training to overcome topology overfitting, achieving zero-shot generalization across unseen power-grid topologies with strong parameter efficiency.
AI.motivation: Single-task fine-tuning on GNNs for power grids leads to topology overfitting, where models encode topology-specific relations that fail on unseen grids despite good in-distribution performance.
AI.method: A multiplex GPS with K task-specific branches on a shared node encoder, cross-branch attention, trained jointly on Static State Estimation (SSE) and AC Power Flow (PF) via self-supervised pre-training and multi-task fine-tuning; evaluated with a 3-fold sliding-window cross-validation over four unseen topologies (14-, 24-, 162-, 300-bus).
AI.result: MxGPS achieves 0% boundary violation rate across all four zero-shot PF topologies. Baseline models with lower in-distribution PF error degrade 190%–1400% under topology shift, while MxGPS degrades by 39%. Parameter count is 1.6M (12x smaller than GridFM).
AI.conclusion: Topology overfitting is mitigated by multi-task joint training, enabling topology-agnostic generalization in power-grid foundation models with strong parameter efficiency; cross-branch attention and shared encoder facilitate learning physics-consistent representations across topologies.

title: Anatomically Faithful but Temporally Blind: Auditing Attribution for Left-Ventricular Ejection-Fraction Estimation from Echocardiography
summary:
