Furthermore, we demonstrate that Cyclone can be distilled to a video diffusion model for temporally consistent weather editing.

AI.tldr: A latent-diffusion-based weather editing framework, Cyclone, enables unpaired, cycle-consistent weather changes across diverse scenes, improving realism and downstream perception, with a path to temporal consistency via distillation to video diffusion.
AI.motivation: To achieve robust perception under diverse weather without relying on paired data or physics-based models, addressing limited realism and poor generalization in weather-augmented training pipelines.
AI.method: Cyclone uses latent diffusion with cycle-consistent constraints and image-text model priors to edit weather in unpaired data. It can generate multiple weather conditions across scenes and can be distilled into a video diffusion model for temporally consistent weather editing.
AI.result: Produces more realistic, structure-preserving outputs than baselines and yields consistent improvements on downstream driving perception tasks; template can be extended to video with temporal consistency via distillation.
AI.conclusion: Cyclone provides a unified, data-efficient framework for weather editing that generalizes beyond training data and can be extended to temporally coherent video diffusion, benefiting autonomous driving perception under varying weather.

title: Lighthouse RL: Sample-Efficient Circuit Optimization via Strategic Reset Points
summary: In this paper, we introduce Lighthouse RL, a sample-efficient reinforcement learning (RL) approach for analog circuit sizing. Traditional methods lack generalization across different performance targets, while standard RL approaches waste resources exploring unpromising regions. Our method addresses these inefficiencies through a strategic reset strategy that initializes episodes from high-performing configurations discovered during training, called "lighthouses". These states, which are closer to the target objectives, guide exploration toward promising regions. When compared to RL and Bayesian optimization methods from the literature, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a 2D benchmark problem and on two analog circuits, showing significant improvements in sample efficiency (up to 1.72x faster), optimization performance (100% vs. 0-87% success rate), generalization (75% vs. 0-50% extrapolation success), and objective maximization. This efficiency is particularly valuable for computationally expensive black-box optimization problems, and our reset strategy can be used as a plug-and-play enhancement for any RL-based optimization approach.

AI.tldr: Lighthouse RL: a sample-efficient RL framework for analog circuit sizing using a lighthouse reset strategy that restarts episodes from high-performing configurations, improving sample efficiency, success rate, and extrapolation generalization compared with RL and Bayesian optimization baselines.
AI.motivation: Overcome RL inefficiencies in analog circuit sizing: insufficient cross-target generalization and wasted exploration in unpromising regions.
AI.method: Introduce a lighthouse reset strategy that seeds each episode from previously discovered high-performing configurations ('lighthouses'), guiding exploration toward promising regions. Evaluated on a 2D benchmark and two analog circuits, comparing against RL and Bayesian optimization baselines.
AI.result: Significant improvements: up to 1.72x faster sample efficiency; 100% success rate versus 0–87% for baselines; 75% extrapolation/generalization success vs 0–50%; improved objective maximization.
AI.conclusion: Lighthouse resets provide a plug-and-play enhancement for RL-based optimization, especially for expensive black-box problems, with broad improvements in efficiency, performance, and generalization.

title: SIVA-RL: Sensitivity-Invariance Visual Alignment for Multimodal Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) drives multimodal reasoning, but answer-level correctness does not guarantee that a vision-language model grounds its predictions in visual evidence. Existing visual-intervention methods contrast policy behavior on original and modified images, yet assign supervision by the type of intervention rather than its observed effect. This assumption fails: identical operators produce heterogeneous outcomes across samples. We propose SIVA-RL, a Sensitivity-Invariance Visual Alignment framework that replaces operator-conditioned regularization with sample-wise, outcome-conditioned supervision. SIVA-RL constructs localized interventions through token-aligned, distance-constrained within-image PatchSwap. A frozen audit policy then scores each clean-intervention pair, and the observed reward drop becomes soft routing weights. Large-drop pairs drive sensitivity alignment, low-drop pairs drive clean-anchored invariance alignment, and ambiguous pairs are down-weighted. This design decouples intervention construction from supervision assignment and is compatible with both GRPO and DAPO backbones. Across nine multimodal reasoning benchmarks spanning mathematical, logical, and vision-dependent tasks, SIVA-RL improves 3B and 7B models over matched RL baselines in every setting. It yields an 8.79 percentage-point gain on vision-dependent reasoning and up to 14.9% relative overall improvement across all four GRPO- and DAPO-based configurations.

AI.tldr: SIVA-RL is a sample-wise, outcome-conditioned visual alignment framework for RL with verifiable rewards, using PatchSwap interventions and a frozen audit policy to drive sensitivity and invariance alignment, improving vision-dependent reasoning across multiple backbones and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Prior visual-intervention methods rely on operator-type supervision which ignores that identical interventions can have different effects across samples; a sample-wise, outcome-conditioned approach is needed to align model grounding with visual evidence.
AI.method: Construct localized intra-image interventions via token-aligned, distance-constrained PatchSwap; evaluate intervention pairs with a frozen audit policy to obtain reward-drop-based soft routing weights; allocate training emphasis by large-drop (sensitivity alignment), low-drop (invariance alignment), and ambiguous (down-weighted) groups; decouples intervention construction from supervision assignment and is compatible with GRPO and DAPO backbones.
AI.result: Evaluated on nine multimodal benchmarks spanning mathematical, logical, and vision-dependent tasks; 3B and 7B models outperform matched RL baselines in all settings; 8.79 percentage-point gain on vision-dependent reasoning; up to 14.9% relative improvement across four GRPO- and DAPO-based configurations.
AI.conclusion: Sample-wise, outcome-conditioned supervision via SIVA-RL yields improved visual grounding for RL with verifiable rewards, with a decoupled, backbone-agnostic design that yields consistent gains across diverse multimodal tasks.

title: Transforming Rank: How Architecture Navigates the Spectral Pathologies of Depth
summary: We investigate how each component of the Transformer feedforward block architecture design determines how much rank survives across depth at initialization. We reinterpret skip connections and normalization, long understood as controlling magnitude, as mechanisms for preserving gradient rank across depth, since the very matrix multiplications and nonlinear activations that make the network expressive also reduce the rank. We show that skip connections trade off rank collapse against ensemble-like behavior, controlled by the relative scales of the branch and the skip: skip connections route the gradient around the residual branch, where rank is lost, rather than along the long gradient paths that encourage the layers to compose. The placement of the normalization layer controls this same tradeoff by setting the branch-to-skip ratio across depth, unifying much of the normalization placement and depth scaling literature, in particular why rank collapses for Post-Norm but plateaus for Pre-Norm. Other aspects of the architecture, like the two-matrix structure that expands and contracts the width, use additional parameters to preserve the representation or branch Jacobian rank. The second matrix decorrelates a coherent mean spike that would grow across blocks with a single matrix and uncentered activation, preventing the residual representation from collapsing. The width expansion between the two matrices keeps the branch Jacobian full rank: applying the rank-reducing activation in this expanded space leaves enough directions to span the original, at a width that follows a Marchenko--Pastur law. The initialization rank of the input--output Jacobian predicts which networks train on CIFAR-10. Taken together, we recast architecture design for deep networks as navigating an intrinsic tradeoff among rank collapse, ensemble-like behavior, and parameter count.

AI.tldr: Transformer feedforward design affects how much rank survives across depth at initialization. Skip connections and normalization are regimes for preserving gradient rank, balancing rank collapse with ensemble-like behavior. A two-matrix width-expansion preserves rank; initialization rank of the input–output Jacobian predicts CIFAR-10 trainability. Overall, architecture design trades off rank collapse, ensemble behavior, and parameter count.
AI.motivation: Understand how architectural choices in Transformers (skip connections, normalization placement, and width-expansion) influence gradient rank preservation and trainability, linking normalization depth placement to rank stability (Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm).
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of rank in Jacobians through the Transformer feedforward block, analysis of skip connections versus residual paths, examination of normalization placement (Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm), two-matrix structure that expands then contracts width, role of activation-induced rank reduction, and the spectral properties following Marchenko–Pastur. Empirical indication on CIFAR-10.
AI.result: Identifies a tradeoff: architecture parameters balance rank collapse and ensemble-like behavior while controlling parameter count. Skip connections bypass the rank-reducing branch; normalization controls the branch-to-skip ratio; width expansion preserves branch Jacobian rank; the expansion ensures enough directions remain after rank-reducing activation, following Marchenko–Pastur distribution. Initialization rank of input–output Jacobian predicts CIFAR-10 trainability.
AI.conclusion: Architectural design for deep networks should navigate intrinsic tradeoffs among rank preservation, ensemble-like behavior, and parameter efficiency. Placement of normalization and the two-matrix width dynamics unify normalization-depth literature (Pre- vs Post-Norm) and offer principled guidelines for maintaining trainability through rank preservation.

title: A novel unsupervised machine learning strategy to handle multimodal cardiac PET/MRI data
summary: Arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy is a genetic myocardial disease difficult to diagnose due to the lack of gold standard criteria. Simultaneous PET/MR imaging, combined with multiparametric quantitative analysis, could facilitate the identification of different profiles related to the phenotype and progression of cardiomyopathy. This preliminary study focuses on a methodological strategy for dealing with PET/MRI data, including inter-patient data linkage and regional analysis. Two-step clustering was applied to T1 and T2 maps, LGE, and 18F-FDG-PET images of 99 patients genetically diagnosed with arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy. Each patient's images were independently z-scored and summed into a single volume, which was clustered into supervoxels. Thirty-two inter-patient groups of supervoxels were obtained by spectral clustering. An "abnormality" score was assigned to each cluster and modality, and used to visualise abnormal regions likely associated with disease. They enabled the generation of automated textual and bullseye health reports for each patient, which were compared with cardiac imager assessments using balanced accuracy in repeated nested cross-validation. This approach was further validated on a larger cohort of 167 numerical phantoms. The reports generated by clustering accurately identified most of the cardiac physicians' observations (BA = 0.76 $\pm$ 0.04 in repeated nested cross-validation on patients, and BA $\ge$ 0.8 on phantoms). Furthermore, the identified abnormal clusters closely matched their visual observations, facilitating the identification of varying degrees of fibrosis or inflammation on the images. This approach enables a more systematic handling of multimodal PET/MRI data to characterise myocardial heterogeneity in arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy patients.

AI.tldr: A multimodal PET/MRI clustering framework enables automated abnormality reporting for arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy (ALVC) with strong agreement to clinicians, handling inter-patient heterogeneity and identifying fibrosis/inflammation.
AI.motivation: ALVC diagnosis is challenging due to lack of gold-standard criteria. Integrating PET/MRI and multiparametric analysis may reveal phenotype/progression profiles and support systematic, automated assessments.
AI.method: Study on 99 genetically diagnosed ALVC patients. Each modality (T1, T2, LGE, 18F-FDG-PET) was z-scored per patient, summed into a single volume, and segmented into supervoxels. Two-step approach: (1) cluster into supervoxels; (2) spectral clustering to form 32 inter-patient groups. An abnormality score per cluster/modality guided visualization. Generated automated textual and bullseye reports; validated against clinicians via balanced accuracy in nested cross-validation. Further validated on 167 numerical phantoms.
AI.result: Clustering-based reports matched most physician observations (BA ≈ 0.76 ± 0.04 in patient data; BA ≥ 0.8 in phantoms). Abnormal clusters aligned with visual assessments, capturing varying degrees of fibrosis/inflammation. Demonstrates systematic multimodal data handling to characterize myocardial heterogeneity in ALVC.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a reproducible, automated method to characterize multimodal PET/MRI heterogeneity in ALVC and generate clinician-aligned reports, potentially aiding diagnosis and monitoring.

title: Improving Wind and Solar Power Prediction with Efficient Wrapper-based Feature Selection: An Empirical Study
summary: With rising global energy demand and growing awareness of climate change and its impacts, the share of renewable energies in the global energy mix continues to grow. Unlike conventional power generation, the output of renewable energy sources cannot be controlled as consistently due to their dependence on environmental conditions. Therefore, reliable prediction of current and future energy production is essential. In this paper, we report findings from two structured literature reviews on real-world renewable energy prediction tasks: wind turbine power curve modeling and photovoltaic power prediction. For the former, we conducted a comprehensive literature review ourselves, while for the latter, we synthesize the key findings regarding frequently selected input features based on an existing survey. Across both domains, our analysis reveals that despite the large number of available monitoring and environmental variables, only limited or unsystematic methods for feature selection exist. To address this gap, we propose Cluster-based Sequential Feature Selection (CSFS), a novel, model-agnostic, clustering-based wrapper method for automatic, efficient, and reliable feature selection in renewable energy prediction pipelines. To support reproducibility and reuse, we provide an open-source implementation of CSFS on GitHub. We empirically evaluate the proposed approach on both use cases and compare it with established feature selection techniques such as wrapper-based sequential feature selection (SFS), filter-based methods, and Random Forest's embedded feature importance. The results show that the wrapper-based methods overall provide better-performing selections of features. CSFS achieves a predictive performance comparable to SFS while reducing computational cost by an average of 21%.

AI.tldr: Proposes Cluster-based Sequential Feature Selection (CSFS) for renewable energy prediction; a model-agnostic, clustering-based wrapper method that reduces computation while matching SFS performance; validated on wind and PV prediction tasks; open-source on GitHub.
AI.motivation: Renewable energy prediction involves many monitoring and environmental variables, but feature selection is often ad hoc, leading to inefficiency and potentially unstable models. A scalable, automatic method is needed to improve predictive accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: Develop two study streams: wind power curve modeling literature review (self-conducted) and PV feature-finding synthesis (based on existing survey). Propose CSFS, a clustering-based wrapper feature selection method. Compare CSFS to wrapper SFS, filter methods, and Random Forest feature importance. Empirically evaluate on wind and PV prediction tasks; assess predictive performance and computational cost. Provide open-source GitHub implementation.
AI.result: Wrapper-based feature selection methods generally outperform others. CSFS achieves predictive performance comparable to SFS but with about 21% lower computational cost on average.
AI.conclusion: CSFS is an effective, model-agnostic, and efficient feature selection approach for renewable energy prediction pipelines, with reproducible implementation. Encourages broader adoption and further exploration of clustering-based feature selection in energy forecasting.

title: Peak-End-Net: A Peak-End Rule Inspired Framework for Generalizable Video Aesthetic Assessment
comment: Accepted to ACM MM 2026, Code: https://github.com/AMAP-ML/Peak-End-Net
summary: Video aesthetic assessment (VAA) aims to predict how aesthetically pleasing a video is, yet remains far less explored than other visual assessment tasks. Its progress is hindered not only by the scarcity of large-scale benchmarks, but also by the intrinsic subjectivity of aesthetic judgment, which is shaped by human perception. In this paper, we revisit VAA from a psychological perspective and propose \textit{Peak-End-Net}, a lightweight and interpretable framework inspired by the \textit{peak-end rule}, which suggests that people tend to judge a temporal experience mainly according to its salient moments and the ending. Building on this intuition, we first transfer knowledge from image aesthetic assessment (IAA) to VAA by introducing a pretrained IAA head to produce frame-wise aesthetic priors, which serve as surrogate signals for identifying aesthetically salient moments and guiding \textit{peak-end rule}-based temporal aggregation. To further capture how a video evolves aesthetically over time, we design an aesthetic rhythm encoder that models temporal progression beyond isolated moments. Additionally, we refine the overall assessment through a dynamic gated fusion mechanism to improve robustness under distribution shift. Our method is built on a frozen vision transformer (ViT) and requires only a small number of trainable parameters, making it scalable and parameter-efficient. Extensive experiments on two existing VAA benchmarks, including in-domain evaluation on VADB and cross-domain testing on DIVIDE-3K, demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, affirming the value of psychologically grounded modeling for VAA. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/Peak-End-Net.

AI.tldr: Peak-End-Net is a lightweight, psychology-inspired framework for Video Aesthetic Assessment (VAA) that leverages a frozen ViT backbone, a pretrained Image Aesthetic Assessment (IAA) head to generate frame-wise priors, a peak-end rule-based temporal aggregation via an aesthetic rhythm encoder, and a dynamic gated fusion mechanism. It achieves state-of-the-art results on VAA benchmarks (VADB in-domain and DIVIDE-3K cross-domain) with strong robustness to distribution shifts, and is released with code and models.
AI.motivation: VAA suffers from subjectivity and limited large-scale benchmarks. A psychology-inspired approach can better capture how humans judge videos by focusing on salient moments and endings, and by transferring knowledge from IAA to VAA to obtain frame-wise priors that guide temporal aggregation.
AI.method: The method freezes a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone and adds lightweight trainable heads: (1) a pretrained IAA head to produce frame-wise aesthetic priors; (2) a peak-end rule-based temporal aggregator informed by these priors; (3) an aesthetic rhythm encoder to model temporal progression; (4) a dynamic gated fusion module to fuse cues robustly. This yields a parameter-efficient architecture with state-of-the-art performance.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on two VAA benchmarks shows state-of-the-art performance: in-domain on VADB and cross-domain on DIVIDE-3K. The method demonstrates robustness to distribution shifts and benefits from the psychology-grounded design. Code and models are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: A psychology-informed, lightweight, and interpretable VAA model can achieve strong performance by leveraging peak-end-based temporal aggregation and transferring IAA priors to VAA. The approach confirms the value of incorporating human perception principles into ML for subjective tasks and offers a scalable, interpretable framework for future research.

title: MetaPerch: Learning from metadata for bioacoustics foundation models
summary: Bioacoustic foundation models rely on large-scale citizen science platforms like Xeno-Canto for geographically and ecologically diverse data. Recent work has shown that supervision alone can produce SotA species detection models when trained on this large-scale data -- however, there remains unutilized potential in the form of recording metadata readily available within these community-driven data hubs. In this work, we explore the use of metadata -- such as location and time -- as auxiliary supervision signals, allowing the model to leverage species-metadata correlations in its learned representation. Auxiliary metadata losses provide additional information beyond vocalizations alone that can encourage a richer, more robust representation that generalizes better to species distribution and acoustic domain shifts -- important challenges for deployment in real-world passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) settings. We introduce MetaPerch, a new foundation model that achieves strong species identification performance across multiple challenging domains and present an extensive empirical study of the effects of 9 diverse metadata sources on 17 bioacoustic datasets.

AI.tldr: Incorporating recording metadata as auxiliary supervision via MetaPerch yields robust, domain-generalized bioacoustic species identification across multiple datasets, with a systematic analysis of 9 metadata sources on 17 datasets.
AI.motivation: Leverage readily available metadata (e.g., location, time) in citizen-science bioacoustic collections to improve representation and generalization, addressing domain shifts in passive acoustic monitoring.
AI.method: Propose auxiliary metadata losses integrated into a new foundation model (MetaPerch); conduct an extensive empirical study across 17 datasets evaluating 9 diverse metadata sources.
AI.result: Metadata-based auxiliary supervision improves learned representations and generalization; MetaPerch achieves strong species identification across challenging domains; detailed empirical results on metadata source effects across datasets.
AI.conclusion: Metadata-enabled training is a promising approach to robust, transferable bioacoustic models; future work to explore more metadata sources and deployment considerations.

title: PlumeQuant: Uncertainty-aware consistency assessment of methane plume masks and emission-rate estimates
comment: 50 pages, 9 figures. Supplementary material provided as an ancillary file. Code and derived data archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21282534
summary: Imaging spectrometers increasingly distribute source-resolved methane plume products in which the plume mask, integrated mass enhancement (IME), plume length, emission rate, and uncertainty are physically and algorithmically linked. Using 63 EMIT-derived Carbon Mapper plume records from 27 scenes, we show that these published scalar quantities do not uniquely constrain the plume boundary: substantially different yet plausible masks reproduce the same IME, plume length, and emission rate. Genetic-algorithm (GA) ensembles conditioned on the published IME and plume length make this equifinality explicit: the high-confidence core selected by nearly all target-consistent masks covers a median of 13% of the plausible footprint envelope, and ambiguity is largest for weak, low-overlap plumes. The diagnostics come from PlumeQuant, which recomputes IME, plume length, emission rate, and five-term uncertainty from distributed product components under stated conventions and evaluates four mask representations: the distributed reference mask, a transparent Carbon Mapper-informed analogue (CM-like), the GA ensemble, and optional expert edits. The CM-like mask is generated per plume without access to the reference mask or published quantities, with settings fixed once on a scene-disjoint 44-plume development split. It reproduced published IME with +0.72% median difference and emission rate with +0.16% (6.98% mean absolute), reached 0.843 median intersection-over-union against the reference masks, and matched the published uncertainty scale (median ratio 1.01). Holdout mean absolute errors were 7.6% (IME), 9.5% (length), and 6.1% (rate). These are product-level consistency diagnostics, not independent validation. They flag weak, offset, or ambiguous plumes for expert review.

AI.tldr: Scalar plume metrics (IME, plume length, emission rate) do not uniquely constrain plume masks; GA-based ensembles reveal persistent equifinality; a CM-like mask reproduces published metrics and enables diagnostics to flag ambiguous plumes.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether published plume-scalar quantities truly constrain the plume boundary, quantify equifinality in distributed plume products, and provide diagnostics (PlumeQuant) to assess mask representations.
AI.method: Analyze 63 EMIT-derived Carbon Mapper plume records (27 scenes); apply GA ensembles conditioned on published IME and plume length; compare four mask representations (distributed reference, CM-like, GA ensemble, expert edits); develop a CM-like mask per plume without access to reference masks or published quantities using a scene-disjoint 44-plume development split; recompute IME, plume length, emission rate, and a five-term uncertainty; report IoU and holdout errors.
AI.result: Published scalars do not uniquely determine plume boundaries; GA ensembles show a high-confidence core covering a median of 13% of the plausible footprint; ambiguity is greatest for weak, low-overlap plumes. The CM-like mask reproduces IME within +0.72% median, emission rate within +0.16% (6.98% MAE), IoU = 0.843 median against reference masks, and matches uncertainty scale (median ratio 1.01). Holdout MAEs: 7.6% (IME), 9.5% (length), 6.1% (rate). These are product-level consistency diagnostics, not independent validation, and they flag weak/ambiguous plumes for expert review.
AI.conclusion: Equifinality in plume boundary estimation is pronounced; the CM-like mask provides a practical, reference-free diagnostic that aligns with published metrics and supports expert review workflows. PlumeQuant enables cross-checks across representations to identify ambiguous cases rather than relying on a single scalar quantity.

title: Linear Independent Component Analysis via Optimal Transport
summary: Linear Independent Component Analysis (ICA) recovers jointly independent source signals from their linear mixtures. To achieve this, classical ICA algorithms attempt to maximize non-Gaussianity, measured by negentropy, which is linked to independence by information theory. Because exact negentropy optimization is intractable, they rely on proxy contrast functions, such as fourth-order cumulants, and parametric log-likelihoods. We propose instead to measure non-Gaussianity using the squared Wasserstein distance $W_2^2$ to a standard Gaussian. We prove that the Wasserstein distance between a standard normal distribution and linear projections of the data is maximized when the projection recovers an independent component. Based on this observation, we propose the OT-ICA algorithm which finds this projection by gradient-based optimization. Empirical evaluation on simulated data shows that OT-ICA outperforms proxy-based methods for different distributions of the latent variables. Application to EEG artifact removal and econometric price discovery confirm OT-ICA can be used for applied ICA tasks without distributional assumptions.

AI.tldr: Introduces OT-ICA, using squared Wasserstein distance to Gaussian as non-Gaussianity measure for ICA; shows W2^2 maximization recovers independent components; gradient-based projection; empirical superiority to proxy-based methods; applicable to EEG and econometrics.
AI.motivation: Negentropy-based ICA relies on proxies to quantify non-Gaussianity; need a principled, distribution-agnostic, tractable criterion for independence in ICA.
AI.method: Define squared Wasserstein distance W2^2 between a standard Gaussian and linear projections of data; prove maximization of W2^2 aligns with recovering an independent component; implement gradient-based optimization to find the projection (OT-ICA); validate on simulated data and apply to EEG artifact removal and econometric price discovery.
AI.result: OT-ICA outperforms proxy-based ICA methods across different latent distributions; demonstrates practical effectiveness in applied tasks without distributional assumptions.
AI.conclusion: W2^2-based ICA provides a principled, distribution-agnostic alternative to negentropy-based ICA and is effective in real-world applications like EEG and econometric analysis.

title: CF-Net: Conflict Fusion with Speaker Normalisation and Certainty Weighting for Ambivalence/Hesitancy Recognition
summary: Detecting ambivalence and hesitancy (AH) in unconstrained video is challenging because the target signal is inherently ambiguous and expressed through subtle cross-modal incongruence rather than prototypical affect. We present CF-Net, a deep multimodal network submitted to the 3rd Edition of the AH Video Recognition Challenge (ABAW 11th, ECCV 2026), targeting the BAH dataset. CF-Net encodes visual, audio, and transcript streams with frozen SigLIP2, HuBERT, and DistilBERT backbones, normalises backbone features per speaker to reduce identity leakage, and fuses them via a ConflictFusion module that explicitly computes pairwise cross-modal incongruence. Training combines certainty-weighted focal loss, manifold mixup, and modality dropout; an auxiliary certainty-regression head leverages ambiguity annotations to stabilise learning on genuinely borderline samples. CF-Net achieves a Macro F1 of 0.7155 on the BAH validation set and 0.7364 (AP = 0.7492) on the private challenge test set.

AI.tldr: CF-Net for ambivalence and hesitancy (AH) detection in unconstrained video using cross-modal incongruence modeling; achieves Macro F1 ~0.716 on validation and ~0.736 on private test (AP ~0.749).
AI.motivation: AH signals are inherently ambiguous and expressed via subtle cross-modal incongruence, not prototypical affect. This demands robust multimodal fusion and uncertainty-aware training to stabilize learning on borderline samples.
AI.method: Multimodal CF-Net with frozen backbones (SigLIP2, HuBERT, DistilBERT) for visual, audio, and transcript streams; per-speaker feature normalization to reduce identity leakage; ConflictFusion module computing pairwise cross-modal incongruence; training with certainty-weighted focal loss, manifold mixup, and modality dropout; auxiliary certainty-regression head leveraging ambiguity annotations.
AI.result: Macro F1 of 0.7155 on BAH validation set; 0.7364 (AP = 0.7492) on the private challenge test set.
AI.conclusion: CF-Net effectively models cross-modal incongruence for AH detection, with per-speaker normalization and certainty-guided supervision yielding stable learning and competitive performance on the BAH dataset.

title: Leveraging unlabelled data for generalizable neural population decoding
summary: Robust and accurate neural decoders are integral to neurotechnologies such as brain-computer interfaces and closed-loop experiments. Recent work has shown that tokenizing neural data at the spike level facilitates multi-session pretraining and delivers state-of-the-art decoding performance. However, current spike-based models are restricted to supervised learning (SL), limiting training to datasets with paired behavioural labels. To address this limitation, we introduce MOJO (Masked autOencoder-based JOint training), a training framework for spike-tokenizing models that jointly leverages self-supervised learning (SSL) via masked autoencoding and SL objectives. We evaluate MOJO on three spiking datasets spanning monkey motor cortex during reaching tasks and multi-regional mouse recordings during vision and decision making tasks, demonstrating superior performance over purely SL-trained models. This improvement is especially pronounced when training with limited labelled data, particularly in few-shot finetuning, where only a small amount of labelled data from a new session is available. Incorporating SSL also yields more interpretable neuronal representations, improving performance on brain region classification and spike-statistics prediction without explicit optimization for these tasks. We further show that MOJO generalizes beyond spiking data to human electrocorticography during speech, where it continues to outperform purely SL-trained models and achieves performance comparable to neuro-foundation models (NFMs) designed specifically for continuous signals. Overall, augmenting spike-tokenizing models with SSL improves performance in label-impoverished settings and enables the use of unlabelled data across various tasks and species, while generalizing to other neural modalities. These results suggest a path towards more flexible and scalable data usage when training NFMs.

AI.tldr: MOJO: a self-supervised masked autoencoder framework for spike-tokenizing models that jointly optimizes SSL and supervised objectives, improving decoding performance, data efficiency, and interpretability across sessions, species, and modalities, including ECoG.
AI.motivation: Current spike-based decoders are SL-only, restricting training to labeled datasets and limiting cross-session and cross-modal generalization. There is a need to leverage unlabeled neural data to improve robustness, data efficiency, and scalability of neural decoders.
AI.method: MOJO combines masked autoencoding SSL with supervised decoding objectives for spike-tokenizing models. It is evaluated on multiple datasets across species (monkey, mouse) and modality (spiking data and human ECoG), including few-shot finetuning scenarios. The training jointly optimizes reconstructive SSL loss and supervised decoding loss to learn tokenized neural representations.
AI.result: MOJO outperforms purely SL-trained models, with especially strong gains in label-scarce settings and few-shot finetuning. SSL leads to more interpretable representations, improving brain region classification and spike-statistics prediction without explicit optimization for those tasks. MOJO generalizes to ECoG data and reaches performance comparable to neuro-foundation models on continuous signals.
AI.conclusion: Integrating SSL with spike-tokenizing models yields robust, data-efficient decoders that leverage unlabeled data across tasks and species, and can extend to continuous neural signals, offering a flexible path toward scalable NFMs.

title: Music-to-Dance Generation via Atomic Movements
summary: Music-driven dance generation aims to produce human motion that is both rhythmically synchronized and semantically consistent with music. While recent neural approaches have achieved impressive visual realism, they typically model motion as a continuous signal and neglect its compositional nature, making generated dances structurally incoherent and difficult to control. In this work, we introduce a structure-aware framework that models choreography as a sequence of atomic movements-semantically interpretable motion events that serve as the building blocks of dance. To construct this atomic movement vocabulary, we first segment large-scale dance data and cluster them into atomic movement groups. We then employ a large language model to semantically relabel and refine the clusters, yielding a set of interpretable and reusable atomic movements. Based on these atomic movement annotations, we design a two-stage generation framework that mirrors the human choreography process. In the atomic movement planning stage, the model predicts the type, duration, and timing of atomic movements conditioned on the input music, forming a symbolic dance allocation. In the completion stage, a transition-aware generator synthesizes smooth and stylistically coherent motion conditioned on the planned structure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces dances with significantly improved structural coherence, rhythmic alignment, and perceptual naturalness compared to existing baselines, while providing enhanced interpretability and controllable editing through explicit structural representation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a structure-aware dance generation framework that represents choreography as atomic movements and uses a two-stage process (planning and completion) to improve coherence, rhythm, and controllability.
AI.motivation: Standard neural dance generation models treat motion as a continuous signal, neglecting the compositional structure of dances, leading to incoherence and limited editability.
AI.method: 1) Build an atomic movement vocabulary by segmenting and clustering large-scale dance data. 2) Refine clusters with a large language model to produce semantically interpretable atomic movements. 3) Two-stage generation: atomic movement planning conditioned on music to allocate types, durations, and timings; transition-aware completion to synthesize motion with smooth transitions.
AI.result: Empirical results show enhanced structural coherence, rhythmic alignment, and perceptual naturalness compared to baselines, along with improved interpretability and editable control via explicit structure.
AI.conclusion: A structure-aware representation enables controllable, coherent, and natural dance generation, highlighting the benefit of semantic atomic units and a planning/completion pipeline.

title: Screening Is Effective for Visual Recognition
summary: Vision Transformer (ViT) has been widely used as a powerful framework for modeling global dependencies among image patches. However, its core component, self-attention assigns softmax-normalized relative weights to all patches, making it difficult to evaluate the relevance between patches independently. In visual recognition, images often contain many background or redundant patches, yet self-attention cannot explicitly reject such irrelevant patches, which may introduce unnecessary information into feature aggregation. To address this limitation, Screening has been proposed in the field of language modeling, where the relevance of each token is independently evaluated based on query-key similarity and low-relevance tokens are explicitly excluded through thresholding. In this work, we propose VisionScreen, a new vision model that extends Screening mechanism to visual recognition. VisionScreen treats image patches as tokens arranged on a two-dimensional grid and extends absolute relevance estimation based on query-key similarity to the two-dimensional spatial domain. This allows each patch to selectively aggregate only content-wise and spatially relevant patches without relying on competition among patches. Experiments on image classification benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional ViT. These results suggest that Screening can be effective for visual recognition, offering an alternative to relative feature aggregation based on softmax attention.

AI.tldr: VisionScreen introduces a 2D screening mechanism for ViT, where patch relevance is independently scored via query-key similarity and low-relevance patches are thresholded out, enabling content- and spatially-relevant aggregation without patch competition, leading to improved image classification over standard ViT.
AI.motivation: Standard ViT relies on softmax-based self-attention which enforces competition among patches and cannot explicitly reject irrelevant background patches. This can introduce noise into aggregation. Screening from language modeling offers token-wise relevance scoring and pruning, suggesting it could improve visual recognition by excluding low-relevance patches.
AI.method: Extend the Screening concept to vision by treating image patches as a 2D grid of tokens. Compute absolute relevance for each patch based on query-key similarity, and apply thresholding to prune low-relevance patches. Patches then aggregate content-wise and spatially relevant neighbors without relying on softmax-based competition across all patches, effectively decoupling relevance estimation from joint attention.
AI.result: Experiments on image classification benchmarks show VisionScreen outperforms conventional ViT, indicating that independent patch relevance estimation and threshold-based pruning can enhance visual recognition performance.
AI.conclusion: Screening is a viable alternative to softmax attention for visual recognition. By evaluating patch relevance independently in the 2D spatial domain and pruning low-relevance patches, VisionScreen improves classification accuracy and suggests broader potential for efficient, selective aggregation in vision transformers.

title: Task-Specific Feature Fusion Method for Multi-Task Affective Behavior Analysis
comment: Extended arXiv version with an appendix. Code will be made publicly available
summary: The 11th Affective Behavior Analysis in-the-wild (ABAW11) Multi-Task Learning Challenge requires a unified system to predict valence-arousal, categorical expressions, and facial action units from the official s-Aff-Wild2 images. Although these tasks are naturally related through facial behavior, our validation experiments show that they benefit from different visual features, temporal processing strategies, fusion mechanisms, and calibration procedures. In this paper, we study task-adaptive feature fusion for ABAW11 multi-task affective behavior analysis. We first adapt two pretrained visual backbones, DINOv2 ViT-L and DINOv3 ConvNeXt-base, on an external expression-oriented facial image set and then freeze them to extract complementary frame-level features from the official ABAW11 data. On top of these frozen features, we systematically compare frame-level prediction heads, temporal convolutional heads, post-hoc temporal smoothing, LightGBM models, feature concatenation, gated fusion, residual fusion, late logit fusion, threshold calibration, and shared MTL structures. The final system selects task-specific fusion and prediction strategies rather than forcing all tasks to share a single architecture. On the ABAW11 validation set, the selected system achieves an EXPR macro-F1 of 0.4222, an AU macro-F1 of 0.5402, and a mean VA CCC of 0.6717, resulting in an overall validation score of 1.6341. The results suggest that task-adaptive fusion of frozen visual features is a simple and effective strategy for ABAW-style multi-task affective behavior analysis.

AI.tldr: Task-adaptive fusion using frozen, pre-trained backbones yields better multi-task affective analysis on ABAW11 by tailoring fusion/prediction per task rather than a single shared architecture.
AI.motivation: Although valence-arousal, expressions, and action units are interrelated, their optimal representations and temporal processing differ; a one-size-fits-all model underperforms compared to task-specific fusion.
AI.method: Freeze two pre-trained backbones (DINOv2 ViT-L and DINOv3 ConvNeXt-base) after adapting on an external expression-focused face dataset; extract frame-level features from ABAW11 images; compare a range of frame-level heads, temporal modules (TCNs, smoothing), machine-learning fusion/prediction strategies (LightGBM, concatenation, gated/residual fusion, late logit fusion), and calibration/shared MTL; select task-specific Fusion/Predictive paths; avoid forcing a single architecture across tasks.
AI.result: On ABAW11 validation: EXPR macro-F1 0.4222, AU macro-F1 0.5402, VA CCC 0.6717; overall validation score 1.6341.
AI.conclusion: Task-adaptive fusion of frozen features is simple yet effective for ABAW-style multi-task affective analysis, outperforming uniform architectures across tasks.

title: Multi-Expert Routing for Multi-Domain Low-Resource OCR: A Manchu Case Study
summary: Historical Manchu OCR must accommodate various visually distinct writing styles, including regular script, running script, and the semi-cursive chancery hand used in palace memorials, despite limited labeled data. We study a multi-expert system that reuses checkpoints from an iterative fine-tuning process as domain specialists and uses a lightweight page-level image classifier to dispatch pages by visual style. When the checkpoint pool lacks a suitable specialist, we train an additional expert for that domain. On three frozen test sets, the routed system matches the selected specialist for each style at two-decimal precision: 0.30 percent CER on regular script, 1.57 percent on memorials, and 4.83 percent on running script. The router achieves 99.3 percent page-level domain accuracy and matches the domain-label oracle at the same precision. Two of the three selected specialists were not trained specifically for their final domain; only the running-script expert was trained with that domain as its target. We report the evaluation protocol, router design, and per-page predictions to make the comparison reproducible.

AI.tldr: A multi-expert routing approach for historical Manchu OCR assigns page images to domain-specialist checkpoints via a lightweight router, enabling near-exact domain matching and strong CER across scripts with limited labels; two of three experts were not trained specifically for their final domain.
AI.motivation: Address limited labeled data and diverse writing styles (regular, memorials, running script) in historical Manchu OCR; leverage checkpoint reuse and domain dispatch to improve accuracy.
AI.method: Iterative fine-tuning to create multiple experts; a page-level image classifier routes pages to an expert; train new experts for domains as needed; a router that achieves 99.3% domain accuracy; evaluation on three frozen test sets; report per-page predictions to ensure reproducibility.
AI.result: CER: 0.30% on regular script, 1.57% on memorials, 4.83% on running script; router domain accuracy 99.3%; matches domain-label oracle at the same two-decimal precision.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation protocol, router design, and per-page predictions are reported to enable reproducibility; shows that specialist routing can approach oracle performance, and that not all final-domain specialists require explicit domain-specific training.

title: From Pixels to States: Rethinking Interactive World Models as Game Engines
summary: Building interactive worlds that respond coherently to player actions has long been a shared goal of computer graphics, games, and artificial intelligence. Recent video generative models provide a data-driven route toward this goal by predicting future observations conditioned on user actions, and are increasingly regarded as potential next-generation game engines. Realizing a genuinely interactive game world, however, requires interaction outcomes that follow rules over evolving game conditions, consequences that persist over long horizons, and a generation loop that operates in real time. Conventional game engines realize these properties through a recurrent action-state-observation loop, in which player actions update an explicit game state according to predefined rules and observations are rendered from the resulting state. Taking this loop as an organizing lens, this paper examines interactive game world modeling along four dimensions: player action control, game state dynamics, state-observation persistence, and real-time interactive generation. For each dimension, we start from the capabilities required by an interactive game world, group existing approaches into representative families, and discuss the strengths and trade-offs of each family. Complementing this analysis, we present a scalable data engine for Black Myth: Wukong that collects over 90 hours of gameplay with frame-aligned player actions, ground-truth game states, and visual observations, together with structured and semantic annotations, as a resource for state-aware game world modeling. We hope this paper offers a clear picture of where the field stands and fosters progress toward interactive game worlds.

AI.tldr: Survey of interactive game world modeling through four dimensions (player action control, state dynamics, persistence of state/observations, real-time generation), offering a taxonomy of approaches, and introducing a large-scale dataset for state-aware game-world modeling to support real-time, persistent, rule-based interactivity.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between data-driven video generation and fully interactive, rule-governed game worlds. Provide a unifying lens to compare methods and identify trade-offs, enabling scalable, state-aware modeling.
AI.method: Frame the problem along four dimensions of interaction; categorize existing approaches into representative families within each dimension; analyze strengths and trade-offs; present a scalable dataset engine (for Black Myth: Wukong) collecting 90+ hours of gameplay with aligned actions, ground-truth states, observations, and semantic annotations as a resource.
AI.result: A taxonomy-guided analysis of current approaches to interactive game world modeling; a practical data resource consisting of 90+ hours of gameplay with rich aligned data; insights into design choices and where the field stands.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a clear organizing picture of interactive game world modeling, highlighting trade-offs among dimensions and offering a concrete data engine resource to spur progress toward real-time, stateful, and rule-based interactive worlds.

title: VideoRAE: Taming Video Foundation Models for Generative Modeling via Representation Autoencoders
summary: Video generative models commonly rely on latent spaces learned by 3D Variational Autoencoders (3D-VAEs). However, conventional 3D-VAEs are mainly optimized for pixel-level reconstruction, which can limit the semantic and spatio-temporal structure captured by their latents. Meanwhile, Video Foundation Models (VFMs) such as V-JEPA 2 and VideoMAEv2 show strong video understanding capabilities, yet whether their frozen representations can be transformed into compact, reconstruction-capable, and generation-friendly video latents remains largely unexplored. We answer this question with VideoRAE, a representation autoencoder that leverages multi-scale hierarchical features from a frozen video foundation encoder and compresses them with a lightweight 1D self-attention projector. VideoRAE supports both continuous latents for Diffusion Transformers and discrete tokens for autoregressive models via multi-codebook high-dimensional quantization. During decoding, a local-and-global representation alignment objective with the frozen VFM teacher improves semantic preservation and enables training without KL regularization. Experiments show that VideoRAE achieves strong reconstruction in both continuous and discrete regimes. On UCF-101, it obtains state-of-the-art class-to-video gFVDs of 40 and 93 with AR and DiT generators, respectively, while converging approximately 5x faster than competing autoencoder baselines. In a controlled 2B-scale text-to-video study, replacing LTX-VAE with VideoRAE leads to faster convergence under comparable settings. These results validate frozen VFM representations as versatile and generation-friendly video latents. The model and code will be released on https://zhxie0117.github.io/VideoRAE.

AI.tldr: VideoRAE introduces a representation autoencoder that reuses frozen video foundation model features, compressed by a lightweight 1D self-attention projector, to produce both continuous and discrete video latents for generation. It achieves strong reconstruction and state-of-the-art gFVD on UCF-101 while converging ~5x faster than baselines; code will be released.
AI.motivation: Conventional 3D-VAEs optimize pixel-level reconstruction, potentially limiting semantic and spatio-temporal structure in latents. Frozen VFMs (e.g., V-JEPA 2, VideoMAEv2) offer strong video understanding, but their latent representations as compact, reconstruction-friendly video latents remain underexplored.
AI.method: Utilize multi-scale hierarchical features from a frozen video foundation encoder. Compress with a lightweight 1D self-attention projector. Support continuous latents for Diffusion Transformers and discrete tokens via multi-codebook high-dimensional quantization. Decode with a local-and-global representation alignment objective against a frozen VFM teacher, enabling training without KL regularization.
AI.result: VideoRAE achieves strong reconstruction in both continuous and discrete regimes. On UCF-101, it attains state-of-the-art class-to-video gFVDs of 40 (AR) and 93 (DiT) and converges ~5x faster than competing autoencoder baselines. In a 2B-scale text-to-video study, replacing LTX-VAE with VideoRAE yields faster convergence under comparable settings.
AI.conclusion: Frozen VFM representations can serve as versatile, generation-friendly video latents. VideoRAE validates this approach and provides a practical autoencoder pipeline with code forthcoming.
